pages.title: A2A
pages.tagline: MCP is how an agent reaches a tool. A2A is how an agent hires another agent — and never learns how it works.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · spec 1.0.0 · stewarded by the Linux Foundation / Agentic AI Foundation
pages.description: A2A (Agent2Agent) cheatsheet: agent cards, tasks and their lifecycle, messages, artifacts, streaming, push notifications and how it differs from MCP.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: The public JSON document at /.well-known/agent-card.json that describes what an agent can do and how to reach it.
terms.detail: Discovery in A2A is a single HTTP GET. The card is the contract: name, description, provider, version, capabilities, securitySchemes, securityRequirements, defaultInputModes and defaultOutputModes, the skills list, supportedInterfaces, and optional signatures. Servers MUST publish one. It is the part a client reads before writing a line of integration code, so it is worth treating as a product surface rather than a config file. A card with three vague skills and no examples is as hard to use as an undocumented API. Required fields Field Holds name, description what this agent is for version the agent's own version, not the protocol's capabilities streaming, pushNotifications, extendedAgentCard supportedInterfaces ordered list of endpoints and bindings defaultInputModes / OutputModes media types accepted and produced skills what it can actually be asked to do When capabilities.extendedAgentCard is true, an authenticated client can call GetExtendedAgentCard for a fuller version — skills that are not advertised publicly. How it relates Cards SHOULD be cacheable: send Cache-Control and an ETag, and have clients use conditional requests.

terms.def: A named capability advertised on the card — the unit a client matches against when choosing an agent.
terms.detail: An AgentSkill carries id, name, description and tags, plus optional examples, inputModes, outputModes and securityRequirements. It is documentation with enough structure to be searched, not a typed function signature. That is a deliberate difference from MCP tools. An MCP tool has a JSON Schema and is invoked with structured arguments; an A2A skill is described in prose and reached by sending a natural-language message. The remote agent interprets — which is exactly why it is an agent and not a function. Writing one that gets picked Field Guidance id stable, machine-friendly, never reused description what it does, its limits, what it will refuse tags how a registry or another agent finds you examples real prompts that work — the most useful field How it relates Per-skill securityRequirements let one agent expose a public skill and a privileged one behind stronger auth.

terms.def: The ordered list of endpoints and protocol bindings the agent speaks — first entry is preferred.
terms.detail: Each entry has a url, a protocolBinding and a protocolVersion, plus an optional tenant. There are three core bindings: JSONRPC (JSON-RPC 2.0 over HTTP, SSE for streaming), GRPC (gRPC over HTTP/2 with TLS, service A2AService) and HTTP+JSON (REST-style, media type application/a2a+json ). Selection is specified, not left to taste: the first entry is the preferred interface, and a client picks the first binding it supports, preferring earlier entries. If the chosen interface declares a tenant, the client must send that value; if it does not, the client must omit it. The three bindings Binding Shape Fits JSONRPC POST, PascalCase methods, SSE the default; easiest to debug GRPC A2AService, HTTP/2, TLS high volume, typed clients HTTP+JSON POST /message:send, GET /tasks/{id} REST-native estates and gateways How it relates All three carry the same semantics, so the choice is operational — see gRPC for when the typed binding earns its complexity.

terms.def: The unit of work: server-created, identified, stateful, and followed rather than awaited.
terms.detail: A Task holds id, contextId, status, artifacts, history and metadata. It is created by the server — a client cannot choose the id — and it exists precisely because agent work is not request/response. It may take an hour, produce several outputs, and stop to ask a question in the middle. A response to SendMessage is therefore either a Message (the agent answered immediately, nothing to track) or a Task (something long enough to need an id). Clients must handle both. Task or message? Situation Response "what currencies do you support?" Message "assess this 40-page application" Task Anything needing approval mid-flight Task Anything producing files Task How it relates Because tasks outlive connections, push notifications exist for clients that cannot hold an SSE stream open.

terms.def: The nine enum values a task moves through, four of them terminal and two of them pauses.
terms.detail: In 1.0.0 the states are enum constants: TASK_STATE_UNSPECIFIED, SUBMITTED, WORKING, COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELED, INPUT_REQUIRED, REJECTED and AUTH_REQUIRED, each prefixed TASK_STATE_. The 0.x spellings ("working", "input-required") are gone. Four are terminal: COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELED, REJECTED. Two are interruptions that expect you to act: INPUT_REQUIRED and AUTH_REQUIRED. Subscribing to a task that is already terminal returns UnsupportedOperationError rather than a stream that never emits. What each means for you State Your move SUBMITTED accepted, not started — wait WORKING in progress, expect updates INPUT_REQUIRED send another message on the same task AUTH_REQUIRED obtain credentials, then continue REJECTED it declined — do not retry unchanged FAILED it tried and could not — retry may help How it relates Treat REJECTED and FAILED differently in your retry policy; see Retry, backoff & jitter.

terms.def: The server-generated id that groups related tasks and messages into one ongoing interaction.
terms.detail: A taskId identifies one unit of work; a contextId ties several together — a follow-up question, a revision, a second task in the same conversation. Both are server-generated, and an agent must reject a message whose contextId and taskId do not belong together. The practical rule: carry the contextId forward when the new request is part of the same conversation, and start fresh when it is not. It is how the remote agent keeps continuity without exposing any of its internal memory to you. How it relates Never invent either id. The server owns the namespace, which is what keeps opaque agents opaque.

terms.def: What the two sides exchange: a role, and a list of parts that may be text, bytes, a URL or structured data.
terms.detail: A Message carries messageId, contextId, taskId, role (ROLE_USER or ROLE_AGENT ), parts, and optional metadata, extensions and referenceTaskIds. In 1.0.0 a Part is one object with a oneof: exactly one of text, raw (bytes, base64 in JSON), url, or data (any JSON value), plus optional mediaType and filename. That shape is why A2A is multimodal without ceremony: a single message can carry a sentence, a PDF by reference and a structured form, and the receiving agent decides what it can use based on the modes it advertised. Which part to use Content Field Instructions, questions text Small inline file raw + mediaType Large file url — do not inline megabytes Form answers, parameters data How it relates referenceTaskIds lets a message point at earlier tasks — the usual way to say "use the output of that one".

terms.def: A durable output of a task, as opposed to the conversational messages that produced it.
terms.detail: An Artifact has artifactId, optional name and description, at least one parts entry, and optional metadata and extensions. It is the deliverable: a report, a dataset, an image, a decision document — the thing a client keeps after the conversation is over. Artifacts can stream. A TaskArtifactUpdateEvent carries append and lastChunk flags, so an agent can emit a long document progressively and the client can render it as it arrives rather than waiting for completion. Message or artifact? Content Put it in "I need the applicant's nationality" a message The finished assessment PDF an artifact Progress commentary a status update message A structured result the caller will store an artifact How it relates Clients that only read the final Task still get the artifacts; streaming them is an experience improvement, not a different result.

terms.def: The method that starts or continues work — PascalCase in 1.0.0, not the 0.x slash form.
terms.detail: Version 1.0.0 renamed every method to PascalCase matching gRPC conventions: SendMessage, SendStreamingMessage, GetTask, ListTasks, CancelTask, SubscribeToTask, the four …TaskPushNotificationConfig methods, and GetExtendedAgentCard. The familiar message/send and tasks/get belong to 0.x. The REST binding maps them onto custom-verb URLs: POST /message:send, POST /message:stream, GET /tasks/{id}, POST /tasks/{id}:cancel, POST /tasks/{id}:subscribe, and the push-config paths under /tasks/{id}/pushNotificationConfigs. Renames to watch for 0.x 1.0.0 message/send SendMessage message/stream SendStreamingMessage tasks/get GetTask tasks/resubscribe SubscribeToTask GetAuthenticatedExtendedCard GetExtendedAgentCard How it relates Most sample code online is still 0.x. A method-not-found against a 1.0 agent is usually this, not a routing problem.

terms.def: Server-sent events carrying status and artifact updates while a task runs.
terms.detail: SendStreamingMessage opens an SSE stream (text/event-stream) whose data: frames are ordinary JSON-RPC envelopes wrapping a StreamResponse — exactly one of task, message, statusUpdate or artifactUpdate. Events arrive in generation order. TaskStatusUpdateEvent carries the new status; TaskArtifactUpdateEvent carries an artifact chunk with append and lastChunk. A dropped connection is recoverable: call SubscribeToTask to attach again, or GetTask to read the current state. Common values Concern Guidance Streaming supported? capabilities.streaming on the card Reconnect SubscribeToTask; terminal tasks refuse Proxies disable response buffering on the route Very long tasks prefer push notifications over a held stream How it relates A reverse proxy with default buffering will hold every event until the task ends, which looks exactly like a broken agent.

terms.def: Webhook delivery of task updates, for clients that cannot hold a connection open for an hour.
terms.detail: A client registers a TaskPushNotificationConfig — a url, a token and an authentication block with a scheme and credentials — and the server POSTs a StreamResponse to that webhook with Content-Type: application/a2a+json. The client returns 2xx; delivery is at-least-once. At-least-once is the design constraint everyone discovers late. The webhook must be idempotent, must validate that the notification really came from the agent, and must not trust the payload as the source of truth — call GetTask to confirm before acting on anything important. Common values Setting Typical Webhook timeout 10–30 s Delivery guarantee at-least-once — deduplicate Auth to your webhook bearer token, or mTLS Advertised by capabilities.pushNotifications How it relates Duplicate deliveries are the same problem as everywhere else — see Idempotency & deduplication.

terms.def: How a client authenticates: declared on the card, obtained out of band, sent on every request.
terms.detail: A SecurityScheme is exactly one of apiKeySecurityScheme, httpAuthSecurityScheme, oauth2SecurityScheme, openIdConnectSecurityScheme or mtlsSecurityScheme — the OpenAPI vocabulary, deliberately. OAuth flows include authorizationCode, clientCredentials and deviceCode; implicit and password are deprecated. The flow the spec describes is plain: read securitySchemes from the card, obtain credentials out of band, send them in headers (or gRPC metadata) on every request. The server MUST authenticate every request, and production deployments MUST use HTTPS or TLS, with TLS 1.3 recommended. Authorization itself is left implementation-specific. How it relates A2A does not define agent identity in its semantics — it is handled at the protocol layer, so it is your existing OAuth 2.0 or mTLS infrastructure doing the work.

terms.def: AUTH_REQUIRED: the remote agent needs credentials for a third system, mid-task.
terms.detail: A travel agent asks a visa agent to check an application; the visa agent needs the user's consent to query a government portal. Rather than failing, the task enters TASK_STATE_AUTH_REQUIRED, letting the agent delegate the authorization step to the client, which can drive a consent flow with the human and then continue the same task. The spec is explicit that an agent MUST NOT treat that state alone as authorization — reaching it is a request, not a grant. The credentials must actually be obtained and validated. How it relates This is the multi-agent equivalent of MCP's elicitation: a pause that puts a human in the loop at the exact moment consent is needed.

terms.def: JWS signatures over the agent card, so a client can verify it was published by who it claims.
terms.detail: The card's signatures array holds AgentCardSignature objects with a required protected header and signature, and an optional header, following JWS (RFC 7515). Canonicalisation uses JCS (RFC 8785), and the signatures field itself is excluded from the signed payload. The protected header MUST include alg and kid, and SHOULD set typ to "JOSE". It matters because the card is the thing you trust before anything else: it tells you where to send work and what the agent claims to do. An unsigned card fetched over a compromised path is a redirection attack with no other defence. How it relates This is the same supply-chain question as connecting an MCP server: verify the publisher before granting access.

terms.def: The A2A-Version header, and why 1.0.0 breaks 0.x clients.
terms.detail: Service parameters travel as HTTP headers (JSON-RPC and REST bindings) or gRPC metadata, including A2A-Version and A2A-Extensions. An unsupported version is rejected with 400 and application/problem+json, which is a far better failure than a mysterious method-not-found. 1.0.0 changed enough to matter: PascalCase methods, supportedInterfaces replacing the single url and preferredTransport, TASK_STATE_* enum spellings, and renamed request and response types. Legacy names are slated for removal, so dual-version code has a deadline. Error codes Range Meaning -32700 … -32603 standard JSON-RPC errors -32001 … -32099 A2A-specific errors -32001 e.g. TASK_NOT_FOUND (gRPC NOT_FOUND, REST 404) How it relates Read the counterparty's card and its protocolVersion first; half of all integration bugs are a version mismatch.

terms.def: The design rule that makes A2A different: you exchange tasks, never internals.
terms.detail: A remote agent does not expose its tools, its prompts, its model, its memory or its plan. You cannot inspect its reasoning and it cannot borrow your context. All that crosses the boundary are messages, task state and artifacts. That constraint is the point. It allows agents from different vendors, written in different languages, holding different credentials, to collaborate without a shared runtime — and it keeps each side's intellectual property and data on its own side of the wire. The consequences You get You give up Cross-vendor interop Visibility into reasoning Independent deployment Shared context and memory Clear trust boundary Fine-grained control Each side keeps its secrets Easy end-to-end debugging How it relates If you need to see inside, you do not want A2A — you want the other agent's tools exposed over MCP, or the same harness running both.

terms.def: Complementary, not competing: one connects agents to tools, the other connects agents to agents.
terms.detail: The official position is that the two are complementary protocols for different aspects of agentic systems. MCP connects a model or agent to tools, APIs and data sources — typed, synchronous, under your control. A2A standardises how separate agents discover each other, exchange tasks and collaborate as peers — prose-described, long-running, opaque. The canonical arrangement: an A2A client asks a remote agent for something substantial; that agent uses MCP internally to reach its own tools. Neither side sees the other's tools, and neither protocol is doing the other's job. Side by side MCP A2A Other side a tool or data source an autonomous agent Interface JSON Schema arguments messages and skills in prose Duration a call a task, possibly hours Visibility you define the tool opaque peer Direction down across How it relates If you control both sides and want determinism, MCP plus your own agent harness is simpler. A2A earns its keep across an organisational boundary.

pages.title: Agent harness
pages.tagline: The model is a function from text to text. Everything that makes it an agent is code you wrote.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · examples use Microsoft.Extensions.AI and the OpenAI Python SDK
pages.description: Agent harness cheatsheet: the loop, tool dispatch, context compaction, budgets, stop conditions, approvals and observability — the code around the model that makes it an agent.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: Call the model, dispatch any tool it asked for, append the result, call again — until a stop condition fires.
terms.detail: Stripped to its essentials the loop is about ten lines, and that is genuinely all there is to the "agentic" part. The model emits either a final answer or one or more tool calls; the harness runs them, appends results as messages, and calls again. Nothing in the model persists between iterations. What varies between harnesses is everything around that: whether tool calls run in parallel, whether the model is shown errors or just a retry, whether intermediate thinking is kept, and what counts as finished. Those choices are worth more than the model choice for most tasks. while (true) { var reply = await model.CompleteAsync(messages, tools); messages.Add(reply); if (reply.ToolCalls.Count == 0) return reply.Text; // done foreach (var call in reply.ToolCalls) messages.Add(await Dispatch(call)); // results go back in if (budget.Exceeded) return Stop(messages); // and the escape hatch } How it relates Without Stop conditions and a Step budget, that while (true) is exactly as dangerous as it looks.

terms.def: The agent's entire memory: an ordered list of messages the harness resends in full on every call.
terms.detail: The model is stateless. There is no session on the provider's side holding your conversation; each request carries the whole list, and the "agent remembers" only because the harness keeps appending. Understanding this explains the cost curve: step 12 is far more expensive than step 1 because it resends everything from steps 1 through 11. The list has structure worth respecting: a system message that rarely changes (which is what makes prompt caching effective), then alternating user, assistant and tool-result messages. Tool results must be linked to the call that produced them, or the model loses track of which answer belongs to which question. What grows fastest Part Growth System prompt fixed Tool definitions fixed, per turn Conversation linear Tool results unbounded — the usual culprit How it relates Cost is quadratic-ish in steps for a fixed tool output size, which is why Tool result shaping pays twice.

terms.def: The set of tools offered on each call — local functions, MCP servers, or other agents.
terms.detail: The registry maps names to implementations and produces the JSON Schema definitions sent to the model. Tools may be plain functions in your process, tools discovered from MCP servers, retrieval over a RAG index, or a delegation to another agent over A2A — the model sees one flat list regardless. The list is a context cost on every turn, and a selection problem: past roughly twenty tools, accuracy falls because descriptions start to overlap. The fix is scoping rather than pruning — offer only the tools relevant to the current phase of the task. Common values Setting Typical Tools offered per call 5–20 Cost of a definition 80–300 tokens each Scoping strategy by phase, by user permission, by task type Parallel calls allow for reads, serialise writes How it relates Permissions belong here too: a user who cannot delete should not be offered a delete tool at all.

terms.def: Validating arguments, running the tool, enforcing timeouts, and turning whatever happens into a message.
terms.detail: Dispatch is where a harness earns its reliability. Arguments arrive as model-generated JSON and must be validated against the schema before anything runs — the schema is advice to the model, not a guarantee. Every tool needs a timeout, a cancellation path and a concurrency limit, because a model will cheerfully ask for forty parallel calls. Writes need more: idempotency keys so a retried call does not duplicate an order, and serialisation so two parallel calls do not conflict. Reads can run concurrently and usually should — it is the cheapest latency win in the loop. Common values Control Typical Per-tool timeout 5–30 s Parallel reads 4–8 at once Writes serialised, idempotency key required Argument validation always, before execution Output cap 2–8k tokens, then truncate with a note How it relates Duplicate side effects from retried tool calls are the same problem as everywhere else — see Idempotency & deduplication.

terms.def: Deciding what the model actually sees from a tool — rarely the raw output.
terms.detail: A query returns 4,000 rows; a file read returns 200 KB; an HTTP call returns a page of HTML. Putting any of those into the message list unchanged burns the window, costs money on every subsequent turn, and buries the three lines that mattered. Shape it: cap rows, project to relevant fields, summarise, and tell the model what was dropped and how to get more. "Showing 20 of 4,312 rows. Narrow the date range or call aggregate_orders for totals." is a better result than the rows, because it is both an answer and an instruction. Shaping rules Output Shape Query rows cap + projection + total count Large file relevant span + offsets, not the file HTML page extracted text, not markup Long logs matching lines + context Binary a reference, never the bytes How it relates Shaping is cheaper than Context compaction and loses nothing, because you discard before it ever enters the list.

terms.def: Summarising or pruning the message list when it approaches the window limit.
terms.detail: Long tasks run out of window. The options are: drop old messages (cheap, loses facts), summarise old messages into one (keeps the gist, loses detail), externalise to a file or store the agent can re-read (keeps everything, costs a lookup), or hand off to a fresh context with a written brief. Compaction must be triggered on a threshold rather than on failure — typically 70–80% of the window — because the summarisation call itself needs room. And it must preserve the load-bearing parts: the original task, decisions made, and anything irreversible that has already happened. Common values Setting Typical Trigger 70–80% of the window Keep verbatim system, original task, last 2–3 turns Summarise everything older, into ~500 tokens Always preserve decisions, side effects already performed Externalise large artefacts to files, keep paths How it relates Compaction is lossy by construction. The best compaction is the tool output you never added — see Tool result shaping.

terms.def: A hard cap on iterations, tokens, wall-clock time and money — enforced by the harness, not hoped for.
terms.detail: Agents fail by looping. A tool returns an error the model misreads, so it tries again; a search returns nothing, so it rephrases forever; two tools disagree, so it oscillates. Without a cap, that runs until something else breaks — usually your bill. Budget on all four axes, because any one alone has a hole: steps miss a single enormous call, tokens miss a slow one, time misses a cheap fast loop, cost is the one finance cares about. And decide what happens at the limit: returning partial work with an explanation is nearly always better than throwing. Common values Task type Steps Tokens Wall clock Question answering 3–5 20k 30 s Research / multi-hop 10–20 100k 3 min Coding task 30–80 500k+ 20 min Background / batch 100+ budgeted in money hours How it relates Alert on how often the budget is hit. A rising rate is a regression signal long before users complain.

terms.def: Every way the loop can legitimately end, including the unhappy ones.
terms.detail: "The model stopped calling tools" is one stop condition, not the only one. A complete list: a final answer, a budget exhausted, a cancellation from the user, a tool signalling terminal failure, a required approval denied, a repeated-state detector firing, or an explicit finish tool the model can call. The repeated-state detector is underused and cheap: hash the last few tool calls and their arguments, and if the same pair repeats three times, stop. It catches the most common loop shape before the budget does, and it can say why it stopped. How it relates Make the stop reason part of the result. "Stopped after 12 steps while searching" is actionable; a timeout is not.

terms.def: Turning a tool failure into something the model can act on, instead of a stack trace or a silent retry.
terms.detail: Errors are prompts. System.NullReferenceException at Orders.Get tells the model nothing and invites an identical retry. "No customer with id CUST-99. Ids look like CUST-4412. Use search_customers to find one by name." tells it exactly what to do next, and it usually does. Classify before reframing. Transient errors (timeout, 503) should be retried by the harness with backoff, invisibly. Permanent errors (not found, forbidden, bad argument) should go to the model as guidance. Fatal errors (credentials revoked) should stop the loop, because no amount of rephrasing will fix them. Three classes Class Who handles it Example Transient harness retries, model never sees it timeout, 429, 503 Semantic model, as a reframed message not found, bad argument Fatal stop the loop auth revoked, budget gone How it relates Harness-level retries use ordinary Retry, backoff & jitter; model-level retries are a different mechanism and must be counted separately.

terms.def: Which actions require a human, and how that is enforced outside the model's judgement.
terms.detail: The model should not decide whether an action is dangerous — it can be persuaded, and it can be wrong. Classify tools in the registry: auto-run, approve once per session, approve every time, never. Enforce it in dispatch, where it cannot be argued with. The approval prompt must show the actual arguments, rendered for a human: "Delete 1,284 rows from orders where status = 'draft'", not "run SQL". Most harmful actions are caught at this step by someone reading the parameters, not the intent. A workable classification Tool Policy Read, search, list auto Write to a draft or sandbox auto, logged Send, publish, charge, deploy approve each time Delete, grant access, move money approve each time, show arguments Anything on production data allow-list, or not at all How it relates Prompt injection turns into action only where a write tool exists without approval. Separating read agents from write agents removes the class.

terms.def: The standing instructions: role, constraints, tool guidance, output format and the refusal path.
terms.detail: It is the one piece of text present in every call, so it is both the most leveraged and the most expensive prose in the system. Useful content: who the agent is and what it is for, hard constraints, when to use which tool, what to do when it does not know, and the required output shape. Keep it stable. Changing it invalidates prompt caching, and it is the variable that most quietly changes behaviour, so it deserves a version number that shows up in your traces and in your evaluation runs. What belongs where Content Put it in Role, constraints, output format system prompt When to use a tool the tool's description Facts about the world retrieval, not the prompt The current task the user message Hard rules code, not prose How it relates Anything that must never happen belongs in the harness. A prompt is a preference; dispatch is a rule.

terms.def: Delegating a bounded piece of work to a fresh context, and getting back only the conclusion.
terms.detail: A subagent is a second loop with its own message list, its own tools and its own budget. The parent sends a brief and receives a summary — which means the subagent's forty tool results never enter the parent's window. That is the main reason to use one: context isolation, not parallelism. It costs real money and two lossy handoffs: the brief you write, and the summary you get back. Use it for genuinely independent work — several searches, several files, several candidate approaches — and not for steps that depend on each other. When it pays Situation Subagent? Search 200 files for a pattern yes — only the answer returns Three independent investigations yes, in parallel Step B needs step A's output no A two-tool-call question no — the overhead exceeds the work How it relates A subagent is a tool from the parent's point of view, so it goes through the same dispatch, budget and approval machinery.

terms.def: The written brief that carries a task across a compaction, a subagent boundary or a session restart.
terms.detail: Whenever context is discarded, something must carry the task forward. A handoff note is that something: the original goal, what has been established, what has already been done irreversibly, what is left, and what "finished" looks like. Written by the model, kept by the harness, prepended to the new context. Its quality is the single best predictor of whether a long task survives compaction. A note that says "continuing the investigation" is worthless; one that lists three ruled-out hypotheses and two file paths lets the next context resume properly. What a good note contains Section Why Original goal, verbatim drift is the main failure Established facts prevents re-discovery Ruled out, with reasons prevents re-trying Side effects already performed prevents repeating them Next step and done criteria resumability How it relates In A2A this is the same idea between agents, and there it is a protocol object rather than a convention.

terms.def: A replayable trace of every call, tool invocation, token count and decision.
terms.detail: Agent bugs are not reproducible from a log line. You need the full sequence — prompts, tool calls, arguments, results, timings, token counts, stop reason — as a trace you can replay. OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions give you spans per model call and per tool call that sit alongside your existing traces. Record prompt and tool-schema versions too, so a behaviour change can be attributed. And store the stop reason as a first-class field: the distribution of stop reasons is the single most informative agent metric there is. What to record per run Field Use steps, tokens in/out, cost budgets and spend tool name, args, duration, outcome debugging stop reason the key health metric prompt + schema version attribution compaction events explains sudden amnesia How it relates Latency here is wildly long-tailed, so report percentiles rather than averages.

terms.def: A fixed set of tasks with checkable outcomes, run on every change to the harness.
terms.detail: Agents cannot be regression-tested by trying three prompts by hand, because they are non-deterministic and the surface is large. An eval suite is a set of tasks with programmatic success criteria — did the right tool get called, is the final state correct, did it stay within budget — run repeatedly and tracked over time. Prefer checking end state over output text: "the ticket is now closed with this label" is objective, "the summary mentions X" is a judgement call. Run each task several times and record the pass rate, because a 70% agent and a 95% agent can both pass a single run. What to measure Metric Tells you Task success rate the headline Steps to success efficiency and drift Cost per task what scale will cost Harmful-action rate the number that must be zero Variance across runs whether you can trust one run How it relates Build evals before tuning the prompt. Otherwise every change is a feeling, and the regressions are invisible.

terms.def: Knowing what a task costs before it is running at a thousand a day.
terms.detail: Agent cost is dominated by resent context. Each step resends everything before it, so total input tokens grow roughly with the square of the step count for a fixed per-step output size. A ten-step task with 5k of tool output per step is not 50k tokens of input — it is closer to 275k. A worked estimate Quantity Value Base prompt + tools 3,000 tokens Added per step ~5,000 tokens Input at step n 3,000 + 5,000n Total input over 10 steps ~305,000 tokens Biggest lever halve the tool output → halve the bill Which is why Tool result shaping is a cost control and not a tidiness preference, and why semantic caching in front of a repetitive agent pays so well. How it relates Put cost in the budget alongside steps and time; it is the limit that most often needs raising deliberately.

terms.def: Constraining what a tool can reach, so a wrong decision has a small blast radius.
terms.detail: Agents take real actions from probabilistic decisions, so containment matters more than it would for ordinary code. Run file and shell tools in a container with a mounted working directory; give database tools a read-only role and a statement timeout; restrict network egress to an allow-list; scope API tokens to the minimum. Pair it with reversibility. A branch rather than a commit, a draft rather than a send, a soft delete rather than a hard one. An agent that can only take reversible actions needs far less approval friction, which makes it both safer and more useful. How it relates Sandbox plus approval plus trace is the full control set: limit what is possible, gate what is dangerous, record what happened.

pages.title: Apache Kafka
pages.tagline: A distributed, append-only log for events: write once, read by many, replay any time.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · release line 4.x (KRaft only)
pages.description: Apache Kafka cheatsheet: architecture, animated produce and consumer-group walk-throughs, key concepts, CLI commands, trade-offs and alternatives.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: One event: optional key, value (bytes), timestamp and headers. Kafka does not care about the format; JSON, Avro and Protobuf are common.
terms.detail: Field Example Notes key user-42 optional; decides the partition and enables compaction value {"status":"paid"} bytes: JSON, Avro, Protobuf… timestamp 1731234567890 creation or append time (ms) headers trace-id: ab12 metadata, e.g. tracing, content type Default maximum size is about 1 MB (message.max.bytes ). Typical events are 0.5–10 KB. Records are batched and compressed (lz4, zstd) by the producer, which is why throughput is so high. Use a schema registry with Avro or Protobuf so producers and consumers agree on the format as it evolves.

terms.def: A named stream of records, like orders or user-signups. Roughly a table name for events.
terms.detail: A topic is a named, partitioned log. Name it after the event, in a consistent style: orders.placed.v1, payments.refunded, user-profiles (compacted). Settings you'll set per topic partitions: parallelism and ordering unit (e.g. 6–12 for a busy topic). replication factor: copies across brokers (3 in production). retention: retention.ms (7 days default) or retention.bytes. cleanup.policy: delete (by age/size) or compact (latest per key). Avoid auto-created topics in production (auto.create.topics.enable=false ): a typo silently creates a new, empty topic with default settings.

terms.def: A topic is split into partitions. Each one is an ordered, append-only log and the unit of parallelism and ordering.
terms.detail: Each partition is an ordered log stored as segment files on a broker's disk, replicated to others. It is the unit of: Ordering: guaranteed within a partition only. Parallelism: in a consumer group, at most one consumer per partition. Placement: each partition has one leader broker. Choosing a count Rule of thumb: max(target throughput / per-consumer throughput, peak consumers). If one consumer handles 5 MB/s and you need 30 MB/s, you need at least 6. Common values: 3–12 for most topics, 30–100 for very high volume. You can add partitions later but never remove them, and adding them changes which partition each key maps to.

terms.def: The position of a record inside a partition (0, 1, 2…). Never reused. Consumers track progress by offset.
terms.detail: An offset is a record's position in its partition: 0, 1, 2… It never changes and is never reused, even after old records are deleted by retention or compaction (gaps are normal). Log end offset: where the next record will be written. Committed offset: where a consumer group will resume. Lag = log end offset − committed offset. The key health metric. Reset where a group starts with auto.offset.reset (earliest / latest) for new groups, or explicitly with kafka-consumer-groups.sh --reset-offsets --to-datetime 2026-11-10T08:00:00.000.

terms.def: A Kafka server. It stores partition replicas on disk and serves producers and consumers. A cluster usually has 3 or more.
terms.detail: A broker is one Kafka server process. It stores partition replicas in log segments on disk, serves producer and consumer requests for partitions it leads, and replicates from leaders for the others. Typical sizing 3 brokers is the minimum for production with replication factor 3. Brokers commonly have 8–32 vCPU, 32–64 GB RAM (much of it used as OS page cache) and fast disks. A single broker can handle hundreds of MB/s and thousands of partitions. Clients connect to any broker via bootstrap.servers, fetch metadata, then talk directly to each partition's leader.

terms.def: The built-in Raft quorum that manages cluster metadata and elects partition leaders. Replaced ZooKeeper, which was removed in Kafka 4.0.
terms.detail: KRaft (Kafka Raft) is Kafka's built-in metadata quorum. A few controller nodes (3 or 5) replicate a metadata log containing topics, partitions, configs, ACLs and who leads what. Elects partition leaders when a broker fails. Replaced ZooKeeper; ZooKeeper mode was removed in Kafka 4.0. Older clusters must migrate on 3.x first. Controllers can run on dedicated nodes (production) or combined with brokers (dev). Benefit: one system to operate and secure, faster failover, and support for millions of partitions.

terms.def: How many copies of each partition exist on different brokers. 3 is the usual production value.
terms.detail: RF = number of copies of each partition, each on a different broker. RF Survives Use 1 nothing: one disk failure loses data local dev only 2 1 broker, but no safety margin with acks=all rarely a good idea 3 1 broker down while still accepting writes production standard Pair RF 3 with min.insync.replicas=2 and acks=all: every acknowledged write is on at least 2 brokers. Storage cost is RF × data size.

terms.def: Each partition has one leader replica that handles reads and writes. Followers copy it and take over if it fails.
terms.detail: For each partition one replica is the leader: producers write to it and (by default) consumers read from it. Followers continuously fetch from the leader to stay in sync. When a leader's broker dies, the controller promotes an in-sync follower within seconds; clients refresh metadata and continue. Leaders are spread across brokers so load is balanced. Consumers can read from a nearby follower (rack-aware fetching) to save cross-zone traffic costs.

terms.def: In-sync replicas: the followers that are caught up with the leader. Only they can become leader without data loss.
terms.detail: The in-sync replica set is the leader plus the followers that have caught up within replica.lag.time.max.ms (30 s by default). With acks=all, a write is acknowledged when every ISR member has it. If the ISR shrinks below min.insync.replicas, producers using acks=all get NotEnoughReplicas errors: Kafka chooses consistency over availability. unclean.leader.election.enable=false (default) prevents an out-of-sync replica from becoming leader and silently losing data. Alert on "under-replicated partitions": it means a broker is slow or down.

terms.def: Producer setting for durability: 0 (fire and forget), 1 (leader only), all (every in-sync replica, the default since 3.0).
terms.detail: acks Producer waits for Risk Latency 0 nothing lost silently on any error lowest 1 the leader lost if the leader dies before followers copy it low all / -1 (default) all in-sync replicas none, with min.insync.replicas ≥ 2 a few ms more Since Kafka 3.0 producers default to acks=all and enable.idempotence=true, so retries can't create duplicates. Only lower them for metrics or logs you can afford to lose.

terms.def: Client that writes records. It batches and compresses them, and picks the partition by hashing the key.
terms.detail: The producer client batches records per partition, compresses them and sends them asynchronously. Settings worth knowing Setting Typical Effect linger.ms 5–20 (default 5) wait a bit to fill bigger batches batch.size 16–256 KB max bytes per partition batch compression.type lz4 / zstd less network and disk enable.idempotence true no duplicates on retry Partitioning: keyed records go to murmur2(key) % partitions; records without a key are spread with a "sticky" partitioner that fills one batch at a time. For atomic writes across partitions, use transactions (transactional.id ).

terms.def: Consumers sharing a group.id. Partitions are divided among them, so each record is processed by one member of the group.
terms.detail: All consumers with the same group.id share the work: each partition is assigned to exactly one member. Different groups are completely independent and each sees every record. Partitions Consumers Result 6 3 2 partitions each 6 6 1 each: maximum parallelism 6 8 2 consumers idle Name groups after the application, not the instance: billing-service. Inspect with kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group billing-service.

terms.def: The group's bookmark per partition, stored in the internal topic __consumer_offsets. A restart resumes from it.
terms.detail: The bookmark a group stores per partition in the internal topic __consumer_offsets. By convention it's the offset of the next record to read. Commit… Crash in between means Delivery after processing reprocessing some records at-least-once (usual) before processing skipping some records at-most-once in a transaction with the output nothing duplicated exactly-once (Kafka-to-Kafka) enable.auto.commit=true commits every 5 s in the background, regardless of whether you finished processing: convenient but imprecise.

terms.def: Reassignment of partitions when consumers join, leave or crash. Processing pauses for affected partitions while it runs.
terms.detail: Triggered when a consumer joins, leaves, crashes (no heartbeat within session.timeout.ms, 45 s default) or takes too long between polls (max.poll.interval.ms, 5 min default). Classic eager protocol: everyone stops, all partitions are reassigned. "Stop-the-world". Cooperative (incremental): only moved partitions pause. New consumer protocol (KIP-848, Kafka 4.0+, group.protocol=consumer ): the broker coordinates assignments; rebalances are faster and less disruptive. Use group.instance.id (static membership) so a restarting pod gets its partitions back without a rebalance.

terms.def: How long records are kept: by time (retention.ms, 7 days by default) or size, whether consumed or not.
terms.detail: Kafka deletes old data per segment file (default 1 GB or 7 days per segment), once the whole segment is older than the retention limit. Setting Default Typical retention.ms 7 days 1–30 days; -1 = forever retention.bytes unlimited cap per partition Retention is independent of consumption: unread records are deleted too, so lag must stay well below retention. Tiered storage can move old segments to object storage (S3, Azure Blob) for cheap long retention.

terms.def: Alternative cleanup policy that keeps only the latest record per key. Turns a topic into a changelog or table snapshot.
terms.detail: With cleanup.policy=compact, Kafka keeps at least the latest record per key instead of deleting by age. The topic becomes a changelog: replaying it rebuilds the current state. Compacting a user-address topic Used for Kafka Streams state stores, CDC tables, configuration and __consumer_offsets itself. Compaction runs in the background and never touches the active segment, so recent duplicates can still be read.

terms.def: Connect moves data between Kafka and other systems (databases, S3). Streams is a Java library for processing topics into new topics.
terms.detail: Kafka Connect A framework to move data in and out of Kafka with configuration instead of code. Source connectors read from systems (Debezium for PostgreSQL/MySQL CDC, JDBC, MQTT); sink connectors write to them (Elasticsearch, S3, Snowflake). Runs as a scalable cluster of workers. Kafka Streams A Java/Kotlin library (not a cluster) for processing topics into topics: filter, map, join, aggregate over time windows, with local state backed by compacted changelog topics and exactly-once support. Scales like a consumer group. Alternatives for processing: Apache Flink (bigger, any language via SQL), ksqlDB, or plain consumers in Python with confluent-kafka or Faust-style libraries.

pages.title: Azure API Management
pages.tagline: One front door for every API you own — and a place to put all the things that are not business logic.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · classic tiers (Developer, Basic, Standard, Premium) plus the v2 tiers and Consumption
pages.description: Azure API Management cheatsheet: the policy pipeline animated end to end, products and subscriptions, backend pools with circuit breakers, revisions versus versions, tiers and gotchas.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: The component that actually receives traffic, runs policies and forwards to backends. Everything else in APIM configures it.
terms.detail: Separate the two planes in your head. The data plane is the gateway handling requests; the control plane is the management API, Bicep and the portal that configure it. They scale, fail and get secured independently. Property Detail Added latency a few milliseconds for a simple policy set; validate-jwt with a cached JWKS adds little Config propagation policy changes reach gateways in seconds, not instantly — do not assume atomicity Network can be injected into a VNet (classic Premium, v2 tiers) so backends are never public Scaling by capacity units; each unit is a fixed throughput envelope, not a CPU percentage A deliberate consequence of putting the gateway in front: backends should refuse traffic that did not come through it. Use private endpoints, VNet integration, or at minimum a shared secret or client certificate the gateway adds — otherwise your policies are a suggestion.

terms.def: An API is a façade with a base path; an operation is one method and URL template within it. Policies can attach to either.
terms.detail: The API in APIM is a façade, not your service. It has its own URL, its own schema and its own operations, and the mapping to the backend is something you configure. Piece Example API base path /orders on https://contoso.azure-api.net Operation GET /orders/{orderId} Backend URL https://orders-prod.internal/api/v3 Rewrite /orders/{orderId} → /api/v3/order?id={orderId} Import from an OpenAPI document rather than clicking operations into existence — you get schemas, examples and descriptions, and validate-content can then enforce the contract. For SOAP backends, import the WSDL and let APIM generate a REST façade. Operation-scoped policies are the right place for anything that is genuinely about one endpoint: a longer timeout on a report, a tighter rate limit on search, a mock while the backend is being built.

terms.def: Four sections — inbound, backend, outbound, on-error — evaluated in order on every request. This is where APIM does its work.
terms.detail: A policy document is XML, and the order of elements is the order of execution. <policies> <inbound> <base /> <!-- inherit the outer scope first --> <validate-jwt header-name="Authorization" failed-validation-httpcode="401"> <openid-config url="https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant}/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration" /> <required-claims><claim name="scp" match="any"><value>orders.read</value></claim></required-claims> </validate-jwt> <rate-limit-by-key calls="600" renewal-period="60" counter-key="@(context.Subscription.Id)" /> <cache-lookup-value key="@($"order-{context.Request.MatchedParameters["orderId"]}")" variable-name="cached" /> <rewrite-uri template="/api/v3/order?id={orderId}" /> </inbound> <backend><forward-request timeout="20" /></backend> <outbound> <base /> <cache-store-value key="..." value="..." duration="60" /> <set-header name="X-Powered-By" exists-action="delete" /> </outbound> <on-error><base /><return-response><set-status code="502" /></return-response></on-error> </policies> Section Runs Typical content inbound before the backend is called auth, limits, validation, cache lookup, rewriting backend the call itself timeout, retry, circuit breaker, backend selection outbound after a response is received transformation, cache store, header stripping on-error whenever any section throws a consistent error envelope, logging the real cause If a policy returns a response early — a cache hit, a 429, a mock — the remaining inbound and backend policies are ski

terms.def: Policies attach at four levels — global, product, API, operation — and <base /> decides where the outer level's policies run.
terms.detail: Each level has its own document. <base /> is a placeholder for everything inherited from the level above; omit it and you silently discard the outer policies, which is one of the most common APIM bugs. Where <base /> sits Effect First in inbound outer policies run first — the usual choice Last in inbound your policy runs before the inherited ones Missing the outer scope is ignored entirely, including your global CORS and correlation id In outbound and on-error the natural order is reversed: put <base /> last so the inner scope transforms the response before the outer one does.

terms.def: Inline C# in @(...) or @{ ... } with access to context. The escape hatch that makes policies programmable.
terms.detail: Single-statement expressions use @(...); multi-statement blocks use @{ ... } and must return a value. <set-header name="X-Tenant" exists-action="override"> <value>@(context.User?.Email?.Split('@')[1] ?? "unknown")</value> </set-header> <set-variable name="isPremium" value="@{ var jwt = context.Request.Headers.GetValueOrDefault("Authorization","") .Replace("Bearer ","").AsJwt(); return jwt?.Claims.GetValueOrDefault("tier") == "premium"; }" /> Useful context members Gives you context.Request / context.Response method, URL, headers, body, matched parameters context.Subscription id, name, key — the natural rate-limit counter key context.User the developer-portal identity, when there is one context.Variables values passed between policies in one request context.LastError in on-error: what actually went wrong .AsJwt(), .AsJObject() parsing helpers on strings and bodies Reading the body needs context.Request.Body.As<JObject>(preserveContent: true), or the backend receives an empty body. Forgetting preserveContent produces a bug that only appears on requests with payloads. Keep expressions short. Policies are not a place to write business logic: they are hard to test, hard to debug and invisible to your IDE.

terms.def: A bundle of APIs with its own terms, policies and quotas, which developers subscribe to. The commercial packaging layer.
terms.detail: Products answer "who may call these APIs, and on what terms". An API can belong to several products, and the product's policies apply to every call made with one of its subscription keys. Product APIs Policy Approval Free Orders (read) quota 1,000 / month, 10 / min automatic Pro Orders, Catalogue quota 1,000,000 / month, 600 / min automatic Partner everything, including write IP allow-list, mutual TLS, no quota manual Internal everything JWT only, no subscription key not published Two flags matter. Published makes the product visible in the developer portal. Requires subscription, when turned off, makes the APIs callable without a key — occasionally right for a public read API, and a very common accident otherwise. Approval workflows put a human in the loop before a key is issued, which is what you want for partner access and rarely what you want for a free tier.

terms.def: A pair of keys issued to a consumer for a product (or a single API, or all APIs). The default unit of identity and throttling.
terms.detail: Each subscription has a primary and a secondary key, sent as Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key. Two keys exist so that rotation needs no downtime: switch clients to the secondary, regenerate the primary, switch back. Scope Use Product the normal case — the key carries the product's terms API one API without product packaging All APIs internal tooling and smoke tests; dangerous if it leaks A subscription key is not authentication. It identifies an application for metering and throttling; it says nothing about a user, it travels in a header that ends up in logs, and in a browser app it is visible to anyone who opens the network tab. Use OAuth 2.0 with validate-jwt for anything that needs to know who is calling, and keep the subscription key for the quota story.

terms.def: The inbound policy that verifies a bearer token's signature, issuer, audience, expiry and claims — before your backend sees the request.
terms.detail: APIM fetches and caches the signing keys from the OpenID configuration endpoint, so validation costs no network call per request. <validate-jwt header-name="Authorization" require-scheme="Bearer" failed-validation-httpcode="401" failed-validation-error-message="Invalid or missing token"> <openid-config url="https://login.microsoftonline.com/{tenant}/v2.0/.well-known/openid-configuration" /> <audiences><audience>api://contoso-orders</audience></audiences> <issuers><issuer>https://sts.windows.net/{tenant}/</issuer></issuers> <required-claims> <claim name="scp" match="any"><value>orders.read</value></claim> </required-claims> </validate-jwt> Check Why it matters audiences without it, a valid token for a different API is accepted issuers pins the identity provider; note v1 and v2 endpoints issue different issuer values required-claims coarse authorization at the edge: scope, role, tenant failed-validation-httpcode 401 for a missing or bad token, 403 for a valid token without the right scope Edge validation is not a substitute for checks in the backend. APIM can confirm the caller holds a valid token with the right scope; only your service knows whether this user may read that order.

terms.def: rate-limit protects against bursts over seconds; quota enforces a volume over days or months. They solve different problems.
terms.detail: Both come in a plain and a -by-key form. The -by-key variants let you choose the counter yourself, which is almost always what you want. <rate-limit-by-key calls="600" renewal-period="60" counter-key="@(context.Subscription?.Id ?? context.Request.IpAddress)" remaining-calls-header-name="RateLimit-Remaining" retry-after-header-name="Retry-After" /> <quota-by-key calls="1000000" renewal-period="2592000" counter-key="@(context.Subscription.Id)" /> rate-limit quota Window seconds to minutes days to months Protects your capacity your commercial terms Response 429, retry soon 403, come back next month Counter per gateway unit, approximate per gateway unit, approximate That last row deserves emphasis: counters are not shared across gateway units or regions. Scale to four units and a 600/min limit becomes roughly 2,400/min in the worst case. For a hard global cap, keep a single-unit gateway in front, or enforce the real limit downstream — see the dedicated page on rate limiting for the algorithms involved.

terms.def: Either the built-in cache-lookup / cache-store pair, or fine-grained cache-lookup-value for arbitrary values. Served from the gateway, so the backend is never called.
terms.detail: The simple form caches whole responses keyed on URL plus whatever you vary by: <inbound> <cache-lookup downstream-caching-type="none" must-revalidate="true" vary-by-developer="false" vary-by-developer-groups="false"> <vary-by-header>Accept-Language</vary-by-header> <vary-by-query-parameter>page</vary-by-query-parameter> </cache-lookup> </inbound> <outbound> <cache-store duration="60" /> </outbound> Cache Available in Notes Built-in all tiers except Consumption small, per gateway unit, not shared between units External Redis any tier shared across units and regions; what you want in production vary-by-developer defaults matter enormously. Leave it false on a response that differs per user and you will serve one caller's data to another — the one APIM mistake that is a security incident rather than a bug. The caching patterns themselves — TTLs, stampedes, invalidation — are the same here as anywhere; see the caching strategies page.

terms.def: A named, reusable target: a URL, credentials and optionally a pool with load balancing and a circuit breaker. Referenced by set-backend-service.
terms.detail: Defining a backend entity rather than hard-coding a URL in each policy gives you one place to change the target, and unlocks pools. <set-backend-service backend-id="orders-pool" /> Pool feature What it does priority lower numbers are used first; higher ones are failover targets weight splits traffic within a priority group — useful for canaries Circuit breaker trips a backend out of rotation after N failures in a window Weighted pools are the cheapest canary you can build: send 5% to the new revision of a service and 95% to the old one, with no deployment slot and no client change. The second animation on this page shows a pool reacting to a failing backend. Remember the breaker is per gateway unit: on a four-unit gateway, each unit must independently observe the failures before it stops sending traffic.

terms.def: How the gateway proves itself to your API: managed identity, client certificate, or a secret from a named value. Never a key the client supplied.
terms.detail: The gateway is a confidential client, so it can hold credentials a browser or mobile app cannot. Use that. <!-- best: no secret exists anywhere --> <authentication-managed-identity resource="api://contoso-orders" /> <!-- for backends that require mutual TLS --> <authentication-certificate thumbprint="{{orders-client-cert}}" /> <!-- last resort: a secret, stored in Key Vault via a named value --> <set-header name="X-Api-Key"><value>{{orders-backend-key}}</value></set-header> Mechanism Rotation Verdict Managed identity automatic, nothing to store the default for Azure backends Client certificate manual, on expiry right for partners and legacy systems Named value from Key Vault rotates with the secret acceptable when nothing better exists Hard-coded secret in the policy never it ends up in source control and in the portal UI Strip inbound credentials before forwarding. The client's subscription key and bearer token should not reach the backend unless it actually needs them: <set-header name="Ocp-Apim-Subscription-Key" exists-action="delete" />.

terms.def: The configuration store: plain strings, secrets, or references to Key Vault, usable in any policy as {{name}}.
terms.detail: They keep environment-specific values out of policy XML, so the same policy document deploys unchanged to dev, test and production. <set-backend-service base-url="{{orders-backend-url}}" /> <set-header name="X-Api-Key"><value>{{orders-backend-key}}</value></set-header> Type Stored Use for Plain visible in the portal and API URLs, tenant ids, feature switches Secret encrypted, masked in the UI legacy secrets with no better home Key Vault reference in Key Vault, fetched by managed identity everything sensitive — it rotates automatically Key Vault references refresh on a schedule (about every four hours by default), not instantly. After rotating a secret, either wait or force a refresh — otherwise you will debug a backend returning 401 while the vault shows the correct value.

terms.def: Non-breaking changes to an API, staged and tested at ?rev=N before one of them becomes current. Same URL for clients.
terms.detail: A revision is a copy of the API's definition and policies that you can edit and call privately, then promote. Clients keep using the same URL throughout. Staging a revision, then making it current Use a revision for Use a version for adding an optional field or query parameter removing or renaming a field a policy change changing a response shape or status semantics a backend URL change anything a client must be told about Making a revision current is instant and reversible: the previous revision is still there, so rolling back is one click. Always fill in the change log — it is published to the developer portal.

terms.def: Breaking changes, exposed deliberately: /v1 and /v2 live side by side, with their own policies and lifecycles.
terms.detail: A version set groups the versions of one logical API. Clients choose which they call; you deprecate on a schedule. Scheme Looks like Trade-off Path /orders/v2/{id} obvious, cache-friendly, easy to route — the usual choice Query string /orders/{id}?api-version=2 easy to default, but easy to forget and awkward for CDNs Header Api-Version: 2 keeps URLs clean, invisible in a browser, harder to debug Each version is a full API in APIM: its own operations, its own policies, its own products. That is the point — v1 can keep a legacy backend and a generous rate limit while v2 points at the rewrite. Deprecation needs a plan, not a date in a wiki: add a Deprecation and Sunset header in an outbound policy, watch per-version metrics in Application Insights to see who is still calling, and contact those subscriptions directly before you remove anything.

terms.def: The auto-generated, customisable site where consumers read the docs, sign up for a product and try calls in the browser.
terms.detail: Generated from your OpenAPI definitions, so the quality of the portal is the quality of your API descriptions and examples. Capability Detail Try-it console real calls with the signed-in developer's key; needs CORS configured at global scope Sign-up and identity built-in accounts, Microsoft Entra ID, or Entra External ID Customisation a visual editor; the whole portal can also be self-hosted from source Publishing edits are not live until you publish — and this catches everyone once Two practical notes. The portal is not available in the Consumption tier. And if you have no external consumers, you may not need it at all — an internal API catalogue is usually better served by your existing documentation site, with APIM just exporting the OpenAPI document.

terms.def: The gateway as a container you run yourself — on-premises, in another cloud, or in Kubernetes — managed from the same Azure control plane.
terms.detail: It solves one specific problem: a backend that cannot be reached from Azure, or data that must not leave a location, while you still want one place to manage every API. Property Detail Availability Premium and Developer tiers Runs as a container; usually a Deployment on Kubernetes, with the APIM Operator available Config pulled from the Azure control plane and cached locally Control-plane outage keeps serving traffic with the cached configuration Telemetry to Application Insights, or locally via OpenTelemetry You now operate it: scaling, upgrades, certificates and capacity are yours. Take it only when the network topology genuinely requires it, not for the idea of hybrid.

terms.def: The pricing tier fixes the feature set (VNet, multi-region, portal, SLA) and the capacity unit fixes throughput. Changing tier later is disruptive.
terms.detail: Choose the tier for its features, not its throughput — throughput is what units are for. Tier Use for Watch out Consumption spiky, low-volume, serverless APIs; pay per call no built-in cache, no developer portal, cold starts Developer non-production only no SLA — never run production on it, whatever the cost argument Basic / Standard ordinary production workloads no VNet injection on the classic tiers Premium VNet, multi-region, self-hosted gateways, workspaces the expensive one; justify it with a feature you actually use v2 tiers faster provisioning and scaling, simpler networking feature parity with the classic tiers is still not complete — check before committing Two operational facts worth knowing early. Classic-tier deployments and scale operations take tens of minutes, so treat them as planned changes. And a tier change usually means recreating the instance, which means a new IP address — plan for it before clients start allow-listing you.

terms.def: What you can see: Application Insights traces, Azure Monitor metrics, resource logs, and the request trace in the test console.
terms.detail: APIM sits between two systems, so it is the natural place to answer "was it us or them". Configure it deliberately rather than relying on defaults. Signal Gives you Application Insights per-request traces, dependency timing for the backend call, failures by operation Azure Monitor metrics capacity, requests, duration, by product and subscription Resource logs (GatewayLogs) the full log, queryable in Log Analytics — the best place for alerting Ocp-Apim-Trace a step-by-step trace of every policy, for one request, from the test console Set the Application Insights sampling rate explicitly. The default of 100% on a busy gateway produces a surprising bill; 5–10% is usually plenty, with failures sampled at 100%. Be careful with request and response body logging: it is invaluable in development and a data-protection problem in production. If you need it, mask the fields that matter in an outbound policy first.

pages.title: Azure Durable Functions
pages.tagline: Write a long-running workflow as ordinary code, and let replay make it survive restarts.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · extension v3.x (in-process and .NET isolated) · Durable Task Scheduler backend generally available
pages.description: Azure Durable Functions cheatsheet: orchestrators, activities and entities, an animated walk-through of replay and fan-out/fan-in, determinism rules, patterns, backends and gotchas.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: The workflow itself, written as sequential code. It decides what to call and in what order, and is replayed from the start every time it resumes.
terms.detail: An orchestrator is a function with a TaskOrchestrationContext (isolated worker) or IDurableOrchestrationContext (in-process). Everything it awaits must come from that context, because only context calls are recorded in the history. [Function(nameof(ProcessOrder))] public static async Task<Receipt> ProcessOrder([OrchestrationTrigger] TaskOrchestrationContext ctx) { var order = ctx.GetInput<Order>()!; var payment = await ctx.CallActivityAsync<PaymentResult>("ChargeCard", order); if (!payment.Succeeded) return Receipt.Declined(payment.Reason); var tracking = await ctx.CallActivityAsync<string>("ShipOrder", order); await ctx.CallActivityAsync("SendConfirmation", (order, tracking)); return new Receipt(payment.TransactionId, tracking); } Allowed in an orchestrator Forbidden CallActivityAsync, CallSubOrchestratorAsync HttpClient, database calls, file I/O ctx.CreateTimer, WaitForExternalEvent Task.Delay, Thread.Sleep ctx.CurrentUtcDateTime, ctx.NewGuid() DateTime.UtcNow, Guid.NewGuid(), Random loops, if, try/catch, LINQ over results Task.Run, ConfigureAwait(false), blocking waits Think of it as a pure function from "the history so far" to "the next thing to schedule". Everything that touches the outside world belongs in an activity.

terms.def: A single unit of real work: call an API, write to a database, send an email. Ordinary code, no determinism rules, executed at least once.
terms.detail: Activities are where all the I/O lives. They receive one serializable input, return one serializable output, and know nothing about the workflow they belong to. [Function("ChargeCard")] public static async Task<PaymentResult> ChargeCard([ActivityTrigger] Order order, FunctionContext ctx) { // ordinary code: HttpClient, EF Core, whatever you like return await _payments.ChargeAsync(order.CardToken, order.Total); } Rules that matter At least once. An activity can run twice — a worker crashes after doing the work but before reporting the result. Make activities idempotent, usually with an idempotency key derived from the instance id. Keep inputs and outputs small. They are serialized into the history. Large payloads belong in Blob Storage, with the activity passing a URL. One job each. Fine-grained activities give you better retry granularity and a far more readable history. Anything that would be unsafe to run twice — charging a card, sending an email — needs a deduplication key. The instance id plus a step name is a good one, because it is stable across replays.

terms.def: Any ordinary function — HTTP, queue, timer — that starts, queries, terminates or raises events against orchestration instances.
terms.detail: The client is the only way in. It gets a DurableTaskClient through a binding and uses it to drive instances. [Function("StartOrder")] public static async Task<HttpResponseData> Start([HttpTrigger(AuthorizationLevel.Function, "post")] HttpRequestData req, [DurableClient] DurableTaskClient client) { var order = await req.ReadFromJsonAsync<Order>(); string id = await client.ScheduleNewOrchestrationInstanceAsync(nameof(ProcessOrder), order); return await client.CreateCheckStatusResponseAsync(req, id); } CreateCheckStatusResponseAsync returns 202 Accepted with a payload of management URLs — status, terminate, raise-event, purge — which gives you a complete async HTTP API for free. Client operation Use ScheduleNewOrchestrationInstanceAsync start, optionally with your own instance id GetInstanceAsync poll status, input, output, custom status RaiseEventAsync deliver an external event (approval, webhook) TerminateAsync / SuspendAsync / ResumeAsync operational control PurgeInstancesAsync delete completed history — schedule this, see the gotchas

terms.def: A small, addressable piece of durable state — a counter, a cart, a device shadow — that processes operations one at a time per entity key.
terms.detail: Entities are the actor model inside Durable Functions. Each entity has an id ("Counter@device-42" ), holds serializable state, and the runtime guarantees that its operations execute serially, so you never need a lock. public class Counter: TaskEntity<int> { public void Add(int amount) => State += amount; public int Get() => State; public void Reset() => State = 0; [Function(nameof(Counter))] public Task RunAsync([EntityTrigger] TaskEntityDispatcher d) => d.DispatchAsync<Counter>(); } Entity Orchestrator holds state, reacts to operations holds a plan, drives a sequence no replay — operations run once replayed many times lives indefinitely, no "end" runs to completion signal (fire-and-forget) or call (await) started by a client Reach for an entity when state is keyed and long-lived and the work is a stream of small updates. Use LockAsync from an orchestrator when one operation must span several entities atomically — that is Durable Functions' version of a transaction.

terms.def: Each time an orchestrator resumes, it runs again from the first line. Completed awaits return their recorded result instead of re-executing.
terms.detail: This is the whole trick, and the thing that confuses everyone on day one. The orchestrator is not suspended and resumed in place — it is re-executed from the top, with the history replayed into it. The orchestrator runs until it awaits something not yet in the history. The function returns; the instance is evicted from memory. When the awaited result arrives, it is appended to the history. The orchestrator starts again at line 1. Each await whose result is already in the history completes instantly, without scheduling anything. Execution reaches the first new await, schedules it, and the cycle repeats. Consequences worth internalising: A log statement in an orchestrator prints once per replay. Use ctx.CreateReplaySafeLogger() to suppress the duplicates. Waiting costs nothing: a three-day timer is a row in a table, not a process holding memory. The cost of an orchestration grows with the number of steps squared in the worst case, because each replay re-reads the whole history. Long loops need ContinueAsNew. The first animation on this page walks through one full cycle.

terms.def: Replayed code must take exactly the same decisions every time. Anything that could return a different value on the second run breaks the orchestration.
terms.detail: Because the orchestrator is re-executed, non-deterministic code makes replay diverge from history — and the runtime fails the instance with a non-determinism error, often long after the offending deploy. Instead of Use DateTime.UtcNow ctx.CurrentUtcDateTime Guid.NewGuid() ctx.NewGuid() new Random() generate it in an activity and return it Task.Delay / Thread.Sleep ctx.CreateTimer(deadline, ct) HttpClient, database, file access an activity function Environment.GetEnvironmentVariable for a value that changes pass it as input, or read it in an activity Task.WhenAny on non-durable tasks ctx.WhenAny over durable tasks only Two subtler traps. First, foreach over a HashSet or Dictionary has no guaranteed order — sort first. Second, parallel Task.Run inside an orchestrator breaks the single-threaded replay model entirely. In .NET, the Durable Task analyzers catch most of these at build time; install them on day one.

terms.def: The append-only list of events for one instance: what was scheduled, what completed, what failed. It is the only state the workflow has.
terms.detail: Event sourcing, applied to a function call stack. A completed two-activity orchestration looks like this: 1 OrchestratorStarted 2 ExecutionStarted name=ProcessOrder input={...} 3 TaskScheduled name=ChargeCard 4 OrchestratorCompleted 5 TaskCompleted result={"txn":"ch_9f3"} 6 OrchestratorStarted 7 TaskScheduled name=ShipOrder 8 TaskCompleted result="TRK-991" 9 ExecutionCompleted output={...} Size matters Shape History size Verdict 10 activities, small payloads a few KB fine 1,000 activities megabytes, replay seconds batch them, or sub-orchestrate Activity returning a 10 MB document huge rows, slow every replay store it in a blob, pass the URL Infinite loop without ContinueAsNew grows forever will eventually fail the instance You can read the history through the management API or the Durable Task Scheduler dashboard. It is the first place to look when a workflow behaves strangely, because it is a literal transcript of what the orchestrator decided.

terms.def: The named container for all the queues, tables and blobs an application uses. Two apps sharing a task hub will steal each other's work.
terms.detail: Configured in host.json, it namespaces everything in the backend: { "extensions": { "durableTask": { "hubName": "OrdersHubProd" } } } Situation What to do Dev, test and prod sharing a storage account a different hubName each — or, better, separate accounts Several developers running locally against one account "hubName": "%UserName%Hub" (the setting supports app-setting substitution) Two apps that must share work same hub name, same storage — this is the only correct reason to share Deleting old data deleting the task hub's tables wipes every instance, including running ones The classic incident: a staging slot and production share a storage account and a hub name, staging picks up a production work item, and an activity runs against the wrong database. Give every environment its own hub, and check it in code review.

terms.def: The unique key of one orchestration run. Supply your own to get deduplication for free.
terms.detail: By default it is a GUID. Pass your own and the task hub enforces uniqueness, which turns "start a workflow" into an idempotent operation: // if order 10427 is already being processed, this throws instead of // starting a second, parallel workflow for the same order await client.ScheduleNewOrchestrationInstanceAsync(nameof(ProcessOrder), order, new StartOrchestrationOptions { InstanceId = $"order-{order.Id}" }); Good instance id Why order-10427 natural key: a duplicate message cannot start a second run invoice-2026-11-ACME readable in the dashboard, greppable in logs {guid} (default) fine when there is no natural key, useless for deduplication Caveat: an id can be reused once the previous instance has completed and been purged, so an id that must stay unique forever needs a date or version segment. Avoid / and @ in ids — @ is reserved for entities.

terms.def: ctx.CreateTimer() instead of Task.Delay. The orchestrator unloads and is woken at the deadline — minutes, days or months later.
terms.detail: A durable timer is a scheduled message, not a sleeping thread. Nothing is in memory while it waits, so a 30-day timer costs nothing but a row. using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource(); var approval = ctx.WaitForExternalEvent<bool>("Approved"); var timeout = ctx.CreateTimer(ctx.CurrentUtcDateTime.AddDays(3), cts.Token); if (approval == await Task.WhenAny(approval, timeout)) { cts.Cancel(); // always cancel the loser await ctx.CallActivityAsync("Publish"); } else { await ctx.CallActivityAsync("Escalate"); } Detail Value Maximum single timer 6 days on the Azure Storage backend; longer waits are split automatically in recent versions Precision seconds, not milliseconds — it is a queue message with a visibility delay Cost while waiting storage only; on the Consumption plan you pay nothing for the idle time Always cancel the losing timer. An uncancelled timer keeps the instance alive until it fires, so the orchestration shows as Running for three days after it has logically finished.

terms.def: WaitForExternalEvent parks the orchestration until something outside — a human, a webhook, another system — raises a named event.
terms.detail: This is what makes human-in-the-loop workflows trivial. The orchestrator awaits a named event; any client raises it by instance id. // in the orchestrator var decision = await ctx.WaitForExternalEvent<ApprovalDecision>("ApprovalReceived"); // anywhere else, days later await client.RaiseEventAsync(instanceId, "ApprovalReceived", new ApprovalDecision(true, "jane")); Behaviour Detail Event before the await buffered in the history, delivered as soon as the orchestrator awaits it Event to an unknown instance silently dropped — check the instance exists first Event to a completed instance dropped; there is nothing to wake Several events, same name queued; each WaitForExternalEvent consumes one Always pair an external event with a timer. A workflow waiting on an event that will never arrive is invisible: it is not failed, not completed, just Running forever.

terms.def: Schedule many activities without awaiting, then Task.WhenAll. The platform parallelises across every available worker.
