terms.detail: The pattern Durable Functions makes almost free, and the main reason to pick it over a chain of queue-triggered functions. var tasks = files.Select(f => ctx.CallActivityAsync<long>("ProcessFile", f)).ToList(); long[] sizes = await Task.WhenAll(tasks); await ctx.CallActivityAsync("WriteSummary", sizes.Sum()); Scale Guidance Up to ~100 parallel activities straightforward; the default concurrency settings cope Thousands batch the inputs, or fan out to sub-orchestrations that each fan out further Per-worker concurrency maxConcurrentActivityFunctions in host.json, default 10 x core count The aggregation step runs in the orchestrator, so it is replayed — keep it cheap and deterministic. If an exception from one activity should not kill the batch, await each task inside a try/catch rather than relying on WhenAll, which surfaces only the first failure.

terms.def: An orchestrator calling another orchestrator. The unit of composition, and the way to keep any single history small.
terms.detail: A sub-orchestration has its own instance, its own history and its own lifetime; the parent awaits it exactly like an activity. var results = await Task.WhenAll(regions.Select(r => ctx.CallSubOrchestratorAsync<RegionReport>(nameof(ProcessRegion), input: r, options: new SubOrchestrationOptions { InstanceId = $"{ctx.InstanceId}:{r}" }))); Use it to Because Split a 1,000-step workflow ten histories of 100 events replay far faster than one of 1,000 Reuse a workflow the same sub-orchestration can be called from several parents Isolate failure a sub-orchestration can fail and be retried as a unit Give a step its own retry policy retries apply to the whole sub-workflow, not one activity Give sub-orchestrations a derived instance id. Searching the dashboard for order-10427 then shows the parent and all of its children together.

terms.def: Restart the orchestration with fresh input and an empty history. The only correct way to write an eternal or long-looping workflow.
terms.detail: Because every replay re-reads the whole history, a loop that runs forever eventually makes replay unbearably slow and then fails outright. ContinueAsNew truncates it. [Function(nameof(MonitorDevice))] public static async Task MonitorDevice([OrchestrationTrigger] TaskOrchestrationContext ctx) { var state = ctx.GetInput<MonitorState>()!; var reading = await ctx.CallActivityAsync<Reading>("PollDevice", state.DeviceId); if (reading.IsCritical) { await ctx.CallActivityAsync("RaiseAlert", reading); return; // stop the loop } await ctx.CreateTimer(ctx.CurrentUtcDateTime.AddMinutes(5), CancellationToken.None); ctx.ContinueAsNew(state with { Polls = state.Polls + 1 }); // fresh history } Rule Why Carry all the state you need in the input the new instance starts with an empty history and no memory of the old one Call it last, and return straight after anything scheduled after it is lost Use it after roughly 100–1,000 iterations before replay cost becomes noticeable Unprocessed external events are carried over, so an eternal orchestration can still receive signals across restarts.

terms.def: Declarative retries on an activity or sub-orchestration call: attempts, delay, backoff, timeout. The orchestrator owns them, so they survive a crash.
terms.detail: Retries are recorded in the history, which means a retry schedule survives the worker that started it dying. That is the difference from an in-process retry library. var options = TaskOptions.FromRetryPolicy(new RetryPolicy(maxNumberOfAttempts: 5, firstRetryInterval: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5), backoffCoefficient: 2.0, // 5s, 10s, 20s, 40s maxRetryInterval: TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5), retryTimeout: TimeSpan.FromMinutes(30))); await ctx.CallActivityAsync("CallPartnerApi", payload, options); Setting Typical maxNumberOfAttempts 3–5 for a transient dependency, 1 for anything not idempotent firstRetryInterval 1–10 s backoffCoefficient 2.0 — exponential; the platform adds no jitter, so stagger at the source retryTimeout bounds the total, which maxNumberOfAttempts alone does not For compensation rather than retry — the saga pattern — wrap the orchestrator body in try/catch and call undo activities in the catch. The catch block is replayed deterministically, so compensation is as durable as the forward path.

terms.def: Changing orchestrator code while instances are mid-flight. The in-flight ones replay against your new code, and a changed shape breaks them.
terms.detail: The single most common production incident with Durable Functions. An instance started on Monday, parked on a three-day timer, replays on Thursday against the code you deployed on Wednesday. If step 2 is now a different activity, replay diverges and the instance fails. Change Safe? Changing the body of an activity yes — activities are not replayed Adding a step at the end yes Adding or removing a step in the middle no Renaming an activity or changing its argument types no Reordering awaits, or changing a loop's iteration count no Strategies Side-by-side: deploy ProcessOrderV2 next to ProcessOrder and point new starts at it. Verbose, and always correct. New task hub / new app: drain the old hub while the new one takes new work. The cleanest option for a big change. Drain before deploy: stop new starts, wait for in-flight instances to finish, then deploy. Only viable for short workflows. Recent extension versions add built-in orchestration versioning, which lets one app run several versions of the same orchestrator — check the version you are on before relying on it.

terms.def: Where the history and queues live: Azure Storage by default, or Durable Task Scheduler, Netherite or MSSQL.
terms.detail: The backend is pluggable and changes throughput, cost and operability far more than anything in your code. Backend Good for Trade-off Azure Storage (default) most workloads; cheap, zero setup lowest throughput; no built-in dashboard Durable Task Scheduler high throughput, a real monitoring UI, managed by Azure a provisioned resource with its own cost Netherite very high throughput via Event Hubs + FASTER more moving parts to operate MSSQL keeping state in your own SQL Server, on-premises or portable you own the database's capacity and backups Switching backends means starting a fresh task hub: history is not portable, so in-flight instances do not migrate. Plan the switch like a migration, not a config change.

terms.def: Querying, suspending, terminating, rewinding and purging instances — through HTTP, the client API, the CLI or the dashboard.
terms.detail: Every instance has a status, and operations are the day-two part of running workflows in production. Status Means Pending scheduled, not yet picked up Running executing, or waiting on a timer or event — the two look the same Completed returned normally Failed an unhandled exception, or replay divergence Terminated killed by an operator; activities already running are not cancelled Suspended paused and resumable — useful while you fix a downstream system SetCustomStatusAsync is underused: it attaches an arbitrary object to the instance, visible to any status query. "Step 3 of 7: awaiting approval from finance" turns an opaque Running into something a support engineer can act on. Completed instances are kept forever unless you purge them, so schedule a timer-triggered purge of instances older than your retention policy. A task hub with millions of stale rows gets slow and expensive.

pages.title: Back-of-the-envelope estimates
pages.tagline: Be roughly right in five minutes instead of precisely wrong in two weeks.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · latency and cost anchors refreshed for NVMe, modern networks and current cloud list prices
pages.description: Back-of-the-envelope estimation cheatsheet: the numbers to memorise, an animated sizing of a real service, the latency ladder scaled to human time, peak factors, Little's Law and cost anchors.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: The power of ten an answer sits at. Getting that right is the whole job; the leading digit is a bonus.
terms.detail: The question an estimate answers is never "what exactly is it" but "which regime are we in", because each regime has a different right answer. Scale What it implies < 100 QPS one machine, one database, no cache. Stop designing. 100–1,000 QPS a few instances behind a load balancer, one database with an index review 1,000–10,000 QPS caching matters, read replicas, connection pooling becomes the bottleneck 10,000–100,000 QPS sharding, CDN, async everything, a dedicated capacity story > 100,000 QPS a different architecture and a different team size < 1 TB total fits on one machine; "big data" tooling is a liability here > 100 TB storage cost is now a product decision, not an infrastructure one Being off by 2x rarely changes the regime. Being off by 100x always does — and that is the error an estimate is designed to catch, usually in the first two minutes.

terms.def: Round every input to one significant figure, preferably to a power of ten, before multiplying. Precision you did not have is precision you cannot keep.
terms.detail: Rounding is not sloppiness; it is what makes the arithmetic doable in your head, and errors in opposite directions cancel as you multiply. Awkward Use Error 86,400 s/day 100,000 +16%, and it rounds toward safety on QPS 365 days 400, or 300 for a lower bound ±10% 1,024 1,000 2.4% 31,536,000 s/year 3 x 10^7 (or π x 10^7) < 5% 7,300 QPS 10,000 +37%, and far easier to carry Two habits worth building. Work in powers of ten and keep the exponent separate: 2 x 10^7 x 5 x 10^3 = 10 x 10^10 = 10^11. And when an input is genuinely uncertain, do the calculation twice with your optimistic and pessimistic guesses — if both land in the same regime, you are done. Finally, round in the direction that would hurt. If overestimating load is safer than underestimating it, round up.

terms.def: Queries per second: daily volume divided by 86,400. The number almost every other number is derived from.
terms.detail: The conversion is one division, and the trick is to use 100,000 seconds per day so you can do it by shifting a decimal point. 1,000,000 requests/day -> 10 QPS 100,000,000 /day -> 1,000 QPS 1,000,000,000 /day -> 10,000 QPS Rough anchors QPS A busy internal line-of-business app 10–100 A popular SaaS product 1,000–10,000 A large consumer app 100,000+ One modest API instance can serve 500–2,000 (simple JSON, cached) One Postgres instance, simple indexed reads 5,000–20,000 One Redis instance 100,000+ Always split reads from writes. The ratio between them decides more of the architecture than the absolute number does — 250:1 means caching and replicas, while 1:1 means the write path is your problem.

terms.def: Traffic is never flat. Multiply the average by 2–4 for a normal daily peak, and far more for an event.
terms.detail: Average QPS is a billing number. Peak QPS is a capacity number, and they are not interchangeable. Why the average line is not the number you provision Workload Peak / average Consumer app, global audience 2–3x Consumer app, single country 3–5x B2B, office hours in one timezone 4–6x Batch or cron-driven 10–100x — it is all peak Flash sale, ticket drop, TV moment 20–100x Above roughly 10x, stop provisioning for the peak: it is cheaper to queue, shed or rate-limit. That is a design decision the estimate just made for you.

terms.def: The ladder from L1 cache to an intercontinental round trip. Knowing the rungs stops you designing something physics forbids.
terms.detail: Approximate, current-hardware values. The exact figures matter far less than the ratios, which have been stable for years. Operation Time vs L1 L1 cache reference ~1 ns 1x Branch mispredict ~3 ns 3x L2 cache reference ~4 ns 4x Mutex lock / unlock, uncontended ~20 ns 20x Main memory reference ~100 ns 100x Compress 1 KB (fast codec) ~2 µs 2,000x Read 1 MB sequentially from RAM ~50 µs 50,000x NVMe SSD random read (4 KB) ~20 µs 20,000x Round trip within a datacenter ~0.5 ms 500,000x Read 1 MB sequentially from NVMe ~0.3 ms 300,000x Spinning-disk seek ~5 ms 5,000,000x Round trip, same continent ~20 ms — Round trip, Europe to California ~150 ms — Three rules fall out of this table and cover most design arguments: memory is ~100x faster than an SSD, a network hop costs more than a local disk read, and the speed of light sets a floor nobody can buy their way past — only a copy nearer the user can. The light-speed floor is worth computing once: light does about 200 km/ms in fibre, so London to New York (5,600 km) is 28 ms one way and 56 ms round trip at best. Real paths are not straight; 70–90 ms is typical.

terms.def: Bytes per field, per row, per object. Estimate by adding up what is actually stored, then double it for overhead.
terms.detail: Most storage estimates fail on this line, usually by forgetting indexes. Thing Size int / bigint 4 / 8 B UUID (binary / text) 16 / 36 B Timestamp 8 B Short text field (name, email) 20–60 B Typical relational row 100–1,000 B JSON document 1–10 KB Log line 200 B–2 KB Web page (HTML only) 50–200 KB Phone photo 2–5 MB Minute of 1080p video ~50 MB Embedding vector (1,536 x float32) 6 KB Multipliers you will forget Indexes: add 20–100% of the table size. A table with five indexes can be larger than its data. Replication: x2 or x3, before backups. Backups and snapshots: often another x1–2 over the retention period. Compression: divide by 3–10 for text and logs, by 1 for already-compressed media. Rule of thumb: whatever you computed, multiply by three. You will be closer than if you did not.

terms.def: Daily volume times retention times replication. The number that most often kills a design, and the one most often left out of it.
terms.detail: Storage is the only resource that accumulates. CPU and bandwidth reset every second; bytes written in January are still being paid for in December. total = items/day x bytes/item x retention_days x replicas x (1 + index_overhead) Example Per day Per year Audit log: 10M events x 500 B 5 GB 1.8 TB App logs: 100M lines x 1 KB 100 GB 36 TB Photos: 20M x 2 MB 40 TB 15 PB Metrics: 10k series x 1 point/10 s x 16 B 1.4 GB 500 GB Two questions turn an unaffordable number into an affordable one: how long must we really keep it, and does it have to stay hot. Dropping log retention from 365 to 30 days is a 12x saving, and archival storage is 5–10x cheaper than hot. Always project three to five years, not one. A design that is fine at year one and impossible at year three is a design you will rewrite under pressure.

terms.def: QPS multiplied by payload size. Convert to bits per second before comparing with any network specification.
terms.detail: The conversion that trips everyone: network links are specified in bits, storage and payloads in bytes. One factor of eight, applied in the wrong direction, is an 64x error. Link Bytes per second 1 Gbps 125 MB/s 10 Gbps 1.25 GB/s 25 Gbps 3.1 GB/s 100 Gbps 12.5 GB/s 50,000 reads/s x 200 KB = 10 GB/s = 80 Gbps # needs a CDN, not a server 1,000 reads/s x 20 KB = 20 MB/s = 160 Mbps # one ordinary instance Useful anchors: a single modern server does 10–25 Gbps comfortably; anything that needs more than roughly 10 Gbps of user-facing egress belongs behind a CDN, and the egress bill will become one of your top three cloud line items long before the bandwidth becomes a technical problem. Also check the time dimension: moving 100 TB over a 10 Gbps link takes about a day of saturated transfer. For a migration, that is the number that decides whether you ship disks instead.

terms.def: concurrency = arrival rate x latency. Three quantities; know two and the third is determined. It sizes pools and queues.
terms.detail: The most useful formula in capacity planning, and the one that explains why a service with plenty of CPU still falls over. L = λ x W concurrent_requests = requests_per_second x seconds_per_request Rate Latency Concurrency needed 1,000 /s 10 ms 10 1,000 /s 100 ms 100 1,000 /s 1 s 1,000 threads or connections 100 /s 2 s 200 Read that third row carefully: nothing about the request rate changed, but a tenfold latency increase demands a thousand concurrent slots. This is exactly what happens when a dependency slows down, and why a pool sized for the happy path exhausts itself during an incident. Run it backwards too. A connection pool of 100 against a database with 20 ms queries can sustain 100 / 0.02 = 5,000 queries per second — and not one more, whatever the CPU graph says.

terms.def: How many reads per write. The single number that decides most of the architecture before any other consideration.
terms.detail: Ratios cluster, and each cluster has a standard answer. Ratio Example Implication 1000:1 news site, product catalogue cache almost everything; the write path is irrelevant 100:1 social feed, e-commerce heavy caching, read replicas, precompute on write 10:1 typical business app ordinary caching, one primary is usually fine 1:1 chat, collaborative editing the write path is the design; caching helps little 1:100 telemetry, IoT ingestion append-only storage, batching, a log, time-series database Estimate it from behaviour, not from the database. "Each user posts twice and scrolls past 200 posts" gives you 100:1 directly, and that is enough to know whether the conversation should be about caching or about ingest. It also tells you where to spend effort: at 1000:1, halving read cost is worth a thousand times more than halving write cost.

terms.def: Not all data is accessed equally. Usually around 20% of it serves 80% of requests, and recent data dominates.
terms.detail: This is what makes caching work at all, and what makes storage affordable: you only need the hot slice to be fast. Pattern Typical shape Social feed 90% of reads touch data from the last 24 hours E-commerce catalogue top 5% of products get 60–80% of views Logs and metrics 99% of queries are over the last 7 days Document archive almost all reads in the first week, then near zero Sizing a cache follows directly: cache the hot slice, not the dataset. For 200 PB of photos where 1% is hot, roughly 2 TB of cache plus a CDN buys an excellent hit ratio — and the caching strategies page covers how to choose the TTLs and eviction policy that keep it that way. The same split drives tiering: hot on SSD, warm on object storage, cold on archival. A 5–10x price difference between tiers applied to 95% of your bytes is usually the largest single cost saving available.

terms.def: Peak load divided by what one machine does, plus headroom. The last step before the number becomes money.
terms.detail: Per-machine capacity is the input people most often guess badly, so anchor it rather than imagining it. Workload One modern instance handles Static files / reverse proxy 50,000–100,000 req/s Simple JSON API, cached 2,000–10,000 req/s API with a database round trip 500–2,000 req/s Heavy computation / rendering 10–100 req/s Postgres, simple indexed reads 5,000–20,000 QPS Redis, single instance 100,000+ ops/s Kafka broker 100 MB/s+ sustained machines = peak_qps / per_machine_qps / target_utilisation = 150,000 / 1,000 / 0.5 = 300 If the answer is under 5, do not design a distributed system: build one service, run three for availability, and revisit when the number changes. If the answer is over 1,000, the interesting question is no longer "how many" but "what else is wrong" — at that scale, cost per request usually dominates the architecture.

terms.def: The gap between what you provision and what you use. Running a system at 90% utilisation is a decision to have no response to anything.
terms.detail: Headroom pays for the things an estimate cannot model: a deploy, an instance failure, an unexpectedly popular feature, a retry storm. Target utilisation Suitable for 30–40% stateful systems, slow-scaling tiers, anything where failover doubles a neighbour's load 50–60% typical stateless services — the usual default 70–80% fast-autoscaling, well-understood workloads > 85% batch jobs that can wait, and nothing else The subtle one is N+1 across a pool: with three instances at 60%, losing one puts the other two at 90%, and they fall over too. With five at 60%, losing one puts the rest at 75%. The smaller the pool, the more headroom each member needs. Queues need headroom in time, not capacity: a queue that drains exactly as fast as it fills has infinite latency the moment anything hiccups. Aim for a consumer that can drain at 2–3x the arrival rate.

terms.def: Rough unit prices, good to a factor of two. Enough to tell whether an idea is cheap, expensive or impossible.
terms.detail: Approximate cloud list prices. Vary by provider, region and commitment — but for a decision, "about $0.02 per GB-month" is all you need. Resource Rough price Object storage, hot $0.02 / GB / month Object storage, archive $0.002 / GB / month Block storage (SSD) $0.08–0.12 / GB / month Managed database storage $0.10–0.25 / GB / month Egress to the internet $0.05–0.09 / GB CDN egress $0.01–0.04 / GB General-purpose VM (4 vCPU, 16 GB) $100–150 / month on demand Same, 1–3 year commitment 30–60% less Two anchors worth memorising because they decide so many arguments: 1 PB of hot object storage is roughly $20,000 per month, and 1 PB of internet egress is roughly $50,000. Once you know those, "we'll just store all of it and serve it from origin" stops being a design and becomes a budget request. Compare against the business, not against other infrastructure. $4M a month is cheap for a product with $100M of revenue and fatal for one with $2M.

terms.def: The last step, and the one people skip: compare the answer with something you already know to be true.
terms.detail: An estimate without a sanity check is a number with no error bars and no defence. Check Question Dimensional do the units actually produce the thing I asked for? Human does this imply every person on Earth does it four times a day? Hardware does this imply a disk faster than any disk? Known system is this larger than a company I know to be much larger than us? Money is this more than the revenue of the product? Dimensional analysis alone catches most arithmetic slips. If you are computing servers and the units come out as "requests per second per byte", you inverted something — and you would never have noticed from the digits. The strongest check is a known reference point. If your estimate of a national bank's daily transactions exceeds the number of card transactions in the world, something is wrong by about a thousand, and knowing that is more useful than any refinement of the inputs.

terms.def: Which assumption dominates the answer. Find it, and spend your remaining time on that one input only.
terms.detail: In a chain of multiplications, the input with the widest uncertainty controls the output. Everything else is noise you do not need to refine. In the photo-service estimate, the inputs are 100M users (known within 20%), 0.2 uploads per user (a guess, possibly 5x off), 2 MB per photo (known within 2x), 5-year retention (a policy choice) and 3 replicas (a design choice). The uploads per user dominates: get it wrong by 5x and the 200 PB becomes 40 PB or 1 EB, and the conclusion flips. Technique How High / low pass run the estimate with optimistic and pessimistic inputs; if both land in the same regime, stop Vary one input double each input in turn and see which moves the answer most Name the dominant term state it out loud: "this whole thing hinges on uploads per user" This is also the honest way to present an estimate. "Somewhere between 40 and 400 PB, driven almost entirely by how often people actually upload — and we can measure that in a week" is a far more useful sentence than a single confident number.

pages.title: Backend-for-Frontend
pages.tagline: One backend per experience, so no client has to negotiate with a general-purpose API.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · the pattern is stable; examples are .NET 10 (LTS) and ASP.NET Core
pages.description: Backend-for-Frontend cheatsheet: animated comparison of one shared API, a BFF per client, gateway aggregation and GraphQL, with round-trip budgets, tail amplification, auth and ownership.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: A server-side component dedicated to one client, owned by that client's team and shaped around its screens rather than around domain resources.
terms.detail: Introduced at SoundCloud and named by Sam Newman. The defining property is not what it does — aggregation and shaping — but who owns it: it is part of the frontend that happens to run on a server. A BFF is A BFF is not one per experience (mobile, web, TV) one per microservice deployed with its client a shared platform component allowed to be ugly and specific a place for domain rules disposable when the client is retired a long-lived public API One per experience, not one per platform: if iOS and Android render the same screens from the same data, they share a BFF. Split them when the experiences genuinely diverge, not because the languages do. The honest test of whether you have a BFF or an API: when the mobile team needs a new field on a screen, do they write the code themselves and ship it today, or do they ask another team? If it is the second, it is not a BFF.

terms.def: An endpoint shaped like a screen — GET /mobile/home — rather than like a resource. The thing a BFF actually exposes.
terms.detail: Resource APIs are designed for generality; experience APIs are designed for one layout. That specificity is a feature, and it is why they must not be shared. Resource API Experience API GET /users/{id} GET /mobile/home GET /baskets/{id} GET /mobile/checkout returns everything about a thing returns everything on a screen stable, versioned, documented changes with the design // the response is the screen, in order { "greeting": "Good evening, Davide", "basket": { "count": 3, "total": "€89.90" }, "panels": [ { "type": "recommendations", "items": [ { "id":"p1", "title":"…", "price":"€12" } ] }, { "type": "loyalty", "points": 420, "nextTier": 80 } ] } Going further, some teams return the layout too — server-driven UI, where the BFF decides which panels appear and in what order. That lets you change a screen without an app release, at the cost of a client that is harder to reason about offline.

terms.def: Receiving far more than the screen renders: the full user aggregate when you needed a name. Wasteful on mobile, and it ties you to a model you do not control.
terms.detail: A general-purpose endpoint has to return everything any consumer might need, so every consumer pays for the union of everyone's requirements. Screen needs GET /users/me returns display name, avatar URL profile, all addresses, preferences, consent history, linked accounts ~120 bytes 28 KB On a good connection nobody notices. On a congested mobile link, 180 KB of padding across six calls is seconds of waiting, and on a metered plan it is the user's money. The subtler cost: every field in that response is now something a client might start depending on, so the shape cannot change. A BFF breaks that by making the transport payload a private detail between the BFF and its own client.

terms.def: The opposite: the response does not contain what you need next, so you make another call — and another. This is what turns one screen into six round trips.
terms.detail: Under-fetching is worse than over-fetching, because extra bytes cost bandwidth while extra calls cost latency, and latency does not improve with a better plan. GET /baskets/current -> { items: [ { productId: 42 }, { productId: 91 } ] } GET /catalogue/items?ids=42,91 -> names and images (needed the first call to know the ids) GET /pricing?ids=42,91 -> prices (and again) Those three calls are sequential: each needs an id from the one before. That is a dependent wave, and three waves on a 150 ms link is 450 ms before a pixel is drawn. Pattern Cost on mobile 6 parallel calls 1 wave — about 150 ms, if connection limits allow 6 calls in 3 dependent waves 450 ms minimum 1 call to a BFF 150 ms, with the waves happening at 5 ms each inside the datacenter The BFF does not remove the dependent waves; it moves them somewhere a round trip is thirty times cheaper.

terms.def: The number of round trips a screen costs. On mobile this dominates everything else, so it is the number to design against.
terms.detail: Give every screen a round-trip budget and treat it like a performance requirement, because it is. Link Typical round trip 6 calls in 3 waves Datacenter-internal 0.5–5 ms ~15 ms Wired broadband 10–30 ms ~90 ms Good 4G/5G 50–100 ms ~300 ms Congested mobile, or rural 150–400 ms 450–1,200 ms Satellite 600 ms+ unusable Two corrections people make that do not help: HTTP/2 multiplexing removes the connection limit but not the dependency between waves, and a CDN helps only if the response is cacheable and shared. A dependent chain of calls is slow on principle. Budget one round trip per screen transition. If a screen needs two, there should be a reason written down.

terms.def: Calling several services in parallel and combining the results. The BFF's main job, and the reason it belongs near the services rather than near the user.
terms.detail: The mechanics are unremarkable; the discipline is in what you do when one of them is slow or broken. var profile = _profile.GetAsync(userId, ct); var basket = _basket.GetAsync(userId, ct); var loyalty = _loyalty.GetAsync(userId, ct); await Task.WhenAll(profile, basket, loyalty); // one wave, not three Rule Why Start every independent call before awaiting any awaiting in sequence turns one wave into N Give every downstream call its own timeout otherwise the slowest defines your latency Degrade rather than fail where you can a home screen without recommendations still works Never let the BFF become a second hop to another BFF chains of aggregators multiply the tail Keep aggregation shallow. A BFF calling services is fine; a BFF calling a BFF calling services is a distributed system with a latency budget nobody is tracking.

terms.def: Returning exactly the fields the screen renders, in the structure it renders them. What turns 180 KB into 4 KB.
terms.detail: Shaping is more than projection. The BFF is the right place to do the formatting, ordering and conditional logic that would otherwise be duplicated in every client. Do in the BFF Leave to the services pick the fields this screen needs what the fields mean format currency and dates for the locale store amounts and instants flatten three responses into one object own their own models decide panel order and visibility business rules and invariants resize or pick an image variant hold the asset The boundary to hold: presentation logic belongs in the BFF, domain logic does not. "Show the loyalty banner when tier is gold and the basket is non-empty" is presentation. "A gold tier requires 2,000 points" is domain, and must live in the loyalty service or it will be wrong in one of your four clients.

terms.def: The BFF is owned, deployed and on-called by the team that owns the client. This is the defining property, not an organisational detail.
terms.detail: Conway's Law applied on purpose. The reason the pattern works is that it removes a hand-off from the most frequently changing part of the system. Owned by the client team Owned by a platform team a new field ships today a new field is a ticket and a sprint deploys with the client release deploys on the platform's schedule free to be specific and ugly must stay general for all consumers deleted when the client is outlives everything, forever If your organisation will not let the client team run a service — no pipeline, no on-call, no budget — you will get a BFF owned by the platform team, which is just a second API with extra hops. In that case prefer gateway aggregation or GraphQL and save yourself the deployment. The same logic says: delete the BFF with the client. A "legacy mobile BFF" still running two years after the app was retired is a sign the ownership was never real.

terms.def: The BFF waits for the slowest of its downstream calls, so its p99 is much worse than any single service's. The cost of fan-out.
terms.detail: Moving the fan-out server-side does not remove the probability maths — it just moves it. If each of six calls is fast 99% of the time, the page is fast only 0.99 6 = 94% of the time. Downstream calls Chance the screen hits a p99 tail 1 1% 6 5.9% 10 9.6% 20 18% So a BFF fanning out to six services with a 500 ms p99 each has roughly a 6% chance of a slow screen — the services' p99 has become the screen's p94. The percentiles page covers the arithmetic and the defences in full. Three mitigations, in order: aggressive per-call timeouts with a degraded response, caching in the BFF so hot panels never fan out, and hedged requests for the one downstream that is genuinely erratic.

terms.def: One downstream is down, and the screen still renders without that panel. A BFF is the natural place to decide this, because it knows what the screen can live without.
terms.detail: A general-purpose API cannot make this decision — it does not know what the caller is drawing. A BFF does, and that is one of its strongest arguments. var recs = await Safe(() => _recs.GetAsync(userId, cts.Token), fallback: []); static async Task<T> Safe<T>(Func<Task<T>> call, T fallback) { try { return await call(); } catch (Exception ex) when (ex is TimeoutException or HttpRequestException) { return fallback; } // log it, count it, and carry on } Downstream If it fails profile fail the request — there is no screen without a user basket fail, or show an explicit error state recommendations omit the panel loyalty omit the panel Decide this per field, write it down, and emit a metric for every degradation. A BFF that silently drops panels is indistinguishable from a product decision, and you will find out months later that a panel has been missing for 4% of users.

terms.def: The BFF is an excellent cache point: it knows the screen, the user and what may be shared. Done wrong, it is where you leak one user's data to another.
terms.detail: Three distinct things can be cached, and conflating them is the classic bug. Cache Key TTL Shared downstream data (catalogue, prices) resource id minutes Per-user downstream data (basket, loyalty) user id + resource seconds, or not at all The assembled screen user id + screen + locale + app version seconds Only the first row is safe to cache globally. Put the user id in the key for the other two, and never set Cache-Control: public on an authenticated response — a shared cache in front of the BFF will happily serve one user's home screen to the next. The caching strategies page covers the patterns and the invalidation traps; the only BFF-specific rule is that the cache key must contain every dimension that changes the screen, including the app version, because an old client and a new one expect different shapes.

terms.def: The BFF sits between a browser or app and the services, which makes it the right place to swap a cookie for a token and to keep tokens off the client entirely.
terms.detail: For a browser SPA this is the strongest security argument for the pattern. Tokens in JavaScript are reachable by any script on the page; tokens in a BFF are not. Client Holds BFF does Browser SPA an HttpOnly, SameSite session cookie keeps the access and refresh tokens server-side and attaches them downstream Mobile app tokens in the platform keychain validates, then exchanges for a downstream token Partner client credentials not a BFF — use the public API This "BFF pattern for SPAs" is now the mainstream recommendation for browser applications precisely because it removes tokens from a place scripts can reach. In .NET, Duende.BFF packages it; the shape is a cookie in, a bearer token out. Do not let the BFF become an authorization service. It should check that the caller is who they claim and pass identity down; whether this user may read that order is the owning service's decision, and duplicating it in four BFFs guarantees a divergence.

terms.def: A BFF can change as often as its client — but on mobile the old client never goes away, so it must serve several app versions at once.
terms.detail: Web is easy: ship the SPA and the BFF together and there is one version in the wild. Mobile is not: users on a two-year-old build still open the app, and you cannot force them to upgrade. Approach Good for Cost Additive-only changes almost everything fields accumulate Version in the path (/v2/mobile/home) a redesigned screen two code paths to maintain Branch on the app version header small divergences if statements that never get deleted Minimum supported version cutting the tail off a forced-upgrade screen and angry reviews Set a support window — "the last four releases, or six months" — before you need it, instrument the version distribution, and put a deletion date on every compatibility branch you add. Without that, a BFF accumulates version checks until it is harder to change than the general-purpose API it replaced.

terms.def: Three BFFs calling the same five services will contain similar code. Some of that duplication is the price of the pattern; some of it is a mistake.
terms.detail: The instinct is to extract the common parts into a shared library, and that instinct, followed too far, recreates the coupling the BFFs were meant to remove. Share Duplicate generated service clients and DTOs aggregation logic auth middleware, tracing, logging response shapes resilience policies and defaults which panel to drop on failure the deployment template anything to do with a screen Rule of thumb: share things that are plumbing, duplicate things that are product. The moment a shared library needs a flag for "but mobile wants it differently", stop and copy the code instead. And watch the version lock: a shared library that every BFF must upgrade in lockstep reintroduces the coordinated release the pattern was adopted to avoid.

terms.def: The BFF depends on the services it calls, so their breaking changes become its problem. A thin BFF makes this manageable; a thick one does not.
terms.detail: You have added a layer, which means a change can now break in two places instead of one. Keep the layer thin enough that a downstream change is a mapping fix rather than a redesign. Keeps coupling cheap Makes it expensive generated clients from OpenAPI hand-written HTTP calls and anonymous JSON mapping at the edge, in one place downstream DTOs flowing through the BFF consumer-driven contract tests finding out in production no business rules in the BFF rules duplicated from the service Contract tests are the highest-value investment here: the BFF publishes what it needs from each service, and the service's pipeline fails if a change would break it. That turns "we found out on Friday" into a red build on the service team's own pull request.

terms.def: The main alternative: one endpoint, a typed schema, and the client declares the shape. Solves over- and under-fetching without a backend per client.
terms.detail: GraphQL and the BFF pattern answer the same question. The differences are about who coordinates, and what it costs to operate. BFF GraphQL Shaping decided by the BFF's code the client's query New client build and run a new service write a new query Coordination none — each team owns its BFF the schema is shared and negotiated HTTP caching normal hard: one URL, usually POST Cost control you wrote the aggregation needs depth and complexity limits N+1 visible in your own code the default, until you add batching # one request, exactly the fields the screen draws query Home { me { displayName avatarUrl } basket { count total } recommendations(limit: 6) { id title price } } They combine well: a GraphQL BFF is one GraphQL server per client, with a schema shaped for that client. You keep declarative shaping and drop the organisation-wide schema negotiation, which is the part most teams find hardest.

pages.title: Backpressure
pages.tagline: When a fast producer meets a slow consumer, the queue between them is not a solution. It is where the outage is hiding.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · examples in C#, Go, Java and Python; the idea is as old as TCP
pages.description: Backpressure cheatsheet: bounded queues, demand signalling and why an unbounded buffer turns a throughput problem into an outage — animated, with the arithmetic that sizes a queue.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: The signal that a consumer cannot keep up, propagated upstream so the producer slows down instead of the queue growing.
terms.detail: It is a flow control mechanism, not a capacity mechanism. It does not make the consumer faster and it does not decide which work to abandon — it only ensures that the mismatch between arrival and service rates becomes visible at a point where somebody can act on it. Almost every implementation reduces to the same two steps: bound the buffer, then choose what happens when the bound is reached. Everything else is a refinement of how politely that is communicated. What it is and is not Mechanism Question it answers Backpressure how do I tell upstream to slow down? Load shedding which work do I refuse? Rate limiting how much is this client entitled to? Circuit breaker should I stop calling a broken dependency? How it relates Backpressure gets the signal to the edge; load shedding is what the edge then does with it.

terms.def: A buffer with a maximum size, which is what turns "the queue grows" into an actual signal.
terms.detail: The bound is the entire mechanism. Once a queue cannot grow, something must happen at the boundary: the producer blocks, the item is dropped, or an error is returned. All three are honest; growing forever is not. Size it from latency, not from memory. If the consumer handles 800 items a second and you are willing to add 25 ms of queueing delay, the queue should hold about 20 items — not the 100,000 that happens to fit in RAM. Sizing by Little's Law Service rate Latency budget Queue size 800 / s 25 ms 20 800 / s 250 ms 200 100 / s 1 s 100 any "as much as fits" wrong question How it relates A connection pool, a thread pool and a semaphore are all bounded queues wearing different names.

terms.def: The default in most libraries, and a reliable way to turn a small overload into a crash.
terms.detail: An unbounded buffer does not prevent failure; it postpones and amplifies it. During the delay, latency climbs past every client timeout, so the consumer spends its capacity on work nobody is waiting for, and the process eventually dies from memory exhaustion rather than from the original 20% overload. The danger is that it looks healthy. No errors are returned, no alerts fire, CPU may even be moderate — right up until the OOM kill. Unbounded by default Thing Default new LinkedBlockingQueue<>() unbounded Channel.CreateUnbounded() unbounded, by name asyncio.Queue() unbounded Go make(chan T) unbuffered — blocks, which is correct An in-memory list "just for buffering" unbounded How it relates The first animation is one unbounded queue, second by second, to the crash.

terms.def: L = λW — the arithmetic that converts a queue depth into a latency, and therefore sizes every buffer you own.
terms.detail: Rearranged as W = L / λ it says: with 2,000 items queued in front of a consumer doing 800 a second, the wait is 2.5 seconds — regardless of how fast any individual item is processed. That is why queue depth is a latency metric in disguise. It also sizes concurrency limits: at 1,000 requests a second and 50 ms of service time, roughly 50 requests are in flight, so a limit of 60 has headroom and a limit of 500 is an unbounded queue with extra steps. The same law, three uses Question Form How long will this queue delay me? W = L / λ How big should the queue be? L = λ × W budget How many workers do I need? L = λ × W service How it relates The Little's Law page works through the identity itself and where it does not apply.

terms.def: Explicit backpressure: the consumer tells the producer exactly how many items it may send.
terms.detail: Instead of discovering fullness by blocking on a write, the consumer publishes its appetite. Reactive Streams calls it request(n), TCP calls it the receive window, gRPC and HTTP/2 call it flow-control windows, Kafka expresses it as fetch sizes and poll limits. The advantage over implicit blocking is that the producer learns the limit before producing, so it can avoid doing expensive work it would then have to throw away — reading fewer rows, rendering fewer items, pulling fewer messages. Credit-based flow control How it relates TCP has worked this way since 1974; most application-level designs are reinventing it badly.

terms.def: The concrete protocol behind demand signalling: a window of permits that the consumer replenishes as it drains.
terms.detail: The consumer advertises a window; the producer decrements it as it sends and stops at zero; the consumer replenishes as it processes. Because the window is a number on the wire, both sides agree on the bound at all times and neither needs a timeout to discover it. The tuning question is window size: too small and the link idles waiting for replenishment, too large and you have rebuilt an unbounded queue. Bandwidth-delay product is the classic sizing rule for networks; for application queues, Little's Law with a latency budget does the same job. Where you already use it System Mechanism TCP receive window HTTP/2, gRPC per-stream and connection windows Reactive Streams request(n) Kafka consumer max.poll.records, pause() AMQP prefetch count How it relates The animation in demand signalling walks one credit cycle.

terms.def: How long an item waits, which matters far more than how many items are waiting.
terms.detail: Depth is a proxy; sojourn time is the thing. A queue of 10,000 drained at 100,000 a second is fine; a queue of 50 drained at 5 a second is a ten-second outage. Measuring the age of the oldest item — or timestamping on enqueue and measuring on dequeue — tells you directly whether you are in trouble. It is also the better shedding signal: algorithms like CoDel drop based on how long items have been waiting rather than on how many there are, which adapts automatically to changes in capacity. What to measure Metric Tells you Queue depth memory pressure Sojourn time (p99) what users actually feel Age of oldest item whether you are falling behind now Enqueue rejections backpressure is engaging How it relates Alert on sojourn time; depth alone will either page too early or far too late.

terms.def: Processing requests whose callers have already given up — the main reason an overloaded system never recovers.
terms.detail: Once the queueing delay exceeds the client timeout, every item dequeued is for a client that has disconnected. The server is now at 100% utilisation with 0% goodput, and because it is busy doing useless work it cannot catch up — the definition of congestion collapse. The fix is to make deadlines travel with the request and to check them on dequeue: if the deadline has passed, drop it without processing. One cheap check recovers the whole capacity. Defences Defence Effect Deadline propagation callee knows when to stop Check deadline on dequeue discard dead work for free Queue timeout < client timeout never start doomed work LIFO under overload serve the freshest, not the stalest How it relates LIFO sounds unfair and is kinder in practice: under overload, FIFO guarantees everyone gets a timeout.

terms.def: Clients retrying a slow system, multiplying the arrival rate exactly when it is least able to cope.
terms.detail: The feedback loop that turns a degradation into an outage. Latency rises past the client timeout, clients retry, arrivals double, latency rises further, more retries. Three layers each retrying three times turns one request into twenty-seven. Backpressure helps by failing fast: a request rejected in a millisecond costs almost nothing, while one that times out after two seconds has consumed two seconds of capacity first. Add jittered exponential backoff and a retry budget so clients cannot collectively exceed a few percent of normal traffic. Controls Control Why Exponential backoff + jitter breaks the synchronised wave Retry budget (e.g. 10%) caps total amplification Never retry at every layer retries multiply, not add Fail fast when shedding a cheap no beats an expensive timeout How it relates A circuit breaker is the strongest form of this control: stop calling entirely for a while.

terms.def: Capping how many requests are in flight at once — the most practical backpressure mechanism in a service.
terms.detail: A semaphore, a thread pool, a connection pool or a worker count all do the same thing: they bound the work in progress, and therefore bound latency by Little's Law. When the limit is reached, new work waits briefly or is rejected — which is backpressure, implemented in one line. It is more robust than a rate limit because it adapts to service time automatically: if each request gets slower, fewer get through, without anyone recalculating a requests-per-second number. Rate limit or concurrency limit? Rate limit Concurrency limit Bounds arrivals per second work in progress Adapts to slowdowns no yes Good for fairness, quotas, billing protecting capacity How it relates The database page's "pool exhausted" animation is a concurrency limit doing its job and being blamed for it.

terms.def: Discovering the right limit at runtime by watching latency, instead of configuring a number that is wrong by next quarter.
terms.detail: Algorithms borrowed from TCP congestion control — Netflix's Gradient and Vegas limiters, and similar schemes in Envoy — track the ratio between current latency and the best latency observed. When latency rises, the limit shrinks; when it recovers, the limit grows. The system finds its own capacity. This matters because static limits are wrong in both directions: too low wastes hardware during normal operation, too high lets the service fall over during a dependency slowdown. Signals used Signal Interpretation Latency > recent minimum queueing has started — shrink Latency at minimum headroom exists — grow Rejections / errors shrink quickly How it relates Start with a static limit sized by Little's Law; adopt adaptive limits once that number is clearly wrong at different times of day.

terms.def: One slow item at the front of a queue delaying everything behind it, however fast those would have been.
terms.detail: A single FIFO shared by cheap and expensive work means the cheap work inherits the expensive work's latency. It appears in HTTP/1.1 pipelines, in a Kafka partition where one poisoned record stalls the rest, and in any thread pool where one slow endpoint occupies every worker. The fix is separation rather than a bigger queue: separate queues or pools per class of work, so a slow class cannot starve a fast one. Separations that help Split by Example Cost fast reads vs heavy reports Priority checkout vs recommendations Tenant one customer cannot starve others Dependency a pool per downstream service How it relates Per-dependency pools are the bulkhead pattern, which is the other half of circuit breaking.

terms.def: The networking name for the same mistake: oversized buffers destroying latency while preserving throughput.
terms.detail: Router vendors added large buffers to avoid dropping packets, and in doing so broke TCP's feedback loop: congestion signals arrived seconds late, so senders kept accelerating and interactive traffic became unusable. The cure — active queue management with CoDel — drops based on how long packets have been waiting. It is worth knowing because the lesson transfers exactly: dropping early is kinder than queueing late, and a buffer's job is to absorb bursts, not to hide a persistent rate mismatch. The transferable lesson Buffer absorbs Verdict A short burst correct use A persistent rate mismatch a crash with a delay How it relates CoDel-style shedding on sojourn time is the application-level version of this fix.

terms.def: Signalling fullness without parking a thread — essential in async and event-driven runtimes.
terms.detail: Blocking a thread on a full queue is fine when threads are cheap and plentiful, and catastrophic in an event loop, where blocking the loop stops everything. Async runtimes therefore return a signal instead: TryWrite returns false, WaitToWriteAsync yields, a Go select falls through to a default branch, a Node stream returns false from write() and emits drain. The failure mode to avoid is the fake-async version: an unbounded in-memory list "so nothing blocks", which is an unbounded queue with better marketing. Idioms Runtime Signal .NET Channels WaitToWriteAsync / TryWrite Go select with default Node streams write() false, then drain Project Reactor onBackpressureBuffer/Drop/Latest How it relates Whatever the idiom, the design question is identical: block, drop, or push the signal further upstream.

terms.def: When you cannot slow the producer — sensors, market data, user events — so you drop deliberately instead.
terms.detail: Some producers genuinely cannot be slowed: a sensor keeps sensing, a market keeps ticking, a user keeps clicking. The correct response is to choose the drop policy rather than let the buffer choose for you — keep the newest, keep a sample, or conflate several updates into one. Conflation is often the best answer for state updates: if three price ticks arrive while you were busy, the consumer only needs the last one, and dropping the first two loses nothing. Drop policies Policy Use for Drop oldest state updates — latest wins Drop newest when order matters more than freshness Conflate / coalesce prices, positions, presence Sample metrics, telemetry Spill to disk when nothing may be lost How it relates This is where backpressure and load shedding meet: a bounded buffer with a chosen drop policy is both.

terms.def: The signal is only useful if it reaches a component that can act — usually the edge, or the job scheduler.
terms.detail: A bounded queue in the middle of a chain stops that queue growing, but if the layer above simply buffers instead, you have moved the bloat rather than removed it. The signal has to travel until it reaches something that can slow down (a batch job, a poller) or say no (the edge talking to a client). The practical test: when the database slows down, does the user get a fast 503, or a two-second timeout? Only the first means your backpressure is connected end to end. Who can actually act Component Possible response Edge / API gateway return 429/503 with Retry-After Batch job, poller genuinely slow down Queue consumer stop fetching; lag builds safely Middle-tier service only propagate — it cannot decide How it relates The second animation is this signal travelling four layers to the one place it is useful.

terms.def: The legitimate use: absorbing short bursts, with a bound set by how long a burst can last.
terms.detail: Queues are not the enemy. A consumer averaging 800 a second against traffic that peaks at 1,200 for two seconds needs somewhere to put 800 items, and a buffer is exactly right. The distinction is that a shock absorber is sized for a known burst and drains afterwards; a bloated buffer is absorbing a mismatch that never ends. So size from the burst, then alert when the queue fails to drain — a queue that is never empty is not absorbing bursts, it is hiding a capacity problem. Healthy or hiding? Observation Meaning Empties several times a minute healthy shock absorber Never empty under-provisioned; bound it Monotonically growing outage in progress How it relates "Does it drain?" is a better health check than any absolute depth threshold.

pages.title: Caching strategies
pages.tagline: Keep the answer near the question — and decide, up front, how wrong you are willing to be.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · patterns are timeless; the examples are .NET 9+, Redis and HTTP
pages.description: Caching strategies cheatsheet: cache-aside, read-through, write-through, write-behind and refresh-ahead, with animated walk-throughs of write paths, stampedes and invalidation races.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: The fraction of lookups answered by the cache. It decides the average latency and, more importantly, how much load reaches the thing behind it.
terms.detail: Hit ratio is the number that turns a cache from a vibe into a measurement. Average latency is hit_ratio x hit_cost + (1 − hit_ratio) x miss_cost, and the miss cost usually dominates. What the numbers actually mean Hit ratio Avg latency (1 ms hit, 50 ms miss) Load reaching the DB 50% 25.5 ms half of it 90% 5.9 ms 1 in 10 99% 1.5 ms 1 in 100 99.9% 1.05 ms 1 in 1,000 Two consequences people miss. First, going from 90% to 99% halves the backend load again — the marginal value of hit ratio grows as it approaches 1. Second, a system tuned to run comfortably at a 99% hit ratio is running at 100x its sustainable load if the cache ever empties, which is why a cold cache after a deploy or a flush can take the database down. Measure hits, misses and evictions separately. A falling hit ratio with rising evictions means the cache is too small; a falling hit ratio with stable evictions means your keys have too much cardinality or your TTLs are too short.

terms.def: Also "lazy loading". Your code checks the cache, and on a miss reads the source and populates the cache itself. The cache knows nothing about the database.
terms.detail: The default pattern, and the one in almost every codebase. The application owns the whole flow: var cached = await cache.GetAsync(key); if (cached is not null) return cached; // hit var value = await db.LoadProductAsync(42); // miss: go to the source await cache.SetAsync(key, value, ttl: 5min); // populate for next time return value; Property Consequence Only requested data is cached no wasted memory on cold items Cache and DB models can differ cache the rendered DTO, not the row A cache outage is survivable every call just becomes a miss — if the DB can take it Every miss pays double a failed lookup plus the real query Writes are your problem you must invalidate, and the race is real Pair it with write-side invalidation (delete the key, do not update it) and a TTL as a backstop for the invalidations you will inevitably miss.

terms.def: The cache sits in front of the source and loads missing entries itself. Your code only ever talks to the cache.
terms.detail: Same read path as cache-aside, but the "go and fetch it" logic lives in the cache library rather than in each call site. In .NET, HybridCache.GetOrCreateAsync is exactly this. // the factory is only invoked on a miss, and only once per key var product = await hybridCache.GetOrCreateAsync($"product:{id}", async ct => await db.LoadProductAsync(id, ct), new HybridCacheEntryOptions { Expiration = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5) }); Why prefer it over hand-rolled cache-aside One implementation instead of one per call site, so the TTL, the serializer and the metrics are consistent. Stampede protection comes for free: concurrent callers for the same key await the same task. Caching a null result (negative caching) is handled once rather than forgotten everywhere. The cost is coupling: your cache now needs to know how to load your data, which makes a cache library harder to swap and makes the loader's failures look like cache failures.

terms.def: Writes go to the cache and to the source synchronously, before the caller is acknowledged. Cache and database never disagree.
terms.detail: The write path mirrors read-through: the cache is the only thing your code talks to, and it forwards the write to the source before returning. Property Effect Consistency strong between cache and source — no stale window Write latency cache write plus full source write (the slower of the two) Durability same as the database: nothing is acknowledged before it is committed Cache contents everything written, whether or not anyone reads it The hidden cost is that last row: a write-heavy, read-light table fills the cache with entries nobody ever reads, evicting the ones people do. Combine write-through with a short TTL, or use write-around for data that is written far more often than it is read. See the first animation for the full write path, and what changes when the same write becomes write-behind.

terms.def: Also "write-back". The write is acknowledged as soon as the cache holds it, and flushed to the source later, usually in batches.
terms.detail: The fastest write path and the only one that can lose data. The cache acknowledges, buffers the change as dirty, and a background flush writes it to the source after a delay or when a batch fills. Knob Typical What it buys Flush interval 100 ms – 5 s batching; longer means fewer, larger writes Batch size 100 – 10,000 rows amortises round trips and index maintenance Data-loss window = flush interval exactly what you lose if the node dies It wins when the same key is written repeatedly — a view counter hit 10,000 times a minute becomes one UPDATE instead of 10,000 — or when the source is slow and the write is not the user's last word on the subject. Never use it for data you cannot reconstruct: payments, orders, audit logs. "We lost 400 ms of writes" is an acceptable sentence about page-view counters and an unacceptable one about money. If you need both speed and durability, write to an append-only log such as Apache Kafka and project into the database asynchronously — same shape, but the buffer is durable.

terms.def: Writes go straight to the source and simply invalidate (or skip) the cache. The entry is only populated when somebody actually reads it.
terms.detail: The quiet default for cache-aside systems: on a write, DELETE the key rather than updating it, and let the next reader repopulate. await db.UpdatePriceAsync(42, 79); await cache.RemoveAsync("product:42"); // not Set — see the invalidation race Compared to Difference write-through does not pollute the cache with write-only data; first read after a write is a miss updating the key in place avoids writing a value you computed from a row you may have read before someone else's write Delete, do not update. A delete is idempotent and always safe; a set can write a stale value computed moments ago, and that value then survives until its TTL. The invalidation deep dive animates exactly how that goes wrong.

terms.def: Refresh popular entries before they expire, in the background, so that no user request ever pays for a miss.
terms.detail: Two flavours. Proactive: a scheduled job recomputes a known set of hot keys on a timer. Probabilistic: on each read, refresh early with a probability that rises as the entry nears expiry — the "XFetch" trick. # refresh early, with increasing probability as the TTL runs out if now - delta * beta * log(random()) >= expiry: refresh_in_background(key) return cached_value Use it for Not for a small, known set of hot keys (homepage, pricing, feature flags) long-tail keys — you would refresh millions of entries nobody wants values that are expensive to compute (reports, aggregations) values that change unpredictably: refresh-ahead still serves the previous one The cost is wasted work: you recompute entries that might never be read again. That is a good trade for the top 100 keys and a terrible one for the next million.

terms.def: Time to live: how long an entry may be served before it is discarded. The simplest, most robust correctness backstop you have.
terms.detail: A TTL is an admission that your invalidation will sometimes fail. It bounds the damage: however badly the invalidation goes, the wrong value disappears within the TTL. Common values Data TTL Why Static assets (hashed filename) 1 year, immutable the name changes when the content does Product catalogue 5–60 min changes rarely, staleness is cheap Prices, stock levels 10–60 s wrong values cost money User session / permissions 1–15 min a revoked permission must not linger Feature flags 5–30 s a kill switch must actually kill Expensive report 1–24 h cost dominates freshness Negative result (not found) 5–30 s short, so a newly created item appears quickly Always add jitter: ttl = base + random(0, base * 0.1). Entries created together — by a deploy, a warm-up script or a bulk import — otherwise expire together and produce a synchronised stampede. Distinguish absolute expiry (dies at a fixed time, predictable) from sliding expiry (extends on each access, keeps hot items alive but can keep a stale value alive forever). Most caches, including .NET's HybridCache, let you set both: a sliding window with an absolute cap.

terms.def: What gets thrown out when the cache is full: least recently used, least frequently used, FIFO, or something smarter. Eviction is not expiry.
terms.detail: Expiry is about correctness (this value is too old); eviction is about capacity (I need the space). A key can disappear for either reason, and your code must handle both identically. Policy Keeps Weak against LRU recently touched entries a scan: one bulk job evicts your whole working set LFU frequently touched entries changing popularity; yesterday's hot key will not leave FIFO nothing in particular almost everything; simple but rarely best W-TinyLFU frequency with a recency window little — it is the modern default (Caffeine, many CDNs) noeviction everything; writes fail instead use for queues and primary data, never for a cache In Redis the choice is maxmemory-policy: allkeys-lru for a pure cache, volatile-lru when the same instance also holds data that must not vanish. Watch evicted_keys — a non-zero and rising number means your cache is too small for its working set, and your hit ratio is paying for it.

terms.def: Removing or replacing an entry because the underlying data changed. The hard half of caching, and the source of the subtlest bugs.
terms.detail: Three strategies, in increasing order of effort and precision: Strategy Precision Effort TTL only coarse: wrong for up to the TTL none Explicit delete on write good, if you find every write path medium, and easy to miss one Event-driven (CDC, outbox, change feed) high: the database itself tells you high, but it catches writes your code did not make Tag-based invalidation ("drop everything tagged product:42 ") is what you want once one entity appears in many cached views — a product page, a category listing and a search result all go stale from one price change. HybridCache.RemoveByTagAsync and CDN surrogate keys both do this. The cache-aside invalidation race Note the shape of the bug: nobody did anything wrong, the operations were individually correct, and the window is a few milliseconds wide. At 5,000 requests per second, a few milliseconds happens constantly.

terms.def: Also "dogpile" or "thundering herd". A hot key expires and every concurrent request misses at once, hitting the source with the full, uncached load.
terms.detail: The counter-intuitive part: the better your hit ratio, the worse the stampede, because the source has been sized for the trickle it normally sees. The four fixes, in order of preference Fix How it works Cost Single-flight / lock one request recomputes, the rest await the same task the waiters still wait once Stale-while-revalidate serve the expired value, refresh in the background a bounded extra staleness Probabilistic early refresh recompute before expiry with rising probability some wasted recomputation TTL jitter spreads expiry so keys do not die together none — always do this In .NET, HybridCache gives you single-flight within an instance and across the distributed layer without extra code, which is the main reason to prefer it over a hand-written IDistributedCache wrapper. In Python or Go, a mutex keyed on the cache key does the same job for the in-process layer; a Redis SET NX lock covers the fleet. The second animation on this page walks through the failure and both fixes.

terms.def: Serve the expired value immediately and refresh it in the background. Latency stays flat; the price is a bounded window of known staleness.
terms.detail: An entry gets two lifetimes: fresh (serve without thinking) and stale but usable (serve, then refresh behind the scenes). It is the single most effective trick for keeping p99 latency flat. Cache-Control: max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300, stale-if-error=86400 Directive Means max-age=60 fresh for 60 s stale-while-revalidate=300 for the next 300 s, serve the old copy and refresh in the background stale-if-error=86400 if the origin is down, keep serving the old copy for a day stale-if-error deserves special mention: it turns your CDN into a last line of defence that keeps the site readable through a complete backend outage. It costs one header. Do not use it where staleness is a correctness bug — account balances, stock levels at checkout, permissions after a revocation.

terms.def: Caching the fact that something does not exist, so that repeated lookups for missing keys do not hammer the source.
terms.detail: Without it, every request for a non-existent id is a guaranteed miss, and an attacker who enumerates random ids gets a direct line to your database — a cache penetration attack. Technique Use when Cache a sentinel "not found" with a short TTL (5–30 s) always, as a baseline Bloom filter in front of the cache huge keyspace, many legitimate misses Validate the key shape before looking it up ids with a checksum or known format — free and effective Keep negative TTLs much shorter than positive ones: a user who just signed up should not be told "no such account" for five minutes because a page load beat the write. Be careful to distinguish "the source says it does not exist" from "the source timed out". Caching the second one turns a blip into a sustained outage.

terms.def: Several caches in series — browser, CDN, in-process, distributed — each with its own hit ratio, TTL and invalidation story.
terms.detail: Latency per layer is what makes the hierarchy worth the complexity. The numbers below are the ones worth memorising: The trap is invalidation across layers. Deleting a key in Redis does nothing to the copy sitting in 40 process-local caches, so an in-process layer needs either a very short TTL (5–30 s) or a broadcast channel. .NET's HybridCache handles both tiers and propagates tag invalidation; Redis pub/sub or key-space notifications do it by hand. Rule: the further a layer is from the source, the shorter its TTL must be, because its invalidation is less reliable.

terms.def: The cache has no schema, so the key naming convention is the schema. It decides cardinality, invalidation granularity and hit ratio.
terms.detail: Include everything that changes the value, and nothing that does not. Each extra dimension multiplies the number of entries and divides the hit ratio. Key Verdict product:42:v3 good — the v3 lets a schema change invalidate everything at once product:42:en-GB:eur good if the rendered value really differs by locale and currency search:{query}:{page}:{sort}:{userId} bad — userId makes every entry unique; hit ratio near zero product:42:{requestId} catastrophic — unbounded cardinality, pure memory leak Normalise before hashing: sort query parameters, lowercase, drop tracking parameters such as utm_*. A CDN that treats ?utm_source=x as a distinct key caches your homepage a thousand times and hits none of them. Put a version segment in the prefix. When the serialized shape changes, bumping v3 to v4 invalidates everything instantly, with no scan and no risk of deserializing an old shape into a new type.

terms.def: How far the cached copy may drift from the source, and for how long. This is a product decision wearing a technical costume.
terms.detail: Every cache is eventually consistent. The only question is the size of the window and who pays when it is exceeded. Staleness budget Strategy that fits Zero (money, permissions at the point of use) do not cache, or write-through with explicit invalidation and read-your-writes Seconds short TTL + delete-on-write; stale-while-revalidate off Minutes cache-aside with a TTL, invalidation best-effort Hours refresh-ahead or a scheduled rebuild; serve stale on error Read-your-writes deserves its own line. A user who edits their profile and immediately sees the old version assumes the save failed and does it again. Fix it by invalidating synchronously on the write path, or by bypassing the cache for the writer for a few seconds (a cookie or a request-scoped flag), even when every other reader gets a cached copy. Write the budget down per data type, next to the TTL. A TTL with no stated budget is a number somebody picked once and nobody can safely change.

terms.def: The cache you get for free: Cache-Control, ETag and conditional requests, honoured by browsers, proxies and CDNs without any code.
terms.detail: Before adding a cache inside your application, check whether the response could simply be cacheable. The cheapest request is the one that never reaches your server. Cache-Control: public, max-age=300, stale-while-revalidate=600 ETag: "a3f9c1" Vary: Accept-Encoding, Accept-Language Directive Effect public / private may a shared cache (CDN, proxy) store it, or only the browser? max-age=N fresh for N seconds s-maxage=N a different, usually longer, freshness just for shared caches no-store never written to disk or memory — the one for personal data no-cache may be stored, but must be revalidated first (not the same as no-store) must-revalidate never serve stale once expired, even if the origin is unreachable With an ETag, a revalidation that finds nothing changed returns 304 Not Modified with no body — still a round trip, but a few hundred bytes instead of a few hundred kilobytes. Vary is the footgun. Vary: Cookie on a page served to logged-in users makes every entry unique and the cache useless; worse, getting Vary wrong on a public response can serve one user's page to another.

pages.title: Circuit breaker
pages.tagline: Stop calling the thing that is broken. You are not helping it, and it is destroying you.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · named by Michael Nygard in Release It!, 2007 · examples use Polly, Resilience4j and Envoy
pages.description: Circuit breaker cheatsheet: closed, open and half-open states, what counts as a failure, bulkheads, and how a breaker stops one slow dependency taking a whole service down.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: A state machine around a dependency that stops calling it once it is clearly failing, and probes later to see whether it recovered.
terms.detail: Borrowed from electrical engineering, where a breaker trips to protect the circuit, not the fault. The software version protects the caller: it stops you spending threads, connections and time on calls that are going to fail anyway, and incidentally gives the struggling dependency some quiet. It is deliberately simple — three states, two thresholds and a timer — and almost all the value comes from the fast failure rather than from any cleverness in the counting. Who it protects Mechanism Protects From Circuit breaker the caller a failing dependency Load shedding yourself your own overload Rate limiting you and other tenants one noisy client Backpressure the whole chain unbounded queueing How it relates Pair it with a fallback: a fast failure is only useful if you have something to do with it.

terms.def: The normal state: calls pass through and their outcomes are recorded in a rolling window.
terms.detail: Closed is not "not monitoring". Every call's outcome feeds a window, and the breaker evaluates the failure rate continuously. The cost is a couple of atomic operations per call, which is why breakers can sit in front of every dependency without being noticeable. The important design decision in this state is what counts as a failure — get that wrong and the breaker either never trips or trips constantly. How it relates A breaker that has never opened in production is usually misconfigured, not lucky.

terms.def: The tripped state: calls fail immediately without touching the dependency.
terms.detail: Two things happen at once. The caller stops paying a timeout per call, so its threads and connections are returned immediately; and the dependency stops receiving traffic, which is frequently what it needs to recover — a service being hammered by retries cannot drain its own backlog. From the caller's perspective the failure is now fast and deterministic: it knows instantly that the feature is unavailable, which is what makes a sensible fallback possible. What changes when it opens Closed and failing Open Latency per call 2,000 ms ~1 ms Workers occupied all of them none Load on dependency full, plus retries zero Caller's other features starved unaffected How it relates Open is where graceful degradation takes over — the breaker hands it a clean signal.

terms.def: The trial state: a strictly limited number of calls are allowed through to test whether the dependency has recovered.
terms.detail: The limit is the entire point. If the breaker simply closed after the cooldown, a recovering service would receive the full traffic rate in one instant and fall straight over, tripping the breaker again — a flapping loop that can continue indefinitely. Allowing two or three concurrent probes while everything else keeps failing fast lets you learn whether it is healthy at almost no cost to it. Why the probe limit exists How it relates Same reasoning as hysteresis in load shedding: never flip state on a single observation.

terms.def: The rate and volume of failures that trip the breaker — expressed as a percentage over a minimum number of calls.
terms.detail: Use a rate rather than a count: "5 consecutive failures" behaves completely differently at 10 requests a second and at 10,000. Fifty percent over a window of twenty calls is a reasonable starting point for most internal dependencies. Lower thresholds for dependencies that are optional (fail fast and degrade), higher for ones you cannot do without (if the breaker opens the feature is dead anyway, so give it more chances). Starting points Dependency Threshold Break Optional enrichment 25% of 20 10 s Normal internal service 50% of 20 30 s Critical, no fallback 70% of 50 5 s Third-party API 50% of 20 60 s How it relates Tune from your actual error-rate distribution, not from a blog post's defaults — including this one.

terms.def: The requirement that enough calls have been seen before the breaker is allowed to trip.
terms.detail: Without it, one failure out of two calls is a 50% failure rate and trips the breaker on a quiet endpoint. With a minimum of twenty calls per window, the breaker ignores statistically meaningless samples — which matters most at night, when traffic is low and a single blip would otherwise disable a feature until morning. How it relates Low-traffic dependencies may need active health checks instead; a breaker needs volume to see anything.

terms.def: The recent history the failure rate is computed over — by count or by time.
terms.detail: A count-based window ("the last 100 calls") reacts consistently regardless of traffic but can hold stale information on a quiet endpoint. A time-based window ("the last 10 seconds") always reflects the present but may contain too few samples to be meaningful. Most libraries offer both; time-based with a minimum-throughput guard is the safer default. Trade-off Count-based Time-based Consistent sample size yes no Always current no yes Needs min-throughput guard less yes How it relates Window length also sets how fast the breaker can close again after recovery.

terms.def: The most consequential configuration choice, and the one most often left at its default.
terms.detail: Timeouts, connection errors and 5xx responses are failures.
