A 404 or a 400 is not — the dependency answered correctly, and counting those means a client sending bad input can trip your breaker and disable a feature for everybody. A 429 is a judgement call: it usually means you should back off, which is breaker-like behaviour, but it also means the service is alive. And business exceptions must never count. "Insufficient funds" is a successful call with an unwelcome answer. Classification Outcome Failure? Timeout, connection refused yes 500, 502, 503, 504 yes Call slower than the limit yes — slow is broken 400, 404, 409, 422 no 429 usually no; back off instead Business exception never How it relates Counting 4xx as failures is the most common way a breaker becomes an outage amplifier.

terms.def: Tripping on latency as well as errors, because a dependency that answers in eight seconds is broken even if it answers correctly.
terms.detail: The dangerous failure mode is not the one that throws — it is the one that slowly succeeds. A dependency returning 200s at eight seconds each will fill every worker you own without ever incrementing an error counter, so an error-only breaker sits closed throughout the outage. Resilience4j calls this the slow-call rate threshold; Polly expresses it through a timeout strategy that converts slowness into a failure the breaker can see. Typical settings Setting Example Slow-call duration 2× the p99 Slow-call rate threshold 50% Timeout below the caller's own deadline How it relates Without a timeout there is no slow-call signal at all, which is why timeouts come first.

terms.def: The prerequisite: a breaker cannot count a failure that never finishes.
terms.detail: A call with no timeout can hang for the lifetime of the connection, and many HTTP clients default to no timeout at all. The breaker sees neither a success nor a failure — just a worker that never comes back — so it stays closed while the service dies. Set the timeout below the caller's own deadline, and make sure it covers connect, TLS, send, and read — "connection timeout" alone is not enough. Order to apply # Layer 1 Timeout — bound every call 2 Bulkhead — bound concurrency 3 Circuit breaker — stop calling 4 Retry — only outside the breaker 5 Fallback — do something useful How it relates Getting this order wrong — especially retry inside the breaker — produces surprising behaviour.

terms.def: A bounded pool per dependency, so no single one can occupy all your workers while it fails.
terms.detail: Named after ship compartments: flooding one should not sink the vessel. Give payments five concurrent slots out of twenty, and a payments outage can consume at most a quarter of your capacity — the other fifteen workers keep serving everything that does not need payments. It is the half of the pattern that works before the breaker trips, during the window when failures are accumulating but the threshold has not been reached. Many cascading failures happen entirely inside that window. Sizing Dependency Share of the pool Critical, most requests use it large Optional enrichment small — 10–20% Known-flaky third party small, plus a tight timeout How it relates Bulkheads apply the same idea as per-queue separation against head-of-line blocking.

terms.def: What you actually do when the breaker is open — the part that turns a fast failure into a working product.
terms.detail: A breaker with no fallback converts a slow error into a fast error, which helps your infrastructure and not your user. The valuable version substitutes something: a cached value, a stale-but-acceptable answer, a default, a reduced feature set, or an honest "unavailable right now" that the UI handles well. Fallbacks must be cheap and must not depend on the thing that is broken — a fallback that calls a second service in the same failing cluster is not a fallback. Fallbacks, best first Fallback Good for Serve stale from cache catalogue, prices, profiles A sensible default recommendations, ranking Omit the section optional page content Queue for later writes that can be async Honest error payments — never fake a success How it relates The graceful degradation page is about designing these fallbacks as a product, not an afterthought.

terms.def: One breaker per downstream service — and often per endpoint — never one global breaker.
terms.detail: A shared breaker means a failing recommendations service can disable your payments calls. Scope each breaker to the thing that can fail independently: usually per service, and per endpoint when one route is much heavier or more fragile than the others. Per- instance scoping matters too: if one of six replicas is bad, a service-level breaker sees a 17% failure rate and never trips, while the bad instance keeps failing a sixth of your traffic. That is what outlier detection solves. Scope Scope Verdict Global never — unrelated failures couple Per service the default Per endpoint when costs differ a lot Per instance outlier detection, usually in a proxy How it relates Envoy's outlier detection ejects individual bad hosts, which a client-side breaker cannot see.

terms.def: Passive per-instance health checking: eject the single bad replica instead of tripping on the whole service.
terms.detail: Service meshes watch per-host error rates and remove a misbehaving instance from the load-balancing pool for a while, returning it gradually. This handles the very common case that a breaker is bad at: one unhealthy pod out of many, which never produces a high enough aggregate failure rate to trip anything. It composes well — outlier detection for instance-level problems, a breaker for service-level ones. Typical Envoy settings Setting Meaning consecutive_5xx errors before ejecting a host base_ejection_time how long it stays out max_ejection_percent never eject the whole pool How it relates In a mesh this is free; without one, client-side load balancers often provide something similar.

terms.def: They interact badly unless you decide which sits inside which.
terms.detail: If the retry is inside the breaker, one logical call produces three recorded failures and the breaker trips three times faster than you configured. If the retry is outside, it will dutifully retry the breaker's instant rejections, converting a fast failure into a fast loop. The usual arrangement: timeout, then retry, then breaker — so the breaker records one outcome per logical operation — and the retry policy must treat the breaker's open-circuit exception as non-retryable. Rules Rule Why One outcome per logical call thresholds mean what you set Never retry an open circuit otherwise it is a busy loop Retry only idempotent calls a timeout may have succeeded Budget retries globally caps amplification How it relates Retry amplification is covered in detail on the backpressure page.

terms.def: The failure where recovery itself re-breaks the dependency, over and over.
terms.detail: Fifty caller instances each open a breaker at the same moment, and thirty seconds later all fifty probe simultaneously. The recovering service receives a synchronised burst, falls over, and every breaker reopens — forever, on a thirty-second cycle. Fixes: cap concurrent probes per instance, jitter the break duration, and increase the cooldown after each failed probe so the system backs off instead of pulsing. Defences Defence Effect Probe limit (1–3) tiny load per instance Jittered break duration desynchronises the fleet Exponential break increase backs off after repeated failures Ramp traffic on close no instant full load How it relates The animation inside half-open walks this failure and its fix.

terms.def: State transitions are incidents in their own right, and should be visible as events rather than inferred from error graphs.
terms.detail: Export the current state per breaker, a counter of transitions, the rolling failure rate, and how many calls were rejected while open. A breaker opening is one of the highest-signal events in a distributed system — it means something downstream is genuinely broken, and it usually precedes the user-visible symptoms. It is also worth alerting on breakers that have never opened: usually a sign of a threshold that cannot be reached, which means the protection does not exist. Metrics Metric Use breaker_state dashboard, per dependency breaker_transitions_total flapping detection breaker_rejected_total blast radius while open fallback_used_total is the fallback actually working? How it relates Rejections while open are shed requests — count them separately from errors, as on the load-shedding page.

pages.title: CQRS
pages.tagline: Writes and reads want opposite things from a schema. Stop making one model do both jobs badly.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · named by Greg Young, 2010; examples in C#, SQL and Python
pages.description: CQRS cheatsheet: separate write and read models, projections, the eventual consistency window and the read-your-own-writes problem — animated, with the levels you can stop at.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: A request to change state, named as an imperative, that can be rejected and returns no business data.
terms.detail: PlaceOrder, CancelReservation, ApproveInvoice. A command is an intention, not a fact: the handler is allowed to refuse it. It is named in the business language, carries exactly the data needed to decide, and ideally carries a client-generated id so retries are idempotent. Commands should not return the new state. Returning an id (or nothing but success) is what keeps the write path from quietly becoming a query path with side effects. Shape Property Convention Name imperative, present tense Returns void, or the new identity Can fail yes — validation and invariants Idempotency client-supplied command id How it relates CQS is the one-object version of this rule; CQRS applies it to whole models. A command typically ends with one or more domain events.

terms.def: A request for data that changes nothing and returns a shape built for a specific screen or caller.
terms.detail: A query returns a DTO, not a domain object. That is the point: the caller gets exactly the fields the screen needs, already joined and formatted, and nothing in the domain model constrains it. Two screens wanting different shapes get two queries, not one flexible one. Because queries never mutate, they are trivially cacheable, safe to retry, safe to run against a replica, and safe to fan out. Query or repository? Need Path Load order 42 to change it repository, write side Order list with customer names query, read side Dashboard totals by month query, read side How it relates The read side is where caching strategies belong — the write side rarely benefits.

terms.def: The single entry point that executes one command: load the aggregate, call one method, save, publish.
terms.detail: One handler per command keeps the write side flat and testable: no service class accumulating twelve unrelated methods, and a one-to-one map from business intentions to code. Cross-cutting concerns — validation, authorisation, transactions, retries, logging — are added as a pipeline around the handler rather than inside it. Keep it thin. Any if about business meaning belongs in the aggregate. Pipeline order that works Step Concern 1 authorisation 2 structural validation 3 idempotency check 4 transaction 5 handler 6 publish events from the outbox How it relates In a DDD context, the handler is the application service.

terms.def: The model optimised for change: aggregates, invariants, small transactions and a normalised schema.
terms.detail: The write model exists to make illegal states impossible. It is normalised because duplication is a correctness risk when you are writing, it is loaded by identity because that is all a command needs, and it has no idea what any screen looks like. A good test: if adding a column for a report changes the write model, the separation has not happened yet. Optimised for Write side Read side correctness latency normalised denormalised few, small transactions no transactions loaded by id indexed by whatever the screen filters on How it relates Aggregates and repositories live here; queries are forbidden here.

terms.def: A denormalised, screen-shaped store of the same data, built from the write side and treated as disposable.
terms.detail: A read model is a cache with a schema: one table (or document, or index) per view, with every join already done and every computed field already computed. Rendering a page becomes a single indexed lookup instead of a six-table join plus mapping. The liberating property is that it holds no authoritative state. You can drop it, change its shape, add a column, and rebuild it from the write side — which means read-side schema changes stop being migrations and become replays. Where read models live Store Good for Same SQL DB, extra tables most cases; cheapest step Materialised view no projector code to maintain Redis / key-value single-key lookups, very hot screens Elasticsearch search, facets, full text Columnar / warehouse analytics and aggregation How it relates Read models are populated by a projection and can always be rebuilt.

terms.def: The code that turns write-side events into read-model rows, and the process that runs it.
terms.detail: A projection is a fold: for each event, update the rows that event affects. OrderPlaced inserts a row into order_list_view; OrderShipped updates its status; CustomerRenamed updates the denormalised name on every row that carries it. Two properties make projections operationally safe: they must be idempotent (the same event applied twice leaves the same state) and they must track a checkpoint, so a restart resumes rather than replays everything. Rebuilding a broken projection How it relates Projections are where the eventual consistency window actually comes from.

terms.def: The position in the event stream a projection has processed up to, stored alongside the read model.
terms.detail: Without a checkpoint a restarting projector either replays everything or skips events. Storing the offset in the same transaction as the rows it produced makes the pair atomic, which is what turns at-least-once delivery into a correct read model. The gap between the writer's latest offset and the projection's checkpoint is the measurable version of "how stale is the read side" — the single most useful metric on the read path. What to monitor Metric Healthy Lag in events near zero, bounded Lag in seconds under your stated window Projection errors zero; one poison event stalls everything How it relates Resetting the checkpoint to zero is how a rebuild starts.

terms.def: The read model trails the write model by a short, bounded delay instead of being updated in the same transaction.
terms.detail: Once the projection is asynchronous, there is a window — usually milliseconds, occasionally seconds under load — in which a committed change is invisible to queries. This is a design decision, not a defect, but it is only acceptable if the window is stated, measured and alerted on. Note the choice is per read model. A dashboard can tolerate thirty seconds; the screen the user lands on after submitting a form usually cannot, and that one may need a synchronous projection or a different mitigation. Typical windows Setup Typical lag Same transaction (synchronous) 0 In-process after commit 1–20 ms Via a broker 20–500 ms Batch rebuild minutes How it relates The second animation is this window being felt by a real user.

terms.def: The guarantee that a user immediately sees the effect of their own change — the first thing CQRS breaks.
terms.detail: The user submits a form, gets redirected to a list, and their item is not there. They submit again. You now have a duplicate caused purely by an architectural choice. Every CQRS system needs an answer to this, chosen per screen. The four workable answers, cheapest first: return the created data from the command so the UI can render it without a query; carry a version token and have the query wait for the projection to reach it; serve the user's own data from the write model; or change the interaction so immediacy is not expected. Mitigations Approach Cost Good when Command returns the data none single-item views Version token / wait some latency lists after a write Read own data from write side two code paths "my orders" screens UI says "processing" product decision genuinely async work How it relates This is why "CQRS everywhere" is a bad default — apply it where the asymmetry pays.

terms.def: The spectrum from two sets of classes over one table to two separate databases — you can stop anywhere.
terms.detail: Almost all of the benefit arrives at level 1, and almost all of the cost arrives at level 3. Most teams should stop at level 1 or 2: commands through the domain model, queries as plain SQL returning DTOs, both hitting the same database inside one transaction. No lag, no projector, no new infrastructure — and the read side is already free of the ORM. Go further only when a specific measurement forces it: reads outgrowing writes, a search requirement SQL cannot serve, or a reporting load that disturbs the transactional store. The ladder Level Shape Consistency 0 one model, one repository strong 1 two models, one schema strong 2 denormalised tables / views, same DB strong or near 3 separate read store, async projection eventual 4 level 3 plus event sourcing eventual How it relates Each step up buys scalability and costs a consistency guarantee.

terms.def: Storing state as an append-only log of events rather than as current rows — frequently paired with CQRS, and independent of it.
terms.detail: Event sourcing changes how the write side persists: instead of updating a row, you append OrderPlaced, ItemAdded, OrderShipped and rebuild current state by replaying them. CQRS changes how you read. They fit together neatly, because an event log is the perfect input for projections, but either works without the other. Treat them as separate decisions with separate costs. Event sourcing brings full history and audit for free, and brings schema versioning of events, snapshotting and a genuinely different debugging experience as the bill. Pick independently You want You need Fast, screen-shaped reads CQRS Full history, temporal queries, audit event sourcing Both both — and a plan for event versioning How it relates Most CQRS systems in production are not event sourced; they project from change events emitted by an ordinary database write.

terms.def: Writing outgoing events into a table inside the same transaction as the state change, then publishing them from there.
terms.detail: Committing to the database and publishing to a broker are two separate systems, so doing both "atomically" is impossible without a protocol. The outbox makes it one transaction: the event row is written next to the state change, and a separate relay reads the table and publishes, marking rows as sent. Without it you get the two classic failures: the write commits and the event is lost (read model permanently stale), or the event is published and the write rolls back (read model shows something that never happened). Guarantees Property Result Delivery at least once Ordering per aggregate, if you keep a sequence Consumer requirement must be idempotent How it relates Change data capture (Debezium and friends) is the other common way to get the same guarantee.

terms.def: Applying the same event twice must leave the read model in the same state as applying it once.
terms.detail: Every realistic delivery mechanism is at-least-once, so a projector will see duplicates after a restart, a rebalance or a retry. Idempotency is what makes that harmless: use upserts keyed by the aggregate id, store the last applied sequence number per row and ignore anything not greater than it, and avoid blind increments like total = total + x. Safe and unsafe projection writes Write Safe? UPSERT … SET status = 'shipped' yes — absolute value SET count = count + 1 no — duplicates accumulate … WHERE seq < @seq yes — guarded by sequence INSERT without a key no — duplicate rows How it relates Idempotency is what makes a rebuild safe to run against a live read model.

terms.def: Dropping a read model and replaying the event history to recreate it — the operational superpower of CQRS.
terms.detail: Because the read model is derived, a bug in a projector or a new column on a screen does not need a data migration: reset the checkpoint, truncate the table and replay. In practice you build the new version alongside the old one, let it catch up, then switch the queries over — zero downtime, and the old table is still there if you need to go back. Plan for it from the start. Rebuild time grows with history, so measure it early and add snapshots or partial replays before it becomes hours. Rebuild checklist Step Note Build the new table alongside no downtime Replay from offset 0 needs retained history Verify row counts and spot checks before switching Switch queries, keep the old table cheap rollback How it relates The animation inside projection walks one rebuild end to end.

terms.def: The read-side counterpart to a command handler: one per query, returning a DTO, with no domain model in sight.
terms.detail: Query handlers are allowed to be boring. Plain SQL, Dapper, a stored procedure, a search client — whatever gets the shape the screen needs in one round trip. Using the ORM's object graph here is the most common way the two sides silently merge back into one. Because they are pure, they are also where caching, pagination and rate limiting naturally belong. Rules of thumb Rule Reason Return a DTO, never an entity stops the domain leaking into the API One handler per screen shape avoids a generic query nobody can optimise No writes, ever makes caching and replicas safe How it relates This is CQS applied at the architecture level rather than the method level.

pages.title: CQS
pages.tagline: Asking a question should not change the answer.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · Bertrand Meyer, Object-Oriented Software Construction, 1988; examples in C#, Python and HTTP
pages.description: Command-Query Separation cheatsheet: every method either changes state or returns an answer, never both — why it makes retries, caching and logging safe, and when to break it on purpose.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: A method that changes observable state and returns nothing.
terms.detail: In CQS terms a command is any method whose purpose is the change: Save(), Cancel(reason), Dequeue(). Returning void is not bureaucracy — it is the signal at the call site that something happened, which is exactly the information a reader needs. Failure is still reported, by throwing. An exception is not a return value in the CQS sense: it says the command did not happen, rather than answering a question. Allowed returns from a command Return Verdict void / Task ideal Throw on failure fine The new identity of a created thing pragmatic, widely accepted The full new state no — that is a query glued on How it relates CQRS applies this distinction to whole models rather than single methods.

terms.def: A method that returns a value and leaves observable state untouched.
terms.detail: A query can be called any number of times, in any order, from anywhere — including from a log statement, an assertion, a debugger watch window or a retry loop — without changing program behaviour. That property is the entire value of the rule. "Observable" is the operative word. A query may write to a cache, open a connection or update a hit counter, as long as no caller can tell the difference in the answers they get. The CQS test Question If no… Can I call it twice safely? it is not a query Can I delete the call if I ignore the result? it is not a query Can I put it in a log line? it is not a query Can a debugger evaluate it? it is not a query How it relates Queries are the methods that can be safely memoized.

terms.def: Any change a method makes beyond returning its value — the thing CQS is organising.
terms.detail: Mutating a field, writing to a database, sending a message, advancing an iterator, consuming from a queue, writing a file. CQS does not forbid side effects — software without them does nothing — it insists they be segregated into methods whose signature announces them. The cost of mixing them is that a reader cannot tell a safe line from a dangerous one, so every refactor becomes an archaeology exercise. How it relates Functional "pure function" is the stricter version of a CQS query.

terms.def: An internal change that no caller can observe — caching, lazy initialisation, metrics — which keeps a method a query.
terms.detail: Meyer's rule is about observable state. A Total() that computes once and caches is still a query: every call returns the same answer and nothing a caller can reach has changed. The same goes for lazily opening a connection, populating an internal index, or incrementing a hit counter used only for monitoring. The line is crossed as soon as the hidden change affects anyone's answers — a cache that goes stale and is never invalidated, or a lazy load that throws on the second call under concurrency. Memoization keeps it a query How it relates This is the loophole that keeps CQS practical in real systems.

terms.def: A method that both returns a value and mutates state — the thing CQS asks you to split.
terms.detail: The classic examples read like queries and behave like commands: Pop(), NextId(), GetOrCreate(key), Read(buffer) on a stream, iterator.next(). Each one is a trap for anyone who assumes an expression is free of consequences. The split is usually mechanical: a query for the value, a command for the change, and the caller writes two lines instead of one. Where atomicity forbids that, keep the mixed method but name it so loudly that nobody mistakes it for a read. Split it Mixed Split into Job Pop() Job? Peek() + void Dequeue() int NextId() int CurrentId + void Advance() bool TryAcquire() keep — atomicity requires it T GetOrCreate(k) keep, but name it as a mutation How it relates The first animation is a mixed method causing a silent data-loss bug.

terms.def: The cases where mixing is correct — atomic operations, iterators, builders — and CQS yields deliberately.
terms.detail: Meyer himself called it a principle rather than an absolute. Concurrency is the honest exception: TryDequeue(out item), CompareAndSwap, Interlocked.Increment must read and write as one indivisible step, and splitting them introduces the exact race the method exists to prevent. Two softer exceptions are widely accepted: a command returning the identity of a thing it created, and fluent builders returning this. Both keep the rule's spirit because the return value is not an answer about state. Break it when… Case Why Atomic test-and-set splitting creates a race Iterators, streams language idiom, deeply expected Fluent builder returning this no state is being reported Create returning the new id the id is not knowable otherwise How it relates Breaking it deliberately and naming it clearly is in the spirit of the rule; breaking it by accident is not.

terms.def: The property that an expression can be replaced by its value without changing the program — what CQS buys you for queries.
terms.detail: If basket.Total() is a genuine query, then every occurrence of it can be replaced by 42 without altering behaviour. That is what makes it safe to hoist out of a loop, compute lazily, run in parallel, cache at the edge or drop entirely when the result is unused. Compilers, ORMs, HTTP caches and retry libraries all depend on this property. CQS is how you make a hand-written object-oriented API honest about having it. What it unlocks Optimisation Needs Caching / CDN referential transparency Hoisting out of loops referential transparency Parallel evaluation no observable writes Automatic retry safety, or idempotency How it relates Caching strategies all assume the read they cache is a query.

terms.def: A function with no side effects whose result depends only on its arguments — a stricter cousin of the CQS query.
terms.detail: A CQS query may read mutable state (a field, a database) and therefore return different answers at different times; a pure function may not. So every pure function is a query, but not every query is pure. order.Total() is a query; Math.Max(a, b) is pure. Pushing towards purity — functional core, imperative shell — is the stronger version of the same instinct, and it composes well with CQS rather than replacing it. Spectrum Kind Reads state Writes state Pure function no no CQS query yes not observably CQS command yes yes Mixed method yes yes, while returning a value How it relates Both give you the same superpower: the ability to reason about a call site locally.

terms.def: Doing something twice has the same effect as doing it once — what a command needs if it is ever retried.
terms.detail: Queries are safe: repeating them changes nothing at all. Commands are not safe, so over an unreliable channel they need idempotency instead — usually a client-supplied key that the server records, so a replayed request is recognised and ignored. The two properties are easy to confuse. Safe implies idempotent; idempotent does not imply safe. DELETE is idempotent and definitely not safe. Safe, idempotent, neither Operation Safe Idempotent Read balance yes yes Set status to shipped no yes Delete order 42 no yes Withdraw 20 no no — needs a key How it relates The second animation is exactly this distinction over a flaky network.

terms.def: GET as query, POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE as command — CQS baked into the protocol since 1997.
terms.detail: HTTP already encodes the rule: GET and HEAD are safe, meaning they must not have side effects, which is precisely why proxies, browsers, CDNs and crawlers feel free to repeat them. The famous cautionary tale is the intranet whose "delete" links were GETs, emptied by a well-behaved prefetching crawler. Honouring this is not pedantry: it decides what your infrastructure may cache and what your clients may retry automatically. Method properties Method Safe Idempotent Cacheable GET / HEAD yes yes yes PUT no yes no DELETE no yes no POST no no rarely PATCH no not necessarily no How it relates A GET that mutates breaks caching and rate limiting at the same time.

terms.def: Caching a query's result so repeated calls are cheap — only safe because the method is a query.
terms.detail: Memoization substitutes a stored value for a computation, which is legitimate exactly when the computation is referentially transparent. Apply it to a mixed method and you silently skip the side effect on every call after the first — a bug that typically appears weeks later under load. The same reasoning extends outwards: an HTTP cache, a CDN, a materialised view and a React useMemo are all making the identical bet. Memoize when Condition Required No observable side effect yes Answer stable for the cache lifetime yes Invalidation story exists yes How it relates The animation inside benign side effect shows memoization preserving query semantics.

terms.def: The architectural scaling of CQS: separate models, and possibly separate stores, for writing and reading.
terms.detail: CQS separates methods; CQRS separates models. The vocabulary is shared and the intuition is the same, but the cost profile could not be more different: CQS is free and local, while CQRS adds projections, eventual consistency and operational surface. Adopt CQS everywhere by default. Adopt CQRS in the one or two bounded contexts where the read and write shapes genuinely diverge, and never because the names sound similar. Side by side CQS CQRS Scope a method a bounded context Cost none real, operational Consistency unchanged often eventual Default answer yes only when measured How it relates A codebase that already respects CQS is much easier to move to CQRS later.

terms.def: Meyer's broader method, which CQS exists to serve: preconditions and postconditions you can state because queries are honest.
terms.detail: CQS was not invented as a style preference. It is a prerequisite for Design by Contract: if assertions could change state, then enabling assertions in debug and disabling them in release would produce two different programs. Queries being side-effect-free is what makes require, ensure and invariant clauses — and modern equivalents like Debug.Assert or property-based tests — trustworthy. The modern restatement: any expression your test suite, logger or debugger evaluates must be free to evaluate. Contract clauses need queries Clause Uses Precondition queries on arguments and state Postcondition queries before and after Invariant queries only, always How it relates This is why assertions must never call a mixed method.

terms.def: The practical dividend: commands are verified by checking state, queries by checking return values — never both at once.
terms.detail: With CQS, a test has an obvious shape. For a query: call it, assert on the result, and assert that nothing changed. For a command: arrange, call, and assert on the resulting state. Mixed methods force every test to do both, and make it ambiguous which behaviour a failure is reporting. It also removes a whole category of mock: you rarely need to verify that a query was called, because calling it is free. Test shape Method Assert on Mocking Query return value stub the inputs Command resulting state verify the interaction Mixed both, ambiguously both How it relates "Don't mock what you don't own" gets much easier when queries are free to call.

pages.title: Database performance
pages.tagline: Index, then query, then schema, then cache, then replicate, then partition — and only then shard.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · examples are PostgreSQL 18 flavoured; the principles carry to MySQL, SQL Server and most engines
pages.description: Database performance cheatsheet: indexes, query plans, partitioning, sharding and connection pools — animated, in the order you should actually try them.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: A balanced tree that turns "find rows matching this value" into a handful of page reads instead of a full table scan.
terms.detail: A B-tree keeps keys sorted, with each node holding hundreds of entries, so the tree stays shallow: even a billion-row table is three to five levels deep. A lookup reads one page per level plus one heap page per matching row — typically four to six page reads in total, against millions for a scan. Because the keys are ordered, the same structure also serves range predicates, ORDER BY and MIN / MAX without extra work. The cost is on the write side: every insert, update of an indexed column and delete must maintain every index on the table. Depth and cost Table rows B-tree depth Page reads for one key 10,000 2 3 1,000,000 3 4 1,000,000,000 4–5 5–6 Index types worth knowing Type Use for B-tree equality, ranges, sorting — the default Hash equality only; rarely worth it GIN / inverted arrays, JSONB, full text BRIN huge, naturally ordered tables (time series) Partial (WHERE) hot subsets, e.g. status = 'open'

terms.def: The fraction of rows a predicate keeps. Low fraction means an index helps; high fraction means it does not.
terms.detail: An index lookup costs a tree descent plus one random heap read per matching row. A sequential scan reads pages in order, which disks and prefetchers love. So beyond roughly 5–10% of the table, scanning sequentially is genuinely faster, and the planner will — correctly — ignore your index. This is why indexing a status column with three values rarely helps, while indexing email always does. For skewed columns a partial index on the rare value gives you the best of both. Rough guidance Rows matched Likely plan Under 1% index scan — big win 1–10% bitmap scan, depends on correlation Over 10% sequential scan, and that is correct How it relates Bad statistics make the planner mis-estimate selectivity, which is the usual cause of a sudden plan flip.

terms.def: An index on several columns, usable only from the leftmost column onwards — the "leftmost prefix" rule.
terms.detail: An index on (customer_id, placed_at, status) is sorted by customer_id first, so it serves queries filtering on customer_id, on customer_id + placed_at, and on all three. It does not serve a query filtering only on placed_at, any more than a phone book sorted by surname helps you find everyone called Ada. Column order rules: equality predicates first, then the range or sort column, then anything you only want to carry along. One well-ordered composite index usually replaces three single-column ones and costs less on writes. What (a, b, c) serves Predicate Uses the index? a =? yes a =? AND b =? yes a =? AND c =? partly — only a narrows b =? no a =? ORDER BY b yes, sort is free How it relates Steps 5–6 of the first animation add the second column and show the extra filtering it removes.

terms.def: An index that contains every column the query needs, so the table itself is never read.
terms.detail: Normally an index tells you where the rows are and the engine then fetches them from the heap — one random read each. If the index also carries the selected columns, the engine can answer entirely from the index: an index-only scan. On a query returning many rows that often removes 90% of the I/O. PostgreSQL spells it INCLUDE (...), SQL Server the same, MySQL/InnoDB gets it for free because secondary indexes already carry the primary key. The cost is a fatter index: more space, more write amplification, and less of it fitting in cache. Trade-off Add columns to the index Effect Reads heap never touched — much faster Writes more pages to maintain Memory index competes for the buffer cache How it relates Postgres also needs the visibility map to be current, so an index-only scan on a table that is never vacuumed quietly stops being index-only.

terms.def: The strategy the planner chose, and the only reliable way to know why a query is slow.
terms.detail: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) shows the plan plus what actually happened. Read it bottom-up and look for two things: a node where rows estimated and rows actual differ by an order of magnitude (bad statistics), and a node that examines far more rows than it returns (missing or unusable index). Plans change on their own as data grows and statistics are resampled. A query that was fast for a year can flip to a scan overnight, which is why plan regressions belong on your dashboards. What to look for Symptom in the plan Usually means Seq Scan on a big table missing or unusable index Estimated 10, actual 100,000 stale or insufficient statistics Nested Loop with a huge outer bad join order from bad estimates Sort spilling to disk work_mem too small High shared read in BUFFERS working set does not fit in RAM How it relates Fix statistics before adding an index — half of "missing index" cases are mis-estimates.

terms.def: Reading every page of a table in order — slow for a needle, and the right choice for a haystack.
terms.detail: A sequential scan is not a bug. Reading pages in physical order is far faster per page than random access, so for anything above roughly 10% selectivity, or for a small table, it wins outright. Forcing an index scan there makes the query slower. It becomes a problem only when it is used for a highly selective predicate — the 555,555:1 ratio in the first animation — or when several concurrent scans push the working set out of the buffer cache and the whole instance slows down. When a scan is correct Case Why Small table (a few hundred pages) the whole thing is already cached Returning most of the rows sequential I/O beats random Analytics and aggregation column scan is the point

terms.def: One query to fetch a list, then one more per item — the most common application-side performance bug.
terms.detail: Fetch 200 orders, then lazily touch order.Customer.Name inside the loop, and the ORM issues 201 round trips. Each one is individually fast, so nothing looks slow in the database; the time is 201 network round trips plus 201 pool acquisitions, and it only appears under load. It is also the fastest way to exhaust a connection pool, because each request now holds its connection for far longer than anyone sized for. Fixes, in order Fix Note Eager load / join Include, selectinload, JOIN FETCH Batch the second query one WHERE id IN (...) Project to a DTO fetch only what the screen needs Fail the build assert query count in tests How it relates Counting queries per request in tests catches this before production does.

terms.def: A bounded set of reusable database connections shared by application threads.
terms.detail: Opening a PostgreSQL connection costs milliseconds and a backend process with its own memory; opening thousands costs the server more than the queries do. A pool keeps a small number open and hands them out, which also acts as a concurrency limiter — its most valuable and least appreciated property. Treat pool saturation as a signal, not a problem to configure away: it means work is arriving faster than the database completes it, and raising the limit only moves the queue somewhere worse. Settings that matter Setting Sensible value Max pool size small — see pool sizing Acquisition timeout 1–5 s; fail fast, do not pile up Statement timeout below the request timeout Idle timeout minutes, to release idle backends Leak detection on — finds unreturned connections How it relates The second animation is a pool saturating because the query got slower, not because the pool was small.

terms.def: How many connections you actually need: arrival rate times time held, by Little's Law — usually a much smaller number than teams expect.
terms.detail: connections = requests per second × seconds held. At 100 requests per second each holding a connection for 50 ms, five are busy on average; a pool of ten has headroom. The famous HikariCP guidance — roughly cores × 2 + effective spindles — lands in the same place from the server's side: a 16-core database rarely benefits from more than about 32 concurrent queries, because beyond that they just compete. Remember to multiply by instances: ten application pods with a pool of 20 each is 200 connections at the server, which is where "too many clients already" comes from. Worked examples Rate Held Busy connections 100/s 50 ms 5 100/s 200 ms 20 500/s 20 ms 10 50/s 2 s 100 — fix the query How it relates This is Little's Law applied to connections; the same arithmetic sizes thread pools and queues.

terms.def: Splitting one logical table into physical pieces inside the same database, by range, list or hash.
terms.detail: Partitioning is a maintenance and locality tool, not primarily a speed tool. Its biggest wins are operational: dropping last year's data becomes DROP TABLE on a partition instead of a DELETE of 400 million rows; vacuum, index rebuilds and statistics run per partition; and indexes stay small enough to cache. Range partitioning by time is the overwhelmingly common case. Hash partitioning spreads writes but gives up pruning on ranges; list partitioning suits tenant or region keys. Choosing a scheme Scheme Good for Watch out for Range (time) logs, events, orders the newest partition is always hot List (tenant, region) multitenancy skew between tenants Hash even write spread no range pruning How it relates Partitioning stays inside one database; sharding crosses machines and loses transactions.

terms.def: The planner skipping partitions that cannot contain matching rows — where the speed-up actually comes from.
terms.detail: A query with WHERE placed_at >= '2026-11-01' on a table partitioned by month touches one partition instead of 36. Pruning only works when the partition key appears in the predicate, which is why a partitioned table with queries that filter on something else is all cost and no benefit. Check it, do not assume it: the plan should show one partition scanned. Functions wrapped around the key, implicit casts and parameters resolved too late are the usual reasons pruning silently fails. Pruning works when Query Pruned? WHERE placed_at > '2026-11-01' yes WHERE date_trunc('day', placed_at) =? often not WHERE customer_id =? no — all partitions How it relates Partition on what you filter by, or do not partition.

terms.def: Spreading one dataset across independent databases, each owning a subset of the rows.
terms.detail: Sharding is the only way past the write throughput or storage of a single machine, and it is the most expensive step on the ladder. Each shard is a separate database: cross-shard joins disappear, cross-shard transactions require a protocol nobody enjoys, unique constraints become application concerns, and every operational task now happens N times. Do it when a single primary genuinely cannot keep up after the cheaper steps — not because the table is large. A well-indexed, partitioned table on a modern machine handles billions of rows. Keys landing on shards, and what resharding costs How it relates Try read replicas and partitioning first; they keep one logical database.

terms.def: The column that decides which shard a row lives on — the single most consequential and least reversible choice in a sharded system.
terms.detail: A good shard key spreads writes evenly, keeps rows that are queried together on the same shard, and appears in almost every query so the router can avoid fan-out. tenant_id and user_id usually qualify; a timestamp almost never does, because all of today's writes land on one shard. Changing it later means moving every row, so model the top five queries against the candidate key before committing. Good and bad keys Key Verdict tenant_id good — natural locality; watch for whale tenants user_id (hashed) good — even spread created_at bad — all writes hit one shard Auto-increment id bad — same hot-shard problem country bad — extreme skew How it relates A hot shard is the sharded version of a hot partition: the median looks fine and one tenant is on fire.

terms.def: A copy of the primary that serves reads, with a replication lag you must design around.
terms.detail: Replicas are the cheapest real scaling step: no schema change, no application rewrite beyond routing. They scale reads only — every replica still applies every write — and they introduce lag, usually single-digit milliseconds but seconds under heavy write load or a long-running query blocking replay. The practical rule is the same as for any eventually consistent read: send a user's own data to the primary right after they change it, and everything else to a replica. What replicas fix Problem Replica helps? Too many reads yes Reporting disturbing OLTP yes Too many writes no — shard or partition Slow individual query no — index it How it relates Replication lag is the same read-your-own-writes problem CQRS has, with the same mitigations.

terms.def: Transactions waiting on each other's row or table locks — latency that no index will fix.
terms.detail: Two shapes dominate. A hot row — a counter, a balance, a sequence table — serialises every transaction that touches it, so throughput is capped at one divided by the lock hold time regardless of hardware. And long transactions hold locks far longer than the statement that took them, especially when an HTTP call happens inside one. Deadlocks are the loud version and are usually fixed by acquiring rows in a consistent order. The quiet version — everything 50 ms slower — is more common and only visible in lock wait metrics. Patterns and fixes Pattern Fix Hot counter row sharded counters, or aggregate asynchronously Long transaction never call out over the network inside one Deadlock consistent lock ordering, short transactions Lock escalation batch updates in chunks How it relates Lock waits inflate the time a connection is held, which is what saturates the pool.

terms.def: The pages actually touched by your queries. Performance falls off a cliff when it stops fitting in RAM.
terms.detail: Databases are fast because the hot pages live in the buffer cache: a hit is about 100 nanoseconds, a miss on NVMe is 50–500 microseconds, several hundred times slower. Most tables have a small hot subset — recent orders, active users — so what matters is not the size of the data but the size of the part you keep touching. The failure mode is non-linear and sudden: the working set grows just past RAM, hit rate drops, I/O climbs, queries slow, connections are held longer, the pool saturates, and the whole thing looks like a pool incident. Keeping it small Technique Effect Partition by time cold months stop competing for cache Narrower rows / TOAST more rows per page Partial and covering indexes fewer pages per query Archive old data the only permanent fix How it relates Cache hit ratio and shared read counts are the early warning; latency percentiles are the late one.

terms.def: Dead row versions left by updates and deletes, and the background work that reclaims them.
terms.detail: In MVCC engines an UPDATE writes a new row version and leaves the old one as garbage. Autovacuum reclaims that space and refreshes the visibility map, but it is throttled by default and loses ground on write-heavy tables — so the table grows, scans read more pages, indexes point at dead tuples and index-only scans silently stop being index-only. Long-running transactions and abandoned replication slots are the usual culprits: vacuum cannot remove a row version that some old snapshot might still need, so a forgotten session can bloat a table for days. Symptoms and causes Symptom Likely cause Table far bigger than its data autovacuum falling behind Index-only scans vanished visibility map stale Vacuum never completes long transaction or stale slot Growing after a bulk delete space reclaimed but not returned to the OS How it relates Bloat quietly grows the working set, which is how a healthy system becomes a slow one without any code change.

pages.title: Docker
pages.tagline: Package an app with everything it needs, then run it the same way on any machine.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · Docker Engine 29.x
pages.description: Docker cheatsheet: architecture, animated docker run and build-cache walk-throughs, key concepts, commands, trade-offs and alternatives.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: A read-only template: a stack of filesystem layers plus metadata (start command, env vars, exposed ports). Built once, run anywhere.
terms.detail: An image is a list of layer tarballs plus a JSON config (entrypoint, env vars, working dir, exposed ports, user). It is immutable and identified by a content hash (digest). Typical base image sizes Base Size Notes alpine ~8 MB musl libc: some Python wheels must compile python:3.13-slim ~45 MB compressed Debian minimal, good default python:3.13 ~400 MB full toolchain, use as build stage distroless / chiseled ~20–50 MB no shell, smallest attack surface One image can target several CPU architectures (linux/amd64, linux/arm64) under the same tag: a multi-platform image.

terms.def: A running (or stopped) instance of an image: an isolated process with its own writable layer. Many containers can run from one image.
terms.detail: A container = image layers (read-only) + its own writable layer + runtime settings (env, ports, mounts, limits) + an isolated process. Lifecycle created → running → paused / exited → removed. A stopped container still exists (and keeps its writable layer) until docker rm. PID 1 inside the container is your app; when it exits, the container stops. Restart policies: --restart unless-stopped keeps services up across crashes and host reboots. Limit resources: --memory 512m --cpus 1.5.

terms.def: The filesystem changes made by one Dockerfile instruction. Layers are content-addressed, cached and shared between images.
terms.detail: Each filesystem-changing instruction (RUN, COPY, ADD) creates a layer containing only the files it added, changed or deleted. Layers are stacked with a union filesystem (overlayfs). Deleting a file in a later layer hides it but doesn't shrink the image: the bytes are still in the earlier layer. Clean up in the same RUN that created the files. Layers are shared: ten images on python:3.13-slim store the base once. Inspect with docker history myapp:1.0 or the dive tool.

terms.def: A text file of instructions (FROM, COPY, RUN, CMD …) that describes how to build an image.
terms.detail: Instruction Does FROM base image (one per stage) WORKDIR set and create the working directory COPY / ADD add files from the build context (prefer COPY) RUN run a command at build time, creating a layer ENV / ARG runtime env var / build-time variable EXPOSE document the port (doesn't publish it) USER run as this user from here on CMD / ENTRYPOINT default command / fixed executable HEALTHCHECK command Docker runs to report health Order instructions from least to most frequently changing so the build cache helps you.

terms.def: Docker reuses a layer when its instruction and inputs are unchanged. Once one step changes, every later step is rebuilt.
terms.detail: For each instruction, BuildKit checks whether it already built the same instruction on the same parent layer with the same inputs (for COPY, a checksum of the copied files). If yes, it reuses the layer. The first cache miss invalidates every later step. RUN apt-get update is cached too, so combine it with install in one RUN. Cache mounts keep package caches between builds: RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip pip install -r requirements.txt. CI runners start empty; export the cache to a registry (--cache-to type=registry) or use the GitHub Actions cache. Force a clean build with --no-cache.

terms.def: A server that stores and distributes images: Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, ECR, ACR, or a private one.
terms.detail: A registry stores images in repositories (ghcr.io/acme/web ), each with many tags. Pull and push use the OCI distribution API; only missing layers are transferred. Registry Notes Docker Hub default for unqualified names; pull rate limits for anonymous users GitHub Container Registry ghcr.io, permissions tied to the repo Azure ACR / AWS ECR / Google Artifact Registry close to your cloud workloads, private networking Harbor self-hosted, with scanning and replication Scan images for known vulnerabilities (Docker Scout, Trivy) as part of CI.

terms.def: nginx:1.27 is a movable tag; nginx@sha256:… is an immutable digest. Pin digests (or exact tags) in production.
terms.detail: nginx:1.27 is a tag: a human-friendly pointer that can be moved to a new image at any time. nginx@sha256:3b2f… is a digest: the hash of the image manifest, which can never change. latest is just the default tag name, not "the newest". Tag your builds with something unique: version (1.4.2) and/or git SHA (sha-9f3c2a1 ). Pin base images by digest in production Dockerfiles for fully reproducible builds; let a bot (Dependabot, Renovate) update the pin.

terms.def: Storage managed by Docker that lives outside the container's writable layer, so data survives when the container is removed.
terms.detail: docker volume create pgdata docker run -d -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:17 A named volume lives in Docker's storage area (/var/lib/docker/volumes ), independent of any container. Remove and recreate the container and the data is still there. Faster than bind mounts on Docker Desktop (stays inside the Linux VM). Back up by running a throwaway container: docker run --rm -v pgdata:/d -v .:/b alpine tar czf /b/pg.tgz -C /d.. docker compose down -v deletes the project's volumes. Careful.

terms.def: Maps a host folder into a container (-v ./src:/app ). Handy for live code reloading in development.
terms.detail: -v ./src:/app/src (or --mount type=bind,…) maps a host path into the container. Changes appear on both sides instantly, which is ideal for hot-reloading code in development. File ownership follows host UIDs, which can cause permission errors with non-root containers. On Windows and macOS, file I/O crosses the VM boundary and can be slow for large trees (node_modules ). Keep the repo inside WSL 2 on Windows. Add :ro to mount read-only. Use volumes for data, bind mounts for source code and config you edit.

terms.def: Virtual network for containers. On a user-defined bridge network, containers reach each other by name (http://api:8000 ).
terms.detail: Driver What it does bridge (default) private network on the host; NAT to the outside user-defined bridge same, plus DNS: containers reach each other by name host container shares the host network stack (Linux only) none no networking Compose creates a user-defined network per project, so api can call http://cache:6379. On the default bridge network, name resolution doesn't work: always create your own network.

terms.def: -p 8080:80 forwards host port 8080 to port 80 inside the container. Without it the service is unreachable from outside.
terms.detail: -p 8080:80 = host port 8080 → container port 80. Docker adds NAT rules on the host so traffic reaching 8080 is forwarded to the container's private IP. -p 127.0.0.1:8080:80 binds only to localhost; plain -p 8080:80 listens on all interfaces, so it's reachable from your network. EXPOSE in a Dockerfile only documents a port; -P publishes all exposed ports to random host ports. Containers on the same network don't need port mapping to talk to each other.

terms.def: Defines a multi-container app (services, networks, volumes) in compose.yaml and starts it with one command.
terms.detail: One compose.yaml describes services (image or build, ports, env, volumes, dependencies), networks and volumes. docker compose up creates them all, in dependency order, on a private network. depends_on with condition: service_healthy waits for a healthcheck, not just a started container. .env files and ${VAR} substitution keep secrets and per-machine settings out of the file. Profiles enable optional services (docker compose --profile debug up ). docker compose watch syncs code changes into containers as you edit. Great for development, CI and small single-host production. For many hosts, the same services move to Kubernetes manifests or Helm charts.

terms.def: Several FROM stages in one Dockerfile: compile in a big image, copy only the result into a small final image.
terms.detail: FROM python:3.13 AS build WORKDIR /src COPY requirements.txt. RUN pip wheel --wheel-dir /wheels -r requirements.txt FROM python:3.13-slim COPY --from=build /wheels /wheels RUN pip install --no-cache-dir /wheels/* && rm -rf /wheels COPY. /app USER 1000 CMD ["python", "/app/app.py"] Compilers, headers and caches stay in the build stage; only the result is copied into the final stage. For Go or .NET apps the final image can be tens of MB instead of a GB. Build a specific stage with docker build --target build. (e.g. for running tests).

terms.def: Lists files not sent to the build (.git, node_modules, .env ). Faster builds and no leaked secrets.
terms.detail: .git .venv __pycache__/ node_modules/ .env *.log dist/ Before building, Docker sends the build context (the folder) to the builder. Without a .dockerignore that includes .git history, virtual envs and secrets. Builds start faster (smaller context). COPY.. doesn't break the cache when irrelevant files change. Secrets like .env never end up in an image layer.

terms.def: The Docker daemon. It exposes the API that the CLI and Compose call, and manages images, networks and volumes.
terms.detail: The Docker daemon runs as a background service (root by default) and exposes a REST API on /var/run/docker.sock (Linux) or a named pipe (Windows). Manages images, containers, networks, volumes and builds (via BuildKit). Delegates running containers to containerd. Access to the socket = root on the host. Never mount docker.sock into untrusted containers or expose the API over TCP without TLS. Rootless mode runs the daemon as a normal user for better security; Podman avoids a daemon entirely.

terms.def: The lower-level runtimes Docker uses: containerd manages container lifecycles, runc creates the process following the OCI spec.
terms.detail: The container stack in layers: Layer Role docker CLI / Compose user interface dockerd high-level API: builds, networks, volumes containerd image pulling, storage, container lifecycle (CNCF project) runc low-level OCI runtime: sets up namespaces and cgroups, starts the process, exits Kubernetes talks to containerd directly through the CRI, skipping dockerd. That's why images built with Docker run unchanged on Kubernetes: they're standard OCI images. Alternative low-level runtimes: crun (faster), gVisor and Kata (stronger isolation).

terms.def: Linux kernel features behind containers: namespaces isolate what a process can see, cgroups limit what it can use.
terms.detail: Namespace Isolates pid process tree: the app sees itself as PID 1 net network interfaces, IPs, ports mnt filesystem mounts: the image's root filesystem uts hostname ipc shared memory, semaphores user UID mapping: root inside, unprivileged outside (rootless) cgroups limit and account resources: --memory 512m (exceed it and the kernel OOM-kills the process), --cpus 1.5 (throttled above it), PIDs and disk I/O. Seeing it yourself: docker run --rm alpine ps lists a single process, and docker stats shows each container's cgroup usage. Kubernetes requests and limits are translated into these same cgroup settings.

pages.title: Domain-Driven Design
pages.tagline: Model the business, not the database — and stop pretending one word means the same thing everywhere.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · Eric Evans, 2003; examples in C# and Python, framework-agnostic
pages.description: Domain-Driven Design cheatsheet: bounded contexts and context maps on the strategic side, aggregates, value objects and domain events on the tactical side — animated.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: One vocabulary shared by developers and domain experts, used in conversation, in documentation and literally in the code.
terms.detail: The ubiquitous language is the deliverable that makes everything else possible. If the business says "a policy lapses" and the code says UpdateStatus(3), every conversation needs a translation step, and translations are where bugs and misunderstanding accumulate. When the model is right, a domain expert can read a method name out loud and say whether it is true. Crucially the language is scoped to one bounded context. "Account" in trading and "account" in support are different words that happen to be spelled the same; forcing one definition across both is the mistake the first animation is about. Translating badly vs well Business says Weak code Ubiquitous the policy lapses status = 3 policy.Lapse() reserve stock qty -= n stock.Reserve(n) settle the invoice paid = true invoice.Settle(payment) How it relates The language is bounded by the bounded context; outside it, it stops being valid. Event storming is the usual workshop for discovering it.

terms.def: The person who actually knows how the business works, and whose vocabulary the model is built from.
terms.detail: DDD assumes continuous access to someone who can answer "what happens if the shipment is refused at the door?" without going to ask. That is not a product owner translating tickets — it is the underwriter, the dispatcher, the credit controller. Without that access the model is a guess dressed in patterns, and most failed DDD efforts fail here rather than on the code. The practical test: can you get an hour a week with someone who would notice if the model were wrong? If not, use something cheaper than DDD. How it relates Their words become the ubiquitous language. They are the ones who tell you which subdomain is actually core.

terms.def: A part of the business problem, classified as core, supporting or generic to decide how much effort it deserves.
terms.detail: Subdomains are discovered in the problem space, before any software exists. The classification is a budgeting decision: the core subdomain is what makes the company money and is worth your best people and full DDD; supporting subdomains are necessary but not differentiating, so keep them simple; generic subdomains are solved problems that you buy. Getting this wrong is expensive in both directions — hand-rolling an invoicing engine, or treating your pricing algorithm as "just CRUD". Classification Type Example Approach Core dynamic pricing, risk scoring full DDD, best team, build Supporting shipping schedules, catalogue simple model, build cheaply Generic auth, invoicing, email buy or use a library How it relates A subdomain is the problem; a bounded context is the solution you build for it — ideally one to one.

terms.def: An explicit boundary inside which one model and one language are consistent and unambiguous.
terms.detail: The single most valuable idea in DDD. Instead of trying to build one enterprise-wide model of "Customer" that satisfies sales, shipping and billing simultaneously — which produces a class with ninety fields and no invariants — you accept that each context has its own model, its own schema and its own meaning for the word, and you translate at the border. The boundary should be aligned with a team, so that one team owns one context end to end. A context that two teams both change is not a boundary, it is a shared mutable object with extra ceremony. Signals you crossed a boundary Signal Meaning The same word needs qualifying two models hiding in one Half the fields are always null two lifecycles in one class Two teams fight over a table boundary runs through it A change is "only for report X" a read model wants its own context How it relates In a modular monolith, a context is a module; in microservices, usually a service. Relationships between contexts are recorded on the context map.

terms.def: A diagram and a document describing every bounded context and the political and technical relationship between each pair.
terms.detail: The context map is the architecture. It names each relationship using a small vocabulary — who depends on whom, who can impose changes, who has to absorb them — and it makes organisational reality visible, including the parts nobody enjoys admitting. Keep it on one page and date it. Its value is in being discussed, not in being complete. Relationship patterns Pattern Means Partnership two teams succeed or fail together; coordinate releases Customer / supplier downstream needs are planned by upstream Conformist downstream adopts the upstream model as-is Anti-corruption layer downstream translates and refuses to adopt it Shared kernel a small shared model, jointly owned Open host / published language upstream publishes a stable contract for everyone Separate ways no integration; duplicate instead How it relates Every arrow on the map is a place where translation code, or a future incident, lives.

terms.def: A translation layer that converts another context's model into yours, so their concepts never leak into your domain.
terms.detail: An ACL is a deliberate, owned piece of code at the border: adapters, mappers and a façade that speak the foreign model on one side and your ubiquitous language on the other. It is how you integrate with a legacy system, a vendor API or another team's service without letting their naming, their nulls and their lifecycle rules spread through your codebase. It costs real effort and it is almost always worth it on the upstream dependency you do not control. When the vendor changes their payload, exactly one package changes. What goes in it Concern Example Naming CUST_TYP=2 → CustomerTier.Gold Missing data default or reject, decided here Shape flatten a 5-level XML into a value object Failure map HTTP 503 to a domain-meaningful error How it relates Shown as the red ACL box in both the context map and the first animation.

terms.def: A small model deliberately shared by two contexts, jointly owned and changed only by agreement.
terms.detail: Sometimes duplicating a concept costs more than sharing it — Money, IsoCountry, a currency conversion table. A shared kernel is the explicit decision to share a small, stable piece, with the condition that neither team changes it unilaterally and both teams' tests run on every change. It is the most abused pattern in DDD, because "shared kernel" is what a shared library of 200 entities calls itself. Keep it tiny, keep it stable, and prefer duplication when in doubt. Share or duplicate? Candidate Verdict Money, Currency, Percentage share — stable, universal Customer, Order, Product duplicate — means different things Event contracts publish instead, versioned How it relates The alternative to a kernel is translation through an anti-corruption layer.

terms.def: An object with an identity that persists through change: two entities differ even when every field matches.
terms.detail: An entity is defined by continuity, not by content. A customer who changes name, address and email is still the same customer, because identity is carried by an id that is assigned once and never reused. Equality is by id; everything else can change. The practical consequence is that entities have a lifecycle — created, modified, archived — and that the model must say who assigns the identity and when, which is usually the moment the aggregate is created rather than the moment the database assigns a key. Entity or value object? Question Entity Value object Do we track it over time? yes no Equality by id by all fields Mutable yes, through methods never — replace it How it relates An aggregate root is always an entity.

terms.def: An immutable object defined entirely by its values, with no identity: two with the same values are interchangeable.
terms.detail: Value objects are the most under-used and highest-return pattern in tactical DDD. Replacing decimal amount and string currency with a Money type removes a whole class of bugs: you can no longer add euros to dollars, you cannot construct a negative price, and the rounding rule lives in one place. They are immutable by definition — "changing" one means producing a new one — which makes them free to share, trivially thread-safe and easy to test. Validate in the constructor so an invalid instance cannot exist. Identity versus value How it relates Most invariants about a single field belong in a value object, not in the aggregate.

terms.def: A cluster of entities and value objects treated as one unit for changes, with a single root as the only entry point.
terms.detail: The aggregate answers the question "what must be consistent right now, in the same transaction?" An Order with its lines is one aggregate because "at most ten items" is a rule about the whole order. The customer who placed it is a different aggregate, referenced by id, because no rule requires the customer and the order to change together. Keep them small. Large aggregates mean long transactions, lock contention and loading hundreds of rows to change one field. The usual advice — one aggregate changed per transaction, other aggregates updated eventually via domain events — is what makes a model scale. Sizing rules Rule Why Reference other aggregates by id keeps the loaded graph small One aggregate per transaction avoids distributed locking Group only true invariants "shown together" is not a reason Prefer eventual consistency outside cross-aggregate rules via events How it relates The second animation loads, mutates and saves exactly one aggregate. The aggregate boundary is also the repository 's unit of work.

terms.def: The single entity through which everything inside an aggregate is reached and changed.
terms.detail: Outside code may hold a reference to the root and nothing else. There is no order.Lines.Add(...) from a service — only order.AddItem(sku, qty), because only the root can see enough state to check the invariant. That single restriction is what keeps business rules from leaking into controllers. Practically: expose child collections as read-only, put behaviour on the root, and give the root the identity that the outside world uses. Allowed or not Call Verdict repo.Get(orderId) yes — roots only order.AddItem(sku, 3) yes — behaviour on the root repo.GetLine(lineId) no — children are not addressable order.Lines.Add(line) no — bypasses the invariant How it relates Step 4 of the aggregate animation is the root refusing to be bypassed.

terms.def: A business rule that must be true before and after every change — the reason an aggregate exists at all.
terms.detail: Invariants are what decide aggregate boundaries. "An order has at most ten items" needs the whole order, so lines belong inside it. "A customer cannot have two orders in flight" needs two aggregates, so it cannot be a transactional invariant — it becomes an eventually consistent check, or the model is wrong. Enforce them in the constructor and in every mutating method, and throw a domain-specific exception rather than returning false. An object that cannot be constructed in an invalid state removes most defensive code elsewhere. Where each rule lives Rule Home Quantity must be positive value object constructor At most 10 lines per order aggregate root method SKU must exist in the catalogue domain service / another context Email must be unique not an invariant — a uniqueness constraint How it relates The last step of the aggregate animation is an invariant rejecting a command.

terms.def: A collection-like abstraction for loading and saving whole aggregates by identity.
terms.detail: A repository hides persistence behind a domain-shaped interface: Get(id), Add(order), Remove(order). One repository per aggregate root, never one per table. It deals in whole aggregates, so partial loads and lazy children are a smell that the aggregate is too big. It is deliberately not a query API. Arbitrary filtering, joins and projections for screens belong on the read side, which is exactly the split that CQRS formalises. Repository or query? Need Where Load order 42 to change it repository List 50 orders with customer names read model / query service Count orders per region read model How it relates CQRS grows naturally out of this restriction.

terms.def: A record that something business-meaningful has happened, named in the past tense and published after the fact.
terms.detail: OrderPlaced, PaymentDeclined, ShipmentDelayed. Domain events are how one aggregate tells the rest of the system what happened without knowing who is listening, and they are the main integration mechanism between bounded contexts. Raising them inside the aggregate and dispatching them after the transaction commits keeps the model clean and avoids publishing events for work that then rolled back. Distinguish internal domain events (rich, private to the context) from integration events (small, versioned, part of your published language). Leaking the internal one across a boundary is how two contexts become coupled again. Naming and payload Rule Example Past tense, business words OrderPlaced, not OrderInsert Carry ids plus what changed orderId, total, placedAt Never carry the whole entity that couples the consumer to your model Version the integration shape OrderPlaced.v2 How it relates Steps 6–8 of the aggregate animation raise, commit and then publish one.

terms.def: A piece of domain logic that does not belong to any single entity or value object, expressed in the ubiquitous language.
terms.detail: Some rules genuinely span several aggregates or need outside knowledge — a transfer between two accounts, a pricing calculation that needs the catalogue and the customer's tier. Putting that on either aggregate would be arbitrary, so it becomes a stateless domain service with a business name: FundsTransferService, PricingPolicy. The trap is using it as a dumping ground. If most of your logic lives in services and your entities are property bags, you have built an anemic domain model with extra layers. Service or method? Logic Goes to Uses only one aggregate's state a method on the root Spans two aggregates domain service Orchestrates transaction + repo + bus application service How it relates Contrast with the application service, which holds no rules at all.

terms.def: The thin orchestration layer: it opens the transaction, loads an aggregate, calls one method on it and saves. No business rules.
terms.detail: Also called a command handler or use-case. Its whole job is plumbing: authorisation, transaction boundaries, fetching the aggregate, invoking a single intention-revealing method, persisting and dispatching events. If it contains an if about business meaning, that if belongs in the domain. Keeping it this thin is what makes the domain testable without a database and what makes the same domain usable from HTTP, a message consumer and a CLI without duplication. Typical body var order = await repo.Get(cmd.OrderId); order.AddItem(cmd.Sku, cmd.Quantity); await repo.Save(order); await bus.Publish(order.ReleaseEvents()); How it relates It is the leftmost box in the aggregate animation.

terms.def: A workshop where domain experts and developers map the business as a wall of past-tense events, then find boundaries in it.
terms.detail: Invented by Alberto Brandolini: orange sticky notes for domain events along a timeline, then commands, actors, policies and external systems layered on top. It is fast — a day gets you a useful map of a domain nobody could previously explain — and it surfaces disagreement between experts, which is usually the most valuable output. The clusters where events stop referring to each other are candidate bounded contexts. That is the cheapest way to find boundaries before committing them to code. The sticky notes Colour Meaning Orange domain event — OrderPlaced Blue command — PlaceOrder Yellow actor / aggregate Purple policy — "whenever X, then Y" Pink external system Red problem, question, disagreement How it relates It is how most teams actually discover their context map.

terms.def: The anti-pattern where entities are property bags and all behaviour sits in services — DDD vocabulary with none of the benefit.
terms.detail: Named by Martin Fowler. The shape is familiar: Order with twenty public setters, OrderService with twenty methods that mutate it, and validation sprinkled across controllers. It is not automatically wrong — for genuine CRUD it is the simpler choice — but it is wrong when the team has paid the cost of DDD and expected the benefit. The tell is that you cannot answer "where is the rule that an order cannot exceed ten items?" by looking at Order. If that rule can be broken by anyone with a setter, the aggregate is decorative. Symptoms Symptom Fix Public setters everywhere private setters, intention-revealing methods Validation in the controller move into constructors and methods Primitive obsession introduce value objects Services named XManager find the missing domain concept How it relates If this describes your code, strategic design — not more patterns — is usually what is missing.

pages.title: Event store
pages.tagline: Store what happened, not what is. Everything else is a fold over the facts.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · examples use PostgreSQL, Marten and KurrentDB 26.0 LTS (renamed from EventStoreDB at 25.0)
pages.description: Event store cheatsheet: append-only streams as the system of record, folding events back into state, optimistic concurrency by stream version, snapshots, subscriptions and schema versioning.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: An immutable record that something happened, named in the past tense and never modified after it is written.
terms.detail: The unit of storage. OrderPlaced, ItemAdded, AddressCorrected.
