An event records a decision that was already taken, so it cannot be rejected and cannot be edited — a mistake is corrected by appending another event, exactly as an accountant posts a correcting entry rather than erasing a line. Keep the payload about the business, not the row. Storing a full entity snapshot inside every event couples consumers to your internal model and destroys most of the benefit. Anatomy Field Why type + version routing and upcasting data what changed, in business terms metadata who, when, correlation, causation stream_id + version position within the aggregate How it relates These are the same orange notes from an EventStorming wall, made durable.

terms.def: The ordered sequence of events for one thing — normally one stream per aggregate instance.
terms.detail: order-42, account-7731, shipment-9c2. The stream is the unit of consistency: you read one to load an aggregate and append to one to change it, and the store guarantees ordering inside it. Stream design is the main modelling decision. Too coarse (all-orders) and every write contends on one stream; too fine and a single business rule spans several, which it must not. The aggregate boundary is almost always the right granularity. Choosing granularity Design Result One per aggregate correct; the default One per entity type write contention, huge streams One per user session invariants span streams — broken Unbounded lifetime stream needs closing and snapshots How it relates A stream is the storage form of a DDD aggregate's consistency boundary.

terms.def: The single rule: events are added at the end and never updated or deleted.
terms.detail: Everything else follows from this. Writes are sequential, which is the fastest thing a disk does; there are no update conflicts at the row level; history is complete by construction; and any derived view can be rebuilt because the inputs never changed. It also means mistakes are permanent in the log. A wrong amount is fixed by appending a correction, not by editing, which is unfamiliar at first and is exactly how financial systems have always worked. What it buys Property Consequence Sequential writes very fast, no in-place updates Immutability projections are always rebuildable Complete history audit is storage, not a feature No deletes GDPR needs a deliberate answer How it relates The deletion problem has its own answer — see crypto-shredding.

terms.def: The sequence number of an event within its stream — the basis for both ordering and concurrency control.
terms.detail: Versions start at 1 (or 0, depending on the store) and increase by one per event. They give deterministic ordering inside a stream and are what a reader uses to resume. They are not global: version 4 of order-42 says nothing about when it happened relative to order-43. Two kinds of position Position Scope Use Stream version one stream concurrency, rehydration Global position whole store projections, subscriptions How it relates Projections checkpoint on the global position, aggregates on the stream version.

terms.def: Appending with the version you expected to find, so a concurrent writer is rejected instead of silently overwriting.
terms.detail: You read order-42 to version 3, decide, and append with expectedVersion: 3. If someone else got there first the stream is at 4 and the store rejects your append with a wrong-expected-version error. No locks are held between read and write, and the aggregate's invariant is still protected. The retry must re-decide, not just re-append: the event that beat you may have invalidated the decision — another item may have taken the order past its ten-item limit. Expected version options Value Means A number stream must be exactly here "no stream" creating it; fails if it exists "stream exists" must already exist "any" no check — gives up the invariant How it relates Steps 7–10 of the first animation are one collision and its correct retry.

terms.def: Rebuilding current state by applying every event in order to an empty starting value. Also called rehydration or replay.
terms.detail: state = events.Aggregate(Empty, Apply). The Apply method must be pure and must never reject anything — an event already happened, so applying it cannot fail. All validation lives in the command handling, before the event is created. That split is what makes the model easy to test: feed a list of events, assert the state, with no database anywhere in the test. Two methods, two jobs Method May reject? Side effects Decide(command) yes — invariants here returns events Apply(event) never mutates state only How it relates A read model is the same fold, kept outside the aggregate and persisted.

terms.def: A stored copy of folded state at a given version, so long streams do not have to be replayed from the beginning.
terms.detail: Load the snapshot at version 9,900 and apply the hundred events after it. It is purely an optimisation and must never become the source of truth: if the fold logic changes, you delete every snapshot and let them rebuild. Most aggregates never need one. Reach for snapshots when a stream genuinely grows without bound — a long-lived account, a device that emits telemetry — and consider whether the aggregate should instead be closed and a new stream started per period. Ten thousand events, or a hundred How it relates Snapshots are to aggregates what read models are to queries: derived, disposable, rebuildable.

terms.def: The order of an event across the whole store, used by anything that reads more than one stream.
terms.detail: Often exposed as a virtual stream ($all in KurrentDB, a seq column in a relational implementation). It is what a projection follows, because a read model usually spans thousands of aggregates and needs a single ordering to checkpoint against. Be careful with its meaning in distributed stores: "global order" may be per partition, and a gap can be an in-flight transaction rather than a missing event. Read your store's guarantees before assuming a dense sequence. How it relates In a Postgres implementation, gaps from concurrent transactions are the classic subtle projection bug.

terms.def: A reader that follows the log — from the beginning, from a position, or from now — and is pushed new events as they arrive.
terms.detail: Two shapes. A catch-up subscription reads history then stays live, with the client owning the checkpoint — the right choice for projections, because you control replay. A persistent (competing-consumer) subscription has the server track position and distribute events across workers, which suits work queues but gives up ordering. Picking one Need Subscription Build a read model catch-up, client checkpoint Rebuild from scratch catch-up from 0 Parallel work queue persistent / competing React only to new events catch-up from "now" How it relates Catch-up subscriptions are what make CQRS projections rebuildable.

terms.def: The position a subscriber has processed up to, stored next to whatever it produced.
terms.detail: Written in the same transaction as the rows it produced, so the pair is atomic: on restart the subscriber resumes rather than replaying or skipping. The gap between the log head and a checkpoint is the lag metric for that reader. How it relates Identical mechanics to a CQRS projection checkpoint — because that is exactly what it is.

terms.def: Any derived view built by folding events — a read model, a report, a search index, an aggregate's own state.
terms.detail: Because the log is immutable, every projection is disposable: delete it, reset the checkpoint, replay, and it comes back. Read-side schema changes become replays instead of migrations, which is the single most liberating operational property of an event store. Projections must be idempotent, since subscriptions redeliver after a restart. Kinds Projection Lives in Read model for a screen SQL table Search index Elasticsearch Aggregate state memory, per request Analytics feed warehouse How it relates An event store plus projections is the fullest form of CQRS.

terms.def: Events are forever, so the code must keep reading the shapes it wrote years ago.
terms.detail: You cannot migrate an immutable log by running an ALTER. A 2024 OrderPlaced with no currency field will still be replayed in 2034, so every change must be backwards compatible: add optional fields, never rename or repurpose, never change the meaning of an existing one. This is the discipline event sourcing demands most consistently, and the one teams underestimate most reliably. Safe and unsafe changes Change Safe? Add an optional field yes Add a new event type yes Rename a field no — upcast instead Change a field's meaning no — new event type Remove a field only once nothing reads it How it relates Internal events can evolve more freely than the integration events other contexts consume.

terms.def: Translating an old event shape into the current one as it is read, so the rest of the code only sees the latest version.
terms.detail: A small function per version transition, applied on the read path: v1 gets a default currency, v2's renamed field is mapped, v3 is passed through. The aggregate and projections only ever handle the newest shape, and the stored bytes stay untouched. The alternative — rewriting the log into a new one — is a big, risky migration and loses the guarantee that history is what actually happened. Prefer upcasting until the chain becomes genuinely unreadable. Strategies Strategy When Upcast on read default; cheap and reversible Weak schema (tolerant reader) additive changes only New event type the meaning really changed Copy-and-transform the stream last resort How it relates Keep upcasters covered by tests built from real old payloads, not from the current class.

terms.def: How you fix a mistake in an append-only world: append the opposite, do not edit the past.
terms.detail: AmountCorrected, ChargeReversed, AddressCorrected. The original stays, the correction follows, and the fold produces the right answer. Anyone who needs to know what the system believed last Tuesday still can — which is the entire reason for the design. Name corrections explicitly rather than re-emitting the original event type, so projections can treat them differently if they need to. How it relates This is exactly how a ledger works, and for the same reasons.

terms.def: Deleting personal data from an immutable log by encrypting it per subject and destroying the key.
terms.detail: "Never delete" meets the right to erasure. The usual answer: store each person's personal fields encrypted with a key held per subject in a separate, mutable key store. Erasure deletes the key, after which the payload is unrecoverable noise while the stream's structure, ordering and versions stay intact. Design it in from the start. Retrofitting it onto a log that already holds plaintext means either a full stream rewrite or a legal problem. Options Approach Trade-off Crypto-shredding standard; needs upfront design Keep PII outside the log simplest; events hold references Rewrite the stream breaks immutability and audit How it relates Projections must handle an unreadable payload gracefully, not crash on replay.

terms.def: Asking what the state was at a past moment, by folding only the events up to it.
terms.detail: "What did this order look like before the address change?" is a filter and a fold, not a feature request. The same mechanism answers "what did we believe when we made that decision?" — which is the question auditors, regulators and incident reviews actually ask. It is also the best debugging tool in the model: replay a customer's exact history into a test and watch the bug happen. How it relates In a state-based database this requires a separate temporal table, maintained by hand and usually incomplete.

terms.def: The log only ever grows, so replay time, storage cost and archiving are planned work, not surprises.
terms.detail: Events are small, so raw volume is rarely the problem; replay time is. Measure a full rebuild early and watch the trend, because a projection that takes eleven hours to rebuild is effectively not rebuildable when you need it at 3 a.m. The usual levers: snapshots for long aggregates, closing streams per period rather than letting them run forever, and archiving cold streams to object storage with a documented way to bring them back. Plan for Concern Lever Slow aggregate load snapshots Slow projection rebuild parallel replay, partitioned projections Unbounded streams close per period, start a new one Cost archive cold streams How it relates Rehearse a full rebuild in CI; it is the test that stops this becoming a crisis.

pages.title: EventStorming
pages.tagline: Put everyone who knows something in front of one very long wall, and find out what the business actually does.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · invented by Alberto Brandolini, 2013 · a workshop format, not a notation
pages.description: EventStorming cheatsheet: the sticky-note grammar, the three levels, how a wall of orange notes becomes bounded contexts, and how the picture maps one-to-one onto code.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: Something that happened in the business, written in the past tense on an orange sticky — the atom of the whole method.
terms.detail: Order Placed, Payment Declined, Parcel Returned. The past tense is not a style rule: it forces the group to describe facts rather than wishes, screens or tables. "Order management" is not an event; "Order Cancelled" is, and it immediately invites the next question — by whom, and what happens next? Events are also the one vocabulary that domain experts and developers already share. Nobody has to learn UML, and nobody gets to hide behind "the system updates the record". Is it an event? Written Verdict Order Placed yes Order Management no — a noun, not a fact Place Order no — that is a command Order Row Updated no — database, not business Payment Declined by Issuer yes — and a useful one How it relates At design level these become the domain events in the code, and the records in an event store.

terms.def: The opening phase: everyone writes events at once, in silence, without agreeing an order or a format first.
terms.detail: Deliberately unmanaged. Parallel writing means a room of fifteen produces in eight minutes what a round-table discussion would produce in two hours — and because nobody is presenting, quiet people contribute as much as loud ones. Resist the urge to tidy. Duplicates, wrong tenses and contradictions are information: a word two people spell differently is a vocabulary problem you were going to discover in production anyway. Facilitator's rules Rule Why Everyone writes simultaneously parallelism is the point No discussion yet discussion serialises the room Past tense, one fact per note keeps notes movable Do not deduplicate duplicates reveal language gaps How it relates Steps 1–2 of the first animation.

terms.def: Arranging the events left to right in the order they happen — the move that turns a wall of notes into a model.
terms.detail: Enforcing an order is where the real work starts, because it forces the room to agree on sequence, and sequence is where people discover they disagree. Parallel branches get stacked vertically; alternative outcomes (Payment Declined beside Payment Taken) sit above or below the happy path. Do not try to make it tidy. A wall with a readable spine and messy branches is far more useful than a neat diagram that smoothed over an argument. Shapes you will see Shape Means A long straight spine the happy path Vertical stacking things happening in parallel A big gap nobody in the room owns that part A dense cluster complexity worth zooming into later How it relates Gaps in the timeline are usually missing people, not missing events.

terms.def: A red sticky placed on a disagreement, an unknown or a risk — parked rather than resolved.
terms.detail: Two people give different answers about when stock is reserved. The instinct is to settle it; the discipline is to write it on a red note, rotate it 45 degrees so it is impossible to miss, and move on. One argument can consume an entire workshop, and it is rarely the most important one. Hotspots are frequently the highest-value output of the session: a list of things the business does not actually know about itself, each one a question to answer before anyone writes code against it. What earns a red note Trigger Example Disagreement "we reserve before payment" / "after" Nobody knows "what happens on a partial refund?" Hidden complexity "this is where the 2019 spreadsheet lives" Missing person "only compliance can answer this" How it relates Photograph the hotspots and turn them into a question list; that list is the agenda for the next session.

terms.def: A moment where the business visibly changes phase — marked with a vertical line that often becomes a boundary.
terms.detail: Order Placed, Payment Settled, Parcel Delivered. Before and after a pivotal event the language changes, the people change, and often the rules change. Those are exactly the seams you want your software to break along. Choosing them is quick and surprisingly uncontroversial: ask the room "where does this stop being one kind of work and start being another?" and the answers usually agree. Pivots becoming boundaries How it relates Pivotal events are the cheapest way to find candidate bounded contexts before committing them to code.

terms.def: A blue sticky naming an intention in the imperative — the thing a person or system tried to do.
terms.detail: For every event, ask what caused it. Usually the answer is a command: Place Order, Cancel Booking, Approve Invoice. The crucial difference from an event is that a command can be refused — which is why the next question is always "who decides?". Commands are also the cleanest handover to code: one command, one handler, one intention. A command with no corresponding event is suspicious; so is an event with no command, unless it came from outside or from time passing. Causes of an event Cause Sticky Someone did something command + actor Another event happened policy Something outside external system Time passed a policy on a schedule How it relates This is the same command/event distinction CQS and CQRS are built on.

terms.def: A small yellow sticky naming the person or role that issues a command, and why they would.
terms.detail: Not a user account — a role with a motivation: "warehouse supervisor chasing a late pick", "customer who has changed their mind". Naming the actor forces the room to ask what that person can actually see before deciding, which is how read models get discovered. If a command has no actor, it is probably automatic, which means there is a policy hiding behind it. How it relates An actor with no read model in front of them is guessing — that is a design smell worth a hotspot.

terms.def: A big yellow sticky between a command and its event: the chunk of business that decides whether the command is allowed.
terms.detail: Brandolini's trick is to leave it nameless at first — just "the thing that decides". Only once the group can state the rule out loud ("an order cannot exceed ten items") does the sticky get a name. That avoids the usual failure of naming entities first and inventing rules to fit them. At Big Picture level you can skip aggregates entirely. They belong to design-level sessions. How it relates Maps directly onto the DDD aggregate: the consistency boundary where the invariant lives.

terms.def: A lilac sticky stating a reaction: "whenever X happened, then do Y" — the glue between one event and the next command.
terms.detail: Policies are where business logic hides. "Whenever payment is taken, reserve the stock" sounds obvious; "whenever payment is taken and the customer is in the EU and it is before 16:00, reserve the stock" is three policies pretending to be one, and finding that out on a wall is far cheaper than finding it out in a code review. Read them aloud. If the sentence needs an "if", or an "except", split the note. Kinds of policy Trigger Example Another event whenever paid, reserve stock Time every night at 02:00, settle A threshold whenever stock < 10, reorder A human decision "someone looks at it" — name the actor How it relates A chain of policies across several contexts is a saga; in code it becomes a process manager.

terms.def: A green sticky naming the information an actor looks at before issuing a command.
terms.detail: "The picker looks at the pick list"; "the approver looks at the customer's credit history". Making this explicit catches a very common design failure: a screen that does not show the one number the decision actually depends on. It also hands you your query requirements directly, which is why design-level EventStorming leads so naturally into CQRS. How it relates Each green sticky is a projection in a CQRS read side.

terms.def: A pink sticky for anything outside the boundary that emits or receives events — and that you cannot change.
terms.detail: Payment providers, carriers, the regulator's filing portal, the 1998 mainframe. Marking them pink makes the integration surface visible at a glance, and pink clusters are where schedule risk lives: every one is a contract you do not control, with its own failure modes and its own vocabulary. How it relates Each pink sticky is a candidate anti-corruption layer in DDD terms.

terms.def: The first level: a whole business or product explored in one session, with the widest possible group of people.
terms.detail: Four hours, fifteen to thirty people, eight metres of paper. Only orange events, plus red hotspots and maybe pink external systems — no commands, no aggregates. The output is a shared map, a list of unknowns, and candidate boundaries. Its real value is usually social: for many organisations it is the first time sales, operations, finance and engineering have described the same process in one room. Shape of the session Setting Typical Duration 3–4 hours People 15–30, mixed roles Stickies used orange, red, (pink) Output boundaries, hotspots, vocabulary How it relates Run this before deciding on services or modules — it is the cheapest boundary-finding tool there is.

terms.def: The middle level: one end-to-end flow worked out in detail, adding commands, policies, actors and read models.
terms.detail: Narrower scope, smaller group, more colours. This is where "how does a refund actually work?" gets answered completely, including the branches nobody documents: partial refunds, refunds after the parcel shipped, refunds on a card that has expired. The output is close to a specification, and usually good enough to start building from. How it relates Policies discovered here are what later become sagas or process managers.

terms.def: The deepest level: one aggregate at a time, producing a model you can type in almost directly.
terms.detail: Three or four people, a couple of hours, one slice. Every command has an aggregate, every aggregate has stated invariants, every actor has a read model. At this point the wall and the code are isomorphic, and the handover is mechanical rather than interpretive. Do not try to reach this level for the whole system. Use it on the complex, differentiating parts — the core domain — and leave the rest alone. Sticky to code Sticky Code Command (blue) command + handler Aggregate (big yellow) aggregate root Event (orange) domain event Policy (lilac) process manager / saga Read model (green) projection External system (pink) anti-corruption layer How it relates Step 9 of the second animation is exactly this table.

terms.def: Reading candidate boundaries off the finished wall, where the language and the people change.
terms.detail: Look for three signals: a pivotal event, a change in vocabulary (the same word meaning something new), and a change in who is talking. Where all three coincide, draw a line — that is a candidate bounded context, and it was found in a morning rather than discovered after six months of building. Treat them as candidates, not conclusions. The wall is evidence, and boundaries are still a design decision. Signals Signal Strength Same word, different meaning strong Different people talking strong Pivotal event medium A gap in the timeline weak — may just be a missing person How it relates This is how most teams actually arrive at a context map.

terms.def: The deliberate constraint that the wall must never run out — because scarcity makes people stop writing.
terms.detail: Brandolini is emphatic about this. A small whiteboard silently tells participants to be selective, and selective is exactly what you do not want during exploration. Eight metres of butcher paper costs almost nothing and changes the behaviour of the room. The same applies remotely: give the board far more canvas than the session could possibly use, and never fit the model to a slide. Practical Setting Advice Paper 6–10 m, at standing height Chairs remove them Remote canvas effectively infinite; never zoom to fit How it relates Standing and a long wall are the two changes with the biggest effect on participation.

terms.def: The small set of behaviours that decide whether the session works: timeboxing, parking arguments, and keeping the loudest person off the wall.
terms.detail: The facilitator does not model. Their job is to keep everyone writing in parallel, to convert arguments into red hotspots, to stop one expert narrating while fourteen people watch, and to keep the timeline moving. A good session feels slightly uncomfortable and ends on time. The two most common failures are both social: an authority figure dictating the model, and the group sliding into solution design before the problem is on the wall. Moves that work Situation Move Two people arguing "that is a hotspot" — write it, move on One person narrating hand everyone a pen, restart parallel writing Drifting into solutions "what happened?", not "what should we build?" Wall gone quiet walk the timeline aloud, end to end Running out of time photograph it; hotspots are a valid ending How it relates Facilitation, not notation, is what separates a useful session from an expensive one.

pages.title: Graceful degradation
pages.tagline: Most of your page is optional. An outage should cost the user those parts, not all of them.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · the product half of resilience engineering; examples in C# and TypeScript
pages.description: Graceful degradation cheatsheet: critical versus optional dependencies, fallback ladders, feature flags and static stability — how to serve a smaller product instead of an error page.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: Designing a feature so that losing part of it costs the user that part, rather than the whole thing.
terms.detail: The opposite is not "ungraceful degradation" but binary availability: the page works perfectly or it returns a 500. Almost every system is built that way by accident, because await makes every dependency look equally mandatory. It is a product discipline supported by technical mechanisms. The breaker, the timeout and the shedder produce a signal; graceful degradation is the decision about what that signal means for the person looking at the screen. Where it sits Layer Job Timeout bound one call Circuit breaker fail fast and deterministically Load shedding choose which requests to refuse Graceful degradation decide what the user still gets How it relates It is the only one of the four that a non-engineer has an opinion about — which is why it needs one.

terms.def: One whose failure genuinely means the feature cannot work — and the list is almost always shorter than the code implies.
terms.detail: The test is blunt: if this returns nothing, can the user still accomplish the thing they came for? For a product page, catalogue and price are critical — you cannot sell an unnamed item at an unknown price. Everything else is decoration, however nice. Critical dependencies get the real engineering: replication, caching, fallbacks of their own, and an honest error page when all of it fails. Pretending something is critical when it is not simply buys you its downtime. The test Question If no… Can the user complete the task without it? critical Would a plausible default be wrong or unsafe? critical Would the user notice within a week? probably optional How it relates Each critical dependency multiplies into your achievable SLO; see composite availability on the SLI/SLO page.

terms.def: One whose failure should change the page and not break it — the large majority, once you look.
terms.detail: Reviews, recommendations, personalisation, loyalty balances, recently-viewed, social proof, A/B assignment, analytics beacons. Each one is a service that can go down, and each one is a panel that can be absent without anyone being unable to buy anything. The engineering requirement is that the call must be unable to break the render: its own timeout, its own breaker, and a result type that permits absence. A null check is not a design. Typical treatment Dependency On failure Reviews omit the panel entirely Recommendations static bestsellers Stock level cached figure, or hide the count Loyalty points hide the row Analytics fire and forget, never await How it relates An optional dependency that can break the page is the single most common degradation bug.

terms.def: The arithmetic that makes this worth doing: mandatory dependencies in series multiply, and the result falls fast.
terms.detail: Eight dependencies at 99.9% give 0.999⁸ = 99.20%, which is about seventy hours a year. Reclassify six of them as optional and the page inherits only 0.999² = 99.80% — four times better, with no change to any service's own reliability. This is the cheapest availability improvement available to most teams: it costs a day of classification and some error handling, rather than replicas, regions or rewrites. Mandatory dependencies in series Count at 99.9% Combined Per year 1 99.90% 8.8 h 2 99.80% 17.5 h 4 99.60% 35 h 8 99.20% 70 h How it relates The first animation is this table, built one dependency at a time.

terms.def: An ordered list of progressively worse but still useful answers, tried in turn before giving up.
terms.detail: Live answer, then fresh cache, then stale cache, then a static default, then omit the element. Most teams implement rung one and rung five and nothing in between, which throws away the most valuable options — a ten-minute-old price is enormously better than no price. Write the ladder down per dependency, including how stale is too stale. "Serve a cached price up to one hour old, then hide the buy button" is a decision; "catch and log" is not. The rungs # Rung Cost 1 Live call normal 2 Fresh cache none 3 Stale cache accuracy 4 Static default relevance 5 Omit the feature How it relates The second animation descends this ladder one rung at a time on a real page.

terms.def: Serving the last known good value when the source is unavailable — usually the highest-value rung on the ladder.
terms.detail: An ordinary cache expires data and then goes to the origin. A degradation-aware cache keeps the expired entry and serves it when the origin fails — the HTTP stale-if-error directive formalises exactly this. The user sees a slightly old answer instead of an error, which is almost always the better trade. Two rules: label staleness where it matters ("as of 14:02"), and set a maximum age beyond which stale becomes dangerous — an hour-old price is fine, an hour-old fraud decision is not. Tolerance by data type Data Acceptable staleness Product description days Price minutes to an hour Stock count minutes, shown as approximate Account balance seconds, clearly labelled Auth / permissions none — never serve stale How it relates This is why a cache is a resilience component, not only a performance one.

terms.def: Designing so that a failure causes the system to keep doing what it was already doing, rather than needing something to work.
terms.detail: Amazon's term for a powerful idea: the failure mode should be "no change" rather than "no service". A load balancer that keeps its last known healthy host list when the control plane is down is statically stable; one that needs the control plane to route is not. Applied to features: pre-compute and cache what the page needs so that an outage freezes the content instead of emptying it. The site keeps working on yesterday's data, which beats working on nothing. Stable or not Design On control-plane failure Cached config, used as-is keeps working — stable Config fetched per request stops — unstable Pre-provisioned capacity keeps serving Scale-up required to serve fails during the incident Two services, one control-plane outage How it relates The strongest version of degradation: nothing degrades, because nothing had to change.

terms.def: The implementation rule for optional dependencies: their failure must be unable to reach the response.
terms.detail: In practice this means every optional call is wrapped: its own short timeout, its own breaker, its own try/catch, and a return type that can be empty. The template must then handle absence — a panel that throws on a null list has merely moved the failure. The subtle version is latency: an optional call with no timeout will not fail your page, it will just make it take eight seconds, which users experience as failure anyway. Checklist per optional call Control Typical Timeout well below the page budget — 100–300 ms Breaker aggressive; it is optional Result type nullable or empty collection Template renders correctly with nothing Never retry on the user's critical path How it relates A circuit breaker supplies the fast failure; fail-soft handling is what turns it into a working page.

terms.def: Named, testable modes — full, reduced, minimal, read-only — rather than an unbounded space of partial failures.
terms.detail: With eight optional dependencies there are 256 combinations, and you cannot test 256 things. Defining three or four named levels collapses that: full, reduced (optional panels off), minimal (critical path only), read-only (writes disabled). Each is a state you can enter deliberately, screenshot, and test. Read-only deserves special mention: for many systems, disabling writes while keeping reads is the difference between a degraded hour and a total outage. A workable ladder Level What is off Trigger Full nothing normal Reduced recs, personalisation load or a breaker Minimal all optional panels heavy overload Read-only writes database failover How it relates Levels make degradation a thing you can rehearse, which is what makes it work when it matters.

terms.def: The manual control: turning expensive features off deliberately during an incident, rather than waiting for them to fail.
terms.detail: Automatic degradation handles dependencies that fail. Flags handle the ones that are merely expensive: an operator can switch off the heavy search ranker, the personalisation model or the live stock lookup and reclaim capacity immediately. For this to be useful the flag must take effect in seconds without a deploy, must be visible in the incident channel, and must be rehearsed — a kill switch nobody has ever pulled is a kill switch that will not work. Requirements Requirement Why Takes effect in seconds deploys are too slow mid-incident Works when its own backend is down cached default, statically stable Audited and announced others must know what changed Exercised regularly untested switches fail How it relates Flags plus named levels give you a degradation runbook rather than improvisation.

terms.def: The decision to show an honest error rather than a plausible-looking wrong answer.
terms.detail: Degradation has a limit. If the fraud check is unavailable, approving the payment is not degradation — it is a security incident with better manners. If the price service is down, inventing a price is worse than showing nothing. The rule: never fall back to an answer that could be wrong in a way that costs money or safety. Correctness-critical paths fail closed; convenience paths fail open. Fail open or closed? Dependency On failure Recommendations fail open — omit Reviews fail open — omit Price stale, or hard fail — never guess Fraud / authorisation fail closed — always Rate limiter judgement — usually fail open How it relates "Fail open or closed?" should be answered per dependency and written next to its classification.

terms.def: Telling the user what is missing, in their terms, instead of silently showing less.
terms.detail: Silent degradation is right for things the user never knew existed — a missing recommendation carousel needs no apology. It is wrong for things they are relying on: a stock figure that is quietly an hour old, or a balance that is quietly stale, erodes trust far more than a small label would. The useful distinction is whether the absence could lead to a bad decision. If it could, say so: "Stock levels may be out of date" costs one line and prevents a complaint. Say something or not? Situation Signal Recommendations missing silent Reviews missing silent, or a quiet note Stock figure stale label it Balance stale label with a timestamp Cannot take the order explicit, with what to do next How it relates Error copy is part of the design; writing it during an incident produces the worst version.

terms.def: The front-end sibling: build the working baseline first, then layer improvements that may not arrive.
terms.detail: Strictly these are opposites in direction — progressive enhancement starts from the floor and adds, degradation starts from the ceiling and removes — but they produce the same system. A form that posts without JavaScript and is enhanced with client-side validation keeps working when the bundle fails to load. The practical value today is less about ancient browsers and more about failure: a third-party script timing out, a CDN region down, a flaky mobile connection. Baseline first Enhancement Baseline that must work Client-side validation server-side validation Async "add to basket" a real form post Infinite scroll paginated links Web font a readable fallback stack How it relates Third-party scripts are optional dependencies; load them async and never block render on them.

terms.def: Degraded paths only work if they are exercised — and they are the least exercised code you own.
terms.detail: The fallback written eighteen months ago and never executed will fail: the cached shape has drifted, the template throws on an empty list, the static default references a deleted product. The only defence is to run it regularly — in tests, in staging, and in production. Make each named level a test fixture and assert that the critical path still works. Then do it in production, deliberately, on a Tuesday afternoon. Ways to exercise it Method Catches Unit tests per fallback shape and null handling Integration test per level template and layout breaks Fault injection in staging timeout and breaker config Game day in production everything the others miss How it relates An untested fallback is a second bug waiting for the worst possible moment.

terms.def: Deliberately breaking a dependency in production, with everyone watching, to find out what actually happens.
terms.detail: Turn off the reviews service at 14:00 on a Tuesday and observe. Teams reliably discover that an "optional" dependency was awaited on the critical path, that a timeout was never configured, or that the empty-state template was never written. Start small and announced: one optional dependency, in one region, with a rollback ready. The goal is information, not heroism. Running one Step Note Pick one optional dependency never a critical one first State the hypothesis "the page renders without reviews" Announce it so alerts are not mistaken for an incident Break it, watch the SLI short window, rollback ready Write down what surprised you that is the whole output How it relates Spend error budget on this deliberately — it is exactly what the budget is for.

terms.def: Tracking which mode you are in, so "degraded" is a state you can see rather than infer.
terms.detail: Count renders per level, fallback usage per dependency, and — most importantly — whether the critical journey still succeeds. A page that renders in reduced mode is a success for availability and a partial failure for experience, and your SLI should say which you are measuring. A good practice is two SLIs: "the user could complete the task" and "the user got the full experience". The first protects the business; the second stops permanent silent degradation. What to export Metric Tells you render_level{level="reduced"} how often you degrade fallback_used{dep=...} which rung, per dependency Critical-journey SLI did the business still work Full-experience SLI silent long-term degradation How it relates Without the second SLI, a feature can be quietly broken for months and look perfectly healthy.

pages.title: GraphQL
pages.tagline: One endpoint, one typed schema, and the client decides what comes back — which moves both the power and the problems to the server.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · examples use Hot Chocolate (.NET) and Strawberry (Python)
pages.description: GraphQL cheatsheet: schema and resolvers, the N+1 problem and DataLoader, nullability, pagination, query cost limits, persisted queries and federation.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: The typed description of everything that exists, written in SDL — the whole contract between client and server.
terms.detail: The schema defines object types, their fields, the arguments each field takes and what it returns. Three types are special roots: Query for reads, Mutation for writes, Subscription for streams. Everything a client can ask is reachable from those. It is checked at query time, not just documented: a query naming a field that does not exist, or passing an argument of the wrong type, is rejected during validation before a single resolver runs. That is a genuine advantage over REST, where the same mistake is a runtime surprise. The building blocks Construct Use type an object with fields input structured arguments — cannot be returned interface shared fields across types union one of several unrelated types enum a closed set of values scalar custom leaf types (DateTime, URL) How it relates Design it around the domain, not around your tables. A schema that mirrors the database is a database with extra steps.

terms.def: The function that produces one field's value — called once per object, not once per query.
terms.detail: Each field can have a resolver taking the parent object, the arguments, a shared context and info about the query. If a field is just a property of the parent, most servers supply a default resolver; you write one when the value must be computed or fetched. The thing to internalise is "once per object". A list of 100 users with a posts field calls that resolver 100 times, with no knowledge that its 99 siblings exist. Everything difficult about GraphQL performance follows from that one sentence. // pseudo-signature, in every implementation resolve(parent, args, context, info) → value | Task<value> How it relates info is how advanced servers do projection — inspecting the requested sub-fields to select only those columns.

terms.def: How the server walks the query: parents before children, siblings in parallel, errors bubbling up through nullable fields.
terms.detail: Execution is breadth-wise and layered. The root field resolves, then its selected sub-fields resolve against each returned object, and so on. Sibling fields at the same level may run concurrently; a child cannot start before its parent has produced an object. Mutations are the exception: top-level mutation fields run serially, in document order, because write order matters. Everything nested under them resolves like a query. How it relates Layered execution is what makes DataLoader possible: all the siblings at one level ask within the same tick, so their keys can be batched.

terms.def: One query for the list, then one more for each item — the default behaviour of a naive resolver tree.
terms.detail: Fetch 50 users with one query, then resolve user.company 50 times, each doing its own lookup: 51 round trips for data that one IN clause would have returned. Nest another level and it multiplies — 50 users × 20 posts × an author lookup is a thousand more. It is not a bug in anyone's code. It is the direct consequence of resolvers being per-object and independent, and it will appear in every GraphQL server that does not explicitly prevent it. How it multiplies Query Naive round trips Batched 50 users 1 1 + company each 51 2 + 20 posts each 101 3 + author of each post 1,101 4 How it relates Log round trips per request in development and fail the build above a threshold — it is the only way to notice before production.

terms.def: A per-request batching and deduplicating cache that collapses N calls into one.
terms.detail: A DataLoader collects the keys requested during one tick of the event loop, then calls a batch function once with all of them and distributes the results. It also deduplicates: ten posts by the same author produce one load. Scope it per request — a shared instance would leak one user's data into another's response. The batch function must return results in the same order as the keys, with a null or a placeholder for misses. Getting that mapping wrong produces wrong data rather than an error, which makes it worth a test. Common values Setting Guidance Lifetime one request, always Max batch size 100–1,000, to bound the IN clause Caching per request; longer-lived caching is a separate layer Ordering results must align with the key array How it relates It fixes round-trip count, not the amount of work. A batch of 10,000 ids is still a very large query — that is what Query cost is for.

terms.def: Every field is nullable unless marked! — and non-null is a promise that propagates failure upward.
terms.detail: GraphQL inverts the usual default: fields are optional by default, and! makes one required. If a non-null field resolves to null or throws, the error cannot stop there — it nullifies the parent, and if the parent is also non-null, its parent, up to data: null in the worst case. So! is a real commitment. Marking a list element non-null means one broken item destroys the whole list. The common advice is to be generous with non-null on scalars you genuinely always have, and conservative on anything fetched from another service. Reading the syntax Type Meaning [Post] list may be null, items may be null [Post!] list may be null, items may not [Post]! list is always present, items may be null [Post!]! both guaranteed — and most fragile How it relates Nullability is part of the contract, so tightening a field later is a breaking change while loosening it is not.

terms.def: Partial data with an errors array, returned under HTTP 200 — which breaks a lot of client assumptions.
terms.detail: A GraphQL response can contain both data and errors: three of four requested fields succeeded and one failed, each error carrying a message, a path and optional extensions. The transport status is 200 even so, because the GraphQL request itself succeeded. Clients and monitoring must therefore inspect the body. An alerting rule based on HTTP status will report perfect health while half the fields on every page are failing — which is one of the most common GraphQL operational blind spots. Where to put what Kind Convey as Malformed query validation error, 400 Unexpected failure errors entry, 200 Expected domain outcome a union or result type in data Not authorised errors with a code in extensions How it relates Modelling expected failures as types — union PayResult = Paid | InsufficientFunds — makes them typed and client-handleable instead of stringly.

terms.def: Cursor-based connections, because offsets break on a graph that changes while you page through it.
terms.detail: The Relay connection pattern is the de facto standard: a field takes first / after (or last / before) and returns a connection with edges (each a cursor and a node) and a pageInfo with hasNextPage and endCursor. It is verbose, and worth it. Cursors are stable under inserts and deletes, the extra indirection gives a place for edge metadata such as addedAt, and first is the argument your cost analysis multiplies by — a list field with no limit is an unbounded query waiting to happen. posts(first: 20, after: "Y3Vyc29yOjIw") { edges { cursor node { id title } } pageInfo { hasNextPage endCursor } } How it relates Require a bounded first on every list field and cap it in the schema — it is the simplest cost control there is.

terms.def: Analysing how expensive a query is before running it, and refusing the ones that are too expensive.
terms.detail: Because the client composes the query, the server cannot know its own workload in advance — unless it computes it. Three controls, usually layered: a maximum depth, a maximum node or complexity score where each field has a cost and list fields multiply by their first argument, and a per-caller budget over time. Depth alone is insufficient: a shallow query asking for 10,000 items of 50 fields each is cheap by depth and ruinous in practice. Complexity scoring catches that, and it runs during validation, so an over-budget query costs one parse rather than a database outage. Common values Control Typical Max depth 7–12 Max complexity 1,000–5,000 points Default list cost 1 per field × first Max first 100, enforced in the schema Per-caller budget complexity points per minute How it relates Rate limiting by request count is nearly meaningless here; limit by complexity points instead — see Rate limiting.

terms.def: Registering allowed operations ahead of time and sending an id instead of a document.
terms.detail: Clients extract their operations at build time, the server stores them, and at runtime the client sends a hash. Three wins at once: the request is tiny, the operation can be GET-able and therefore CDN-cacheable, and — if you allow only registered documents — arbitrary queries become impossible, which retires the entire query-cost attack surface. That last mode is often called trusted documents, and it is the single best answer for a private API serving your own clients. It does not fit a public API where third parties compose their own queries. How it relates With trusted documents you can also disable Introspection in production without inconveniencing your own build pipeline.

terms.def: The schema querying itself — what powers tooling, and what hands an attacker a map.
terms.detail: __schema and __type let any client discover every type, field, argument and description. This is how GraphiQL, code generators, IDE completion and client typing all work, and it is a genuine advantage of the ecosystem. In production on a private API it is also a complete inventory of your internal model, including deprecated fields and descriptions nobody meant to publish. The usual posture is: on in development, off in production, with the schema distributed to your own builds as a file. How it relates Disabling it is obscurity, not security. Field-level authorization still has to be correct.

terms.def: Permission checks per field, because one request can touch twenty types across three services.
terms.detail: There is no endpoint to protect. A single request may read a user, their orders, each order's customer and that customer's billing details — and the right to see each of those may differ. Authorization therefore lives on fields and types, typically as directives or attributes resolved during execution. The subtle failure is through traversal: a user may legitimately read Order, and Order.customer may expose a customer they should not see. Permission must be evaluated on the object actually being returned, not only on the entry point. Where to enforce Layer Catches Schema directive coarse role checks, declaratively Resolver per-object ownership Data layer row-level rules — the backstop How it relates Enforce in the data layer too. It is the only place that cannot be bypassed by a traversal nobody anticipated.

terms.def: HTTP caching mostly stops working; a normalised client cache replaces it.
terms.detail: One URL, POST bodies, and a response shape that differs per client: URL-based caches have nothing to key on. CDN and browser caching largely do not apply unless you use persisted queries over GET. What replaces it is a normalised cache in the client. Apollo Client, Relay and urql split responses into objects keyed by type and id, so a User fetched by one screen is reused by another and a mutation returning an updated object updates every view at once. That is genuinely powerful — and it requires every type to expose a stable id. What caches where Layer Works? CDN / browser HTTP cache only with persisted GET queries Normalised client cache yes — the main mechanism Per-request DataLoader yes, within one request Server-side object cache yes, inside resolvers (Redis) How it relates Always expose a globally unique id. Without it, client caches cannot normalise and lose most of their value.

terms.def: No v1 and v2 — you add fields, deprecate old ones, and watch who still uses them.
terms.detail: Because clients request fields explicitly, adding a field breaks nobody. That is the strongest practical argument for GraphQL in a multi-client estate: the mobile app from eighteen months ago keeps working while the web app uses fields that did not exist then. Removal is the hard part. Mark a field @deprecated(reason: "..."), track per-field usage in your telemetry, and remove it only when usage reaches zero — which is a thing you can actually know, unlike with REST response bodies. Breaking or not Change Breaking? Add a field or type no Add an optional argument no Remove or rename a field yes Make a nullable field non-null no for clients, risky for you Make a non-null field nullable yes Add an enum value yes, in practice How it relates Run schema-diff checks in CI against the registered schema; breaking changes should fail the build, not surprise a client.

terms.def: Server-pushed updates over a persistent transport, for the cases polling cannot cover.
terms.detail: A subscription operation opens a long-lived stream — WebSocket, or SSE in newer transports — and the server pushes a result each time an event fires. The payload is shaped by the selection set like any other operation. They carry real operational weight: persistent connections per client, state in the server, a pub/sub backbone so any instance can publish, authentication at connect and ongoing, and a reverse proxy configured not to buffer or time out. For many use cases polling or SSE on a plain endpoint is less machinery for the same user experience. How it relates If you add subscriptions, plan the pub/sub layer and the proxy configuration first — they are where the effort actually goes.

terms.def: Composing one graph from several independently owned subgraphs.
terms.detail: Instead of one monolithic server, each team owns a subgraph that declares which types it contributes and which it extends by key. A gateway composes them into a supergraph, plans each query across subgraphs, and stitches the results. It solves a real organisational problem — one graph, many owners — and introduces a distributed query planner into your request path. Query planning bugs, cross-subgraph N+1s and composition failures at deploy time are all new operational categories. Worth it at the scale that needs it; a heavy price below that. How it relates A Backend-for-Frontend is the lighter answer when the problem is per-client shaping rather than multi-team ownership.

pages.title: gRPC
pages.tagline: A typed method call that happens to cross a network — with HTTP/2 doing the multiplexing and protobuf doing the bytes.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · examples use proto3, grpc-dotnet and grpcio
pages.description: gRPC cheatsheet: protobuf contracts, the four call types, HTTP/2 framing, status codes and trailers, deadlines and cancellation, channels, retries and gRPC-Web.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: The IDL and the binary wire format: a schema both sides compile, and bytes neither side can read by eye.
terms.detail: A .proto file declares messages and services. protoc turns it into types and stubs in your language. On the wire each field is a varint tag — field number and wire type — followed by its value, with no field names and no padding, which is why payloads are typically 3–10× smaller than the equivalent JSON and parse several times faster. The cost is that a packet capture is unreadable without the schema, and so is a message sitting in a log or a queue. That trade is fine between services you own and poor for anything a human has to debug by eye. Rough comparison JSON Protobuf A small order message ~420 B ~95 B Parse speed baseline 3–10× faster Readable in a log yes no Schema required to read no yes How it relates Protobuf is useful without gRPC — as a message format on Kafka, for instance — and gRPC can in principle carry other codecs.

terms.def: The small integers that are the real identity of every field — names are only for humans.
terms.detail: Each field carries its number on the wire, not its name. Renaming a field is therefore a non-event for compatibility; changing its number, or reusing one that used to mean something else, silently reinterprets old data as the new type. Numbers 1–15 encode their tag in a single byte, so spend them on the fields present in every message. Always reserved the numbers and names of deleted fields, so nobody can accidentally resurrect them. Common values Range Tag size Use for 1–15 1 byte hot, always-present fields 16–2047 2 bytes everything else 19000–19999 — reserved by protobuf itself message Order { reserved 4, 7 to 9; // never reuse these reserved "legacy_total"; string id = 1; int64 amount_cents = 2; } How it relates In proto3 every field is optional on the wire, so adding one is always backward compatible — which is what makes rolling deploys safe.

terms.def: Unary, server streaming, client streaming and bidirectional — all on one HTTP/2 stream.
terms.detail: Because a stream can carry a sequence of messages in each direction, the method signature chooses the shape. Streaming is not an add-on here — it is the same mechanism with different cardinalities, which is why it is so much less painful than bolting streaming onto REST. How it relates Streaming calls hold server state and a stream slot for their lifetime, so they need their own limits — they are not free.

terms.def: Each call is an independent stream on a shared connection — which is both the performance story and the load-balancing problem.
terms.detail: One TCP connection, one TLS handshake, and then thousands of concurrent calls as multiplexed streams with no head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer. Headers are HPACK-compressed, so repeated metadata is nearly free. This is why gRPC is fast in a chatty service mesh. It is also why an L4 load balancer fails here: it balances connections, and there is one long-lived connection per client. Three clients can spread perfectly across three backends while 90% of the requests land on one. Common values Setting Typical Max concurrent streams 100 (often raised) Max connection age 30–60 min, to force re-dial Keepalive ping ≥ 30 s; too aggressive and the server resets you Initial window 64 KB, raised for streaming How it relates The full failure mode and its fixes are on the L4 vs L7 load balancing page — it is the canonical example.

terms.def: The outcome arrives after the body, in trailers — a design choice with wide consequences.
terms.detail: A call ends with a grpc-status and optional grpc-message in HTTP/2 trailers. The HTTP status is almost always 200, even for failures, because the HTTP exchange itself succeeded. This is what lets a server start streaming results and only later discover an error — it has not committed to an outcome by sending headers. The consequences show up everywhere: proxies must support trailers, browsers cannot read them (hence gRPC-Web ), and monitoring based on HTTP status reports a perfectly healthy service while every call fails with INTERNAL. Codes worth knowing Code Meaning Retry? OK (0) success — INVALID_ARGUMENT (3) caller's fault no DEADLINE_EXCEEDED (4) budget gone rarely NOT_FOUND (5) no such entity no RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED (8) quota or rate limit with backoff FAILED_PRECONDITION (9) wrong state — do not retry no ABORTED (10) conflict — retry higher up yes UNAVAILABLE (14) transient yes How it relates Alert on grpc-status, never on HTTP status — the same trap GraphQL has with its errors array.

terms.def: Key-value pairs sent as HTTP/2 headers: auth tokens, trace context, tenant ids.
terms.detail: Metadata is the out-of-band channel. Keys ending in -bin carry base64-encoded binary values; everything else is ASCII, and keys are lower-cased. Initial metadata goes with the request headers, and trailing metadata can accompany the final status. Because HPACK compresses repeated headers on a long-lived connection, metadata that is the same on every call is close to free — which makes it the natural place for tokens, traceparent and tenant identifiers. Common keys Key Carries authorization Bearer … traceparent W3C trace context grpc-timeout the deadline, set by the library x-tenant-id your own routing keys grpc-status-details-bin rich typed error details How it relates Attach it in an interceptor, not at every call site; that is the difference between a convention and a guarantee.

terms.def: An absolute point in time, sent with the call and propagated down the chain — not a per-hop timeout.
terms.detail: The caller sets a deadline; the library converts it to a grpc-timeout header. A server receiving one knows how long it has, and when it calls another service it passes along what is left. The budget shrinks down the tree instead of each hop inventing its own. Two rules follow. Always set one — the default in most languages is infinity, which turns a slow dependency into exhausted threads. And always propagate the incoming deadline rather than starting a fresh timeout, or the chain's total can exceed what the caller is still waiting for. Common values Call Deadline Interactive read 200–500 ms Write with side effects 1–3 s Batch or report 30–120 s Streaming per message, not per stream How it relates Deadline propagation is one of the few genuinely distributed features built into the protocol rather than into your code.

terms.def: When a caller gives up, the whole subtree finds out and stops working.
terms.detail: A cancelled or expired call resets its HTTP/2 stream, and the server's handler receives a cancelled context or token. If that handler is itself waiting on downstream calls, their streams reset too, and the signal flows all the way to the leaves. That only works if your code honours it: pass the cancellation token into every database call, HTTP request and loop. A handler that ignores it keeps burning a connection and a thread for a result nobody will ever read — which under load is how a slow dependency becomes an outage. How it relates This is the cheapest load-shedding you have: work for abandoned requests stops by itself, for free.

terms.def: The client-side object holding the connection, name resolution and load-balancing policy — expensive, and meant to be shared.
terms.detail: A channel resolves a target name to addresses, maintains a subchannel per address, and applies a load-balancing policy across them. Creating one is costly — DNS, TCP, TLS — so create it once per target and keep it for the process lifetime. Creating a channel per call is the classic performance bug, and it also defeats HTTP/2 multiplexing entirely. Channels have state: IDLE, CONNECTING, READY, TRANSIENT_FAILURE, SHUTDOWN. Watching it is useful — a channel stuck in TRANSIENT_FAILURE is a resolution or TLS problem, not a server problem. Common values Setting Typical Lifetime process-wide singleton Name resolution dns:///, xds:///, or a custom resolver DNS re-resolve 30 s — not once at startup LB policy pick_first (default) or round_robin How it relates In .NET, register it with AddGrpcClient so the factory manages lifetime, handler reuse and DNS refresh for you.

terms.def: Spreading calls across backends when one connection carries all of them.
terms.detail: The default pick_first policy connects to one address and sends everything there. round_robin opens a subchannel to every resolved address and alternates — which is what most internal services actually want, and it requires a resolver that returns all the addresses (headless DNS in Kubernetes, not the Service VIP). The three workable shapes are: client-side balancing with round robin, an L7 proxy or sidecar balancing per request, or a proxyless mesh using xDS. An L4 balancer in front of gRPC is the one that does not work, and it fails invisibly — connection graphs look perfect while one backend takes everything. Options Approach Fits round_robin + headless DNS internal services, no extra hop Sidecar / L7 proxy per-request balancing, central policy xDS (proxyless mesh) large estates, dynamic config L4 balancer does not spread load — avoid How it relates If you must stay on L4, set a maximum connection age so clients re-dial and redistribute periodically.

terms.def: Configured declaratively in the service config, with a budget — not hand-written at every call site.
terms.detail: gRPC has built-in retry support driven by a service config: which methods, which status codes, how many attempts, the backoff curve, and a retry throttling budget that disables retries when the ratio of failures gets high. That budget is the part hand-rolled retry logic always lacks, and it is what prevents a retry storm from finishing off a struggling service. Only retry on codes that are genuinely safe — UNAVAILABLE, sometimes RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED. Retrying ABORTED or INTERNAL on a mutation duplicates work unless the method is idempotent. "retryPolicy": { "maxAttempts": 3, "initialBackoff": "0.1s", "maxBackoff": "1s", "backoffMultiplier": 2, "retryableStatusCodes": ["UNAVAILABLE"] } How it relates Retries consume the same deadline, so a 200 ms budget with three attempts means each attempt gets less — see Retry, backoff & jitter.

terms.def: HTTP/2 windows stopping a fast producer from overwhelming a slow consumer, per stream and per connection.
terms.detail: Each stream has a receive window; the sender may only have that many unacknowledged bytes in flight, and the receiver sends WINDOW_UPDATE as it consumes. Backpressure is therefore built in: a server streaming faster than a client reads simply blocks, rather than buffering without limit. The default 64 KB window is small for high-throughput streaming over a high-latency link, which is the usual cause of "gRPC streaming is slower than I expected". Raising it, or enabling dynamic window sizing, often multiplies throughput. How it relates This is backpressure provided by the transport — but only if your handler actually awaits writes instead of queueing them itself.

terms.def: Middleware for calls: auth, logging, tracing, retries and error mapping in one place.
terms.detail: Interceptors wrap unary and streaming calls on both client and server, so cross-cutting concerns live in one place instead of in every method. The standard set: attach credentials, inject and extract trace context, record metrics per method and status, enforce deadlines, and map domain exceptions to proper status codes. The error mapping one matters most. Without it every unhandled exception becomes UNKNOWN, and callers cannot tell "you sent nonsense" from "try again later" — which makes correct retry behaviour impossible for them. How it relates Streaming interceptors run once per stream, not per message; per-message concerns go inside the handler.

terms.def: How browsers call gRPC at all, and why it cannot be the same protocol.
terms.detail: Browsers cannot control HTTP/2 frames or read trailers, so native gRPC is impossible from a page. gRPC-Web is a compatible protocol that encodes trailers into the response body and works over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2, usually with a proxy translating — Envoy, or middleware in the server itself. The limitation to plan around: client streaming and bidirectional streaming are not supported. Server streaming works. If a browser is a first-class client, consider plain HTTP with JSON transcoding instead of adding a translation layer. How it relates CORS, preflight and exposing grpc-status headers are all part of this; budget for the configuration, not just the library.

terms.def: Serving the same service as a REST/JSON API from annotations in the proto file.
terms.detail: With google.api.http annotations, a method can be exposed at a REST path — GET /v1/orders/{id} — with JSON in and out, while internal callers keep using native gRPC. The server, or a gateway, handles the translation. This is often the right compromise: protobuf efficiency and generated clients between services, an ordinary JSON API for browsers, partners and curl. One contract, two surfaces, no duplicate implementation. rpc GetOrder(GetOrderRequest) returns (Order) { option (google.api.http) = { get: "/v1/orders/{id}" }; } How it relates It also gives you OpenAPI generation, which is usually what a partner integration actually needs.

terms.def: The server describing its own services at runtime, which is what makes grpcurl possible.
terms.detail: Without the .proto file, a binary request is unconstructable by hand. The reflection service lets a client ask the server for its service descriptors, so tools like grpcurl and Postman can list methods and build messages from plain JSON. It is enormously useful in development and a free inventory of your internal API in production. The usual posture is on in development and staging, off in production, with descriptors distributed as a file to the tools that need them. How it relates Pair it with health checking (grpc.health.v1.Health ), which gives probes and balancers a standard way to ask if you are ready.

terms.def: The 4 MB default receive limit, and why hitting it means you wanted streaming.
terms.detail: gRPC defaults to a 4 MB maximum received message size. The first instinct is to raise it; the better reaction is usually to switch to server streaming, so the data arrives as many small messages with flow control instead of one buffer that must be fully materialised in memory on both sides. A single huge message also cannot be cancelled usefully, cannot report partial progress and allocates a large contiguous buffer. Streaming fixes all three. Common values Setting Default Advice Max receive size 4 MB raise deliberately, not reflexively Max send size unlimited (client) bound it Streaming chunk — 32–256 KB per message How it relates For genuinely large binaries, a signed URL to object storage beats both options.

terms.def: Adding fields is safe, changing numbers and types is not, and both sides must be able to deploy independently.
terms.detail: In proto3, unknown fields are preserved rather than rejected, and every field has a default when absent. So adding a field, adding a method or adding an enum value is backward compatible; removing a field, reusing a number, changing a type or renaming an enum value is not. The practical discipline is a schema registry or a linter in CI that diffs the proto against the deployed version and fails on breaking changes. buf breaking does this well, and it is the gRPC equivalent of a schema diff check in GraphQL. Breaking or not Change Safe? Add a field with a new number yes Rename a field yes on the wire, breaks source Change a field's type no Reuse a deleted field number no — and silently wrong Add an RPC yes Remove or rename an RPC no How it relates Reserve deleted numbers and names in the message; it turns a silent data corruption into a compile error.

pages.tagline: Exactly-once delivery does not exist. Exactly-once effect does, and this is how you build it.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · examples in C#, Python, SQL and Kafka · the impossibility result is the Two Generals Problem
pages.description: Idempotency cheatsheet: why exactly-once delivery is impossible, how idempotency keys and dedup windows give you effectively-once processing, and how to size the window.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: One whose repetition changes nothing beyond the first application — naturally safe to retry.
terms.detail: Setting a value is idempotent; adding to it is not. status = 'shipped' applied five times leaves the same state, while balance = balance + 10 applied five times does not. The distinction is the first thing to check before adding any retry. Where you have a choice, prefer absolute values to increments. Writing the new total rather than a delta turns an operation that needs deduplication into one that does not. Naturally idempotent or not Operation Idempotent? SET status = 'shipped' yes UPSERT … SET total = 42 yes DELETE WHERE id = 7 yes balance = balance + 10 no INSERT with a generated id no Send an email, charge a card no How it relates HTTP already classifies this: PUT and DELETE are idempotent, POST is not.

terms.def: A client-generated identifier for one logical operation, stable across every retry of it.
terms.detail: It is what lets a server make a non-idempotent operation safe. The client generates a UUID once, before the first attempt, and sends the same value on every retry. The server records it and recognises the repeat. The single most common implementation bug is generating the key inside the retry loop, so each attempt carries a fresh one and the server sees three unrelated requests. Generate it with the intent, not with the attempt. Properties Property Requirement Generated by the client, before attempt 1 Stable across every retry of that operation Unique across different operations, always Form UUIDv4/v7, or a hash of the intent How it relates The second animation follows one key through a first call, a retry and a concurrent duplicate.

terms.def: What the key is unique within — and the thing that decides whether one tenant can affect another.
terms.detail: Scope the key to the authenticated caller, not globally. A global namespace lets one client guess or collide with another's key and either read their response or suppress their request — a cross-tenant leak dressed as a correctness feature. The usual key is (client_or_tenant_id, endpoint, idempotency_key), which also stops the same key being reused accidentally across different operations. Scoping Scope Verdict Global unsafe — cross-tenant collisions Per tenant minimum acceptable Per tenant + endpoint the usual choice How it relates In a multi-tenant system the tenant comes from the validated token, never from the request body.

terms.def: A hash of the request body stored with the key, so the same key with different content is rejected rather than silently answered.
terms.detail: If a client sends key K with a €40 charge and later sends K with a €4,000 charge, replaying the first response would silently swallow the second request. That is a client bug, and the only safe behaviour is to say so. Stripe returns a 422 in this case. Hash the canonical body at write time, compare on every repeat, and fail loudly when it differs. Responses Situation Return New key process; 200/201 Same key, same body, complete replay the stored response Same key, same body, in flight 409 or wait Same key, different body 422 — never replay How it relates Canonicalise before hashing, or whitespace and key order produce false mismatches.

terms.def: Returning the stored result of the first attempt, so a retry is indistinguishable from the original.
terms.detail: Deduplication that returns a bare 409 is only half useful: the client still does not know whether the charge succeeded and still cannot show a result. Storing the status code and body against the key makes the retry transparent — the client receives exactly what it would have received the first time. Store it in the same transaction as the effect, so there is never a moment where the charge exists and the recorded response does not. What to store Field Why Status code + body replay the exact answer Request fingerprint detect a changed body State: in-flight / done handle concurrency Created-at window expiry How it relates Replay the response for failures too — a stored 422 avoids re-running a doomed request.

terms.def: Two attempts in flight at once — the case a naive check-then-act misses entirely.
terms.detail: "Look up the key; if absent, process" has a race: both attempts look up, both find nothing, both process. Retries with low backoff make this likely rather than theoretical. The fix is an atomic claim: insert the key first and let the unique constraint decide. Exactly one insert succeeds and does the work; the other sees the conflict and either waits briefly or returns 409. Approaches Approach Safe? Check, then insert no — a race INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING yes SET NX in Redis yes A lock on the key yes, with a timeout How it relates An in-flight record also needs a timeout, or a crashed attempt blocks its own retry forever.

terms.def: Never retry: no duplicates, and silent loss whenever something goes wrong.
terms.detail: Fire and forget. It is the correct choice when a lost item is genuinely cheaper than a duplicate one and nobody will miss it: a metrics sample, a log line, a presence ping. It is the wrong choice for anything a human or a ledger will notice, because the failure is invisible — there is no artefact to find, no alert to fire, and nothing to reconcile against. How it relates Choosing it should be deliberate. Most at-most-once systems got there by forgetting to handle an error.

terms.def: Retry until acknowledged: nothing is lost, and duplicates are guaranteed to happen eventually.
terms.detail: The right default, for one asymmetry: duplicates are detectable and losses are not. A repeat carries an identifier you can match; a message that never arrived leaves no trace anywhere. Accepting it means accepting an obligation: every consumer must tolerate repeats. That is not a caveat to note in a document — it is a requirement to test, by replaying the same message twice. Where duplicates come from Source Frequency Client or library retry routine Broker redelivery after a restart routine Consumer group rebalance routine Outbox relay restart routine An operator replaying a queue rare, and large How it relates The outbox pattern produces at-least-once by construction, which is why it mandates idempotent consumers.

terms.def: The thing that cannot be built — and the phrase to push back on in a design review.
terms.detail: It would require the sender to distinguish "lost on the way there" from "processed, lost on the way back". Doing so needs a reliable acknowledgement, which needs a reliable acknowledgement of the acknowledgement, and so on. The regress is the proof. When a product claims exactly-once, it almost always means at-least-once delivery plus deduplication inside its own boundary — which is genuinely useful and stops at the edge of that boundary. What the claims mean Claim Actually Kafka "exactly-once" idempotent producer + transactions, within Kafka Flink "exactly-once" checkpointing + transactional sinks Queue "exactly-once" at-least-once + a dedup window How it relates The moment an effect leaves the system — an email, a card charge — the guarantee ends.

terms.def: At-least-once delivery whose duplicates have been made harmless. What everyone means by exactly-once.
