terms.detail: Three parts: delivery that retries until acknowledged, a key that is stable across those retries, and a store that remembers which keys have been handled — written atomically with the effect itself. The atomicity is the part that gets skipped. Recording the key in Redis and then writing to the database leaves a window where a crash loses one and keeps the other, which reintroduces exactly the problem. The three parts Part Supplied by At-least-once delivery retries, broker, outbox A stable key the client or the producer Dedup, atomic with the effect one transaction in your store How it relates If the dedup record and the effect are in different stores, you need an outbox between them.

terms.def: Where processed keys live — a table or a cache, read and written on the hot path.
terms.detail: A relational table alongside the business data is the simplest correct answer, because the dedup record and the effect commit together. Redis is faster and introduces a second store, which means the atomicity has to be designed rather than inherited. Whatever you choose, the key must be the primary key, and expiry must be automatic — a dedup table nobody prunes becomes the largest table you own. Options Store Trade-off Same database atomic with the effect; simplest Redis with TTL fast, self-expiring, not atomic with the DB Broker-native dedup free, but only within the broker Bloom filter tiny; false positives drop real work How it relates A Bloom filter's false positives mean "silently discarded a genuine request" — rarely an acceptable trade.

terms.def: How long a key is remembered. Too short and duplicates slip through; too long and you store everything forever.
terms.detail: Outside the window the same key looks new, and the operation runs a second time. The window is therefore not a storage decision dressed up as a correctness one — it is the correctness boundary. Twenty-four hours is the common default (Stripe uses it) because it comfortably exceeds any plausible client retry horizon while keeping the table bounded. What happens at the edge of the window How it relates Broker-side dedup windows are usually far shorter — check yours before relying on it.

terms.def: The window must outlast every mechanism that could redeliver — retries, broker redelivery, operator replays.
terms.detail: Add up the worst cases: the client's full retry schedule, the broker's maximum redelivery delay, any dead-letter replay you might perform, and a margin for clock skew. The window must exceed that sum, not the typical case. Then check the cost: storage is roughly rate × window × row size. At 1,000 operations a second over 24 hours that is 86 million rows, which is why the row should be small and the index tight. Worked sizing Input Value Client retry horizon 5 min Broker max redelivery 1 h Manual replay window 12 h → dedup window 24 h, comfortably → storage at 1k/s ~86M rows How it relates If a replay older than the window is ever needed, dedup on a business key instead — it never expires.

terms.def: Deduplicating on something the domain already guarantees unique, instead of a separate key with a window.
terms.detail: A unique constraint on (order_id, line_no) or on an invoice number does the job permanently, with no window to size and no table to prune. Where the domain offers such a key, it is strictly better than an idempotency key. It also survives replays from any era, which is the one case a windowed dedup store cannot handle. Prefer a business key when Situation Key Creating an order line (order_id, line_no) Recording a payment provider's transaction id Importing a row source system's primary key Arbitrary client command idempotency key — no natural one exists How it relates A unique index is deduplication; catching the conflict and returning success is the whole implementation.

terms.def: The consumer-side table recording processed message ids, written in the same transaction as the work.
terms.detail: The mirror of the outbox. On receipt, insert the message id; if the insert conflicts, this message has already been handled and you acknowledge without doing anything. Because the insert and the business change share a transaction, a crash cannot leave one without the other. That atomicity is the entire value. Checking a cache and then writing to the database is the same pattern with the guarantee removed. How it relates Outbox plus inbox is the complete transactional messaging pair.

terms.def: What Kafka and friends provide — real, useful, and bounded to the broker.
terms.detail: Kafka's idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true) stops a retried produce creating duplicate records, using a producer id and sequence numbers. Transactions extend that to atomic read-process-write across partitions. Both guarantees end at the broker boundary. The moment your consumer charges a card or sends an email, you are back to needing your own idempotency — which is why "we use exactly-once Kafka" is not an answer to "can this charge twice?". What it covers Scenario Covered? Producer retry duplicating a record yes Read → process → write, within Kafka yes, with transactions Consumer writing to your database no — your inbox Consumer calling an external API no — idempotency key How it relates The Kafka page covers the producer and consumer settings in detail.

terms.def: Duplicates are not the only hazard — a redelivered older message can overwrite a newer state.
terms.detail: A retry can arrive after a later update has already been applied. Blindly applying it reverts the record, which is a correctness bug deduplication alone does not catch. Carry a monotonic version or sequence number and guard the write: apply only when the incoming version is greater than the stored one. That makes the operation both idempotent and order-insensitive. Guarded write Write Safe? SET status=… WHERE seq < @seq yes SET status=… unconditionally no — can revert total = total + x no — duplicates accumulate How it relates CQRS projections need exactly this guard, for exactly this reason.

terms.def: Emails, charges and webhooks leave your transaction boundary — and your guarantees with it.
terms.detail: A database write can be made idempotent locally. Sending an email cannot: once it is gone, a duplicate is visible to a human. The only defence is to push the idempotency outward — use the provider's idempotency key, or record "sent" atomically with the send attempt and accept the small ambiguity that remains. Order matters here. Do the local, reversible work first and the irreversible external call last, so a failure in between leaves less to explain. Making externals safer Effect Defence Card charge provider's idempotency key Email / SMS dedup on a message id you generate Outbound webhook send a delivery id; the receiver dedups File write write to a temp name, then rename How it relates This is the pivot point in a saga: after it, you can only retry forwards.

pages.title: JWT & token handling
pages.tagline: Signed, not secret. Verifiable, not revocable. Everything else follows from those two facts.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · RFC 7519 (JWT), RFC 7515 (JWS), RFC 7517 (JWK), RFC 8725 (BCP) · examples in C# and Python
pages.description: JWT cheatsheet: the three segments, the validation checks in order, the alg-confusion and none attacks, the revocation problem, and where to store a token.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: A signed JWT — the kind you almost always mean. Three segments, integrity-protected, publicly readable.
terms.detail: JSON Web Signature is the structure behind the familiar a.b.c string. The signature covers the Base64URL-encoded header and payload exactly as transmitted, which is why re-encoding a token can invalidate it even when the JSON is equivalent. "JWT" in conversation almost always means a JWS. A plain unsecured JWT — alg: none, no signature — is part of the spec and should be treated as a forgery in every production context. How it relates Compact serialisation is what makes it fit in a header; the JSON serialisation exists but is rarely used.

terms.def: An encrypted JWT, five segments instead of three — for when the claims themselves must be hidden.
terms.detail: JWS gives integrity; JWE gives confidentiality. If a token must carry something the holder should not read — an internal identifier, a sensitive attribute — encryption is the mechanism, not base64. In practice JWE is uncommon. The usual and better answer is to keep sensitive data out of the token and look it up server-side by sub. Which one Need Use Nobody may tamper with it JWS Nobody may read it JWE, or keep it out Both JWS inside JWE (nested) How it relates Reaching for JWE is usually a sign the token is carrying data that belongs in a database.

terms.def: The first segment: which algorithm signed the token and which key to verify it with.
terms.detail: Three fields matter. alg names the algorithm — and is attacker-controlled, so it must never decide how you verify. kid selects a key from the JWKS, which is what allows rotation. typ distinguishes token types and matters where several kinds circulate. The correct use of alg is as a filter against your own allow-list: if it is not in your list, reject before doing anything else. Fields Field Use Trust it? alg algorithm no — check against your list kid which public key as a lookup hint only typ token type useful for token confusion defence How it relates Both attacks in the second animation are header manipulation.

terms.def: The claims — and a reminder that Base64URL is an encoding, not a protection.
terms.detail: Anyone holding the token can read every claim: paste it into a decoder and it is plain JSON. This surprises people regularly, and it is how internal identifiers, email addresses and role structures end up visible to users and to anyone who finds the token in a log. The payload is also the thing that grows. Large group lists and custom claim sets produce tokens of several kilobytes, which then hit header size limits in proxies. Do not put in it Never Instead Secrets, keys, passwords nowhere near a token Personal data you would not log look up by sub Hundreds of group ids a claim pointing at a lookup Anything that changes often your own session store How it relates "It's encoded" is not a security property; treat the payload as public.

terms.def: The standard seven: iss, sub, aud, exp, nbf, iat, jti — each with a defined meaning and a reason to check it.
terms.detail: They exist so that validation can be generic. A library given an issuer and an audience can check a token from any provider, because these names mean the same thing everywhere. jti is the one most often ignored and the one you need if you ever want replay protection or a revocation list — it is the token's unique id. The seven Claim Meaning Check iss issuer exact match sub subject key your data on it aud intended recipient must be you exp expires at now < exp nbf not before now ≥ nbf iat issued at sanity / max age jti token id replay and revocation lists How it relates All times are seconds since the Unix epoch, in UTC — not milliseconds, which is a common integration bug.

terms.def: The only part that makes the other two trustworthy, and the only part an attacker cannot forge.
terms.detail: Computed over the exact Base64URL text of the header and payload. Any change to either — a single character in a claim — invalidates it, which is what lets a service trust claims it did not create. Verification must be constant-time and must happen before any claim is read. Code that decodes the payload, acts on it, and verifies afterwards is code that trusts an attacker's input. How it relates Decoding without verifying is fine for logging and debugging, and a vulnerability anywhere else.

terms.def: HS256 shares one secret; RS256 and ES256 split signing from verification. The choice decides who can mint tokens.
terms.detail: With HMAC, the key that verifies is the key that signs — so every service able to validate a token is also able to forge one. That is acceptable inside a single application and unacceptable across a fleet. With RSA or ECDSA the issuer holds a private key and everyone else holds only the public one. That asymmetry is what makes JWKS and key rotation possible, and it is the right default for anything multi-service. Choosing Algorithm Use when HS256 one app signs and verifies its own tokens RS256 the default for an identity provider ES256 same, smaller signatures; good for mobile EdDSA modern, fast; check library support none never How it relates Using one key for both HMAC and RSA is what makes algorithm confusion possible.

terms.def: The issuer's public keys as JSON, fetched over HTTPS and cached — what makes rotation invisible.
terms.detail: Each key carries a kid; the token's header names the one it used. Providers publish a new key before signing with it, so a client that caches the set and refreshes on an unknown kid keeps working across a rotation with no coordination. Rate-limit that refresh. A stream of tokens with random kid values is otherwise a cheap denial-of-service against your identity provider — and, through it, against you. Caching rules Rule Why Cache for minutes to hours never fetch per request Refresh on unknown kid handles rotation Rate-limit the refresh prevents amplification HTTPS, validated certificate the keys are the trust anchor How it relates Most frameworks do all of this if you give them the authority URL instead of a hard-coded key.

terms.def: Forging a token by changing the header so the verifier uses an algorithm — and a key — the attacker controls.
terms.detail: The API expects RS256 and verifies with a public key. The attacker edits the header to say HS256 and signs the token using that same public key as the HMAC secret. A library that reads the algorithm from the header will dutifully run HMAC-SHA256 with the key it has — and the signature matches, because the attacker used the same key. The sibling attack is alg: none: strip the signature and declare the token unsecured. Both exist only because the verifier asked the token how to verify itself. The fix, in both cases Do Not Pin an algorithm allow-list read alg from the token One key, one algorithm reuse a key across algorithms Reject none explicitly assume the library does How it relates The second animation walks both attacks and the one configuration line that ends them.

terms.def: exp and nbf decide whether a token is current — and servers whose clocks disagree decide whether that works.
terms.detail: Both are Unix seconds in UTC. Because clocks drift, validators allow a small tolerance — but several libraries default to five minutes, which quietly extends every token's life by five minutes in both directions. Thirty seconds is plenty on machines running NTP, and shortening it is one of the cheapest hardening changes available. Skew defaults Setting Recommended Clock skew 30 s (not the 5 min default) Access token lifetime 5–60 min ID token lifetime minutes Require exp always — reject tokens without it How it relates Lifetime is also your revocation window, which is the next concept.

terms.def: The thing a JWT cannot do. Validation is offline, so nothing server-side can stop an issued token early.
terms.detail: Deactivate a user at 10:05 and their token minted at 10:00 with a 10:15 expiry keeps working until 10:15, because the API never asks anyone whether it should. That window is the price of stateless validation. There are three answers, in increasing cost: short lifetimes so the window is small; a denylist of jti values for high-value tokens; or introspection, which gives immediate revocation and reintroduces the per-request dependency JWTs existed to remove. The revocation window How it relates Short access tokens plus revocable refresh tokens is the standard compromise.

terms.def: The token's unique id — the hook for one-time use and for denylists.
terms.detail: A bearer token can be used any number of times until it expires, which is usually fine for an access token and unacceptable for a one-shot artefact like a password-reset or magic-link token. Recording the jti on first use and rejecting repeats turns it into a single-use credential. The same store doubles as a revocation denylist for high-value tokens — small, bounded by the token lifetime, and cheap to check. When to track jti Token Track? Password reset, magic link yes — one use only Refresh token yes — rotation and reuse detection Ordinary access token no — that is a session store again How it relates Tracking every access token's jti reintroduces exactly the state JWTs were chosen to avoid.

terms.def: Which service the token was minted for — and the check whose absence turns one compromise into many.
terms.detail: Without it, any token your issuer ever signed is accepted by your API: a token for another service, an ID token meant for a client, a token obtained by a different application entirely. One service can then replay a token at another and act as the user. When a service genuinely needs to call another on the user's behalf, exchange the token for one with the right audience rather than forwarding yours. How it relates This is the single most commonly skipped check, and the most commonly exploited.

terms.def: Accepting a token of the wrong kind — an ID token where an access token belongs, or a refresh token at an API.
terms.detail: All of them are JWTs from the same issuer with valid signatures, so signature-only validation accepts all of them. Audience catches most cases; the typ header and an explicit check on token-type claims catch the rest. Deciding which token types your API accepts, and rejecting everything else, is a five-line policy that closes a whole class of confusion. How it relates The OIDC page's first animation is this failure mode in full.

terms.def: JWTs are sent on every request, and a fat one costs bandwidth, cache space and sometimes a 431.
terms.detail: A token with a few standard claims is around 500–800 bytes. Add group memberships, permissions and custom claims and it reaches several kilobytes — at which point proxies start rejecting the request, because default header limits are commonly 4–8 KB. The fix is to carry an identifier rather than the data: put sub and a tenant in the token, and look up roles and groups server-side with a cache. Rough sizes Contents Size Standard claims only ~0.5 KB Plus a few roles ~1 KB Plus 200 group ids 8 KB+ — expect 431s How it relates Cookie storage makes this worse: browsers cap total cookie size per domain at around 4 KB.

terms.def: Where a browser keeps a token, and why every option is a trade rather than a solution.
terms.detail: localStorage is readable by any script on the page, so one XSS or one compromised dependency is a full account takeover. An httpOnly cookie is unreadable by scripts but is sent automatically, which reintroduces CSRF and needs SameSite plus a token or origin check. The honest answer for a browser application is not to hold tokens at all: a BFF keeps them server-side and gives the browser a session cookie instead. Options Where XSS CSRF localStorage exposed safe httpOnly cookie protected needs SameSite + checks In memory only partly safe; lost on reload BFF, server-side best available cookie rules apply How it relates The BFF page covers the server-side-token arrangement in detail.

terms.def: Binding a token to the client that obtained it, so a stolen copy cannot be used — DPoP or mTLS.
terms.detail: Everything above assumes a bearer token: possession is sufficient. Sender-constraining breaks that by requiring an additional proof only the legitimate client can produce — a per-request signed JWT in DPoP, or a client certificate with mTLS. It is the strongest defence against theft, and it is the direction the specifications are moving, but support across providers and SDKs is still uneven. How it relates It does not remove the need for short lifetimes; it removes the value of a stolen token.

terms.def: Token validation is a solved problem with many sharp edges — use a maintained library and configure it.
terms.detail: The failures are not exotic: algorithm confusion, missing audience checks, unverified signatures, generous clock skew, non-constant-time comparison, mishandled kid. Every one has appeared in widely used code written by competent people. Your job is configuration, not cryptography: pin the algorithms, set the issuer and audience, tighten the skew, point at the authority and let it manage JWKS. How it relates If you find yourself splitting a token on '.' in application code, stop.

pages.title: Kubernetes
pages.tagline: You declare what should run; it keeps a fleet of machines making that true, forever.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · release line 1.36
pages.description: Kubernetes cheatsheet: architecture, animated deployment and self-healing walk-throughs, key concepts with deep dives, kubectl commands, trade-offs and alternatives.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: A set of machines (nodes) plus a control plane that manages them as one big computer for containers.
terms.detail: A cluster is the unit you create, upgrade and secure. You talk to it only through its API server; the machines behind it are interchangeable. Control plane: API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager. Managed services (AKS, EKS, GKE) run and patch it for you. Worker nodes: where your pods actually run. Typical sizes Setting Nodes Laptop (kind, minikube) 1–3 containers pretending to be nodes Small production 3–10 nodes Large hundreds; the documented limit is 5,000 nodes Many companies run several clusters (dev, staging, prod, per region) rather than one giant one: a smaller blast radius and easier upgrades.

terms.def: A worker machine (VM or physical) that runs pods. Each runs a kubelet, kube-proxy and a container runtime.
terms.detail: A node offers allocatable resources to pods: its total CPU and memory minus what is reserved for the OS and Kubernetes' own agents. On every node kubelet: the agent. Watches the API server for pods assigned to this node and starts or stops their containers. container runtime: usually containerd; pulls images and runs containers. kube-proxy (or a CNI like Cilium): implements Service routing on the node. Common sizes Production nodes are often 4–16 vCPU with 16–64 GiB of memory (e.g. Azure Standard_D4s_v5: 4 vCPU, 16 GiB). Several medium nodes usually beat one huge node: losing one costs less. Statuses: Ready, NotReady (kubelet stopped reporting), SchedulingDisabled (cordoned for maintenance).

terms.def: The smallest deployable unit: one or more containers that share an IP address and volumes and are always scheduled together.
terms.detail: You almost never create pods directly; a Deployment, StatefulSet, DaemonSet or Job creates them for you and replaces them when they die. Containers in one pod talk over localhost and can share volumes. Typical shape: one main container, optionally a sidecar (log shipper, proxy) and init containers that run first. Pods are ephemeral: a replacement gets a new name and a new IP. Reach them through a Service. Lifecycle phases Pending → Running → Succeeded / Failed. Common trouble states you'll see in kubectl get pods: ImagePullBackOff (wrong image or no registry access), CrashLoopBackOff (container keeps exiting), OOMKilled (exceeded memory limit).

terms.def: The CPU unit Kubernetes counts in: 1 CPU = one vCPU or hyperthread = 1000 millicores (1000m ).
terms.detail: A vCPU is one virtual CPU as sold by a cloud provider: usually one hyperthread of a physical core. Kubernetes measures CPU in these units and lets you ask for fractions, written in millicores: 1000m = 1 vCPU, 250m = a quarter. Common values Request Typical workload 50m–100m sidecars, small agents, idle-most-of-the-time services 250m–500m a typical web API or worker replica 1 – 2 CPU-heavy services, JVM apps at startup, build jobs 4+ databases, ML inference, batch processing A node with 4 vCPU has roughly 3.8 vCPU allocatable after system reservations. The scheduler only places a pod where the sum of requests fits. CPU on a 4-vCPU node How it relates Requests reserve vCPU for scheduling; limits cap usage. Going over the CPU limit only slows the container (throttling); going over the memory limit kills it (OOMKilled ). The HPA measures CPU usage as a percentage of the request, so a wrong request makes autoscaling wrong too. Node size in vCPU sets how many pods fit; cloud cost is mostly "vCPU × hours".

terms.def: Per-container CPU and memory settings: requests are reserved for scheduling, limits are the hard ceiling.
terms.detail: resources: requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi } limits: { memory: 512Mi } Requests: what the scheduler adds up to decide if a pod fits on a node. Your guaranteed share. CPU limit: usage above it is throttled. Many teams set no CPU limit to avoid needless throttling, relying on requests for fairness. Memory limit: exceeding it gets the container killed (OOMKilled) and restarted. Always set one. Quality of Service classes Class When Evicted Guaranteed requests = limits for CPU and memory last Burstable requests set, lower than limits middle BestEffort nothing set first Memory units: Mi / Gi are powers of 2 (256Mi ≈ 268 MB); M / G are powers of 10.

terms.def: Declares how many replicas of a stateless pod should run and rolls out new versions gradually.
terms.detail: The workhorse object for web apps, APIs and workers. You change the image tag; the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and shifts pods over. Rolling update knobs maxSurge: 25%: how many extra pods may exist during a rollout. maxUnavailable: 25%: how many may be missing. Set to 0 for zero downtime. New pods must pass their readiness probe before old ones are removed. kubectl rollout undo deployment/web switches back to the previous ReplicaSet in seconds. Kubernetes keeps 10 old revisions by default. For stateful software with stable identities (databases, Kafka brokers) use a StatefulSet instead.

terms.def: Keeps exactly N identical pods running. Deployments create and manage ReplicaSets for you.
terms.detail: A ReplicaSet runs the simplest reconcile loop: count the pods matching my label selector; create or delete pods until the count equals replicas. You rarely touch them directly. During a rollout a Deployment owns two ReplicaSets, old and new, and scales one down while scaling the other up. Their names carry the pod-template hash: web-7d9f8c, and pods are named web-7d9f8c-x2k4q. Deleting a pod by hand is safe: the ReplicaSet notices the shortfall and creates a replacement within seconds.

terms.def: A stable virtual IP and DNS name that load-balances to the Ready pods matching a label selector.
terms.detail: Pods come and go with new IPs; a Service gives clients one address that never changes: web.shop.svc.cluster.local, or just web from the same namespace. Types Type Reachable from ClusterIP (default) inside the cluster only NodePort every node's IP on a port 30000–32767 LoadBalancer a cloud load balancer with a public or private IP Headless (clusterIP: None) DNS returns pod IPs directly (used by StatefulSets) Only pods passing their readiness probe are listed as endpoints, which is how rollouts and failures avoid sending traffic to broken pods.

terms.def: HTTP(S) routing from outside the cluster to Services by host name and path, with TLS termination.
terms.detail: Instead of one cloud load balancer per Service, a single entry point routes shop.example.com/api to the api Service and / to web. Ingress: the original API; needs an ingress controller (NGINX, Traefik, cloud-specific) installed in the cluster. Gateway API: the newer, more expressive successor (traffic splitting, header matching, roles for platform vs app teams). Prefer it for new setups. TLS certificates are usually issued automatically by cert-manager with Let's Encrypt.

terms.def: A virtual folder inside a cluster for grouping and isolating objects, quotas and permissions.
terms.detail: Names must be unique only within a namespace, so team-a and team-b can both have a Service called api. Built-in: default, kube-system (cluster components), kube-public, kube-node-lease. Attach ResourceQuotas (max CPU/memory per team), RBAC roles and NetworkPolicies per namespace. Namespaces are not a security boundary by themselves: pods can still talk across them unless NetworkPolicies say otherwise. Common layouts: one namespace per team, per app, or per environment in a shared dev cluster. Select one with -n shop or set it as default for your context.

terms.def: Key/value tags on objects (app=web) and the queries that pick objects by them. The glue of Kubernetes.
terms.detail: Kubernetes rarely references objects by name. A Service, ReplicaSet or NetworkPolicy finds its pods with a selector such as app=web,tier=frontend. metadata: labels: { app: web, version: "1.4", team: shop } --- selector: matchLabels: { app: web } Recommended keys: app.kubernetes.io/name, /version, /component, /part-of. Query from the CLI: kubectl get pods -l app=web. Gotcha: a typo in a selector means a Service with zero endpoints, silently. Check with kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web.

terms.def: Configuration and credentials stored separately from the image and injected as env vars or files.
terms.detail: The same image runs in dev and prod; only its ConfigMaps and Secrets differ. ConfigMap: plain settings (feature flags, URLs, config files). Secret: passwords, tokens, TLS keys. Only base64-encoded, not encrypted, unless you enable encryption at rest. Restrict access with RBAC. Mounted as files they update in place after a short delay; as env vars they're read only at container start, so you need a rollout (kubectl rollout restart) to pick up changes. Production teams often sync secrets from a vault (Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault) with the External Secrets Operator.

terms.def: A pod's request for durable storage ("10Gi, read-write"), fulfilled by a PersistentVolume from a StorageClass.
terms.detail: Container filesystems disappear with the pod. A PVC asks for a disk that outlives it; the cluster provisions one dynamically (an Azure Disk, an EBS volume…) via a StorageClass. Access modes Mode Meaning Typical backend ReadWriteOnce one node mounts it read-write cloud block disks ReadWriteMany many nodes read-write NFS, Azure Files, EFS ReadOnlyMany many nodes read-only shared datasets Block disks are tied to one availability zone: a pod using one can only be rescheduled to nodes in that zone. Check the reclaimPolicy: Delete removes the disk with the claim.

terms.def: Like a Deployment, but each pod gets a stable name, stable DNS and its own persistent volume.
terms.detail: Pods are named db-0, db-1, db-2, created in order and keep their name and disk across restarts. A headless Service gives each one a DNS name like db-0.db. Used for databases, Kafka brokers, Elasticsearch, ZooKeeper-style clusters: software where members are not interchangeable. Running databases on Kubernetes is possible but demanding (backups, upgrades, failover). Operators such as CloudNativePG or Strimzi automate it; managed cloud databases are often simpler.

terms.def: Runs one copy of a pod on every node (or a chosen subset), for node-level agents.
terms.detail: When a node joins, the DaemonSet adds its pod there automatically; when it leaves, the pod goes with it. Typical uses: log collectors (Fluent Bit), metrics agents (node-exporter, Datadog agent), network plugins (Cilium), storage drivers. Use a nodeSelector or tolerations to target, say, only GPU nodes.

terms.def: Health checks the kubelet runs: liveness restarts a stuck container, readiness controls traffic, startup protects slow boots.
terms.detail: Probe If it fails… Check readiness pod removed from Service endpoints (no restart) "can I serve traffic now?" (DB connected, cache warm) liveness container is restarted "am I deadlocked?" Keep it cheap and local startup other probes wait until it passes for apps that take a minute to boot readinessProbe: httpGet: { path: /healthz/ready, port: 8000 } periodSeconds: 5 Classic mistake: a liveness probe that checks the database. When the database is slow, every pod restarts at once and turns a blip into an outage.

terms.def: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler: adds or removes replicas based on CPU, memory or custom metrics.
terms.detail: kubectl autoscale deployment web --cpu-percent=70 --min=2 --max=10 Every 15 s it computes desired = ceil(current × actual / target). With 3 pods at 140% of their CPU request and a 70% target, it scales to 6. Needs metrics-server and CPU requests on the pods, since utilisation is measured against them. Scales down slowly by design (5-minute stabilisation window) to avoid flapping. It adds pods, not machines: the Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter adds nodes when pods stay Pending. KEDA scales on queue length, Kafka lag and more.

terms.def: The package manager for Kubernetes: templated YAML bundles ("charts") installed and upgraded as releases.
terms.detail: helm repo add bitnami https://charts.bitnami.com/bitnami helm install cache bitnami/redis -n shop --set auth.enabled=true helm upgrade cache bitnami/redis -f values-prod.yaml helm rollback cache 1 A chart is templates plus a values.yaml; you override values per environment. Helm records each install as a numbered revision you can roll back to. Alternatives: Kustomize (built into kubectl, patches plain YAML without templates) and GitOps tools like Argo CD or Flux that apply either from a Git repo.

pages.title: L4 vs L7 load balancing
pages.tagline: One reads the envelope, the other opens the letter. That single difference explains every trade-off between them.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · examples use nginx, HAProxy, Envoy, YARP and Kubernetes Gateway API
pages.description: Load balancing cheatsheet: what an L4 balancer can and cannot see, what L7 buys you, why HTTP/2 breaks connection-level balancing, and the power of two choices.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: Choosing a backend from the TCP/UDP five-tuple, then forwarding packets without inspecting them.
terms.detail: The decision is made once, when the connection is established, and every subsequent packet follows the same path. Because nothing is parsed, it runs at line rate — in the kernel with IPVS or eBPF, or on dedicated hardware — and it works for any protocol: HTTP, gRPC, Postgres, SMTP, a custom binary protocol. Its blindness is the whole trade. It cannot route by path, cannot retry a failed request elsewhere, and cannot tell the difference between a connection carrying one request and one carrying ten thousand. Where you meet it Product Notes Kubernetes Service kube-proxy / IPVS — L4 AWS NLB, Azure Load Balancer L4, very high throughput HAProxy in mode tcp L4 IPVS, eBPF, Maglev kernel-level L4 How it relates A Kubernetes Service is L4; an Ingress or Gateway is L7. Knowing which you have explains a lot of behaviour.

terms.def: Terminating the connection, parsing the request, and choosing a backend per request.
terms.detail: Once the request is parsed, everything becomes possible: route /api and /static to different pools, send 5% of traffic to a canary, retry an idempotent request on another backend, inject headers, enforce per-user rate limits, serve from cache. It also balances the right unit. An L7 balancer picks a backend for each request, which is what keeps distribution even when one connection carries thousands of them. What it unlocks Capability Needs L7? Route by path or host yes Retry on another backend yes Canary by header or percentage yes Per-request balancing yes Rate limit per user yes Raw TCP throughput no — use L4 How it relates A service mesh sidecar is an L7 balancer placed next to every workload.

terms.def: How an L4 balancer picks: hash the connection's identity and map it onto a backend.
terms.detail: Source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port, protocol. The source port varies per connection, so a single client spreads naturally across backends — unless the balancer hashes on source IP alone, which is sometimes done deliberately to pin a client. With plain modulo hashing, adding or removing a backend reshuffles nearly every connection. Production balancers use consistent hashing or Maglev hashing so a change moves only a small fraction. Hash inputs Input Effect Full 5-tuple even spread, new connection may move Source IP only pins a client; uneven behind NAT Consistent hash minimal disruption when the pool changes How it relates Source-IP hashing behind a corporate NAT sends an entire office to one backend.

terms.def: Choosing per request rather than per connection — the thing HTTP/2 makes essential.
terms.detail: Under HTTP/1.1 a connection carries one request at a time, so balancing connections approximately balances requests. Under HTTP/2 and gRPC, a single long-lived connection multiplexes thousands of concurrent streams — and an L4 balancer still sees one connection. The result is that connections can be perfectly distributed while requests are not distributed at all. Only something that parses the protocol can pick a backend per request. How it relates The second animation is this failure, with numbers.

terms.def: The classic gRPC-behind-an-L4-balancer problem: even connections, wildly uneven load.
terms.detail: A handful of long-lived clients — a gateway, a mesh, a batch worker — each open one connection and keep it for hours. Every request on that connection lands on the backend chosen at connection time, so one backend can take the overwhelming majority of traffic while others idle. It is worse than uneven: it also defeats scaling out, because new backends receive no traffic until someone dials a new connection. Fixes, best first Fix Note L7 balancer or sidecar per-request; the real answer Client-side balancing gRPC name resolver + picker Max connection age forces periodic re-dial Max requests per connection same idea, request-based How it relates Queueing theory names the underlying problem: per-connection pinning is dedicated queues, and pooling beats them.

terms.def: Where encryption ends — and the thing that decides whether L7 features are available at all.
terms.detail: Three arrangements. Termination decrypts at the balancer, enabling every L7 feature and leaving the last hop in plaintext. Passthrough forwards encrypted bytes, so only L4 decisions are possible — though SNI can still be read for routing. Re-encryption decrypts, inspects and re-encrypts to the backend, which is the usual answer when the internal network is not trusted. The three Mode L7 features Backend hop Termination all plaintext Re-encryption all encrypted Passthrough none (SNI only) end-to-end TLS How it relates SNI routing is the useful middle ground: route by hostname without decrypting anything.

terms.def: Round robin, least connections, least response time — and why the obvious one is rarely best.
terms.detail: Round robin ignores load entirely, so one slow backend keeps receiving its full share. Least connections approximates load well and is a good default. Least response time (or a latency EWMA) reacts fastest to a degrading instance. The subtlety is that "send to the least loaded" behaves badly across many independent balancers: they all observe the same idle backend and all send to it at once, producing a herd. Power of two choices How it relates Envoy's default is weighted least-request using two random choices, for exactly this reason.

terms.def: Sample two backends at random and take the less loaded one — nearly optimal, with no global state.
terms.detail: The surprising result from randomised load balancing: picking the better of two random samples reduces the maximum load from roughly log n / log log n to log log n. One extra sample buys an exponential improvement. Practically, it gets you most of least-connections' quality without needing a consistent global view, and without several balancers stampeding the same idle backend. Comparison Strategy State needed Herding Random none none, but uneven Round robin a counter none; ignores load Least connections global view yes, across balancers Two choices local only no How it relates It is the default in Envoy, Finagle and several meshes; worth knowing why before changing it.

terms.def: How a balancer learns a backend is unfit — actively by probing, or passively by watching real traffic.
terms.detail: Active checks probe an endpoint on a schedule. They are predictable and catch a dead instance even with no traffic, but a shallow check (TCP connect, or a handler that returns 200 unconditionally) tells you only that the process is running. Passive checks observe real responses and eject a backend that starts failing. They catch problems a synthetic probe misses, and they are what the sidecar page calls outlier detection. Designing the probe Check Catches TCP connect process is dead HTTP 200 on /healthz app is running Readiness incl. dependencies cannot serve — careful, cascades Passive 5xx ejection partial, real failures How it relates A readiness check that fails when a shared dependency is slow removes every backend at once — the check becomes the outage.

terms.def: Removing a backend gently: stop sending new work, let in-flight requests finish.
terms.detail: Without it, every deploy produces a burst of errors: the instance disappears while requests are still being served. With it, the balancer stops routing new requests, waits for the existing ones, and only then lets the instance go. The drain timeout must exceed your slowest normal request, and the application must fail its readiness check before it stops accepting connections, so the balancer learns first. Shutdown order # Step 1 fail readiness — balancer stops sending 2 wait for the balancer to notice 3 finish in-flight requests 4 close and exit How it relates Step 2 is the one teams omit, and it is why "we drain properly" still produces 502s.

terms.def: Ramping traffic to a new backend instead of giving it a full share immediately.
terms.detail: A freshly started instance has a cold cache, an unJITted runtime and empty connection pools. Sending it an equal share immediately makes it slow, which with a least-connections algorithm can even attract more traffic — because it has few open connections. Slow start gives it a linearly increasing weight over a warm-up window, typically 30 to 60 seconds, so it has time to become as fast as its peers. How it relates Without it, scaling out during an incident can briefly make latency worse.

terms.def: Pinning a client to a backend — useful, and a constraint you pay for in every other dimension.
terms.detail: L4 does it by hashing the source IP; L7 does it properly with a cookie, which survives NAT and mobile network changes. Either way it trades away even distribution, easy scaling and graceful draining. Prefer removing the need: put session state in Redis or a signed cookie, and any instance can serve any request. Keep affinity for genuine cases — in-memory caches with high hit rates, stateful connections like WebSockets. Cost of affinity You lose Because Even load clients are not equal Easy scale-out existing clients stay put Clean draining pinned sessions must move Pooling gains dedicated queues, by definition How it relates Queueing theory prices this exactly: at ρ = 0.8, pinning costs about four times the queueing delay.

terms.def: Mapping keys to backends so that adding or removing one moves only a small fraction of them.
terms.detail: With plain modulo, changing the pool size reshuffles nearly everything — disastrous when the hash is choosing a cache node or a sticky session. Consistent hashing with virtual nodes moves roughly 1/n of keys instead. Google's Maglev adds near-perfect evenness with minimal disruption, which is why it is the scheme in several cloud L4 balancers. How it relates Use it whenever the hash picks something stateful: a cache shard, a session, a partition owner.

terms.def: Behind a balancer every request appears to come from the balancer — unless you arrange otherwise.
terms.detail: L7 balancers add X-Forwarded-For; L4 balancers can use the PROXY protocol to prepend the original addresses. Without one of these, rate limiting, geo-rules and audit logs all see a handful of balancer addresses. And X-Forwarded-For is client-supplied until you prove otherwise: trust only the hops you control, counting from the right, or an attacker simply sets whatever address they like. Mechanisms Mechanism Layer X-Forwarded-For L7, trust-boundary aware Forwarded (RFC 7239) L7, standardised PROXY protocol L4, prepends a header to the stream Direct server return backend sees the real client How it relates Rate limiting on an untrusted X-Forwarded-For is trivially bypassed.

terms.def: An L4 technique where responses bypass the balancer and go straight to the client.
terms.detail: Requests go through the balancer, responses do not. Since most traffic is outbound — a small request, a large response — this removes the balancer from the expensive direction and lets modest hardware front enormous bandwidth. The cost is sophistication: it needs layer-2 adjacency or tunnelling, backends configured with the virtual IP, and it rules out anything requiring the balancer to see the response. How it relates Common in large CDN and video deployments; rarely needed below that scale.

terms.def: Choosing a region or a point of presence before any connection is made — DNS or anycast.
terms.detail: DNS-based steering returns different addresses per client, which is flexible but slow to change because of caching and resolvers that ignore TTLs. Anycast advertises the same address from many locations and lets BGP pick, which fails over in seconds but gives coarse control. Either way this is a separate tier above your L4 and L7 balancers, with its own failure modes and its own health signals. Comparison DNS Anycast Granularity per client per network path Failover speed minutes (TTL) seconds Control fine coarse How it relates DNS TTLs are advisory; plan for clients that cache far longer than you asked.

terms.def: An L7 balancer can resend a failed request to another backend — which is powerful and easy to misconfigure.
terms.detail: Because it sees the request, it can retry on a connection failure or a 503 without the client knowing. The dangers are the usual ones: retrying non-idempotent requests, and adding another layer to an already-retrying stack. Restrict retries to safe methods and connection-level failures, cap them, and set a retry budget so a broad failure does not multiply load. Safe defaults Setting Value Retry on connect failure, reset, 503 Methods idempotent only, unless keyed Attempts 1–2 Budget 10–20% of active requests How it relates Count the balancer's retries when auditing your total amplification — they are easy to forget.

terms.def: Hardware, cloud service, software proxy or sidecar — the same decisions at different places.
terms.detail: Cloud L4 and L7 services cover most needs with no operations. A software proxy — nginx, HAProxy, Envoy, YARP — gives full control at the cost of running it. A sidecar puts an L7 balancer next to every workload, which is how a mesh does per-request balancing for east-west traffic. North-south (internet to you) and east-west (service to service) have different requirements, and it is common to use different tools for each. Typical stack Tier Usually Global DNS or anycast Edge cloud L4 — volume, DDoS Ingress L7 — routing, TLS, canary East-west sidecar or client-side L7 How it relates The sidecar page covers the per-workload case, including what it costs per pod.

pages.title: Little's Law
pages.tagline: How many are inside = how fast they arrive × how long they stay. That's the whole thing.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · proved in 1961 and not going to change; the examples are .NET 10 (LTS), PostgreSQL and Prometheus
pages.description: Little's Law cheatsheet: L = lambda x W animated from a real queue, the three ways to rearrange it, what it does not tell you about utilisation, and the boundary mistake that makes it look wrong.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: The three quantities: items inside, arrival rate, time inside. Fix any two and the third is determined.
terms.detail: Everything on this page is about these three letters and the fact that they are not free to move independently. Symbol Is Measured in In your system L average number in the system items (dimensionless) in-flight requests, busy connections, queue depth λ average arrival rate items per second requests/s, queries/s, messages/s W average time an item spends inside seconds latency, residence time, time-in-queue All three are averages over the same window. That sounds pedantic and is the source of most arithmetic that does not reconcile: a λ taken over five minutes and a W taken over the last ten seconds will not multiply to the L you measured at this instant. And all three are means, which is why this page and the percentiles page pull in opposite directions. Little's Law is exact about averages and says nothing whatsoever about your p99. A system can satisfy L = λW perfectly while a tenth of its users are having an unacceptable time.

terms.def: The one precondition: over the window you measure, as many items leave as arrive. Without it there is no stable L to talk about.
terms.detail: Little's Law needs remarkably little, but it does need this. If arrivals exceed departures the population grows without bound, and an "average number in the system" over a growing quantity is not a meaningful number. Condition Status Arrivals ≈ departures over the window the law applies exactly Arrivals > departures unstable — L grows, W grows, no steady state Arrivals < departures draining; fine once it settles Bursty but balanced over the window applies — burstiness is irrelevant to the identity Note what is not required: no assumption about the arrival distribution, the service time distribution, the number of servers, or the queue discipline. FIFO, LIFO, priority, random — the law does not care. That is what makes it an identity rather than a model, and why it needs no calibration. In practice "steady state" means: pick a window long enough that start-up and drain effects wash out. For a web service a few minutes is usually plenty; for a batch pipeline it may be a whole run.

terms.def: The box you draw around "the system". Move it and all three numbers change — which is why an unstated boundary makes the law look broken.
terms.detail: The law holds for any boundary you care to draw, and it holds separately for each one. The mistake is mixing numbers from different boxes. Boundary L is W is The whole request in-flight requests end-to-end latency Just the queue queue depth waiting time only Just the servers busy servers service time only The connection pool checked-out connections checkout-to-return time A downstream call outstanding calls that call's latency One quantity is shared: in steady state λ is the same through every nested boundary, because everything that enters the outer box also passes through the inner ones. That is what lets you chain the law across layers. So the discipline is one sentence long: say which box you mean, every time. "We have 100 in flight" is not a fact until somebody says in flight where.

terms.def: W is the whole time inside the boundary — waiting plus being served. Substituting service time is the most common error.
terms.detail: Your service's own stopwatch usually starts when a handler begins and stops when it returns. That is service time. The request was in your system before that: in the accept queue, waiting for a thread, waiting for a connection. residence time W = waiting time Wq + service time S If you use You get S, but L from the whole system numbers that do not reconcile; you conclude the law is wrong S, consistently, with servers-only L correct — and L is then just utilisation × servers W end to end, with in-flight L correct, and the one you usually want The gap between the two is the single most useful diagnostic on this page. If end-to-end W is 200 ms and your handler reports 8 ms, then 192 ms is queueing somewhere you are not instrumenting — and that is where the fix is.

terms.def: ρ = λ/μ, the fraction of capacity in use. Little's Law does not mention it, and that omission is the point.
terms.detail: μ is the service rate — how many items a server could finish per second if never idle. ρ is how much of that you are using. ρ What it feels like < 50% queue mostly empty, W ≈ service time 70% queueing becomes visible in the tail 85% W is several times service time; p99 is much worse 95% W is around 20× service time for a simple queue ≥ 100% unstable: the queue grows until something sheds it For a single-server queue with exponential service, W = S / (1 − ρ). That denominator is the whole story: it is why the last 10% of capacity costs more than the first 70%. Little's Law is perfectly happy at ρ = 0.99 — it will multiply your enormous W by your λ and hand you an enormous L. It is an identity, so it cannot warn you. The warning has to come from the utilisation curve.

terms.def: As utilisation approaches 1, waiting time rises hyperbolically. Nothing got slower; there is simply nowhere for arrivals to go.
terms.detail: The shape matters more than the formula. Latency is nearly flat for most of the range and then goes vertical, which is why systems feel fine right up until they do not. ρ W as a multiple of service time Add 10% traffic and W becomes 0.5 2× 2.2× 0.7 3.3× 4.2× 0.8 5× 7.7× 0.9 10× 50× 0.95 20× unstable Read the last column. At 50% utilisation a traffic bump is a rounding error; at 90% the same bump is an incident. This is the real argument for the headroom numbers on the back-of-the-envelope page, and it is why "the CPU is only at 85%" is not the reassurance it sounds like. It is also why autoscaling thresholds belong in the flat part of the curve. By the time a metric shows you are on the steep part, the queue has already grown and the new capacity arrives late.

terms.def: Bursty arrivals or uneven service times move the wall closer. Kingman's formula puts a number on it.
terms.detail: Little's Law ignores variability entirely — correctly, because it is an identity. But what causes W is extremely sensitive to it. Wq ≈ (ρ / (1 - ρ)) × ((ca² + cs²) / 2) × S The middle term is the variability penalty: ca and cs are the coefficients of variation of arrivals and of service time. With perfectly regular arrivals and constant service both are 0 and there is no queueing at all below ρ = 1. With exponential arrivals and service both are 1, the term is 1, and you get the familiar curve. Situation Effect Bursty traffic (ca > 1) queueing at much lower utilisation Mixed cheap and expensive requests (cs > 1) same — one slow request parks the server Smoothing arrivals (a leaky bucket) lowers ca, buys back utilisation Splitting slow work onto its own pool lowers cs for the fast path This is the theory behind two practices that otherwise look unrelated: rate limiting with a leaky bucket, and giving expensive endpoints their own thread pool. Both are attacks on variability rather than on load.

terms.def: The main thing people use the law for: how many connections, threads or permits you need to carry a given rate at a given latency.
terms.detail: The arithmetic is one line; the judgement is in what you put in it. connections = queries_per_second × seconds_per_query = 2000 × 0.040 = 80 → a pool of 100 leaves headroom Rate Query time Minimum pool 500 /s 10 ms 5 2,000 /s 40 ms 80 2,000 /s 200 ms 400 — and now the database is the problem 10,000 /s 5 ms 50 Two refinements that matter. Size for peak λ, not average — a 3× daily peak means a 3× pool or a queue at the peak. And use the latency you expect under load, not the one you measured on an idle box, or you will size the pool for a world that only exists at 3am. Bigger is not safer. An oversized pool lets your service push more concurrent work at a database that cannot take it, converting a polite queue in your application into a slow one in the database. The pool is a concurrency limit, and that is a feature.

terms.def: What happens when W grows and the pool is fixed: the pool fills, arrivals queue outside it, and the whole service stalls on one slow dependency.
terms.detail: This is Little's Law as a failure mode. The pool size L is fixed by configuration, so when W rises, λ must fall — the identity has no other option. pool = 100 connections normal: λ = 100 / 0.020 = 5,000 req/s degraded: λ = 100 / 0.500 = 200 req/s ← the dependency slowed 25× Nothing about your service changed. Its capacity fell by 96% because a downstream call went from 20 ms to 500 ms, and your pool arithmetic followed the identity down. Symptom What it means Pool at 100% checked out, CPU low you are waiting, not working Throughput collapses, latency climbs classic L-fixed, W-rising Timeouts cluster at the pool-wait timeout the queue outside the pool is the bottleneck The defences are all about not letting W run away: aggressive timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads so one dependency cannot consume the whole pool, and shedding load rather than queueing it.

terms.def: The law applies at every layer at once, and λ is shared between them. That is what makes a latency budget add up.
terms.detail: Because every request that enters the outer boundary passes through the inner ones, the same λ flows through all of them — so the L values add up in a way you can budget with. Layer W L at λ = 500 /s Whole request 40 ms 20 — pool wait 12 ms 6 — the query 8 ms 4 — everything else (CPU, serialisation) 20 ms 10 The inner W values sum to the outer W, and so the inner L values sum to the outer L. That gives you a direct way to find where the in-flight work actually sits: instrument each layer, multiply by the shared λ, and the layer with the largest L is where your concurrency is going. It also explains fan-out. If one request makes three parallel downstream calls, the downstream boundary sees λ = 1,500 /s even though your service sees 500 /s — the rates differ because the boundary differs, not because something is wrong.

terms.def: All three quantities must come from the same interval, long enough for start-up and drain to wash out.
terms.detail: Most "Little's Law doesn't work here" reports are a window problem. Mistake Effect Instantaneous L, 5-minute λ L jumps around; the product never matches Window shorter than W most items neither arrive nor leave inside it Window spanning a deploy or a scale-out two different systems averaged together Window including a drain departures exceed arrivals; not steady state Rule of thumb: the window should be at least ten times W, and should not contain a change in the system. For a 40 ms service that means anything from a few seconds up; for a batch job with a 2-hour residence time it means days. Prometheus makes this easy to get right by accident and easy to get wrong on purpose: use the same rate() interval for λ and for the histogram you derive W from, and take L from a gauge averaged over the same interval.

terms.def: The same identity outside software: cap work in progress and cycle time falls, because λ is fixed by demand.
terms.detail: Kanban's central claim is Little's Law rearranged. With throughput set by how fast the team actually finishes things, W = L / λ says the only lever you control directly is L. WIP (L) Throughput (λ) Cycle time (W) 30 items 5 / week 6 weeks 15 items 5 / week 3 weeks 5 items 5 / week 1 week Starting more work does not make the team finish faster; it just increases L, and W rises to match. The counter-intuitive consequence — that limiting WIP shortens delivery time without anyone working harder — is the identity, not a management theory. The same argument applies to an incident queue, a code review backlog, or a support rota. If you want things to come out faster and λ is fixed by capacity, the only honest move is to put fewer in.

terms.def: Carry the units through. If they do not cancel to "items", you have mixed two boundaries or two windows.
terms.detail: The cheapest error check on this page, and it catches the boundary mistakes too. L = λ × W [items/s] [s] = [items] ✓ [items/min] [s] = nonsense ✗ mixed units [items/s] [ms] = 1000× too big ✗ classic Common slip Fix λ per minute, W in seconds convert λ to per-second first W in milliseconds divide by 1,000 — or expect a 1000× answer λ counted per user rather than per request pick one item type and stay with it The "one item type" rule is worth stating explicitly. If λ is page views and W is the time of an API call, the product is not anything. The item flowing in must be the same kind of item whose residence time you measured.

terms.def: When arrivals exceed departures there is no steady state, L grows without bound, and the law has nothing to describe.
terms.detail: The identity does not break — it simply has no finite average to be about. What happens instead is mechanical and always the same. Stage What you see λ creeps above μ queue depth starts climbing and never comes back down L grows linearly with time memory for queued work grows too W grows linearly timeouts begin firing for the oldest items Clients retry λ increases — the feedback loop that turns a blip into an outage The important detail is the last row: retries make an overloaded system more overloaded, which is why the rate limiting page insists on backoff with jitter and on shedding rather than queueing. The only cures are the three that reduce λ or raise μ: shed load, add capacity, or make the work cheaper. A bigger queue is not a cure — it just converts a fast failure into a slow one, with the same ending.

terms.def: The gap between λ and μ. Little's Law tells you what you need; headroom is what keeps W off the wall.
terms.detail: Having sized a pool or a fleet with the law, the follow-up question is where on the utilisation curve you intend to sit. Target ρ Suitable for 30–50% bursty traffic, slow-scaling tiers, anything where a failover doubles a neighbour's load 50–70% ordinary stateless services — the usual default 70–80% smooth, well-understood, fast-autoscaling workloads > 85% batch work that can wait, and nothing a user is waiting for These are the same numbers as on the back-of-the-envelope page, and now you can see where they come from: they are the region where 1/(1−ρ) is still small enough that a traffic bump costs you a little latency rather than an incident. Lower the target when variability is high. Kingman's middle term scales the whole curve, so bursty arrivals mean the wall arrives at a utilisation you would otherwise have considered comfortable.

terms.def: How to actually get λ, W and L out of a running system, and how to use the law to check your instrumentation.
terms.detail: Two of the three are usually easy; the third is the one worth deriving as a cross-check. Quantity Where it comes from λ a request counter, rate(requests_total[5m]) W a duration histogram — but use the mean, not p99 L an in-flight gauge, or a pool's active-connection metric The trick: measure all three, then check that L = λW. If it does not hold, one of your three metrics is lying, and the law has just found a bug in your instrumentation. Common culprits are an in-flight gauge that is not decremented on the error path, a histogram that excludes queue time, and a counter that misses rejected requests. The one that catches people out: a duration histogram's mean is rate(sum) / rate(count), not histogram_quantile(0.5, …). Little's Law wants the mean. The percentiles page explains why those two numbers are usually far apart.

pages.title: Load shedding
pages.tagline: Past capacity you will fail some requests whatever you do. Shedding is choosing which ones, instead of letting the overload choose for you.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · examples in C#, Go, Envoy and Python; the arithmetic is from queueing theory
pages.description: Load shedding cheatsheet: why goodput collapses past capacity, how to choose what to drop by priority and cost, and which signal to shed on — animated.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: Deliberately refusing a portion of incoming work, quickly and cheaply, so the remainder can be served within its SLO.
terms.detail: The premise is unsentimental: past capacity, some requests will fail no matter what you do. Shedding does not change how many fail — it changes which ones, how fast they find out, and whether the survivors get a good experience. It is the response to your own overload, which separates it cleanly from its neighbours: rate limiting enforces a contract regardless of your health, and a circuit breaker reacts to somebody else's failure. Four mechanisms, four questions Mechanism Question Load shedding which work do I refuse right now? Backpressure how do I tell upstream I am full? Rate limiting how much is this client entitled to? Circuit breaker should I stop calling a broken dependency? How it relates Backpressure carries the signal to the edge; shedding is the decision the edge then makes.

terms.def: Requests completed successfully and within their deadline — the only throughput number that means anything under overload.
terms.detail: A server at 100% CPU processing 1,000 requests a second, all of which time out before they are returned, has a throughput of 1,000 and a goodput of zero. Measuring the first and ignoring the second is how teams conclude that an overloaded service is "working hard". Goodput is also the right objective: you are not trying to maximise requests touched, you are trying to maximise requests that helped somebody. Under 3× overload Metric No shedding With shedding Throughput high moderate Goodput ~150 / s 1,000 / s p99 latency timeout normal Failures ~95% ~67%, chosen How it relates The first animation is this table drawn as a curve.

terms.def: The regime where offered load rises and useful output falls — the failure shedding exists to prevent.
terms.detail: Three reinforcing effects produce it. Queues grow past client timeouts, so completed work is discarded unread. Clients retry, multiplying arrivals exactly when capacity is scarcest. And the machine itself gets slower under memory pressure, context switching and cache thrashing, so each request costs more than it did. The important property is that it does not self-correct. A collapsed system stays collapsed after the original spike has passed, because it is still busy with the backlog; recovery usually requires shedding, or a restart. The three loops Loop Effect Queue > timeout work completed for nobody Clients retry arrivals multiply Resource pressure per-request cost rises How it relates The term comes from 1980s internet congestion; the dynamics are identical at the application layer.

terms.def: The component that decides, before any real work begins, whether a request gets a slot.
terms.detail: Its defining property is that it is cheap and early. Parse enough to classify, check the signal, then admit or refuse. Anything expensive — a database lookup, a downstream call, deserialising a large body — must happen after the decision, or the rejection costs as much as the work. It lives wherever it can act: an API gateway, a sidecar proxy, or the first middleware in the application. Order of operations Step Cost Read headers, classify priority microseconds Check shedding signal one atomic read Reject with 503 + Retry-After ~0.1 ms — everything expensive below this line — Authenticate, query, call downstream milliseconds How it relates A sidecar proxy is a natural home for this, since it sees every request before the application does.

terms.def: Labelling traffic by business value so that shedding sacrifices the least important work first.
terms.detail: Without classes, shedding is random, and random shedding destroys a third of your checkout traffic to save a third of your recommendation traffic. With classes, you keep 100% of revenue and lose 100% of something nobody will notice. Keep the ladder short — three or four levels — and assign classes at the edge, where the business meaning of a request is still visible. Google's internal criticality levels work exactly this way, and the levels propagate through every downstream call. A workable ladder Class Example Shed Critical pay, place order never Standard browse, search last Background recommendations, analytics beacons first Batch exports, reindexing first, with Retry-After How it relates Shedding a background class is usually implemented as graceful degradation in the UI.

terms.def: Carrying the priority of the originating request through every downstream call, so the whole chain sheds consistently.
terms.detail: If the edge knows a request is critical but the inventory service does not, the inventory service may shed it while serving a background recommendation query — and the checkout fails anyway. The class has to travel, as a header or in the RPC metadata, exactly like a deadline. A useful rule: a service may never raise the criticality of work it issues. A background request cannot spawn critical calls, which stops low-value traffic laundering itself into protected capacity. What should travel with a request Field Purpose Criticality what to shed first Deadline when to stop bothering Tenant / account fairness Trace id debugging the decision afterwards How it relates Same plumbing as deadline propagation, and best added at the same time.

terms.def: The measurement that decides when to start refusing — and the choice that determines whether shedding helps or flaps.
terms.detail: CPU is the tempting signal and the worst one: it saturates late, it is noisy, and it says nothing about latency when you are blocked on I/O. Queue sojourn time is the best general-purpose signal, because it is expressed in the same unit as your SLO and adapts automatically when capacity changes. Concurrency in flight is a good second choice — by Little's Law it is proportional to latency — and it is trivial to implement with a semaphore. Signals, ranked Signal Verdict Queue sojourn time best — matches the SLO, self-adapting Concurrency in flight good — simple, proportional to latency Observed latency vs target good — direct, slightly laggy Queue depth poor — meaningless without a drain rate CPU utilisation poor — late, noisy, blind to I/O waits Why depth is the wrong trigger How it relates CoDel applies the sojourn-time idea to network queues; the same logic works for request queues.

terms.def: How long a request has already waited — the signal that stays correct when capacity changes underneath you.
terms.detail: Timestamp on enqueue, measure on dequeue. If the oldest waiting item has been there longer than your latency budget allows, you are behind and should shed. A halved capacity shows up immediately as doubled sojourn time, while the depth-based rule sees nothing until it is far too late. It composes with deadlines: a request whose remaining budget is already exhausted should be dropped on dequeue without being processed at all. CoDel-style parameters Parameter Typical Target sojourn 5–20 ms Interval before acting 100 ms Action drop / reject, increasing in rate How it relates Envoy and several gRPC middlewares ship CoDel-style overload filters out of the box.

terms.def: Rejecting before the expensive part, and accounting for the fact that not all requests cost the same.
terms.detail: A rejection issued after authentication, a database lookup and a downstream call is not a rejection — it is a full-price request with a 503 on the end. Admission has to happen in the first few microseconds. The second half is that a "request" is not a unit of capacity. One report query can cost as much as a thousand key lookups, so shedding by request count protects you badly. Weighting by expected cost, or giving expensive endpoints their own smaller limit, fixes it. Weighting ideas Approach Use when Per-endpoint concurrency limits costs differ by route Weighted admission (cost units) cost is predictable per request Separate pool for heavy work reports, exports, search Shed by measured p50 cost cost varies with parameters How it relates Separate pools per class of work are the bulkhead pattern applied to admission.

terms.def: Refusing in a fraction of a millisecond, which is what makes shedding cheap enough to work.
terms.detail: The arithmetic is the argument. A rejection costing 0.1 ms lets a single server refuse tens of thousands of requests a second while still serving its full real capacity. A rejection that arrives as a two-second timeout costs 20,000 times more, and consumes the very capacity you were trying to protect. Say no with a real status code and a real hint — 503 with Retry-After, or 429 when the cause is a quota — so clients can behave sensibly instead of hammering. Status codes Code Means 503 + Retry-After I am overloaded; come back 429 + Retry-After you exceeded your quota 504 a dependency timed out — not shedding Silence / timeout the expensive mistake How it relates Fast rejections only help if clients back off; pair with jitter and a retry budget.

terms.def: Telling the client when to come back, so your fast rejection does not become their fast retry loop.
terms.detail: A rejection that costs 0.1 ms is a gift to a client that retries immediately: you have built an efficient way to be hammered. Retry-After, jittered exponential backoff and a client-side retry budget are what convert cheap rejections into actual relief. Jitter is not optional. Without it, every rejected client returns at the same instant and you get a synchronised thundering herd on a system that has not yet recovered. Client-side contract Control Typical Backoff exponential, full jitter Retry budget ≤ 10% of request volume Retry on 503, 429, connection errors Never retry 4xx other than 429 How it relates Retry amplification is the failure this prevents; see the backpressure page for the full loop.

terms.def: Shedding part of a response rather than the whole request — degrade the answer instead of refusing it.
terms.detail: Instead of a 503, return the page without recommendations, without personalisation, with a cached price, or with ten results instead of a hundred. The user gets something useful and you spend a fraction of the capacity. This is usually the better first move for user-facing traffic: a page that renders with less on it beats an error page, and most pages contain far more optional content than critical content. What to drop first Drop Keep Personalisation the product and its price Recommendations the add-to-cart button Live stock count a cached estimate Full search ranking a cheap ranking How it relates The graceful degradation page is this idea developed into a product strategy.

terms.def: Making sure shedding does not fall entirely on one tenant, region or unlucky client.
terms.detail: Naive shedding is biased in ways you did not intend: the client with the most retries wins, the nearest region wins, and one heavy tenant can consume all the admitted capacity. Shedding per tenant, or weighting admission by recent usage, keeps a single noisy customer from eating everybody's share. This is where load shedding and rate limiting genuinely overlap — per-tenant quotas provide the fairness, shedding provides the overload response, and most real systems need both. Approaches Approach Effect Per-tenant concurrency limit hard isolation Weighted fair queueing proportional shares Shed heaviest user first protects the long tail of small users Global FIFO simplest, and least fair How it relates In a multi-tenant system this is the difference between one customer's incident and everybody's incident.

terms.def: Different thresholds for starting and stopping, so the system does not oscillate between shedding and not shedding.
terms.detail: A single threshold produces flapping: you shed, load drops below the line, you stop shedding, load returns, you shed again — many times a second, with wildly variable behaviour for clients. Shedding in at a higher mark and out at a lower one, with a ramp rather than a cliff, keeps it stable. A proportional response is better still: shed 10% of background traffic, then 40%, then all of it, rather than switching the whole class off at once. Stability measures Measure Why Separate in/out thresholds prevents oscillation Ramp the shed fraction no cliff edge Smooth the signal (EWMA) ignores single-sample noise Minimum dwell time bounds the switching rate How it relates Same reasoning as a circuit breaker's half-open state: never flip instantly on one observation.

terms.def: At the edge, in the service, or in a sidecar — each sees different information and can take different action.
terms.detail: The edge is the only place that can talk to the client, so final rejections belong there. But the edge does not know which internal dependency is struggling, so services need their own admission control too — and a sidecar proxy can apply uniform limits without each service implementing them. In practice you want both: cheap global protection at the edge, and local protection per service so that one slow dependency does not take everything with it. Division of labour Layer Knows Can do Edge client, criticality, global load 503 with Retry-After Sidecar per-service latency uniform concurrency limits Service which dependency is slow shed by feature, brownout How it relates Envoy's overload manager and adaptive concurrency filter do this at the sidecar layer.

terms.def: Shed rate, goodput and the SLO — because shedding that nobody measures looks exactly like an outage.
terms.detail: Count rejections separately from errors, labelled by class and reason, or your error rate graph will show a catastrophe when the system is in fact working as designed. Then watch goodput and p99 latency for admitted traffic — those are the numbers shedding is supposed to protect. It is worth deciding in advance whether shed requests count against your SLI. Usually they should: the user did not get served, and pretending otherwise makes the error budget meaningless. Dashboard Metric Expectation shed_total by class zero normally; bursts under load Goodput flat at capacity during overload p99 for admitted traffic unchanged under load Critical class shed always zero — page if not How it relates "Critical traffic shed > 0" is one of the few alerts worth paging on immediately.

pages.title: Model Context Protocol
pages.tagline: A standard socket between a model and everything it is allowed to touch — so N×M integrations become N+M.
pages.description: MCP cheatsheet: the stateless 2026-07-28 revision — hosts, clients and servers, tools, resources, prompts, multi round-trip requests, transports and OAuth authorization.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: The host runs the model and owns policy; it creates one client per server; each server fronts one system.
terms.detail: The host is the application the user sees — an IDE, a chat app, an agent runtime. It holds the model, the conversation and all the policy: which servers are connected, which tools are enabled, what needs approval. The client is a connector object inside the host that speaks to exactly one server. The server is a separate program or service that exposes capabilities and holds the real credentials. The one-to-one client/server pairing is deliberate: it keeps each server's capabilities, authorization and failures isolated. A server that crashes or misbehaves takes down one client, not the host's whole tool catalogue.
