Load shedding is dynamic and global: it reacts to your health signals — queue depth, p99 latency, CPU, pool saturation — and rejects whatever keeps the service alive. Priority-aware: shed background sync and analytics before interactive traffic. Tag requests with a criticality on the way in. Shed early: rejecting at the front door costs microseconds; rejecting after the database call has already cost you the database call. Drop the oldest: a request that has waited 5 s probably belongs to a client that already timed out. Under overload, LIFO sheds better than FIFO. Signal it with 503 and Retry-After, not 429: the caller did nothing wrong, and the distinction tells their on-call engineer where the problem actually is.

terms.def: Pushing the "slow down" signal upstream instead of silently queueing. A bounded queue that blocks the producer is backpressure; an unbounded one is a time bomb.
terms.detail: Every unbounded buffer turns an overload into a latency disaster: memory grows, requests sit behind work nobody is waiting for any more, and recovery takes longer than the incident. Bound every queue, and decide what happens when it is full: block the producer, drop the newest, or drop the oldest. Give every queued item a deadline and discard it when the deadline passes, rather than serving a response nobody will read. In a pull-based system — a consumer group reading from Apache Kafka, or a job queue — backpressure is automatic: the consumer simply fetches more slowly and the broker holds the backlog. A rate limiter is backpressure made explicit at an HTTP boundary, where no protocol-level mechanism exists.

terms.def: Randomness added to retry delays and to window or cache expiry so that clients do not all come back at the same instant.
terms.detail: Without jitter, a limiter creates the herd it is meant to prevent: every rejected client is told the same reset time, sleeps the same number of seconds, and returns in the same millisecond. // exponential backoff with full jitter delay = random(0, min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt)) Strategy Spread Verdict Fixed delay none synchronises the herd Exponential, no jitter none still synchronised, just later Exponential + full jitter excellent the sane default Decorrelated jitter excellent better throughput during long outages Cap the total attempts and respect Retry-After when it is present. Retries that ignore a 429 are the single most effective way to turn a small limit breach into an outage.

pages.title: Redis
pages.tagline: An in-memory data structure server: a key-value store that answers in microseconds.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · latest release line 8.10
pages.description: Redis cheatsheet: architecture, animated SET and cache-aside walk-throughs, key concepts, commands, trade-offs and alternatives.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: A binary-safe string that names a value, by convention namespaced with colons: user:1, cart:7. Max 512 MB, but keep keys short.
terms.detail: Keys are binary-safe strings. Redis has no tables or schemas, so the naming convention is your schema: object-type:id:field. Good Why user:1042 type + id, easy to SCAN MATCH user:* session:9f3c short, unique, set a TTL rl:{user:42}:2026-11-10T10:05 rate-limit bucket; {…} is a Cluster hash tag Keep keys short: with 100M keys, every extra 20 bytes is ~2 GB of RAM. Avoid unbounded patterns (one key per request) without a TTL.

terms.def: The set of all keys in a database, stored in one big in-memory hash table. Lookups are O(1).
terms.detail: All keys of a database live in one big hash table, so GET, SET and DEL are O(1) whatever the size. Redis grows the table incrementally (rehashing a little on each command) to avoid long pauses. DBSIZE counts keys; INFO keyspace shows keys and expiring keys per database. Redis has 16 numbered databases (SELECT 0..15 ), but Cluster supports only db 0. Prefer key prefixes over database numbers. Scale: tens of millions of keys per instance are normal; the limit is RAM, not count.

terms.def: What a key holds: String, Hash, List, Set, Sorted set, Stream, Bitmap, HyperLogLog, Geo, JSON, Vector set. Each has its own commands.
terms.detail: Type Think of it as Typical use String bytes, number, JSON blob (≤ 512 MB) cache entries, counters, locks Hash a small object / dict user profile, session fields List linked list, push/pop at both ends queues, recent-items feeds Set unique unordered members tags, "who liked this" Sorted set members ordered by score leaderboards, scheduling, sliding windows Stream append-only log with consumer groups event streams, job queues with acks JSON, Vector set, HyperLogLog, Bitmap, Geo specialised structures documents, similarity search, unique counts, flags, "nearby" Pick the type by the operations you need: if you'd read-modify-write a JSON string to change one field, use a Hash instead.

terms.def: A time-to-live on a key. When it runs out, Redis deletes the key. The basis of caching and sessions.
terms.detail: SET session:9f "{...}" EX 1800 # set with 30 min TTL EXPIRE cart:7 3600 # add/replace a TTL TTL cart:7 → 3597 # seconds left (-1 none, -2 missing) PERSIST cart:7 # remove the TTL Expired keys are removed two ways: lazily when someone touches them, and actively by a background job that samples keys with TTLs several times per second. Memory is therefore reclaimed slightly after expiry, not at the exact second. Common values Cache entries: 1–60 min, with random jitter to avoid stampedes. Sessions: 30 min to 24 h, refreshed on activity. One-time codes: 5–10 min. Gotcha: SET without EX / KEEPTTL on an existing key removes its TTL.

terms.def: The RAM cap. When it is reached, the maxmemory-policy decides what to drop (e.g. allkeys-lru) or to reject writes (noeviction ).
terms.detail: maxmemory caps the RAM Redis uses for data. When a write would exceed it, maxmemory-policy decides what happens. Policy Evicts Use for noeviction (default) nothing: writes fail with OOM data you can't lose (queues, primary data) allkeys-lru least recently used key pure caches (most common) allkeys-lfu least frequently used key caches with stable "hot" keys volatile-lru / volatile-ttl only keys with a TTL mixed cache + persistent data allkeys-lru in action Size it: set maxmemory to ~70–80% of the machine's RAM to leave room for fragmentation, replication buffers and fork during RDB saves.

terms.def: Commands run one at a time on the main thread, so a single command like INCR never races with another.
terms.detail: Commands execute one at a time on the main thread, so INCR, SET NX, LPUSH or ZINCRBY can never interleave with another client's command. Two app servers incrementing the same counter never lose an update. But a sequence of commands from your app is not atomic: between your GET and SET another client can sneak in. Options: A single command that does it all (INCR, SET … NX GET, GETDEL ). MULTI/EXEC with WATCH for optimistic locking. A Lua script or Function: the whole script runs atomically. Since Redis 6, network I/O can use extra threads, but command execution stays single-threaded, so atomicity is unchanged.

terms.def: Send many commands without waiting for each reply. Cuts network round trips; usually the biggest client-side speedup.
terms.detail: Without pipelining each command waits for its reply: 1,000 commands × 0.5 ms round trip = 0.5 s, mostly waiting on the network. With a pipeline you send all 1,000, then read 1,000 replies: a few milliseconds. var batch = db.CreateBatch(); // client-side batching, not a transaction var tasks = userIds.Select(id => batch.HashGetAllAsync($"user:{id}")).ToArray(); batch.Execute(); // one round trip for the whole set var profiles = await Task.WhenAll(tasks); pipe = r.pipeline(transaction=False) for uid in user_ids: pipe.hgetall(f"user:{uid}") profiles = pipe.execute() Pipelining is a client-side batching trick, not a transaction: other clients' commands can still run in between. Keep batches to a few thousand commands to bound memory.

terms.def: A transaction: queued commands run together with nothing interleaved. There is no rollback if one fails.
terms.detail: WATCH stock:42 GET stock:42 → "3" MULTI DECR stock:42 LPUSH orders "…" EXEC → nil if stock:42 changed since WATCH Commands are queued and run back-to-back with nothing interleaved. No rollback: if one command fails at runtime (wrong type), the others still apply. WATCH gives optimistic locking: EXEC aborts if a watched key changed; retry in a loop. In Cluster all keys must share a hash slot. For logic with conditions ("decrement only if > 0"), a Lua script is simpler than WATCH retries.

terms.def: Server-side scripts that run atomically. Use them for read-modify-write logic, such as rate limiters.
terms.detail: A script runs entirely on the server, atomically, so it can read, decide and write in one step. Classic fixed-window rate limiter: -- KEYS[1] = rl:{user:42}:minute, ARGV[1] = limit local n = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1]) if n == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], 60) end return n <= tonumber(ARGV[1]) EVAL sends the script each time; EVALSHA reuses a cached one. Redis 7+ Functions (FUNCTION LOAD, FCALL) store named scripts in the server and persist them with the data. Keep scripts short: while one runs, every other client waits.

terms.def: Point-in-time snapshot of the whole dataset to disk. Compact and fast to load, but you lose writes made since the last snapshot.
terms.detail: Redis forks; the child writes the whole dataset to dump.rdb while the parent keeps serving. Fork uses copy-on-write, so memory use can briefly grow under heavy writes. save 3600 1 300 100 60 10000 # snapshot after N changes in T seconds BGSAVE # snapshot now LASTSAVE # when was the last one Pros: compact file, fast restarts, perfect for backups (copy it to object storage). Cons: a crash loses every write since the last snapshot, often minutes. Replicas also bootstrap from an RDB sent by the primary.

terms.def: Append-only file: every write command is logged. With appendfsync everysec, at most about 1 second of writes is lost on a crash.
terms.detail: The append-only file logs every write command; on restart Redis replays it. appendfsync Data at risk on crash Speed always ~none slow (fsync per write) everysec (default) ~1 second fast, the usual choice no up to ~30 s (OS decides) fastest The log is rewritten in the background to stay compact. Modern Redis uses a multi-part AOF with an RDB base plus incremental files. Common production setup: AOF everysec + periodic RDB for backups.

terms.def: Replicas keep an asynchronous copy of a primary. They serve reads and can be promoted if the primary fails.
terms.detail: A replica connects to the primary (REPLICAOF host 6379 ), receives an RDB snapshot, then a continuous stream of write commands. Asynchronous: the primary acknowledges the client before replicas have the write. A failover can lose the last few writes. WAIT 1 100 blocks until 1 replica has it (still not a guarantee). Replicas are read-only and can serve reads, but may lag a few ms behind. Typical setup: 1 primary + 1–2 replicas in different availability zones. Replication alone doesn't fail over automatically: that's Sentinel's or Cluster's job.

terms.def: Processes that monitor a primary and its replicas, run automatic failover and tell clients the new primary's address.
terms.detail: Sentinel is a separate process (run at least 3, on different machines) that watches a primary and its replicas. Sentinels ping the primary; if a quorum (e.g. 2 of 3) agrees it's down, they elect a leader Sentinel. The leader promotes the most up-to-date replica and reconfigures the others. Clients ask Sentinel "who is the primary for mymaster ?" and reconnect. Use Sentinel when data fits on one machine and you need automatic failover. If you need to shard data across machines, use Cluster instead; it has failover built in. Managed services (ElastiCache, Azure Cache) handle this for you.

terms.def: Redis Cluster shards keys over 16,384 slots (CRC16(key) mod 16384 ). {tags} in a key force related keys into the same slot.
terms.detail: Redis Cluster splits the keyspace into 16,384 hash slots: slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384. Each primary owns a range of slots; each primary has replicas for failover. Node Slots A 0 – 5460 B 5461 – 10922 C 10923 – 16383 Clients cache the slot map; a MOVED reply tells them the map changed. Multi-key commands (MGET, MULTI, Lua) need all keys in one slot. Force it with a hash tag: only {user:42} is hashed in cart:{user:42} and profile:{user:42}. Resharding moves slots between nodes online.

terms.def: Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget broadcast. Streams are a persistent, append-only log with consumer groups and acknowledgements.
terms.detail: Pub/Sub Streams Storage none: delivered and forgotten kept in a log (trim with MAXLEN) Offline consumers miss messages catch up from their last ID Load balancing every subscriber gets every message consumer groups split the work Acks / retries no XACK, pending list, XCLAIM Use for live notifications, cache invalidation, chat presence job queues, event sourcing, activity feeds Streams look a lot like a mini Kafka: IDs like 1731234567890-0 are timestamp-based offsets. For days of retention or very high volume, use Kafka itself.

pages.title: Retry, backoff & jitter
pages.tagline: Retrying is the cheapest way to survive a blip, and the cheapest way to turn one into an outage.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · examples use Polly 8 and Tenacity; the jitter analysis is AWS's, from 2015
pages.description: Retry cheatsheet: which errors are worth retrying, why exponential backoff without jitter just rearranges the thundering herd, retry budgets, and how three layers turn one request into twenty-seven.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: A failure likely to go away on its own — the only kind worth retrying.
terms.detail: Connection resets, timeouts, 503s, lock contention, leader elections. They share a property: nothing about the request was wrong, so the same request may well succeed shortly. A 400, a 404 or a validation failure is deterministic. Retrying it wastes capacity, delays the error the caller needs to see, and in aggregate looks exactly like an attack. Retry or not Outcome Retry? Connection reset, DNS blip yes Timeout yes, if idempotent 503, 429 (honour Retry-After) yes 500 cautiously — may not be transient 400, 404, 409, 422 never 401 / 403 no — refresh the token instead, once How it relates A circuit breaker is what you add when "transient" turns out to mean "for the next twenty minutes".

terms.def: A retry is only safe if repeating the operation cannot do the work twice.
terms.detail: The dangerous case is the timeout, because it is ambiguous: the request may have been processed and only the response lost. Retrying a GET is free; retrying a payment on a timeout can charge the customer twice. Reads and natural replacements are safe by construction. For anything that creates or moves money, attach an idempotency key so the server can recognise the repeat. Safety by operation Operation Safe to retry? GET, HEAD yes — no effect at all PUT, DELETE yes — idempotent by definition POST that creates only with an idempotency key Increment, append no — needs a key or a dedup window How it relates The idempotency page covers the server-side half: keys, windows and delivery semantics.

terms.def: Doubling the wait after each failure, so a persistent problem is not hammered.
terms.detail: base × 2ⁿ. With a 100 ms base: 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600. It adapts automatically — a one-off blip costs a tenth of a second, while a real outage quickly drops your request rate by orders of magnitude. It is necessary and, on its own, not sufficient: it spaces out each client's attempts without doing anything about the fact that all clients are stepping in time. Strategies Strategy Waits Use Immediate 0 one quick retry on a fresh connection Constant 1, 1, 1 polling a known-slow resource Linear 1, 2, 3 rarely the right answer Exponential 1, 2, 4, 8 the default How it relates Always pair it with jitter and a cap; the three together are the actual pattern.

terms.def: Randomising the wait so that clients which failed together do not return together.
terms.detail: The failure event synchronises every client. Deterministic backoff preserves that synchronisation perfectly, so the retries arrive as a spike no matter how far apart the spikes are. Randomness is the only thing that breaks the lockstep. AWS's analysis compared the options and found full jitter — random(0, min(cap, base × 2ⁿ)) — gave the lowest contention and the shortest completion time. It is the default worth using unless you have a reason otherwise. Three ways to randomise the wait How it relates The first animation is the same point at the scale of a thousand clients.

terms.def: Many clients retrying in unison, producing a spike far above capacity exactly when the system is weakest.
terms.detail: Anything that fails everyone at once creates it: a restart, a failover, a cache flush, an expiring token with a round-number lifetime, a cron job at the top of the hour. The clients were independent until a shared event put them in step. Jitter fixes the retry case. The others need the same medicine — randomised cache TTLs, staggered cron schedules, token lifetimes with a random component. Other herds worth jittering Source Fix Cache entries expiring together randomise the TTL ±10% Cron at :00 spread over the window Token refresh refresh at a random point before expiry Reconnect after a deploy jittered reconnect backoff How it relates From the server's side, this is a load-shedding problem; from the client's, a jitter problem.

terms.def: Retries at several layers multiplying rather than adding — the reason one blip becomes an outage.
terms.detail: Three layers each retrying three times is 3³ = 27 requests from one user action, all aimed at a dependency that is already failing. The load arrives precisely when there is least capacity to absorb it, which is how a recoverable degradation becomes congestion collapse. The rule is to retry at exactly one layer. Usually the one closest to the failure, because it knows most about the error and wastes the least work; sometimes the edge, if only it can see the whole operation. Multiplication Layers retrying Calls per request 1 3 2 9 3 27 4 81 How it relates The second animation builds this number step by step.

terms.def: A cap on retries as a fraction of total traffic, so the system cannot retry itself to death.
terms.detail: A per-request attempt limit does nothing about aggregate load: if every request fails, a limit of three still triples your traffic. A budget works on the whole client — typically "retries may not exceed 10% of successful requests" — and once exhausted, failures are returned immediately. This is what turns retry from a local decision into a system-level one, and it is the control that gRPC and modern service meshes expose for exactly this reason. Two different limits Limit Bounds Attempts per request one request's latency Retry budget total extra load on the dependency How it relates Without a budget, a widespread failure means every client retries at once — which is the amplification case again.

terms.def: How many tries, and the longest a single wait may become.
terms.detail: Three to five attempts covers almost all genuinely transient faults; beyond that you are no longer riding out a blip, you are waiting for an outage to end — which is a circuit breaker's job. The cap matters because unbounded doubling reaches absurd waits quickly: without one, the eighth attempt is 25 seconds away and the user left long ago. Sensible defaults Setting Interactive Background Attempts 2–3 5–8 Base delay 50–200 ms 1 s Cap 1–2 s 30–60 s Total budget the request deadline minutes How it relates An interactive request's real limit is the user's patience, which the deadline encodes.

terms.def: Retrying only while there is time left in the caller's budget, rather than a fixed number of times.
terms.detail: A retry that starts 50 ms before the caller gives up is pure waste: it consumes a connection and a worker to produce a result nobody will read. Checking the remaining deadline before each attempt removes that work entirely. It also bounds latency honestly. With a propagated deadline, the user's two-second budget is the limit regardless of how many layers would like to retry inside it. Before each attempt Check If no Time left > expected attempt duration? fail now Budget left in the retry quota? fail now Circuit closed? fail now How it relates Deadline propagation is the same plumbing the backpressure page recommends for discarding dead work.

terms.def: Retries multiply the timeout: three attempts at two seconds is a six-second wait unless something stops it.
terms.detail: Teams set a per-attempt timeout and forget that the caller experiences the sum. With backoff added, three attempts at two seconds plus waits is closer to seven — well past the point the user refreshed the page and created a second request. Size the per-attempt timeout so that the attempts plus their waits fit inside the overall deadline, not the other way round. How it relates Without a timeout there is nothing to retry on: the call simply hangs, which is worse than failing.

terms.def: The server telling you when to come back — and the one input that beats any backoff formula.
terms.detail: Returned with 429 and often with 503, as seconds or an HTTP date. The server knows more about its own recovery than your exponential curve does, so honour it — and add a small jitter on top, because every client received the same value and would otherwise return together. Precedence Signal Priority Retry-After highest — obey it Your backoff schedule when no header Immediate retry at most once, on a fresh connection How it relates Jitter the value you were given; identical sleeps re-synchronise the herd you were avoiding.

terms.def: Retry handles a blip; a breaker handles an outage. They need to be arranged deliberately.
terms.detail: If the retry sits inside the breaker, one logical call records three failures and the breaker trips three times faster than configured. If it sits outside, it will retry the breaker's instant rejections and spin. The arrangement that works: timeout, then retry, then breaker — one recorded outcome per logical operation — with the open-circuit error marked non-retryable. How it relates The circuit breaker page covers the full ordering, including bulkheads and fallbacks.

terms.def: Sending a second request before the first has failed, to cut tail latency rather than to handle errors.
terms.detail: If the p99 is ten times the p50, issue a duplicate once the p95 has elapsed and take whichever answer arrives first. It trades a few percent extra load for a dramatically shorter tail, and it is how large systems hide slow replicas. It demands idempotency and a tight budget — typically hedging at most 5% of requests — because it adds load by design rather than only on failure. Retry vs hedge Retry Hedge Triggered by an error slowness Fixes failures tail latency Extra load only on failure always, by design How it relates Both are retries in the server's eyes, so both must respect the same budget.

terms.def: One layer, chosen deliberately — not everywhere a library made it easy.
terms.detail: Closest to the failure wastes the least work and knows most about the error. The edge sees the whole operation and can decide whether a retry is still useful. Both are defensible; doing both is not. Watch for retries you did not write: HTTP client defaults, SDK policies, service mesh configuration and database drivers all retry silently, and they compose with yours. Audit these Layer Often retries by default HTTP client / SDK yes — check the policy Service mesh (Envoy) yes, if configured Database driver yes, on connection errors Message consumer yes — redelivery is a retry How it relates Count the real attempt multiplier before adding one more layer of "resilience".

terms.def: Where a message goes when the retries are exhausted, so the queue keeps moving.
terms.detail: In message-driven systems a failing message is redelivered, which is a retry under another name. Without a maximum delivery count, one poison message is retried forever and blocks everything behind it. Move it aside after a bounded number of attempts, with the error and enough context to replay it later. An empty dead-letter queue nobody monitors is as bad as not having one. How it relates Alert on dead-letter depth; it is usually the first signal of a systematic failure rather than a transient one.

terms.def: Counting attempts separately from requests, so retries are visible before they become an incident.
terms.detail: If retries are invisible, a dependency degrading shows up as "traffic increased" — and the obvious response, scaling up, feeds the amplification. Separating attempts from logical requests makes the real story legible. The most useful single number is the attempt multiplier: attempts divided by logical requests. At 1.0 nothing is retrying; at 3.0 you are sending three times the load you think you are. What to export Metric Watch for attempts / requests rising above ~1.1 retries_exhausted_total real failures, not blips retry_budget_rejected the budget is engaging Dead-letter depth poison messages How it relates Trace spans should record the attempt number, or a retried call looks like several unrelated ones.

pages.title: Reverse proxy
pages.tagline: One public door in front of many private rooms — and the only place where "every request" is a thing you can say.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · examples use nginx, Envoy, Caddy, Traefik and YARP
pages.description: Reverse proxy cheatsheet: TLS termination, routing, header rewriting, upstream keepalive, buffering, timeouts and the X-Forwarded-For trust chain.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: A forward proxy represents clients to the internet; a reverse proxy represents servers to clients.
terms.detail: The code is nearly identical — accept a connection, open another, copy bytes with some rewriting — but the trust direction inverts. A forward proxy is configured by the client and is trusted by the client; a reverse proxy is configured by the server operator, chosen by DNS, and the client usually does not know it exists. That inversion decides everything else. A forward proxy filters outbound requests and can be bypassed by a client that stops using it. A reverse proxy cannot be bypassed — it owns the public address — which is exactly why it is the right place for TLS, authentication, rate limiting and logging. Side by side Forward Reverse Configured by the client the server operator Hides the client the servers Typical use corporate egress, filtering TLS, routing, edge policy Examples Squid, corporate proxies nginx, Envoy, Traefik, CDNs How it relates A service mesh sidecar is both at once: a reverse proxy for inbound traffic and a forward proxy for outbound.

terms.def: Decrypting HTTPS at the proxy so everything behind it can be plain HTTP — or re-encrypted.
terms.detail: Terminating TLS at the edge is what makes a proxy useful: nothing can be routed by path, cached, compressed or rate limited while it is still encrypted. It also centralises certificates — one place to renew, one place to configure ciphers and protocol versions, one place to enable HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. What happens on the second hop is a separate decision. Termination leaves it plain inside the network, re-encryption opens a fresh TLS session to the upstream, and passthrough forwards the encrypted stream untouched — which keeps the proxy blind and therefore unable to do its job at layer 7. Common values Setting Typical Protocol floor TLS 1.2, prefer 1.3 Certificate source ACME / Let's Encrypt, auto-renew HSTS max-age=31536000 once you are sure Upstream leg plain inside a trusted network, mTLS in a mesh Session tickets on, rotated — cuts handshake cost How it relates Terminating means the proxy sees your traffic in clear text. That is a trust and compliance decision as much as a technical one.

terms.def: The hostname the client announces in the TLS handshake, before any HTTP exists.
terms.detail: Server Name Indication solves a chicken-and-egg problem: the proxy must pick a certificate before it can decrypt anything, but the hostname lives in the encrypted HTTP request. SNI puts the hostname in the clear part of the ClientHello, so one IP address can serve hundreds of certificates. It is also the only routing signal available to a proxy doing TLS passthrough — which is how "route by domain without decrypting" works. And because it is in clear text, it is visible to the network, which is what Encrypted Client Hello is designed to fix. How it relates An SNI that disagrees with the HTTP Host header is a classic request-smuggling and domain-fronting vector; strict proxies reject the mismatch.

terms.def: The named set of backend addresses a route forwards to, with a balancing policy and health checks.
terms.detail: Routes do not point at servers, they point at pools. A pool holds addresses (static, DNS-resolved or discovered), a balancing policy, health-check configuration, connection limits and a slow-start ramp. Splitting routing from pooling is what makes canaries, blue/green and scale-out a configuration change. How the pool learns its members matters more than the policy. Static lists go stale; DNS needs re-resolution on a timer (and many proxies resolve once at startup unless told otherwise); service discovery or the Kubernetes API is the usual answer in dynamic environments. Common values Setting Typical Policy least-request, or power of two choices DNS re-resolve every 5–30 s, not once at boot Max connections per upstream bounded, to protect the backend Slow start 30–60 s ramp for cold instances How it relates The policies themselves are the subject of L4 vs L7 load balancing; this page is about everything else the proxy does.

terms.def: Choosing a route from the Host header, the path, and sometimes a method or header.
terms.detail: One proxy, one address, many sites: the Host header selects a server block, then the longest matching path prefix selects a route. This is what lets shop.example and admin.example live on the same machine, and /api/ and /static/ go to entirely different services. Match ordering is the usual source of confusion. nginx prefers exact matches, then the longest prefix, then regular expressions in file order — which is not "first rule wins". Envoy and the Gateway API evaluate in declared order with explicit precedence rules. Read your proxy's rules once; guessing produces a route that works in staging and shadows another in production. Common matchers Matcher Use Host multi-tenant domains, environments Path prefix service boundaries Header canary (x-canary: 1 ), API version Method splitting reads from writes Weight percentage-based canary rollouts How it relates Routing by header is how canary releases become a config change instead of a deployment.

terms.def: Changing the request path between the public URL and the one the backend expects.
terms.detail: The public surface rarely matches the internal one: /api/orders/77 must arrive at the orders service as /orders/77. Rewriting is simple to write and easy to get subtly wrong — trailing slashes, double slashes, URL-encoded segments and the difference between a redirect and a rewrite. The trailing slash is the classic. In nginx, proxy_pass http://api; and proxy_pass http://api/; behave differently: the second strips the matched location prefix, the first does not. Half of all "404 from the backend but the route looks right" tickets are this character. Things that bite Issue Symptom Trailing slash on proxy_pass paths doubled or truncated Backend generates absolute URLs links point at internal hosts Encoded slashes %2F decoded, then routed somewhere unintended Cookie Path attribute cookies not sent after a rewrite How it relates Backends that build absolute URLs need X-Forwarded-Prefix, or they will emit links the public cannot follow.

terms.def: The hop-by-hop headers that tell the backend who the real client was and how they connected.
terms.detail: Once a proxy is in the path, the backend's socket shows the proxy's address, and the scheme is http even though the user typed https. The X-Forwarded-* family carries the lost context: -For (client IP, appended at each hop), -Proto (original scheme), -Host (original Host) and -Prefix (the path segment that was stripped). RFC 7239's Forwarded header does the same in one line and is less widely used. They are plain headers, so a client can send them. Everything about trusting them is covered in Trusted proxy chain — and skipping that is how rate limiters get bypassed. The set Header Carries X-Forwarded-For comma-separated client, then each proxy X-Forwarded-Proto https — needed for redirects and secure cookies X-Forwarded-Host the Host the client asked for X-Forwarded-Prefix the stripped path prefix X-Request-Id correlation across proxy and app logs How it relates Missing X-Forwarded-Proto is the cause of infinite redirect loops: the app sees HTTP, redirects to HTTPS, the proxy forwards again as HTTP.

terms.def: The rule that decides which forwarded addresses to believe and which to discard.
terms.detail: X-Forwarded-For is appended to, never replaced, so after a CDN and your own proxy it reads client, cdn, edge. A client can pre-populate it with anything — X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4 — and that value will sit at the left, exactly where naive code looks for "the client". The correct algorithm walks the list from the right, discarding addresses that belong to proxies you control, and takes the first one that does not. Equivalently: trust as many hops as you actually operate, no more. Frameworks implement this — ASP.NET Core's ForwardedHeadersOptions.KnownProxies, Express's trust proxy, Django's USE_X_FORWARDED_HOST — and all of them default to something you must change. Worked example Hops you operate Header Client IP 2 (CDN + proxy) 1.2.3.4, 203.0.113.9, 198.51.100.4 203.0.113.9 0 (naive, takes leftmost) same 1.2.3.4 — spoofed The belt-and-braces fix: have the outermost proxy you control strip any inbound X-Forwarded-For and set it fresh from the socket address. How it relates Every rate limit, geo-rule, ban list and audit log built on an untrusted address is bypassable by setting a header.

terms.def: A small preamble that carries the real client address on connections where headers are not available.
terms.detail: When an L4 balancer or a TLS-passthrough proxy forwards a connection, there is no HTTP to add a header to. The PROXY protocol prepends a short line (v1, text) or binary block (v2) before the first byte of the real stream, carrying source and destination addresses and ports. It must be enabled on both sides. Enabled on the sender only and the receiver treats the preamble as request data, producing bizarre parse errors; enabled on the receiver only and every normal connection fails. It is also unauthenticated, so the listener must only accept it from known addresses. PROXY TCP4 203.0.113.9 10.0.0.5 51882 443\r\n GET /api/orders/77 HTTP/1.1 Host: shop.example How it relates This is how a Kubernetes Service of type LoadBalancer can preserve client IPs without an L7 hop.

terms.def: Reusing upstream connections across requests instead of dialling a new one every time.
terms.detail: Each new upstream connection costs a TCP handshake, possibly a TLS handshake, and a slow-start window. At any real request rate, keepalive to the backend is the difference between a proxy that adds a millisecond and one that adds twenty. nginx notoriously does not keep upstream connections alive unless you add a keepalive directive and set proxy_http_version 1.1 with an empty Connection header. Pool sizes must be bounded, and the idle timeout on the proxy should be shorter than the backend's. If the backend closes first, the proxy can send a request into a connection that is already closing — which surfaces as rare, unexplained 502s under load. Common values Setting Typical Idle connections per upstream 32–128 Proxy idle timeout 60 s Backend idle timeout 75 s (longer than the proxy's) Max requests per connection 1,000–10,000, to rebalance How it relates Long-lived pooled connections are exactly what breaks connection-level balancing under HTTP/2 — see L4 vs L7 load balancing.

terms.def: Whether the proxy holds the whole request or response in memory before passing it on.
terms.detail: With buffering on, the proxy reads the complete response from the backend, frees the backend connection immediately, and then dribbles it out to a slow client at whatever rate the client can manage. This is a real protection: it stops slow mobile clients from occupying expensive application threads, and it is why buffering defaults to on. It is also why streaming appears broken. Server-sent events, chunked progress output, long downloads and LLM token streams all arrive as one lump at the end, because the proxy is waiting for the response to finish. Those routes need buffering explicitly disabled. Common values Setting Typical Note Response buffer on protects backends from slow clients Buffer size 8–64 KB in memory spills to disk beyond that SSE / streaming routes proxy_buffering off plus X-Accel-Buffering: no Request body buffer on needed for retries; breaks uploads How it relates Request buffering is what makes a retry possible — you cannot replay a body you have already streamed away.

terms.def: The proxy's own deadlines and second attempts, which stack with everyone else's.
terms.detail: A proxy has at least four timeouts — connect, send, read, and total — and each one has a default that is almost certainly wrong for your workload. nginx's 60-second read timeout is an eternity for an API and far too short for a long export. Retries are more dangerous. A proxy retrying an idempotent GET on a connection error is good. A proxy retrying a POST that the backend actually processed is a duplicate order. Retry only on connect errors and on explicit, safe conditions, cap attempts, and use a retry budget so a broad failure cannot multiply load. Common values Timeout Typical Connect 1–3 s Read (API) 5–30 s Read (streaming / SSE) hours, with keepalive frames Total request client timeout minus a margin Retries 1, on connect errors only How it relates Timeouts must decrease outward: client > proxy > backend. Inverted, the proxy keeps waiting on work the client abandoned.

terms.def: How the proxy decides an upstream should stop receiving traffic.
terms.detail: Active checks poll an endpoint on a schedule; passive checks (outlier detection) watch real traffic and eject an instance after N consecutive failures. Passive reacts faster and costs nothing, active notices recovery — most mature setups run both. The classic mistake is a readiness endpoint that calls the database. When the database is slow, every instance fails its check at once and the proxy ejects the entire pool: the check causes the outage. Readiness should test only what this instance needs to serve, and shared-dependency failures should be handled with ejection limits. Common values Setting Typical Interval 2–10 s Unhealthy after 3 consecutive failures Healthy after 2 consecutive successes Max ejected ≤ 50% of the pool How it relates A deploy should fail readiness first, wait longer than the check interval, then drain. The wait is the step everyone omits.

terms.def: WebSockets, SSE and gRPC need the proxy to step out of the way rather than parse and buffer.
terms.detail: A WebSocket starts as HTTP and then stops being HTTP: the proxy must forward the Upgrade and Connection headers, switch to a byte pipe, and raise its read timeout to something measured in hours. Default configurations drop the connection after 60 seconds of silence, which is why "the socket disconnects every minute" is such a common first bug. Server-sent events and token streams need buffering off. gRPC needs HTTP/2 end to end, including on the upstream leg, and separate handling of trailers. What each needs Protocol Requirements WebSocket upgrade headers forwarded, long read timeout SSE buffering off, long read timeout, no compression gRPC HTTP/2 upstream, trailers, no request buffering Large uploads request buffering off, body size limit raised How it relates Each of these conflicts with a protection the proxy provides by default. Scope the exception to the route, never globally.

terms.def: The cross-cutting rules — size limits, rate limits, compression, caching, security headers — applied in one place.
terms.detail: This is the real reason to run a reverse proxy. A request body cap stops a memory-exhaustion attack before any application code runs. Compression at the edge means no service implements gzip. A shared response cache for static assets removes most traffic from the backends entirely. Security headers get set once instead of in every framework. The blast radius is the flip side: a bad regular expression, a wrong cache key or a mistyped limit at this layer is an outage for everything behind it. Treat proxy configuration as production code — reviewed, tested, versioned and rolled out gradually. Sensible defaults Policy Typical Max request body 1–10 MB, raised per upload route Max header size 8–16 KB Compression gzip/brotli over 1 KB, text types only Static cache public, max-age=31536000, immutable for hashed assets Security headers HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, CSP How it relates Doing this in the proxy is why Azure API Management and other gateways exist — they are reverse proxies with a product around the policy layer.

terms.def: Rejecting excess traffic before it reaches a backend that would have queued it.
terms.detail: The cheapest request is one the proxy refuses. Edge limits protect against scrapers, retry storms and accidental loops, and they do it without consuming an application thread. nginx uses a leaky bucket (limit_req with a burst); Envoy supports local and global token buckets; gateways usually offer per-key quotas. The key is the hard part. Limit by raw socket address and you throttle an entire corporate NAT or a mobile carrier; limit by X-Forwarded-For without a trusted chain and anyone can bypass it; limit by API key or authenticated user and you need the proxy to parse the token. Common values Surface Limit Login / password reset 5–10 per minute per IP Public API, per key 100–1,000 per minute Expensive search 10–60 per minute Burst allowance 2–5× the steady rate How it relates The algorithms, keys and headers are covered in depth on the Rate limiting page.

terms.def: Applying new configuration without dropping the connections already in flight.
terms.detail: Because the proxy owns every connection, restarting it is an outage. Mature proxies reload instead: nginx forks new workers with the new config, lets old workers finish their current requests, then retires them. Envoy performs hot restart with socket handover; Caddy and Traefik reload from a watched file or API. Validate before reloading — nginx -t exists precisely so a typo fails at the gate rather than taking the site down. In Kubernetes the ingress controller does this for you on every Ingress change, which is also why a bad annotation can quietly break reloads for everyone in the cluster. How it relates Validate in CI, roll out to one proxy instance first, and watch error rates before continuing — config is a deployment.

terms.def: A reverse proxy whose configuration is generated from Kubernetes objects instead of a file.
terms.detail: An ingress controller watches the API server for Ingress or Gateway API resources and rewrites the proxy's configuration to match, with pod IPs as the upstream pool. The proxy underneath is usually nginx, Envoy, HAProxy or Traefik — the controller is the translation layer, not a new kind of proxy. The Gateway API is the current direction: typed resources for listeners, routes and policies, with role separation between cluster operator and application team, replacing the annotation soup that Ingress accumulated. How it relates A Kubernetes Service is L4; the ingress controller is the L7 reverse proxy in front of it. Knowing which layer you are looking at explains most routing surprises.

pages.title: Saga pattern
pages.tagline: You cannot roll back a transaction that already committed in someone else's database. You can only do something that undoes it in business terms.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · Garcia-Molina & Salem, 1987; examples in C#, Python and workflow engines
pages.description: Saga pattern cheatsheet: local transactions with compensating actions, choreography versus orchestration, the pivot step, and the isolation anomalies nobody warns you about.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: A business transaction spread across several services as a sequence of local transactions, each with a way to be undone in business terms.
terms.detail: The term comes from a 1987 paper about long-lived database transactions, and was adopted by the microservices world for the same reason: holding locks across several systems for the duration of a business process is not viable, so you give up atomicity and buy consistency back with explicit compensation. What you lose is isolation. A saga's intermediate states are visible to everyone while it runs, which is the source of most of its surprises and all of its countermeasures. ACID, minus one Property In a saga Atomicity simulated by compensation Consistency eventual Isolation gone — needs countermeasures Durability yes, per local transaction How it relates Each step publishes its events reliably with an outbox; the saga assumes nothing is ever lost.

terms.def: One step: a single ACID transaction inside one service, which commits and becomes permanent immediately.
terms.detail: Each step does its own work and publishes the event (or replies to the command) that moves the saga along. The critical property is that it commits: by the time step 3 starts, steps 1 and 2 are real, durable and visible to every other reader in the system. Keep steps small and single-purpose. A step that does three things cannot be compensated precisely, and partial failure inside a step is the hardest case to reason about. A step's obligations Obligation Why Commit atomically it is the unit of durability Publish its outcome reliably outbox, not a direct broker call Be idempotent it will be retried Have a compensation, or be after the pivot otherwise the saga cannot unwind How it relates The outbox pattern is what makes "publish its outcome reliably" true rather than hopeful.

terms.def: A new transaction that undoes a previous step's effect in business terms — never a rollback.
terms.detail: Refund the charge, cancel the reservation, release the stock, mark the order failed. Each is a forward transaction of its own, with its own rules and its own side effects — a cancellation may incur a fee, a refund may take three days, a released seat may already have been taken by someone else. Two hard requirements: compensations must be idempotent, because they will be retried, and they must be designed to always eventually succeed, because there is nothing to compensate a failed compensation with. Anything that might genuinely fail belongs after the pivot instead. Forward and back Step Compensation Not Charge card issue refund delete the charge Reserve room cancel reservation delete the row Reserve stock release reservation re-add the quantity blindly Send email — none possible put it after the pivot How it relates Steps 6–8 of the first animation are three compensations running in reverse order.

terms.def: The acknowledgement that undoing is a business act with its own trail, not the erasure of what happened.
terms.detail: A database rollback leaves no trace. A saga compensation leaves two: the original fact and its reversal. The customer sees a charge and a refund; the ledger shows both; the audit log shows both. That is usually correct — it is what actually happened — but it surprises stakeholders who expected "the booking just didn't happen". Agree the trail explicitly. Decide what the customer sees, what finance reconciles, and whether a cancellation fee applies, before you write the code. Who needs to agree Question Owner Does the customer see both lines? product Is a fee charged on cancellation? business / legal How does finance reconcile it? finance What does support see? operations How it relates This is why compensations are designed in a workshop, not invented during implementation.

terms.def: The step after which the saga can no longer be undone — everything before it must be compensatable, everything after it must be retriable.
terms.detail: Every saga has one, whether or not you named it. Charging the card, dispatching the parcel, filing with the regulator, sending the confirmation email — past that point the only acceptable outcome is forward completion, so the remaining steps must be designed to retry until they succeed. Identifying it changes the design: irreversible actions get pushed as late as possible, and anything that can genuinely fail gets pulled before it. The three zones Zone Requirement Before the pivot every step compensatable The pivot the point of no return After the pivot every step retriable, never compensated How it relates Ordering the steps around the pivot is the single highest-leverage design decision in a saga.

terms.def: A step after the pivot: it may fail temporarily but must eventually succeed, so it is retried rather than undone.
terms.detail: Issuing the ticket, printing the label, notifying the warehouse. These are retried with backoff forever, because the alternative — unwinding a charged card and a dispatched parcel — is worse. They therefore need to be idempotent and to have an escalation path when "eventually" becomes "two hours". An alert on retriable steps stuck beyond a threshold is not optional: this is precisely where a saga quietly stops and nobody notices. Retry policy Setting Typical Backoff exponential with jitter Cap minutes, not milliseconds Give up never — escalate to a human instead Alert after a stated business threshold How it relates Retries make duplicates certain, which is why idempotency is a saga-wide requirement.

terms.def: Each service reacts to the previous one's events and publishes its own. No coordinator exists.
terms.detail: Attractive at the start: nothing new to deploy, no central component, and each service only knows the events it subscribes to. For a two or three step flow that rarely changes, it is the right answer. It degrades badly with size. The flow exists only as the sum of everyone's subscriptions and is written down nowhere, so nobody can answer "where is order 42?", adding a step means editing several services, and cyclic dependencies appear quickly. Compensation logic is scattered across every participant. Good and bad signs Sign Meaning 2–4 steps, stable choreography fits Nobody can draw the flow you have outgrown it Service A listens to its own downstream a cycle; time to orchestrate Compensation logic duplicated time to orchestrate How it relates Steps 1–5 of the second animation; the purple policies on an EventStorming wall are choreography drawn out.

terms.def: A coordinator owns the flow as an explicit state machine and tells each service what to do.
terms.detail: The orchestrator sends commands and waits for replies, holding the whole sequence — including compensation order and timeouts — in one readable artefact. You can query it, test it, draw it and change it in one place. The costs are real: a component that knows about every participant, and one that must itself be durable, because a crash mid-saga must not lose the state. The usual mistake is letting it accumulate business rules that belong in the services. Trade-offs Choreography Orchestration Flow visible nowhere one place Coupling pairwise, implicit hub, explicit Adding a step several services one "Where is order 42?" unanswerable a query Extra infrastructure none durable state How it relates Durable execution engines exist precisely to make the orchestrator's state somebody else's problem.

terms.def: The implementation of an orchestrator: a stateful object that receives events, decides the next command, and remembers where it is.
terms.detail: In DDD terms it is the lilac policy made durable. It holds the saga's state, handles the replies, applies the timeout rules and, on failure, runs the compensations in reverse. It should contain sequencing logic and nothing else — pricing, eligibility and validation belong to the aggregates in the services. Model it explicitly as a state machine. Implicit state spread across boolean flags is how sagas become unmaintainable. What it owns Owns Does not own Step order business rules Compensation order pricing, validation Timeouts data the services own Saga state and history the aggregates themselves How it relates An EventStorming lilac policy that spans contexts usually becomes a process manager.

terms.def: Durable storage of which step a saga reached, so a crash resumes instead of losing the business process.
terms.detail: Without it, an orchestrator restart leaves a trip half booked and nobody tracking it. The log records the saga id, the current step, the data gathered so far and the compensations already run, updated transactionally with each decision. It also becomes your operations console: the list of in-flight sagas, how long each has been in its current step, and which ones are stuck. That table is the first thing support will ask for. Minimum columns Column Why saga_id correlation state current step data jsonb ids collected so far updated_at stuck detection compensated[] never compensate twice How it relates Update the log and enqueue the next command in one transaction, which is the outbox pattern again.

terms.def: The identifier carried through every message so that replies can be matched to the saga that is waiting for them.
terms.detail: Every command carries the saga id; every reply echoes it. Without it an orchestrator cannot tell which of five hundred in-flight bookings a PaymentCompleted belongs to. It is also what makes distributed tracing usable: one id ties together six services and twenty messages. Generate it when the saga starts, never later, and propagate it through every hop including the external ones you control. Ids worth carrying Id Purpose saga_id which saga instance message_id deduplication causation_id which message caused this one trace_id observability across services How it relates The message id comes from the outbox row; the saga id comes from the orchestrator.

terms.def: The property a saga gives up: its half-finished state is visible to everybody while it runs.
terms.detail: Between step 2 and step 4 the hotel is reserved and the flight is not. Any other process reading that data sees a trip that does not exist yet, and may act on it. The classic anomalies are the database ones: dirty reads of uncommitted saga state, lost updates when another process writes over a saga's work, and fuzzy reads where a value changes mid-saga. These are not theoretical. A support agent refunding an order mid-saga, and the saga then compensating as well, is a real and common double-refund. A dirty read, and the semantic lock that stops it How it relates Every saga needs at least one countermeasure; "we'll be careful" is not one.

terms.def: The standard techniques for coping with a saga's missing isolation, from cheap to thorough.
terms.detail: Chris Richardson catalogues five. A semantic lock marks the record as in-progress (PENDING) and makes every reader handle that state. Commutative updates are designed so order does not matter, so compensation is exact. A pessimistic view reorders the steps so the risky data is written last. Re-read value checks nothing changed before writing, which is optimistic locking. A version file records operations so out-of-order ones can be reconciled. Start with the semantic lock — it is cheap, it is explicit, and it makes the intermediate state legible to humans as well as to code. The five Countermeasure Cost Use when Semantic lock low almost always Commutative updates low counters, balances Pessimistic view medium reordering is possible Re-read value medium concurrent writers Version file high out-of-order is unavoidable How it relates Semantic locks show up in the UI too: "processing" is a countermeasure, not a loading state.

terms.def: Every step and every compensation must tolerate being executed more than once.
terms.detail: Messaging is at-least-once, orchestrators restart, and retries are routine, so duplicates are certain. A refund handler that refunds twice is not a rare bug; it is the default behaviour unless you prevent it. The standard defences: an inbox table keyed by message id, natural upserts, and state checks that make a repeated step a no-op ("already cancelled → return success"). Where duplicates come from Source Frequency Broker redelivery routine Outbox relay restart routine Orchestrator crash and resume occasional Manual replay by an operator rare and dangerous How it relates The inbox table from the outbox pattern is the ready-made answer.

terms.def: An instance that stopped: a reply never arrived, a step keeps failing, or a compensation cannot complete.
terms.detail: Sagas fail quietly. No request is pending, no user is waiting on a response, no HTTP 500 is logged — there is simply a row in the saga log that has not moved for three hours while a customer's money sits in limbo. Treat the age of the oldest in-flight saga per state as a first-class metric, and build a console where an operator can inspect, retry or force-compensate an instance. Both will be needed in the first month. Operational minimum Need Why Age of oldest saga per state the only alert that catches this Per-step timeouts a saga must never wait forever Manual retry / force-compensate someone will have to Full history per instance support cannot work without it How it relates Same failure shape as outbox lag: everything looks healthy while nothing is progressing.

terms.def: The deadline on each step, after which the saga gives up waiting and takes a decision.
terms.detail: Every step needs one, and the timeout has to be a business decision rather than a technical default: if the payment provider has not replied in ninety seconds, do we compensate, or do we wait — given that the charge may have gone through and we simply have not heard? This is where sagas get genuinely hard. A timeout is not knowledge of failure; it is the absence of knowledge, and the compensating action has to be safe in both cases. Querying the provider before compensating is usually the honest answer. Choosing one Step Typical timeout On expiry Internal service call seconds retry, then compensate Payment provider 1–2 min query status, then decide Human approval hours or days escalate, do not compensate Overnight batch partner a day alert a human How it relates In an orchestrated saga all the timeouts live in one file, which is a strong argument for orchestration.

pages.title: Semantic caching
pages.tagline: A normal cache asks "have I seen this exact key?". A semantic cache asks "have I answered this question before, in any words?".
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · examples use Redis vector search, pgvector and Microsoft.Extensions.AI
pages.description: Semantic caching cheatsheet: caching LLM answers by meaning instead of by exact key — thresholds, namespaces, false hits, invalidation and the savings arithmetic.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: The cosine score above which a stored question is treated as "the same question".
terms.detail: This single number decides both your savings and your error rate, and the two move in opposite directions. Lower it and more questions hit — including ones that are merely related. Raise it and every hit is safe, but paraphrases stop matching and the hit rate collapses. There is no universal value, because it depends on the embedding model and on how close your question space is. Short, templated questions cluster tightly and need a high threshold; long, varied questions spread out and tolerate a lower one. Derive it from data: embed a few hundred real question pairs, label each pair same/different, and plot precision and recall against the threshold. Common values Workload Threshold Reasoning FAQ / support 0.95–0.97 questions are short, a wrong answer is costly Internal docs assistant 0.93–0.96 varied phrasing, tolerant audience Classification / tagging 0.90–0.94 outputs are coarse, errors are cheap Anything transactional or financial exact match only do not guess How it relates A threshold alone is a blunt instrument. Pair it with a Cache namespace so it is only ever comparing questions that could legitimately share an answer.

terms.def: Serving a cached answer to a question that only looks similar — a wrong answer delivered fast.
terms.detail: Embeddings measure topical closeness, not equivalence. "How do I cancel my order?" and "How do I cancel my subscription?" differ by one token and share almost all their semantic content, so cosine similarity lands around 0.93–0.95 — above many thresholds. Negations are worse: "can I get a refund?" and "can I not get a refund?" are nearly identical vectors with opposite meaning. The reason this is dangerous rather than annoying is invisibility. The answer is fluent, plausible and instant; nothing in the response says it came from a different question. Unless you log the similarity score and the matched question id with every hit, false hits are undetectable in production. Classic false-hit pairs Pair Why it matches cancel my order / cancel my subscription one noun differs refund for EU / refund for US entity swap, same shape price in 2025 / price in 2026 numbers carry little signal is X allowed / is X not allowed negation barely moves the vector How it relates The cheap mitigations are a higher threshold, entity and number checks, and a second-stage verification before serving.

terms.def: The partition key that keeps answers from leaking across tenants, users, models and prompt versions.
terms.detail: A semantic cache keyed only by question text is a data-leak waiting to happen. Two users in different tenants can ask the same words and must get different answers — or must not get each other's answers at all. The partition must be a hard pre-filter in the vector query, never a post-filter applied to results. The namespace should also include everything that could change the correct answer even for the same user: the model id, the system-prompt version, the retrieval index version, the locale. Bump any of them and the old entries should stop matching rather than quietly serving answers produced by yesterday's prompt. A workable key namespace = sha1(tenantId + ":" + visibilityScope // public | role:support | user:4412 + ":" + modelId // gpt-4.1-mini + ":" + promptVersion // v7 + ":" + indexVersion // docs-2026-11-18 + ":" + locale) // en-GB How it relates If answers depend on the individual user, the only safe scope is that user — which usually makes the cache worthless and tells you to cache something else.

terms.def: The share of requests served from the cache — the number that decides whether any of this is worth it.
terms.detail: Hit rate is a property of your traffic, not of your implementation. Support and FAQ workloads are famously head-heavy: a few hundred distinct intents cover most of the volume, and semantic caching captures all the paraphrases of each. Open-ended chat and personalised assistants have a long flat tail and cache badly. Measure it before building: take a day of real questions, embed them, and count how many have a previous neighbour above your candidate threshold. It is an afternoon of work and it tells you whether the hit rate is 35% or 3%. What to expect Workload Typical hit rate Public FAQ bot 40–70% Internal docs assistant 20–40% Support agent copilot 15–30% Open-ended chat 2–10% Agentic / multi-turn tasks near zero on full context How it relates A low hit rate is not a failure of the cache. It is a signal that Prompt caching or a cheaper model is the better lever.

terms.def: The back-of-the-envelope that says whether the cache pays for itself.
terms.detail: Every request now costs an embedding call plus a vector search, whether it hits or not. Hits avoid a generation. So the saving is hitRate × generationCost − embeddingCost − searchCost, and the break-even hit rate is usually tiny because generation is two to three orders of magnitude more expensive than an embedding. A worked example Item Per request Embedding (cache key) ~$0.00001 · 8 ms Vector lookup ~$0 · 5–20 ms RAG + generation on a miss ~$0.004 · 1.9 s At 30% hit rate, 1M req/month saves ~$1,200 and 300k × 1.9 s of waiting Break-even hit rate < 1% The latency saving usually matters more than the money: a cached answer lands in 25–40 ms, which is the difference between a progress spinner and an instant reply. How it relates The same reasoning appears in Back-of-the-envelope estimates: find the dominant term, and ignore the rest.

terms.def: Removing cached answers when the underlying knowledge, prompt or model changes.
terms.detail: A cached answer is a frozen snapshot of a corpus, a prompt and a model. Any of the three can change, and when they do the cached answer becomes confidently out of date — with none of the signals a stale page has. Three mechanisms, used together. Version in the namespace handles prompt and model changes: bump the version and the old entries become unreachable without a delete. TTL bounds everything else. Targeted invalidation handles document updates: store the retrieved chunk ids alongside each cached answer, and when a document is re-ingested, delete every cache entry that cited it. Common values Content TTL Product documentation 24 h – 7 days Policy and legal text 1–24 h, plus event-driven purge Pricing, stock, anything live do not cache the answer; cache the retrieval Classification results 30 days or more How it relates Reverse-indexing cache entries by cited chunk id is the one piece people skip, and the reason retracted content keeps being quoted.

terms.def: Canonicalising the question before embedding so trivial variations collapse to one key.
terms.detail: Lowercasing, trimming whitespace, stripping trailing punctuation and removing greetings costs microseconds and raises the hit rate on the exact tier for free. "Hi! How do I reset my password?" and "how do i reset my password" become the same string, which means a hash lookup answers them before any embedding call happens. Be careful what you strip. Removing numbers, dates or identifiers raises the hit rate and manufactures false hits — those tokens are often the entire question. Normalise form, never content. Safe and unsafe Transformation Verdict lowercase, trim, collapse whitespace safe strip greetings and sign-offs safe drop trailing? and! safe remove stop words risky — drops negations strip digits, dates, ids unsafe How it relates Normalisation is what makes the free Exact-match tier actually land.

terms.def: A plain hash lookup in front of the semantic cache, catching identical questions for free.
terms.detail: A surprising share of repeated traffic is byte-identical after normalisation — the same button, the same suggested prompt, the same retry. Those questions do not need an embedding call at all: a Redis GET on sha256(namespace + normalised) answers them in under a millisecond with zero risk of a false hit. So the real shape is three tiers: exact, semantic, generate. The exact tier is cheap, perfectly safe and often handles half of all hits; the semantic tier is what catches paraphrases. exact → 0.4 ms, 0 risk, ~15% of requests semantic→ 20 ms, threshold risk, ~18% of requests generate→ 1.9 s, full cost, ~67% of requests How it relates Build this tier first. It is twenty lines and it is the part that cannot be wrong.

terms.def: A cheap second check, after the vector match, that the two questions really are the same question.
terms.detail: Because a false hit is a correctness bug, it is worth spending 20–80 ms to avoid one. The candidate match from the vector search is verified before being served: a cross-encoder scores the pair properly, or a rules check compares the entities, numbers and negations in both questions, or — for high-value flows — a small, fast model is asked "are these the same question? yes/no". This lets you lower the vector threshold deliberately, raising the hit rate, because the verification stage catches what the looser threshold lets through. Recall from the index, precision from the verifier — the same division of labour as retrieval and reranking in RAG. Cost of each check Verifier Latency Catches Entity / number / negation rules < 1 ms the classic pairs Cross-encoder 20–60 ms most paraphrase errors Small LLM judge 150–400 ms nearly all, at a real cost How it relates If verification costs more than generation, you have reinvented the expensive path. Keep it to rules and a cross-encoder.

terms.def: The provider-side cache of a shared prompt prefix — a different mechanism, often confused with this one.
terms.detail: Prompt caching is offered by the model provider: you mark a long, stable prefix — system instructions, a tool catalogue, a fixed document — and repeated requests that share it are billed and processed more cheaply, because the provider reuses the computed attention state. The model still runs; only the prefix work is saved. Semantic caching skips the model entirely. The two are complementary and solve different problems: prompt caching lowers the cost of every miss, semantic caching removes some misses altogether. Side by side Semantic cache Prompt cache Where your infrastructure the provider Saves the whole call part of the input cost Keyed on question meaning exact token prefix Can be wrong yes no Latency ~25 ms total faster first token, still seconds How it relates Put the stable parts of your prompt at the front — it is what makes prompt caching land, and costs nothing.

terms.def: Remembering that a question had no good answer, so you do not pay to fail twice.
terms.detail: When retrieval finds nothing above the cut-off and the system answers "I don't have enough information", that outcome is worth caching too — with a much shorter TTL, because it is the entry most likely to be fixed by someone adding a document. Negative entries also double as a content backlog. A ranked list of questions that repeatedly produce refusals is the most honest documentation gap report you will ever get. Common values Outcome TTL Answered hours to days Refused ("don't know") 5–30 minutes Error / timeout do not cache How it relates Purge negative entries whenever the index is updated — that is exactly the event that might have fixed them.

terms.def: An empty cache serves nothing, and the first hours look like pure added latency.
terms.detail: Every entry has to be paid for once. On day one the hit rate is zero and every request carries an extra embedding call and vector search. This is small — under 15 ms — but it is the reason a cache evaluated for an hour looks useless. Warming helps where the head of the distribution is known: replay the top few hundred historical questions, or seed from your FAQ, during deployment. Flushing on every deploy is the opposite mistake — version the namespace instead, so old entries age out rather than disappearing at once. How it relates Watch hit rate over days, not minutes, and segment by question type — one long-tail segment can hide a 60% hit rate in another.

terms.def: You can cache the final text, or just the retrieved chunks — and the trade-offs are different.
terms.detail: Caching the answer saves everything but freezes the output: if the documents change, or the answer should be personalised, it is wrong. Caching the retrieval result — the chunk ids for a question — saves the search but still runs generation, so the answer reflects the current text of those chunks and can be tailored to the user. For live data, caching retrieval is often the only safe choice. It also has a much weaker scoping requirement, because chunk ids with ACL filters re-applied at read time cannot leak the way a rendered answer can. Which to cache Situation Cache Stable docs, impersonal answers the answer Answers vary by user the retrieval Underlying text changes hourly the retrieval Classification / extraction the answer, long TTL How it relates Caching retrieval cuts about 120 ms and the search cost; caching answers cuts about 1.9 s and nearly all the cost.

terms.def: How entries leave a cache that would otherwise grow without limit.
terms.detail: Semantic caches grow one entry per distinct question, and each entry carries a vector of several kilobytes plus the answer text. A million entries at 1536 dimensions is roughly 6 GB of vectors before the index — affordable in Redis or Postgres, but not free, and every extra entry slightly slows the search and slightly raises false-hit risk. LRU or LFU by access is the usual policy, combined with a TTL. Because hit distribution is head-heavy, evicting the cold tail costs almost no hit rate: in most workloads the top 5% of entries serve the large majority of hits. Common values Setting Typical Max entries 100k – 1M Policy allkeys-lru or LFU, plus TTL Vector size 6 KB at 1536 dims × float32 With int8 quantisation 1.5 KB How it relates The eviction policies here are the ordinary ones from Redis and Caching strategies; only the key is unusual.

terms.def: Logging the similarity, the matched entry and the served source on every request — the only way false hits become visible.
terms.detail: A semantic cache that logs only a hit/miss counter is unauditable. Three fields per request make it debuggable: the similarity score, the id of the matched entry, and whether the answer came from exact, semantic or generation. With those you can replay any complaint, plot the score distribution, and see exactly where the threshold sits relative to real traffic. Two alerts are worth having: a rising hit rate with no traffic change (the threshold may have become too loose after a model swap) and a cluster of hits in the 0.92–0.95 band, which is where false hits live. What to record Field Why cache.source exact / semantic / miss cache.similarity histogram, threshold tuning cache.matched_id replay the original question cache.namespace catch scoping bugs user feedback on cached answers the real false-hit signal How it relates Serve a small "this answer was reused" affordance in internal tools; the first false hit a user reports pays for the whole instrumentation.

pages.title: Sidecar pattern
pages.tagline: Put the cross-cutting concern in a container next door, not in every application's dependency list.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · Kubernetes native sidecar containers are GA since 1.29; examples use Istio/Envoy, Fluent Bit and Cloud SQL Proxy
pages.description: Sidecar pattern cheatsheet: a helper container sharing the pod's lifecycle and network, what it moves out of your code, the lifecycle traps it brings, and when sidecarless beats it.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: A helper container deployed in the same unit as the application, sharing its lifecycle and extending it without changing its code.
terms.detail: The defining properties are co-location and co-lifecycle: the sidecar is scheduled onto the same node, starts and stops with the application, and reaches it over loopback. That makes it fundamentally different from a shared service — there is no network partition between the two, and no multi-tenancy to reason about. The motivation is language independence. A retry policy as a library must be written once per language and released once per service; as a sidecar it is one image everybody uses, including the Python script and the 2009 Java application nobody dares to touch. What usually goes in one Concern Typical sidecar mTLS, retries, routing Envoy / Linkerd proxy Log shipping Fluent Bit, Vector Metrics translation an exporter Secrets and config Vault agent, config reloader Database access Cloud SQL Proxy, PgBouncer How it relates A service mesh is this pattern applied to every pod, plus a control plane.

terms.def: The deployment unit the pattern depends on: one or more containers that are scheduled, scaled and deleted together.
terms.detail: A pod gives the sidecar everything it needs: the same node, the same IP, the same lifecycle, and optionally the same volumes. Scaling the application scales the sidecar with it, one to one — which is both the pattern's convenience and the source of its cost. Outside Kubernetes the same idea appears as a companion process under systemd, an ECS task with two containers, or a daemon on the same VM. The pattern predates the word "pod". What is shared Resource Shared? Network namespace / IP yes — always Lifecycle and node yes Volumes opt in Process namespace opt in Filesystem root, memory limits no — per container How it relates Kubernetes is the page to read for how pods, probes and scheduling actually work.

terms.def: Both containers see the same loopback interface, so they reach each other on 127.0.0.1 with no network hop.
terms.detail: This is what makes a sidecar cheap enough to be useful. Traffic between the app and the proxy never leaves the kernel: no DNS, no TLS, no routing, just loopback. It also means the two containers share one port space, so a collision is a startup failure rather than a subtle bug. And it is a security boundary you have given up: anything in the sidecar can talk to anything the app binds on localhost, including the admin port you assumed was private. Conventional ports Port Meaning (Istio) 15001 outbound capture 15006 inbound capture 15020 / 15090 health and metrics your 8080 the app, reached over loopback How it relates Never bind a debug or admin endpoint on 0.0.0.0 in a pod with a sidecar.

terms.def: An emptyDir or similar mounted into both containers — how log and config sidecars exchange data.
terms.detail: The app writes /var/log/app.log, the shipper reads it and forwards to the logging backend; or a config sidecar writes a rendered template into /etc/app and signals the app to reload. It is the filesystem equivalent of the loopback interface: a private channel with no network in it. Watch the medium. An emptyDir on disk shares the node's filesystem and will fill it; emptyDir: {medium: Memory} is fast but counts against the pod's memory limit. Choices Volume Use emptyDir logs, scratch — dies with the pod emptyDir (Memory) secrets, fast handoff; costs RAM projected tokens and certs from the platform How it relates Rotating files without a size cap is the classic way a log sidecar fills a node.

terms.def: Redirecting the pod's inbound and outbound traffic into the proxy, usually with iptables or eBPF, so the app needs no changes at all.
terms.detail: An init container rewrites the pod's iptables rules so everything arriving on the pod IP goes to port 15006 and everything leaving goes to 15001. The application opens an ordinary socket to payments:8080 and has no idea the connection was captured, encrypted and load balanced. That transparency is the pattern's best trick and its worst debugging experience: curl from inside the pod behaves differently from curl on the node, and "connection refused" may mean the proxy is not ready rather than the destination being down.
