Mechanisms Mechanism Note iptables REDIRECT classic; needs NET_ADMIN once eBPF lower overhead, newer kernels Explicit proxy config no magic; app must cooperate How it relates Interception is why startup ordering matters so much — see startup ordering.

terms.def: A sidecar that owns outbound connections on the app's behalf: discovery, load balancing, retries, circuit breaking.
terms.detail: The app connects to localhost:6379 and the ambassador decides which Redis shard that really is, whether to retry, and when to trip a breaker. Cloud SQL Proxy and PgBouncer-as-a-sidecar are the same idea for databases: the application holds a plain local connection string and the hard parts happen next door. It is the most immediately useful variant for legacy applications, because it needs no interception magic — just a changed connection string. Common ambassadors Sidecar Hides Envoy discovery, retries, mTLS Cloud SQL Proxy IAM auth, TLS, instance routing PgBouncer connection pooling How it relates An ambassador is where connection pooling and rate limiting naturally land.

terms.def: A sidecar that normalises what the application exposes, so the platform sees a uniform interface.
terms.detail: The app emits metrics in its own format on /stats; the adapter translates them into Prometheus exposition format on /metrics. Or it turns an idiosyncratic health endpoint into a standard one, or unstructured log lines into JSON with the right fields. It is the pattern of choice for third-party software you cannot modify, which is exactly the software that never speaks your platform's conventions. Examples Adapter Turns Exporter sidecar app stats → Prometheus Log parser text lines → structured JSON Health wrapper a TCP check → an HTTP probe How it relates Ambassador points outwards, adapter points inwards — both are sidecars.

terms.def: The sidecar pattern applied to every workload, with a control plane distributing policy to all the proxies.
terms.detail: Istio, Linkerd and friends inject a proxy into every pod and configure them centrally. The payoff is uniform mTLS, uniform retries and timeouts, uniform golden metrics, traffic splitting for canaries, and the ability to change any of it for the whole fleet with a config push instead of a release train. The cost is a second distributed system that sits in the data path of every request. Adopt it for the capability you actually need — usually mTLS everywhere, or traffic shifting — not because it is the default diagram. What it gives you Capability Alternative without a mesh mTLS everywhere per-language TLS libraries Uniform retries, timeouts a client library per language Golden metrics for free instrument every service Canary traffic splitting gateway or client-side routing How it relates Kubernetes provides the pod; the mesh provides the proxies and the policy.

terms.def: The sidecars that actually carry traffic, as opposed to the control plane that configures them.
terms.detail: The separation matters operationally: if the control plane goes down, the data plane keeps running on its last configuration, so requests keep flowing. What stops is change — new pods cannot get config, which is why a control plane outage shows up first as failing deployments rather than failing traffic. It also sets the upgrade shape: control plane first, then data plane, pod by pod, which means a mesh upgrade is a fleet-wide rolling restart. Failure modes What fails Effect Control plane existing traffic fine; new pods stuck One sidecar that pod is down — blast radius of one Bad config push fleet-wide; this is the scary one How it relates Roll config changes out gradually; a mesh config push is a global deploy.

terms.def: Kubernetes' first-class support: an init container with restartPolicy: Always, which starts before the app and stops after it.
terms.detail: Stable since Kubernetes 1.29, this fixes the three lifecycle problems that plagued sidecars for years: the sidecar is started and becomes ready before the application containers start, it is terminated after they exit, and it does not prevent a Job's pod from completing. Declaring a sidecar this way removes most of the folklore — the sleep loops, the preStop hacks, the /quitquitquit calls at the end of a batch job. Before and after Problem Old workaround Native sidecar App starts first retry loop in the app ordered startup Proxy dies first preStop sleep ordered shutdown Job never completes curl /quitquitquit terminated automatically How it relates The second animation walks all three failures and this fix.

terms.def: The race where the application is ready before its proxy, and its first outbound calls fail.
terms.detail: With traffic interception in place, every outbound connection is redirected to a proxy that may still be fetching its configuration. A service that connects to its database on boot therefore gets "connection refused" and crash-loops — at every deploy, on the pods that happen to lose the race. Declare the proxy as a native sidecar with a startup probe and the problem disappears. On older clusters the honest workaround is a readiness-aware retry loop in the app's entrypoint. Symptoms Symptom Cause Connection refused on boot only proxy not listening yet Fails on some pods, not others it is a race Fine locally, broken in the cluster no sidecar locally How it relates Steps 1–4 of the lifecycle animation.

terms.def: The mirror race: the proxy exits while the application is still draining in-flight requests.
terms.detail: On deletion every container receives SIGTERM at the same time. A proxy that exits in 100 ms takes the network away from an application that needs 20 seconds to finish what it was doing — so every rollout produces a small burst of 5xx right at the end. Native sidecars terminate after the main containers. Before that, the standard fix was a preStop hook on the sidecar that simply sleeps for longer than the app's drain period. Checklist Setting Rule terminationGracePeriodSeconds longer than the app's drain App SIGTERM handler stop accepting, finish in flight Sidecar ordering native sidecar, or preStop sleep How it relates The same errors show up as a dip in your SLI at every deploy — worth an error-budget look.

terms.def: The CPU, memory and money a sidecar costs, multiplied by every replica of every service.
terms.detail: A proxy sidecar typically requests 50–100 mCPU and 64–128 MiB. That is unremarkable per pod and significant per fleet: 2,000 pods at 100 mCPU and 128 MiB is 200 cores and 250 GiB spent on proxies. For small services the sidecar can out-consume the application it is helping. It also changes scheduling: every pod is bigger, so bin packing is worse and you need more nodes for the same workload. The fleet multiplication How it relates Back-of-the-envelope arithmetic is the right tool before adopting a mesh fleet-wide.

terms.def: The extra hops a sidecar adds: two proxies on every service-to-service call.
terms.detail: A call from A to B passes through A's sidecar and B's sidecar, so the fixed cost is roughly 0.5–2 ms per request in a healthy mesh, plus the TLS handshake on new connections. For most request paths that is noise. For a service in a tight internal loop, or one making twenty downstream calls per request, it is not. The tail is what bites: a saturated or restarting proxy adds far more than its median, and it does so on every call, so one bad sidecar shows up across the whole dependency graph. Rough costs Hop Typical added latency Loopback to local proxy 0.1–0.5 ms Full A→B with two proxies 0.5–2 ms New mTLS handshake a few ms, amortised How it relates Measure it as a percentile, not a mean — the median hides the cost entirely.

terms.def: Adding the sidecar automatically at admission time, so application teams never write it into their manifests.
terms.detail: A mutating admission webhook rewrites the pod spec as it is created, inserting the proxy container, the init container that sets up iptables and the volumes it needs. Enabled per namespace with a label, it is what makes a mesh adoptable without touching hundreds of repositories. It also means the pod that runs is not the pod you wrote, which is a surprise worth documenting: always debug from kubectl get pod -o yaml, never from the manifest in git. Consequences Effect Note Manifests stay clean the point Running spec differs from git confusing during incidents Version comes from the webhook upgrades need pod restarts Opt-out per pod an annotation; useful for jobs How it relates Injection plus a control plane is what turns "a sidecar" into "a mesh".

terms.def: Doing the same work without a per-pod proxy: eBPF in the kernel, a per-node agent, or an ambient mesh.
terms.detail: The counter-trend. Cilium pushes policy and encryption into the kernel with eBPF; Istio's ambient mode replaces per-pod proxies with a per-node component for mTLS and routing, adding a Layer-7 proxy only for the workloads that need one. Both cut the per-pod tax dramatically. The trade is blast radius and isolation: a per-node agent serves many pods, so its failure or saturation affects all of them, and the neat "one proxy per workload" security story becomes a shared one. Compared Sidecar Per-node / eBPF Overhead per pod per node Blast radius one pod a whole node Isolation strong shared Kernel requirements none recent kernels L7 features full often opt-in per workload How it relates A per-node DaemonSet agent is the older, simpler version of the same trade — common for log shipping.

terms.def: The failure where a batch job finishes but its pod never completes, because the sidecar is still running.
terms.detail: A Kubernetes Job's pod is only Completed when every container has exited. A proxy or log shipper is designed to run forever, so the job hangs: the work is done, the pod is alive, and the Job controller waits for a container that will never stop. The old fixes were all ugly — have the job curl localhost:15020/quitquitquit at the end, or exclude jobs from injection entirely. Native sidecars solve it properly: once the main container exits, the sidecar is terminated for you. Options Approach Verdict Native sidecar correct; needs 1.29+ Exclude jobs from injection fine if they need no mesh Call the proxy's quit endpoint works; couples the job to the mesh How it relates Step 7 of the lifecycle animation; the same issue applies to CronJobs and to init-style migrations.

pages.title: SLI, SLO & SLA
pages.tagline: Measure what users feel, promise a number you can keep, sign only what you can afford to break.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · vocabulary from Google SRE; examples use Prometheus, OpenSLO and Sloth
pages.description: SLI, SLO and SLA cheatsheet: how a good-events ratio becomes a target, a target becomes an error budget, and a budget becomes the alert that wakes you up.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: A Service Level Indicator: a ratio of good events to valid events, expressed as a percentage of things that worked.
terms.detail: An SLI is always a fraction, never a gauge. CPU usage is not an SLI; "99.94% of checkout requests returned a non-5xx within 300 ms" is. Writing it as good / valid forces you to define both halves explicitly, which is where most of the thinking happens. Measure it as close to the user as you can afford. The same journey measured at four points gives four different numbers, and the one furthest from your code is the one the user actually lives with. Where to measure Vantage point Catches Misses Application logs handler errors crashes, LB failures, DNS Load balancer / ingress 5xx, timeouts, most outages client network, CDN, DNS Synthetic probe full path incl. DNS and TLS real traffic mix, real users Client / RUM what users truly see noisy, hard to attribute How it relates An SLO is just a threshold applied to an SLI over a window. The valid events denominator decides what you are even allowed to be judged on. The first animation is one SLI being computed from four log lines.

terms.def: The denominator: the events that count towards the SLI at all. Everything else is excluded, not counted as bad.
terms.detail: Choosing the denominator is the most consequential and least discussed decision in an SLO. A 400 Bad Request caused by a malformed client payload is not your service failing; counting it as bad means a single broken integration can eat your budget. A 429 from your own rate limiter is usually excluded too — it is the system working as designed. The rule of thumb: an event is valid if your service could in principle have handled it correctly. Be careful, though — exclusions are also how teams quietly make an SLO unfalsifiable. Every exclusion should be written down and reviewed. Typical treatment Event Usual call 5xx from your service valid, bad 4xx from a client bug not valid 429 you issued on purpose not valid Health-check and bot traffic not valid Timeout with no response valid, bad How it relates Rate limiting decides how many 429s exist, so the two designs interact directly. Step 8 of the first animation drops a 429 out of the denominator entirely.

terms.def: A Service Level Objective: the target value of an SLI over a stated window, chosen internally and with no contractual force.
terms.detail: An SLO is three things in one sentence: an SLI, a threshold and a window. "99.9% of checkout requests succeed within 300 ms, measured over a rolling 28 days." Drop any of the three and it stops being actionable — especially the window, since the same target over an hour and over a quarter mean completely different things. Pick the number from evidence, not ambition. Measure what you already deliver for a month, then set the SLO slightly below it. If current performance is 99.95%, a 99.9% SLO gives you headroom and still means something; a 99.99% SLO invented in a meeting just guarantees a permanently breached objective that everybody learns to ignore. Window choices Window Behaviour Rolling 28 days most common; no month-boundary amnesty, four whole weeks Rolling 7 days reacts fast, very noisy for low traffic Calendar month matches billing and SLAs; budget resets on the 1st Calendar quarter planning-friendly, far too slow to act on How it relates The error budget is mechanically 100% − SLO. The SLA should be a looser number than the SLO, never the same one.

terms.def: A Service Level Agreement: a contract with a customer stating a service level and the financial consequence of missing it.
terms.detail: An SLA is a legal document that happens to contain a number. It specifies what is measured, by whom, over what period, what counts as excluded (planned maintenance, force majeure, the customer's own misconfiguration), how the customer claims, and what they get — almost always service credits rather than real damages. The engineering rule is simple: the SLA target must be meaningfully weaker than the SLO. The SLO is where you start worrying; the SLA is where you start paying. If they are equal, the first bad week costs money. A typical gap is one nine: internal SLO 99.95%, contractual SLA 99.9%. Typical public SLAs Tier Monthly target Allowed downtime Single VM / instance 99.9% 43 min Multi-AZ managed service 99.95% 22 min Global control plane 99.99% 4.4 min How it relates Service credits are the enforcement mechanism. Many services have an SLO and deliberately no SLA at all — that is a perfectly good answer for internal platforms.

terms.def: The amount of unreliability the SLO permits in a window: 100% minus the SLO, expressed in bad events or in minutes.
terms.detail: The error budget is what converts an SLO from a report into a decision-making tool. It is a quantity you are entitled to spend: on a risky deploy, a schema migration, a chaos experiment, or simply on bad luck. Spending it is not failure — not spending it means your SLO is too loose and you are shipping too slowly. Express it in whichever unit the audience understands. Engineers tend to prefer "40,000 bad requests left"; managers hear "30 minutes of full outage left this month". Budget for a 28-day window SLO Budget (time) Budget at 40M req 99% 6 h 43 m 400,000 99.9% 40 m 19 s 40,000 99.95% 20 m 10 s 20,000 99.99% 4 m 2 s 4,000 How it relates Burn rate is the speed at which you are spending it. The error budget policy is the pre-agreed rule for what happens when it runs out.

terms.def: How fast the error budget is being consumed, relative to the rate that would exactly exhaust it over the full window.
terms.detail: Burn rate is a unitless multiplier: burn = observed error rate / (1 - SLO). At 1× the budget runs out precisely at the end of the window. At 14.4× it runs out in under two days — which, for a 28-day window, means 2% of the budget is gone in a single hour. It is the right thing to alert on because it is scale-free and window-independent: the same thresholds work for a service doing 10 requests a second and one doing 10,000, and they translate directly into "how long until we have a problem". Standard thresholds (28–30 day window) Burn Long window Short window Budget used Action 14.4× 1 h 5 m 2% page 6× 6 h 30 m 5% page 3× 1 d 2 h 10% ticket 1× 3 d 6 h 10% ticket How it relates The second animation walks a 14.4× spike and a slow 3× leak through exactly this table.

terms.def: The share of valid requests that did not fail: the default SLI, and usually the first one a team writes.
terms.detail: Request-based availability counts events, not seconds: non-5xx / valid requests. That is usually better than time-based availability, because "the minute was up" hides a minute in which 40% of requests failed. Time-based availability still has a place in contracts, where "minutes of downtime" is easier to litigate. Watch the difference when you translate between the two: a service that is 99.9% available by request count during peak hours can look far better by minute count, because quiet minutes dilute the bad ones. Two definitions, same service Definition Formula Favours Request-based good req / valid req users; weights peak traffic Time-based good minutes / total minutes providers; dilutes short peaks How it relates Pair it with a latency SLI: a service returning 200s slowly is "available" and useless.

terms.def: The share of requests served faster than a threshold — a ratio, not a percentile.
terms.detail: Write it as "99% of requests under 300 ms", not "p99 under 300 ms". They sound identical and behave differently: the first is a counter you can add up, aggregate across services and subtract from a budget; the second is a quantile that cannot be averaged, cannot be summed across instances, and tells you nothing about how bad the slow 1% was. In Prometheus this maps straight onto histogram buckets, so pick the threshold to match a real bucket boundary — interpolating between buckets is where most latency SLI inaccuracy comes from. Two thresholds beat one Tier Example target Protects against Typical 90% under 200 ms the median getting worse Tail 99% under 1 s a slow minority being ignored How it relates The percentiles page explains why quantiles cannot be averaged, which is exactly why this SLI is defined as a ratio.

terms.def: The trailing period the SLI is evaluated over — typically 28 days, moving forward continuously instead of resetting.
terms.detail: A rolling window means yesterday's outage keeps counting until it ages out, and the budget recovers gradually rather than being forgiven on the 1st of the month. That is usually what you want: it removes the perverse incentive to take risks on the 31st, and it keeps the number continuous. 28 days rather than 30 is deliberate — it is exactly four weeks, so weekend and weekday traffic patterns are always represented in the same proportion and the number does not wobble with the calendar. Consequences Window type Budget recovery Good for Rolling 28 d gradual, day by day engineering decisions Calendar month instant on the 1st billing, SLA credits How it relates Burn-rate alert windows (1 h, 6 h) live inside this window; they are not the same thing.

terms.def: Shorthand for availability targets — 99.9% is "three nines" — and the downtime each one allows.
terms.detail: Each extra nine divides the allowed downtime by ten and multiplies the engineering cost by considerably more. Three nines is reachable with good practices, a load balancer and a competent on-call rotation. Four nines requires removing single points of failure, automated failover and deploys that cannot cause a full outage. Five nines usually means the thing is not allowed to depend on a human at all. Be honest about what the number has to include: if a planned deploy takes the service down for 90 seconds once a week, you have already spent more than a four-nines monthly budget. Allowed downtime Target Per day Per 30 days Per year 99% 14 m 24 s 7 h 12 m 3 d 15 h 99.9% 1 m 26 s 43 m 12 s 8 h 46 m 99.95% 43 s 21 m 36 s 4 h 23 m 99.99% 8.6 s 4 m 19 s 52 m 36 s 99.999% 0.9 s 26 s 5 m 15 s How it relates Chaining dependencies multiplies nines downwards — see composite availability.

terms.def: A specific thing a user is trying to accomplish, used as the unit an SLI is defined around. Often abbreviated CUJ.
terms.detail: SLOs attach to journeys, not to services. "The payments service" is not a journey; "a customer completes checkout" is, and it may touch six services. Defining the journey first stops you from shipping a dashboard where every microservice is green and the product is broken. Keep the list short. Three to five journeys per product is plenty, and each one should be something a non-engineer would recognise as a thing people do. Journeys and their natural SLI Journey SLI Browse catalogue page renders under 1 s Complete checkout payment accepted, non-5xx under 300 ms Receive order email sent within 2 min of order Nightly export file delivered before 06:00 How it relates Each journey gets its own budget; they are not pooled.

terms.def: The agreement, written before anything breaks, that says what the team does at each level of budget consumption.
terms.detail: Without a policy, an error budget is a chart nobody acts on. The policy names thresholds and the consequence of crossing each one, and — this is the part that matters — it is signed off by product and engineering together while everyone is calm. Once the budget is gone, the decision has already been made and there is no negotiation. The classic escalation is: healthy budget means ship freely; half spent means review risky changes; exhausted means feature freeze and reliability work only until the window recovers. Repeated exhaustion means the SLO itself goes back on the table. A typical policy Budget remaining Action Above 50% ship normally, run experiments 20–50% risky changes need a second reviewer Below 20% no non-essential deploys 0% freeze; reliability work takes priority 0% three windows running renegotiate the SLO or fund the fix How it relates This is the only mechanism that makes an SLO change anyone's behaviour.

terms.def: An alert that fires only when a high burn rate shows up in both a long qualifying window and a short confirming window.
terms.detail: A single-window burn alert is either slow to fire or slow to clear. The multi-window multi-burn-rate pattern fixes both: the long window (say 1 h) decides whether the problem is big enough to care about, and the short window (1/12 of it, so 5 m) confirms that it is still happening right now. Both must be over threshold. The effect is that a two-minute blip never pages anyone, and a resolved incident stops paging within minutes instead of an hour. Two severities — fast burns page, slow burns raise a ticket — are enough for almost every service. Behaviour Property Single window Multi-window Detection time long short Reset time up to a full window minutes False pages frequent rare How it relates The middle of the burn-rate animation is this rule firing and then clearing.

terms.def: What happens to a target when a journey depends on several services in series: the availabilities multiply.
terms.detail: If a request must pass through auth, the API and the database, and each is independently 99.9% available, the journey is 0.999 cubed = 99.70% — three times the downtime of any single component. Dependencies in series subtract nines; this is why a four-nines promise on top of three-nines infrastructure is arithmetic fiction unless you add redundancy or graceful degradation. Redundancy works in the other direction: two independent replicas each at 99% give 1 − 0.01 squared = 99.99%, provided the failures really are independent — which shared power, shared control planes and shared deploys quietly ensure they are not. Nines draining through a chain How it relates Set component SLOs above the journey SLO, not equal to it.

terms.def: The usual remedy in an SLA: a percentage of the bill refunded when the target is missed, capped and claimed by the customer.
terms.detail: Credits are deliberately small. A typical ladder refunds 10% of the monthly fee below 99.9%, 25% below 99%, and 100% only in extreme cases — and almost always as credit against future invoices rather than cash. They are a signal of seriousness, not compensation for the customer's actual loss, which is usually orders of magnitude larger. Two details decide whether credits ever get paid: the customer normally has to file a claim within a short window, and the measurement is the provider's own. Both are worth reading carefully from either side of the contract. A common ladder Monthly uptime Credit Below 99.9% 10% Below 99.0% 25% Below 95.0% 100% How it relates Credits are why the SLA number must sit below the SLO number.

pages.title: Vector database
pages.tagline: Every other index answers "equal to". This one answers "near" — and it is allowed to be slightly wrong about it.
pages.asOf: As of Nov 2026 · examples use pgvector, Qdrant and Postgres
pages.description: Vector database cheatsheet: HNSW and IVF indexes, recall and ef_search, quantisation, filtered search, sizing arithmetic and when Postgres is enough.

sections.title: When to use / when not to

terms.def: Trading a few percent of correctness for one to three orders of magnitude of speed.
terms.detail: Exact search compares the query to every vector: perfectly correct, and linear in the number of rows. At a million rows and 1,536 dimensions that is about six billion floating-point operations per query — hundreds of milliseconds even with SIMD. ANN indexes look at a few thousand candidates instead and get the right answer almost always. The word "almost" is the whole topic. There is no error, no warning and no log line when recall drops; results just get slightly worse. This is why recall must be measured explicitly, against a brute-force baseline, on your own data. Rough numbers, 1M vectors × 1536 dims Method Latency Recall Brute force 200–800 ms 100% IVF, nprobe=8 5–15 ms ~90% HNSW, ef_search=40 1–3 ms ~95% HNSW, ef_search=200 5–12 ms ~99% How it relates Below roughly 50,000 vectors, brute force is fast enough and exactly right. Do not build an index you do not need.

terms.def: A layered graph of "small world" links: long hops at the top, short ones at the bottom.
terms.detail: Hierarchical Navigable Small World is the default index in almost every engine. Each vector is a node; each node has up to m neighbours on layer 0 and progressively fewer nodes exist on higher layers. A search enters at the top, greedily walks to the closest node it can see, drops a layer, repeats — so the top layers cover distance quickly and the bottom layer refines. Its strengths are high recall at low latency and support for incremental inserts. Its costs are memory (the graph lives beside the vectors, in RAM) and a build time that is substantial on large collections. Common values Parameter Typical Raising it m 16 (32 for high recall) better recall, more memory, slower build ef_construction 64–200 better graph, much slower build, no query cost ef_search 40–200 better recall, slower queries — set per query m and ef_construction are build-time and need a rebuild to change; ef_search is per query. Tune the cheap one first. How it relates Deletions are tombstones in the graph, not removals — see Segments and compaction for why that matters.

terms.def: The size of the candidate list during the layer-0 walk — the one knob that trades recall for latency at query time.
terms.detail: During the final layer the algorithm keeps a dynamic list of the ef_search best candidates found so far and keeps expanding their neighbours until none improves. A larger list explores more of the graph, so it is less likely to get stuck in a local minimum — and does more distance comparisons. It must be at least k, and in practice 2–10× k. It can be set per query, which is the useful part: raise it for the queries that matter, keep it low for cheap ones. Common values Goal ef_search Effect Fast, good enough 40 ~95% recall, 1–3 ms Balanced default 100 ~98% recall High recall 200–400 ~99.5%, several times slower With a reranker after higher than you think recall matters more than order How it relates If RAG quality is poor, raising this is the cheapest experiment available — one session setting, no rebuild.

terms.def: Partition the space into clusters, search only the few nearest clusters.
terms.detail: An inverted file index runs k-means over a sample to find nlist centroids, assigns every vector to one, and at query time compares the query to the centroids and scans only the nprobe closest lists. Much less memory than HNSW, much faster to build — and lower recall at the same speed. Its weakness is the boundary problem: a true nearest neighbour sitting just across a cluster boundary is invisible unless nprobe covers that cluster. It also needs training on representative data, and a collection whose distribution drifts away from the training sample degrades until it is retrained. Common values Parameter Typical nlist √n, so ~1,000 for 1M vectors nprobe 1–5% of nlist Training sample 30–256 × nlist vectors Best for huge collections, memory-constrained How it relates IVF-PQ combines it with product quantisation for billion-scale collections where HNSW would not fit in memory at any price.

terms.def: The share of the true top-k that your index actually returned — the number nobody measures and everybody should.
terms.detail: Measuring it is easy and nobody does it: take a few hundred real queries, run them with the index off (brute force) to get ground truth, run them with the index on, and compute the overlap of the two top-k sets. Thirty lines of code, run once per configuration change. Without it you are tuning blind, and the symptom of bad recall is indistinguishable from a bad embedding model, bad chunking or a weak LLM. With it, you know within an hour which of those to work on. How to read the number recall@10 Verdict > 0.98 index is not your problem 0.90–0.98 raise ef_search; usually free < 0.90 check filters, quantisation, m How it relates In RAG, index recall multiplies with retrieval recall. 95% here caps everything downstream at 95%.

terms.def: Cosine, inner product or L2 — and it must match what the embedding model was trained for.
terms.detail: Cosine measures angle and ignores magnitude; inner product rewards magnitude as well; L2 is straight-line distance. For normalised vectors cosine and inner product rank identically, and L2 ranks identically too — which is why the choice only bites when vectors are not normalised. Nearly every text embedding model is trained for cosine. Pick it unless the model card says otherwise, and store the metric alongside the model name as part of the index's identity. Common values Metric Use when pgvector operator Cosine text embeddings, the default <=> Inner product recommenders, trained that way <#> L2 images, some vision models <-> How it relates Build the index with the matching operator class — a cosine index does not accelerate an L2 query, it is simply not used.

terms.def: Combining "nearest" with "where" — the feature that most differentiates engines in practice.
terms.detail: Three strategies. Post-filter: do the ANN search, discard non-matching results — fast, and catastrophic with a selective filter, because the top-k can contain zero matches. Pre-filter: find matching ids, then compare exactly — correct, and linear in the matching set. Filtered traversal: walk the graph but only accept matching nodes — good, until the matching subgraph is disconnected and the walk cannot reach parts of it. Good engines estimate selectivity and switch: brute force below a threshold, filtered traversal above it. That is why the same query can be fast and correct for a tenant with 2 million documents and slow or empty for one with 200. Which strategy, by selectivity Matching share Best strategy < 1% pre-filter + exact comparison 1–20% filtered traversal, raise ef_search > 20% filtered traversal, or even post-filter How it relates Never post-filter an ACL. The result is not just wrong, it is a permissions bug with no error.

terms.def: The JSON stored next to each vector: tenant, permissions, source, date, and the text itself.
terms.detail: A pure vector store would be useless: you need to know what you matched, whether the user may see it, and where it came from. The payload carries that, and fields used in filters need their own index — usually a keyword, integer or geo index maintained separately from the vector index. Keep it lean. Payloads sit beside vectors, often on disk but cached, and a megabyte of original text per row turns a 7 GB collection into a 60 GB one. Store a reference and fetch the body from your primary store when you need it. Typical fields Field Indexed? tenant_id yes — always filtered acl / groups yes updated_at yes, for freshness source, url, title no — returned, not filtered Full text only if small; otherwise a reference How it relates In Postgres this is just other columns, which is the single strongest argument for pgvector.

terms.def: Storing smaller, lossier copies of the vectors so more of them fit in memory.
terms.detail: Scalar quantisation maps each float32 to an int8: 4× smaller, usually 1–2% recall lost. Binary quantisation keeps one bit per dimension: 32× smaller, with distance computed as a Hamming distance that is extraordinarily fast but much lossier. Product quantisation splits the vector into sub-vectors and codebooks them, reaching 16–64×. The standard pattern is oversample and rescore: search the quantised index for 4–10× more candidates than you need, then rescore those few with the full-precision vectors. You get most of the memory saving and nearly all of the recall. Common values Mode Size for 1536 dims Recall impact float32 6,144 B baseline int8 scalar 1,536 B −1–2% binary 192 B −5–15%, rescore essential product (PQ) ~100–400 B −3–10%, needs training How it relates Many newer embedding models are Matryoshka-trained, so truncating 3072 dims to 1024 often beats quantising — try that first.

terms.def: Arithmetic you can do in two minutes that decides your architecture.
terms.detail: Per vector: 4 × dims bytes for float32, plus the graph. A reasonable HNSW estimate is 1.1 × (4 × dims + 8 × m) bytes, plus payload and filter indexes. Everything performance-critical wants to be in RAM; spilling to disk is supported by most engines and costs an order of magnitude. Worked examples Collection dims Mode RAM 100k chunks 1536 float32 ~0.7 GB — a laptop 1M chunks 1536 float32 ~6.9 GB 1M chunks 1536 int8 ~1.9 GB 10M chunks 1536 float32 ~69 GB — now it is a cluster 10M chunks 768 int8 ~9 GB — still one machine The lesson from the last two rows: halving dimensions and quantising is a 7× saving, and usually costs less recall than you fear. How it relates Same spirit as Back-of-the-envelope estimates — one multiplication tells you whether this is a table or a cluster.

terms.def: How long each vector is — and the fact that you can often shorten it for free.
terms.detail: Dimensions drive storage, memory and comparison cost linearly: 3072 dims cost twice 1536 in every respect. Bigger is usually slightly better for recall, but the curve flattens quickly, and the difference between 1536 and 3072 is often under a percent on real retrieval tasks. Matryoshka representation learning changes the calculus: models trained this way put the most information in the leading dimensions, so a 3072-dim vector can be truncated to 1024 and renormalised with a small loss. Always check whether your model supports it before paying for the full width. How it relates Changing dimensions, like changing models, means rebuilding the collection — so decide before the first million rows, not after.

terms.def: How writes land, why deletes are tombstones, and why a collection gets slower with churn.
terms.detail: Most engines write into immutable segments, each with its own index, and a query searches all of them and merges. Deletes mark a tombstone rather than removing a node, because removing from an HNSW graph would break its connectivity. Updates are a delete plus an insert. So a collection with heavy churn accumulates dead nodes that are still traversed and still occupy memory. Compaction rebuilds segments without them. If search slows down over weeks while row counts stay flat, this is almost always why. Common values Signal Action Deleted ratio > 20% compact / vacuum Many small segments merge — each is searched Latency up, rows flat tombstones Bulk load insert first, build the index after How it relates In Postgres this is ordinary VACUUM territory — see Database performance.

terms.def: How quickly a new or changed vector becomes searchable, and the deletion path nobody builds.
terms.detail: HNSW supports incremental insertion, so new vectors are usually searchable within seconds. The problems are at the edges: a bulk load is far faster if you insert first and build the index afterwards, and a document that is deleted at source must be deleted here too. Use deterministic ids (docId#chunkIndex) so re-ingestion is an upsert, delete by document id on removal, prune trailing chunks when a document shrinks, and run a periodic reconcile that diffs source ids against index ids. Without the last one, retracted content stays retrievable indefinitely. How it relates The ingestion half of RAG is exactly this, and the Outbox pattern is the usual way to make it reliable.

terms.def: One collection with a tenant filter, or one collection per tenant — and when to switch.
terms.detail: A shared collection with a tenant_id filter scales to many tenants cheaply and is the right default. It relies on filtered search working well at your tenants' selectivity, and on the filter being applied inside the search rather than after it. A collection per tenant gives perfect isolation and perfect recall per tenant, but each collection carries fixed overhead — so ten thousand small tenants becomes expensive. Several engines offer a middle option: one collection, partitioned by a tenant key, with the graph built per partition. Choosing Situation Shape Many small tenants shared collection + filter A few very large tenants collection per tenant Strict data residency collection per tenant, per region Wildly uneven sizes partitioned, or split the whales out How it relates The same trade-off, with the same names, as on the Multitenancy strategies page.

terms.def: Retrieve more than you need, then rescore the few exactly — the universal recall repair.
terms.detail: Whenever an approximation is in the path — a quantised index, a low ef_search, a binary first pass — the fix is the same: ask for 4–10× k candidates, then rescore that small set with full-precision vectors or a proper reranker, and keep the best k. It works because the approximation is good at excluding the obviously distant and bad at ordering the close ones. Oversampling covers exactly that weakness, and rescoring 100 vectors is microseconds. Common values First pass Oversample int8 quantised 2–4× binary quantised 8–16× Low ef_search 3–5× Feeding a cross-encoder 10–25× How it relates It is the same shape as retrieve-wide-then-rerank in RAG, applied one layer lower.

terms.def: Running keyword search alongside vector search and fusing the results.
terms.detail: Embeddings are weak on exact tokens: identifiers, SKUs, error codes, rare proper nouns. BM25 is strong on exactly those and weak on paraphrase. Running both and fusing with Reciprocal Rank Fusion is the single most reliable quality improvement available, and most engines now support it natively. It changes what the database must store: a keyword index as well as a vector index, over the same rows, with filters applied consistently to both. In Postgres that is a tsvector column beside the vector one. How it relates The fusion maths and when each retriever wins are covered on the RAG page.

terms.def: No index at all — and the right answer far more often than vendors suggest.
terms.detail: A full scan with SIMD compares roughly 10–50 million dimensions per millisecond per core. At 1,536 dimensions that is a few thousand vectors per millisecond, so 50,000 vectors is a 10–30 ms query — with 100% recall, no parameters, no index build, no rebuild on model change, and no tombstones. A great many production systems have fewer than 100,000 chunks. For those, an exact scan in Postgres is simpler, cheaper and more correct than any index, and it is also the ground truth you measure recall against later. Where the crossover sits Vectors Advice < 50k no index; exact scan 50k–1M HNSW in Postgres is usually plenty 1M–50M a dedicated engine starts to pay > 50M quantisation and sharding, seriously How it relates Also use it as the recall baseline: the same query with the index disabled is your ground truth.
